- **photograph** the camera's own focal length (EXIF); heading, tilt and roll fitted on the near summits only, for each model
- skyline residual, photo placed as each model prefers: globe k 2.9′ · straight 1.8′ · plane 2.2′

*Figure caption:* **From the plateau de Caussols, bend the Earth and watch the sea horizon fall.** The view east from 1,210 m, drawn from the IGN's LiDAR and, beyond 45 km, the Copernicus model: the Riviera, Mont Agel, Monte Ceppo in Italy, Corsica 222 km out to sea. It starts on a plane, where the sea rises towards eye level and Mont Agel, 77 m lower than the eye, sits 7′ below the horizon. Its height here is the terrain model's, 1,133 m, not the published 1,148 m: the IGN's LiDAR has no data on the summit, a military site, and the models that fill the gap differ by up to 30 m around it ([Basics](/ai/phys.md#phys-h2dem), terrain models). With 1,148 m it would sit 5′ below the plane's horizon instead of 7′, and 48′ above the refracted globe's instead of 47′. The Earth is then curved to its measured radius, 6,371 km: the horizon falls to 67′ below eye level and Mont Agel rises clear of it. Refraction comes last, and it works the other way: bending light along the curve, it acts as a larger radius, R/(1−k) with k = 0.13, and lifts the far scene back by a few arcminutes (horizon 62′ below). The terrain between the three computed models is interpolated for the animation; the horizon and the named summits are computed at every step. Last, once the model has stopped changing, [Xyphophor](https://x.com/Xyphophor)'s photograph from this spot fades in, then blinks fully on and off to show how well it lands on the drawing. It is framed as the refracted globe prefers (focal length from the camera, heading, tilt and roll fitted on the near summits): its sea horizon lies within 0.1° of that model's and about 45′ below a plane's, and Mont Agel stands 42′ above it.

*Figure caption:* **Globe.** The surface keeps its shape; only the observer moves. Raise the eye and the tangent point slides outward as √h while the sightline tips further below horizontal: **840.4′ = 14.007°** down, horizon at **36 km**. Everything in the red band beyond it is geometrically hidden.

*Figure caption:* **Flat plane.** Same frame, same scales. The observer rises but nothing else changes: no tangent point ever forms, the surface runs straight to the frame edge, and the only "horizon" is the eye‑level line itself — reached at infinity, dip 0.0′ = 0.000°. At 36 km, where the globe's horizon sits, the plane still shows open ground 9.6′ (0.161°) below eye level.

$$\operatorname{Dip} = \arccos\frac{R}{R+h} \approx {1.76'\times\sqrt{h}}$$
$$\operatorname{Horizon} = \sqrt{2Rh + h^2} \approx {3.86\,\text{km}\times\sqrt{h}}$$

h in metres. The bold constants are the *refracted* values printed in every nautical almanac and dip table (geometric: 1.93′√h and 3.57 km·√h). On a flat plane both formulas collapse: **dip = 0 at every height**, and the ground never reaches a horizon at all.

**What each model predicts at the current eye height**

| Model | Dip below eye level | Distance to horizon | Sharp edge? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Globe — geometric | 19.3′ = 0.321° | 36 km | yes, sharp |
| Globe + refraction (k=0.13) | 18.0′ = 0.299° | 38 km | yes, sharp |
| Flat plane — any height | 0.0′ = 0.000° | ∞ (no tangent) | no — haze only |

At h = **100 m** the geometric dip is **19.3′ = 0.321°** — the √h rule gives 1.93′×√100 = **19.3′ = 0.322°**, matching the exact arccos formula to within a whisker. The flat prediction is 0.0′ = 0.000° at this and every other height.

## Solve the triangle: the flat model contradicts itself [evidence: prediction]

Suppose the flat model is granted the *measured* dip angle δ — the one a dip meter actually reads. On a flat plane the eye, the point straight below it, and the point where the sightline meets the ground form a **right triangle**: height h, horizontal run d, right angle at the foot. That triangle is solvable, and it fixes where the ground must be:

$$\tan\delta = \frac{h}{d} \implies {d = \frac{h}{\tan\delta}}$$

Feed the measured dip into flat geometry and it says the sightline strikes the ground at distance d. But δ ≈ √(2h/R), so d ≈ h/√(2h/R) = √(hR/2) = **½·√(2Rh)** — exactly **half** the measured horizon distance, at every height. And on a plane nothing ends there: the ground simply continues, seen at ever‑smaller angles.

*Figure caption:* Granting the measured dip **δ = 19.3′ = 0.321°**, flat trigonometry puts the ground contact at **18 km**. The horizon actually ranged sits at **36 km** — a factor of **2.00**. On the plane the surface neither ends at the first distance nor at the second; on the globe both numbers are the same tangent point.

**Grant the measured dip, then solve the flat triangle — and compare with the horizon that can actually be ranged**

| Eye height | Measured dip δ | Flat: d = h / tan δ | Measured horizon | Ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 m | 2.7′ · 0.045° | 2.5 km | 5.0 km | **2.00×** |
| 10 m | 6.1′ · 0.102° | 5.6 km | 11 km | **2.00×** |
| 100 m | 19.3′ · 0.321° | 18 km | 36 km | **2.00×** |
| 1.4 km | 71.9′ · 1.199° | 67 km | 133 km | **2.00×** |
| 10 km | 192.5′ · 3.208° | 178 km | 357 km | **2.00×** |

> **Three statements, no consistent flat answer.** (1) The dip is real and measured — so the flat triangle puts the ground at h/tan δ. (2) The horizon is real and ranged — radar, known landmarks and ship disappearance all put it twice as far. (3) On a plane the surface has no edge at either distance. The globe satisfies all three at once with a single number: the tangent point of a sphere of radius R sits at √(2Rh), and the angle to it *is* the dip. The factor of 2 isn't a fudge — it's the signature of a tangent line on a circle versus a chord to a plane.

## The surface you never drew [evidence: prediction]

Here is the same measurement with **no ground drawn at all**. Every line is one sightline to the horizon, taken from a real vantage point on the *same vertical* — a beach, a ship's bridge, a lighthouse, a cliff, a summit, an airliner — each tipped below horizontal by its own measured dip δ(h). Nothing else is plotted: no circle, no arc, no Earth. Yet the lines cannot enter a certain region, and that forbidden region has a shape. The dip angles alone carve the planet out of the negative space. **Click any sightline** to see which altitude it came from.

Click any sightline in the figure to see the height it was taken from, the dip it produces, and how far its horizon lies.

*Figure caption:* Seven real vantage points on one vertical, from a beach to an airliner, each line tipped by its own dip. Notice the wedge below them that none of the lines enters, and how its upper boundary curves. **Click any line** for its numbers, or press **reveal the surface** to see what fills the void.

This is what a mathematician calls an **envelope**: a family of straight lines whose boundary traces a curve that none of them crosses. Because a tangent to a circle touches at one point and lies outside it everywhere else, the sightlines can only be tangents of one specific circle — the one whose radius satisfies cos δ = R/(R+h) at *every* height simultaneously. A flat plane produces no envelope at all: with δ = 0 at all heights, every line is horizontal, they never fan, and the empty region is an unbounded half‑plane with no curve anywhere in it.

## Measuring the Earth from one dip angle [evidence: measurement]

Turn the formula around. If you can measure your height h and the dip δ, you can solve for R — no satellites, no travel, no second observer:

$$\cos\delta = \frac{R}{R+h} \implies {R = \frac{h\cos\delta}{1-\cos\delta}} \approx {\frac{2h}{\delta^2}}$$

δ in radians for the approximation. One hill, one angle, one number — and it must come out the same from a sea cliff, a mountain, or an aircraft window. That consistency is the test; a single value would prove nothing on its own.

**Solving for R from the current height, and what refraction does to the answer**

| Dip used | Value at current h | R = h·cos δ/(1−cos δ) | Compared with 6,371 km |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Geometric dip (vacuum) | 19.26′ = 0.321° | 6,371 km | +0.0% |
| Refracted dip, used as-is | 17.97′ = 0.299° | 7,323 km | +14.9% |
| Refracted dip, corrected by (1−k), k=0.13 | 17.97′ = 0.299° | 6,371 km | -0.0% |

From h = **100 m** the geometric dip returns R exactly. Feed in the *refracted* dip — which is what any real instrument reads — and the naive answer is about **15% too large**, because light bending makes the Earth look flatter than it is. Correcting by the refraction coefficient recovers the right value. This is the one systematic error that dogged the method for nine centuries.

### Who did it first: al‑Bīrūnī, around 1018

An astrolabe, a hill in the Salt Range, and an answer within a fraction of a percent — partly by luck, since he had no way to correct for refraction

> **Who did it first: al‑Bīrūnī, around 1018.** The Persian scholar Abū Rayḥān al‑Bīrūnī carried out exactly this measurement from a hill at Nandana, in the Salt Range of what is now Pakistan. He first obtained the hill's height by triangulating it from the plain below, then used an astrolabe to measure the dip of the horizon — reporting roughly 34 arcminutes — and applied the same relation R = h·cos δ/(1 − cos δ). Depending on which cubit he used, his answer corresponds to an Earth radius of about 6,300–6,340 km, within a fraction of a percent of the modern 6,371 km[10]. Eratosthenes had measured the Earth some 1,250 years earlier, but by a completely different route — comparing midday shadow angles at two latitudes — so the *dip method* is credited to al‑Bīrūnī. His accuracy involved some luck: as the table above shows, refraction biases this method by more than 10%, and he had no way to correct for it.

## Your own dip, measured on a photograph — and the radius it gives [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the camera's level is set by summits whose angles need their distances in km.]

The page's author photographed the sea from the plateau de Caussols on 13 June 2026 at 15:23, the eye 1,210 m above it — the photograph used in the Caussols figure above. It can measure the dip itself, without assuming a globe. The sea horizon lies at the same depression all the way round, on a globe and on a plane alike (where that depression is zero), so its slope in the picture gives the camera's roll, and its height is left free. The level is fixed by the two nearby summits, the dome of the Puy de Tourrettes and the Pic de Courmettes, about 7 km off, whose elevation angles come from the LiDAR terrain with flat trigonometry — no curvature at all, the choice most favourable to a plane (with the globe's own geometry they move by under 2′). The scale is the camera's EXIF focal length: one pixel is 1.27′. The horizon is found in 1,350 columns of open sea, scattering 0.9 px about a straight line; the summits are matched to 2.6 px rms. Result: the sea horizon lies **65.0′** below the level. A plane says 0′.

Turning a dip into a radius needs the bending of the light, and the standard coefficient k = 0.13 is an average for sightlines near the ground. From 1,210 m what counts is the air at the two ends of the grazing ray: the dip depends almost only on the difference between the air at eye level and the air at the apparent horizon, whatever lies in between.[2] For an atmosphere in spherical layers this is exact: n·r·cos α keeps the same value all along a ray (Bouguer's invariant), so the ray that grazes the sea, where the index is n_sea, reaches the eye with n_sea·R = n_eye·(R + h)·cos δ. The reanalysis for that afternoon gives 22.2 °C and 889 hPa at the eye, 21.9 °C and 1,021 hPa over the sea where the ray grazes it[6]; with the refractive index of air for visible light[5], a globe of 6,371 km predicts a dip of 60.4′ that day — more bending than standard, as if k were 0.19, because the air at 1,210 m was almost as warm as the air over the sea. Solved for R, the photograph's 65.0′ gives **R = 5,645 km**. With the standard k instead: 5,888 km; with no refraction at all: 6,768 km.

$$R = \frac{n_{\text{eye}}\,h\cos\delta}{n_{\text{sea}} - n_{\text{eye}}\cos\delta}$$

h = height of the eye above the sea · δ = measured dip · n = refractive index of the air at the eye and where the ray grazes the sea, n − 1 = 79.01·10⁻⁶·P/T (P in hPa, T in K) · with n_sea = n_eye it is the formula of the table above

**Each decision of the measurement changed alone: the dip, and the radius under three assumptions about the air**

| Variant | Dip | R, no refraction | R, k = 0.13 | R, the day's air | Fit (summits / horizon) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| central measurement | 65.0′ | 6,768 km | 5,888 km | 5,645 km | 2.6 / 0.9 px |
| horizon taken at the top edge of the sea | 62.3′ | 7,379 km | 6,420 km | 6,064 km | 2.5 / 0.7 px |
| skyline threshold 25 (more sensitive) | 66.4′ | 6,490 km | 5,646 km | 5,450 km | 2.2 / 0.9 px |
| skyline threshold 60 (less sensitive) | 63.1′ | 7,180 km | 6,246 km | 5,929 km | 4.1 / 0.9 px |
| summits given the globe's geometry | 67.0′ | 6,368 km | 5,540 km | 5,364 km | 2.7 / 0.9 px |
| 5 m of scrub on the summits | 62.2′ | 7,394 km | 6,433 km | 6,074 km | 2.5 / 0.9 px |

*Figure caption:* **The photograph, and the lines measured on it.** Top: the strip of the photograph from the two summits to the open sea, at uniform scale. Yellow dots: the skyline found on the summits; white line: the LiDAR relief projected by the fitted camera; orange dashes: the level (eye level, where a plane puts the horizon); white: the sea horizon measured. Bottom: a magnified piece of the horizon, with the measured points, and for comparison only the globe's horizon for that day's air and for no refraction. No axis is stretched.

The measurement is imprecise, and the table shows how much. Changing each decision alone — where the hazy horizon is taken, how the skyline is found, whether the summits are given the globe's geometry, a few metres of scrub on them — moves the dip between 62.2′ and 67.0′; with three states of the air, R runs from 5,355 km to 6,139 km. One pixel is 1.27′, and one minute of dip is 3.1 % of the radius. The central dip lies 4.6′ (3.6 px) deeper than the globe predicts for that day's air. The air cannot explain that — it bent the light more than standard, which raises the horizon — so the difference points at the camera: scrub on the summits, residual lens distortion away from the centre of the frame, or where exactly the hazy horizon lies. Taking the free air above the sea at eye height (19.1 °C) instead of the air of the sunny plateau gives 5,702 km. A plane gives no radius at all: its horizon would lie on the level line, 65.0′ above the one photographed.

Experiment 4 · horizon dip

Climb, and measure how far the sea horizon falls

Stand at the shore with a levelled instrument and measure the angle between true horizontal and the sea horizon. Then climb — a cliff path, a tall building, a hill — and measure again from a known height.

Independent variable
**What you change:** your **eye height h** above sea level. You choose it by where you stand: 2 m, then 50 m, then 300 m. Set it with the height control at the top of this tab.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the **dip angle** — how far the horizon sits below level. The world decides this.

IV h = 100 m (set above)
DV flat prediction: dip = 0.0′ = 0.000°
DV globe prediction: dip = 18.0′ = 0.299° (with refraction)
geometric, no refraction: 19.3′ · rule of thumb 1.76′×√h = 17.6′

**Verdict rule:** a single non-zero dip, repeated and larger from higher up, refutes the flat model outright — there is no value of any parameter that turns zero into 18.0′. And because the globe predicts dip ∝ √h, plotting your readings against √h should give a straight line whose slope hands you the Earth's radius.

## Below eye level and still in the sky — the band the Sun has to cross [evidence: prediction]

Everything above treats the dip as a correction. Turn it round and it becomes something you can *watch*. If the horizon sits δ below your eye level, then there is a strip of sky, δ tall, that is **below the level line and above the horizon at the same time**. Anything in that strip — the Sun, the Moon, a planet, a distant aircraft — is seen whole, against sky, with nothing in front of it, while a bubble level says it is beneath you. From a mountain or an airliner the strip is several Sun‑widths tall and it takes the Sun a quarter of an hour to cross it.

On a flat plane that strip cannot exist, and not by a little. The ground's depression angle is atan(h/x), which shrinks toward zero as the ground recedes: eye level *is* the vanishing line, and the surface fills every direction below it out to the limit of visibility. An object seen below your own eye level would have to be seen through the ground. The flat model does not predict a thin strip, or a strip that needs good conditions. It predicts a strip of width **zero**, at every height, which is rule 4 again: an absence against a presence.

$${\delta(h) \gt 32'}$$
$${\delta - 32'}$$
$${\frac{\delta - 32'}{15.04^\circ/\text{h}\times\cos\varphi}}$$

The Sun spans about 32′[4], so its whole disc is under your eye level once its centre is 16′ below, and it is still wholly clear of the horizon until its centre reaches 16′ above the horizon line. Subtract: the window opens at a dip of one Sun‑width, which is an eye height of about 330 m. The rate is the equinox rate at latitude φ; away from the equinox it is slower still, which only lengthens the window.

*Figure caption:* Eye height 100 m: the horizon lies 19.3′ (0.321°) below eye level, so the shaded band is 0.60 Sun-widths tall. At this height the band is narrower than the Sun itself, so the disc cannot fit inside it — climb above about 330 m and it can. On a flat plane the two lines coincide and the band has zero height at every altitude.

**The band below eye level, at documented heights, and how long the Sun spends inside it**

| Eye height | Dip δ | Band, in Sun‑widths | Whole disc below level and clear | Time to cross, φ = 45° | Flat plane |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.7 m standing at the waterline | 2.5′ · 0.042° | 0.08× | — too low | — | 0.0′ · 0 s |
| 276 m Eiffel Tower, top platform | 32.0′ · 0.533° | 1.00× | — too low | — | 0.0′ · 0 s |
| 555 m Burj Khalifa, At the Top SKY | 45.4′ · 0.756° | 1.42× | 13.4′ = 0.42× | 75 s | 0.0′ · 0 s |
| 1,395 m Sommet de Viériou | 71.9′ · 1.199° | 2.25× | 39.9′ = 1.25× | 3.8 min | 0.0′ · 0 s |
| 3,275 m Karagöl subpeak | 110.2′ · 1.837° | 3.44× | 78.2′ = 2.44× | 7.4 min | 0.0′ · 0 s |
| 11,000 m airliner at cruise | 201.9′ · 3.364° | 6.31× | 169.9′ = 5.31× | 16.0 min | 0.0′ · 0 s |

Times are for the equinox at 45°, where the Sun descends at 10.64° per hour; nearer the solstices, or nearer the poles, it descends more slowly and every figure above gets longer. Sunset from an airliner is also **later** than at sea level by the whole band: 19 minutes at this latitude, for the 202′ of dip alone. A plane predicts the same instant from the beach and from 11 km.

> **This is not the Sun setting, and that is the whole point.** Occultation is a separate event that happens later, when the disc finally reaches the horizon line. The claim here is about the interval *before* it: the Sun entire, nothing covering any part of it, sky visible underneath it, and a levelled instrument reading it as below the horizontal. You can photograph the state directly — one frame containing the Sun, the sea horizon under it, and a plumb line or a levelled bar in the same field of view. There is no version of a flat plane in which that frame exists.

> **Three things that can spoil it, stated in advance.** First, the level has to be a real level: in an aircraft the apparent vertical follows the resultant of gravity and acceleration, so a bank or a climb tilts it — take the reading in steady cruise, and prefer the angle from the Sun *to the horizon*, which no instrument error can manufacture. Second, refraction lifts objects near the horizon by roughly 34′[1] and shrinks the dip by about 8%[2]; both are already in the numbers above, and both work *against* the effect rather than creating it. Third, over land the horizon is terrain, not the geometric horizon, so this is a sea‑horizon measurement. None of the three turns a zero into 3°.

Experiment 4b · the doubled sunset

Watch the same sunset twice, and get the radius of the Earth out of a stopwatch

Sit at the water's edge facing west and watch the Sun's last edge disappear. Then stand up — or run up a dune, or take a lift, or take off — and it comes back. The delay is not an illusion and it is not small: it is δ(h₂) − δ(h₁) divided by the rate at which the Sun sinks. Rawlins proposed this in 1979[3] as a way to measure the planet with a wristwatch and a metre stick, and Minnaert did the six‑metre version by running up a dyke.[2]

Independent variable
**What you change:** your **eye height**, between the first sunset and the second. Sitting to standing is half a metre; a stairwell is ten; an aircraft is eleven thousand.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the **delay** in seconds between the two disappearances — one number, from a stopwatch.

Dip at 1.2 m: 1.97′ · at 6.0 m: 4.40′ → Δδ = **2.43′**

Globe predicts a delay of 15.8 s at 52.0° · flat plane predicts 0.0 s

Your 16.0 s, inverted: Rₑff = **7,107 km**, i.e. R = **6,183 km** after removing k = 0.13

**Verdict rule.** The flat prediction is that the second sunset never happens: raise your eye and the Sun stays gone, because the vanishing line does not move. Time a delay of **0 s**, repeatably, from a height difference big enough that the globe predicts 16 s, and the globe prediction is refuted. Conversely a delay that tracks √h₂ − √h₁ across several height pairs, and returns the same R each time, is a measurement no flat arrangement reproduces. Expect scatter: coastal air can shift the dip by minutes of arc, so repeat it and take the open sea over a river mouth.

> **It is measured, not inferred.** A dip meter (or a theodolite levelled with a bubble, or a sextant's artificial horizon) reads the angle between the true horizontal and the sea horizon directly. From a 10 m bridge it is about 5.6′ (0.093°); from a 100 m cliff about 17.6′ (0.293°); from an airliner at 10 km about 3.0°. Those numbers are tabulated, reproducible with hardware costing a few hundred euros, and they track √h exactly as arccos(R/(R+h)) requires. A plane predicts 0.0′ = 0.000° at every one of those heights.

## The doubled sunset, on an instrument: Mauna Loa and the coast below it [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the Sun's altitude from an ephemeris, the observatory's horizon from a terrain model; the coast's sunset is computed.]

Experiment 4b asks for a stopwatch. NOAA's observatory on Mauna Loa, 3,397 m up on the island of Hawaii, runs something better: a pyrheliometer, a tube that follows the Sun and records its direct light every minute. The record is open to anyone.[7] It says, to the minute, when sunlight stops reaching the mountain each evening. 55 km away towards the summer sunset, at Keahole Point on the coast (4 m), there is also a station.[8] It measures only the light of the whole sky, which does not mark the sunset, so its sunset is computed. Both are put on one clock.

*[Figure: An animated cross-section through the Earth in the direction of the sunset, with Mauna Loa Observatory on its mountain and Keahole Point on the coast 55 km closer to the Sun. As the clock runs, the last ray of sunlight, grazing the sea, sweeps upward: Keahole falls into the Earth's shadow first, the mountain minutes later. Below, the western sky from each place, and the direct sunlight measured at Mauna Loa on the same clock.]*

- Keahole sunset, computed: 18:51:16 (18:49:07 without refraction)Mauna Loa, last edge computed: 18:57:37 (18:54:54 without refraction)Mauna Loa, last direct light measured: 18:53:51, Sun's centre 1.89° below the horizontal2016: 104 clear evenings with a sea horizon; last light with the Sun's centre 1.72° below the horizontal (median), 1.9 min after Keahole's computed sunset

*Figure caption:* **One clock, two sunsets.** Top: a cross-section through the Earth in the direction of the setting Sun on a typical evening, chosen by a rule fixed in advance: of the year's clear evenings, the one whose last light came closest to the median. The Sun is to the left. The yellow line is the last ray that still reaches the ground, grazing the sea. The grey band behind the Earth is its shadow. Rule 1: to show a 3.4 km mountain beside the curve of the sea, the Earth is drawn smaller and the distances along the ground shortened, by the factors printed on the figure. The heights are true, and the ray and its tangent point land where they would on the real Earth. The terrain between the two places is the Copernicus surface model. Middle: the western sky from each place, at true angular scale, with eye level dashed. From the mountain the sea horizon lies 1.7° below eye level, and the Sun sinks into that gap before it sets. Bottom: the direct sunlight measured at Mauna Loa that evening (black), with the computed sunsets. Click to pause.

$$a_{\odot} = -(\varphi + \rho_0 + s)$$
$$\varphi = \dfrac{1}{1-k}\arccos\dfrac{R_e}{R_e + h}, \qquad R_e = \dfrac{R}{1-k}$$
Keahole (h = 4 m): a = −0.81° · Mauna Loa (h = 3,397 m): a = −2.75° (−2.13° without refraction)

a is the true altitude of the Sun's centre at the moment its upper edge disappears. The last ray that reaches the eye grazes the sea at a tangent point, an arc φ away. Beyond that point it bends a further ρ₀ ≈ 34′ in the air[1], and the centre of the Sun is s ≈ 16′ below its edge.[4] Refraction near the ground enters through Rₑ = R/(1 − k), k = 0.13.[2] The mountain keeps the Sun until it is almost 2° lower than at the coast, about 9 minutes of the Sun's motion on a summer evening there. Keahole lies 55 km further west, which alone gives it about 2 minutes more, so the mountain's lead is 6 to 7 minutes.

One evening proves little, so here is the whole of 2016. The direct light ended on 331 evenings, 286 of them clear. On 104 of those, the Sun set where the observatory's horizon is the sea: April to August. In the other months it sets further south, behind the slopes of Mauna Loa itself (the Copernicus terrain model[9]). Those evenings are left out by that rule alone. On the 104, the light stopped with the Sun's centre 1.72° below the horizontal (median), and below it on 90 evenings. It stopped a median 1.9 minutes after Keahole's computed sunset, and later than that sunset on 70 evenings. The geometry predicts more: the last edge at −2.75°, 6.6 minutes after Keahole (6.0 without refraction). The instrument loses the beam about a degree early, because a ray grazing the sea crosses hundreds of kilometres of low air and arrives too dim for the 5 W/m² threshold. That loss works against the effect, not for it.

> **What the plane predicts, and what would have vindicated it.** On a plane, nothing is ever seen below eye level. And a lamp at height H and distance D is seen at atan((H − h)/D): lower from a mountain than from the shore. If anything, the mountain would lose the Sun *first*. On a globe the mountain loses it minutes *later*, and the record agrees on most evenings. What would vindicate the plane: on the same clear evening, the mountain's last direct light coming no later than the coast's, measured by the same kind of instrument at both places. That second instrument is what this section lacks. Keahole's sunset is computed, so the comparison is between a measurement and a prediction, not between two measurements.

> **Limits, stated in advance.** The tracker is aimed by the same astronomical calculation used here, and it sees a patch of sky several degrees wide. On its own, then, it cannot place the Sun to a fraction of a degree. What it fixes is the *time* the light stops, and the Sun's position at that time is ordinary astronomy, the same that predicts every sunset at sea level. The threshold makes the measured last light come early, by about a degree, and the amount varies with the haze. Near azimuth 300° the summit of Hualālai, 35 km away, rises just above the sea horizon. No evening of 2016 set there, and the rule would have left it out. This is one year of one observatory; the build script redoes any other year.

Why a plane has no horizon at all. On an infinite plane the ground's depression angle below eye level is atan(h/x), which shrinks toward zero as x grows but never reaches it. The surface would fade into haze at a distance set by air clarity — blurry, weather‑dependent, and different for every camera. What is actually seen is a *sharp, hard edge* at a definite distance that sharpens with better optics, sits lower the higher you climb, and hides ships hull‑first. The right panel shows the flat model's depression at the same distance where the globe places its horizon: a number that is not zero, but is far too small and in the wrong place.

Refraction, again. Air bends light downward, pushing the horizon farther away and reducing the dip by roughly 8%. That is why the almanac constant is 1.76′√h rather than the geometric 1.93′√h. Toggle it above: it changes the numbers by a few percent, never the sign, and never rescues zero.

The through‑line. Same R again — the dip is simply the elevation angle of the tangent sightline, the limiting case of the Simulator's geometry when the target's height goes to zero. It is the horizon whose dip the perspective panel already draws, and the same R that fixes k = 1/R and converts Δλ into kilometres.

**See also**[Refraction](/ai/ref.md)[Hidden height](/ai/hh.md)[Elevation angles](/ai/elev.md)[Observation](/ai/obs.md)

# The Earth is curved everywhere. The horizon only looks curved from high up.

> Tab "Horizon curve" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-curv. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Horizon curvature · two different curves*

Two curves are easy to mix up. The **curvature of the Earth** belongs to the ground: it is the same everywhere, one turn per 40,000 km, and it makes the surface fall below a level line by about d²/2R — 7.8 cm at 1 km, 7.85 m at 10 km, 785 m at 100 km. The **curvature of the horizon** belongs to your viewpoint. The horizon is the ring where your sightlines just graze the sphere, and every point of that ring lies at the same angle δ below eye level — the dip.[3] A ring seen from just above its own plane is seen almost edge-on, and a ring seen edge-on looks like a straight line. How curved it looks depends on how high you are, and on how wide a slice of it your eye or your camera takes in.

> **The objection this tab answers.** “The horizon looks perfectly flat from the beach, from mountains, even from airliners — so the Earth is flat.” The globe predicts exactly that. From 2 m, across a 60° field, the horizon of a globe sags by 0.010 % of the frame's width: 0.4 px on a photograph 4,000 pixels wide. From an airliner at 35,000 ft it is 0.724 % of the width, and the one careful study of the question calls it “subtle”: it is not seen in a field narrower than about 60°.[1] A flat-looking horizon at those heights is not evidence against the globe. It is what the globe says you should see.

*Figure caption:* **The two curvatures in one drawing.** Side view, drawn for the height set in the simulator below. The ground falls away below the level line (the Earth's curvature, the same at every height); the sightlines that graze it meet the surface on a ring, all at the dip δ below eye level (the horizon, which depends on the height). To make a few kilometres of height visible next to the planet, the Earth is drawn *smaller* — at uniform scale, never stretched — and the factor is printed on the figure; the angles written on it are the real ones, computed, not measured on the drawing.

## In depth the curve is easy to see; left to right it is not [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: distances to the tower read on a map.]

The Earth's curvature shows **in depth**: look along the surface and the far ground falls below your sightline, so distant things lose their base. **Left to right** it hardly shows: the horizon is the ring at the dip δ, and it bends only by δ·a²/2. Both come from the same radius, but the first grows with the square of the distance, the second with the square root of your height.

*Figure caption:* **In depth, not left to right.** Left: what the camera records, in true perspective, nothing exaggerated. While it moves away the lens zooms to keep the tower readable (the field is printed), then widens to 90° with the horizon through the centre. At each of the author's shots the animation stops and the red line marks the height he measured as hidden. Dashed orange: eye level, which is the horizon of a plane, and the whole tower as a plane would show it. Right: the same instant in profile. To fit a tower 48 km away in one drawing, the Earth is drawn up to 2,000 times smaller and ground distances about √2,000 ≈ 45 times shorter, at uniform scale. With that pairing d²/2R does not change, so every height and every hidden height in the drawing is the real one. The factors are printed, and the angles written are the true ones. Drawn without refraction; the refracted hidden height is printed beside.

$$H = \frac{(d - d_0)^2}{2R},\quad d_0 = \sqrt{2Rh}$$
$$s \approx \delta\,\frac{a^2}{2},\quad \delta \approx \sqrt{2h/R}$$

H = hidden height of a distant target · d = its distance · d₀ = distance of the horizon · h = eye height · R = 6,371 km · s = sagitta of the horizon, as an angle at the centre of the frame · a = half the horizontal field (ordinary lens, horizon centred)

A documented case shows both at once. On 26 February 2016 Mathias Kp filmed the Turning Torso in Malmö, 190 m tall, from the Danish side of the Øresund: six shots from 25 to 47.9 km with his eye 2 to 4 m above the water, then a seventh from 17.6 m at the last spot.[12] He counted how many of the tower's nine segments the water hid and converted them into metres.[13] At 47.9 km, 114 m of it was gone (the geometric globe says 143 m); climbing to 17.6 m brought 50 m back. From the same 2.1 m, the horizon across a 90° lens bends by 0.7 px on a photograph 4,000 pixels wide. The animation replays his shots, then keeps climbing. From 180 m the whole tower is in view again, and the horizon still bends by only 6.2 px; the bend becomes plain only kilometres up: 48 px from an airliner, 304 px from 400 km.

**The Turning Torso shots, 26 February 2016: the part hidden by the water, measured by the author[13] and predicted**

| Shot | Eye height | Distance | Measured hidden | Globe, geometric / k = 0.13 | Plane hides | k that would fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 3.7 m | 25.0 km | **23 m** (0.75 seg.) | 25.8 / 21.2 m | 0.0 m | 0.080 |
| B | 2.9 m | 28.4 km | **34 m** (1.32 seg.) | 39.1 / 32.7 m | 0.0 m | 0.103 |
| C | 2.9 m | 34.7 km | **54 m** (2.35 seg.) | 64.3 / 54.2 m | 0.0 m | 0.133 |
| D | 2.4 m | 40.3 km | **76 m** (3.46 seg.) | 94.9 / 80.7 m | 0.0 m | 0.173 |
| E | 2.7 m | 45.1 km | **101 m** (4.72 seg.) | 120.8 / 102.9 m | 0.0 m | 0.143 |
| F | 2.1 m | 47.9 km | **114 m** (5.40 seg.) | 143.3 / 122.5 m | 0.0 m | 0.183 |
| F2 | 18 m | 47.9 km | **64 m** (2.86 seg.) | 85.1 / 69.2 m | 0.0 m | 0.174 |

Every measurement lies below the geometric globe and close to the refracted one. The refraction coefficient that would make the globe fit each shot exactly runs from 0.08 to 0.18 — around the usual 0.13 and as variable as it is measured to be near the sea.[4] The author's own estimates, with a slightly different refraction model, run from 0.076 to 0.187.[13] The plane hides nothing. Over a flat sea the base of a building sits a hair below eye level, at atan(h/d), and a wave hides it only by about the wave's own height — unless the wave, close to the camera, reaches almost to the eye, and then it hides the sea and the horizon as well. The author gives no wave data for that day, only that waves there are usually very small; the eye heights are his own, and a segment read by eye is uncertain by a few metres. Those uncertainties are metres; the hidden parts are 23 to 114 m, they grow with distance and shrink when the eye rises, as d²/2R says.

The same depth effect gives two sunsets. Watch the Sun's top edge vanish, then climb: the horizon drops as the dip grows, and the Sun comes back. Drone pilots film it. One describes the first sunset at about 80 ft above the ground and the second at about 400 ft[10]; another does it over the Atlantic from Ireland with a DJI Phantom 3 SE[11]. Between 80 and 400 ft the geometric dip grows from 9.5′ to 21.3′. On a plane the horizon stays at eye level at every height, so climbing cannot bring back a Sun that has gone below it. These videos give only the pilots' own rough heights: they show the effect, they do not measure it. The [Dip](/ai/dip.md) tab turns the delay between two sunsets into a radius of the Earth.

## Why the curve of the horizon is so small [evidence: prediction]

From a height h the dip is cos δ = R/(R + h), about √(2h/R) — 1.93′·√h with h in metres, the figure every navigator subtracts from a sextant sight.[2][3] Standard refraction bends sightlines along the curve and acts like a larger radius R/(1 − k), with k ≈ 0.13 near the ground[3][4]; it lowers the dip by about 7% (the almanacs, allowing for slightly stronger refraction, use 1.76′·√h[2]), and both values are shown everywhere on this page. Aim a camera at the horizon and take in a half-width a on each side. The middle of the horizon sits at the dip; the two ends sit at the dip too, but they are seen off to the side, and an ordinary lens draws them lower. The gap between the middle and the straight line joining the two ends — the **sagitta**, the measure Lynch used[1] — is, for an ordinary (rectilinear) lens:

$$s = f\,\tan\delta\,(\sec a - 1) \approx \delta\,\frac{a^2}{2}$$

s in pixels (or, divided by f, as an angle at the centre of the frame) · f = focal length in pixels · a = half the horizontal field · exact for a level camera; the page computes every case by projecting the horizon ring point by point

Two small factors multiply. The dip grows only as the square root of the height: 2.7′ (2.5′ refr.) at 2 m, 3.31° (3.09° refr.) at 35,000 ft. And a²/2 is small unless the field is wide: 0.14 for a 60° field, 0.31 for 90°. That is the whole story of the flat-looking horizon. The ground's curvature never changes; what changes with height is how steeply you look down on the ring, and a ring looked down on at 3° still looks nearly straight. Lynch's photograph from 35,000 ft, horizon on the optical axis, 62.7° across, measures a sagitta of **0.51°**[1]; the formula gives 0.57° without refraction and 0.53° with it.

## Simulator: the horizon a camera should record [evidence: prediction]

Set a height and a field of view. The picture is a true projection of the ring onto the sensor — nothing is exaggerated, so at low heights there is nothing to see, which is the point. The sea is drawn below the refracted horizon (solid line); the geometric horizon, a little lower, is dashed. The dotted line joins the two ends of the horizon; the gap to it at the centre is the sagitta. The orange line is eye level: the horizon of an infinite plane, at every height. With the camera level the horizon sits below the centre by the dip; “horizon centred” tilts the camera down by the dip, as Lynch recommends for a measurement.[1]

Dip of the horizon: 3.09° refracted · 3.31° geometric

## What a lens does to a horizon

Most photographs “of the curvature of the Earth” show something else, and the reason fits in three sentences. The focal length deforms nothing: changing it multiplies the whole image by a constant, a zoom that only sets the field of view. What changes shapes is the **projection law** — how the angle θ between a direction and the optical axis becomes a distance r from the centre of the image — and the residual distortion of the lens design[5]: an ordinary lens follows r = f·tan θ and keeps every straight line straight; real wide-angles fall a little short of it towards the edges (barrel distortion); fish-eyes follow other laws altogether. And every one of these laws is **radial**: it moves a point along the line joining it to the centre of the image and never changes its angle about the centre. A straight line through the centre is one of those lines, so *every* lens leaves it straight. Anywhere else, only the ordinary law does. That is the whole reason for Lynch's rule — horizon through the centre — and it is what he showed by photographing the sea from 8 ft, effectively sea level, with the horizon near the top, the middle and the bottom of the frame: near the top it arched upward, near the bottom downward.[1]

*Figure caption:* **horizon near the top**plane 95 px (2.37 %)
globe 95 px (2.39 %)

*Figure caption:* **horizon through the centre**plane 0.2 px (0.005 %)
globe 0.7 px (0.017 %)

*Figure caption:* **horizon near the bottom**plane −94 px (−2.36 %)
globe −94 px (−2.35 %)

*Figure caption:* **One scene, one lens, three framings** — as Lynch photographed it.[1] The camera is tilted so that the middle of the visible horizon sits near the top, on the centre, or near the bottom of the frame; nothing else changes. The pale grid is a flat sheet held square in front of the lens: every line on it is straight, so wherever it bends, the lens is bending it. The orange line is a perfectly flat horizon at eye level; the teal line is the globe's, with standard refraction. Under each frame, how much each one sags on a photograph 4,000 pixels wide (positive = arched upward). The eight laws are those of the [Star trails](/ai/star.md) tab; the barrel coefficients are typical of their class of lens, not the measurement of a particular model.

Start with the 14 mm from 2 m, where the globe's own sag is below half a pixel: the flat horizon arches by 2.85 % of the width near the top and sags by as much near the bottom — more than twice what the globe gives from an airliner, horizon centred, with an ordinary lens over the same 100° field (1.26 %). Switch to the 35 mm law and nothing bends anywhere: the grid stays square, the flat horizon stays straight, and the globe's sag barely depends on where the horizon sits (from 35,000 ft, 62.7° field: 30.3–30.6 px on a 4,000-px frame across tilts of ±20°). The fish-eyes bend everything that is not through the centre, by several percent. Hence the rule for any photograph offered as evidence, either way: an ordinary lens, or a lens whose distortion has been calibrated, and the horizon through the centre of the frame.

## Calculator: from what height does the curve show in a photograph? [evidence: prediction]

Choose a camera. Phones are listed by the 35 mm-equivalent focal length their maker publishes, and their lenses are corrected in software, so they are treated as ordinary lenses[6][7]; Apple's own figures agree with that geometry (13 mm equivalent gives a 118.0° diagonal against the published 120°, 120 mm gives 20.4° against 20°). For a camera with interchangeable lenses, pick the sensor format[9], the focal length and the lens type. Enter the real width of your image in pixels — it is in the file's details — since the threshold is in pixels. The calculator places the horizon through the centre, assumes a sharp horizon, and finds the height at which the sagitta reaches the chosen number of pixels — the least a careful measurement could detect — and the height at which it reaches the bend of Lynch's photograph from 35,000 ft, 0.758 % of the width, which he describes as subtle but discernible.[1] It also says how much the lens alone bends a flat horizon that is not through the centre. Below, the same camera is taken to each height at which someone has reported on the horizon.

| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3,116 m | Haleakalā summit: Lynch could not convince himself he saw any curvature. | 20 px (0.505 %) / 19 px (0.471 %) | 0.0 px |
| 4,205 m | Mauna Kea summit: the same — no curvature he could be sure of. | 24 px (0.587 %) / 22 px (0.547 %) | 0.0 px |
| 10,668 m | Airliner, clear horizon: “subtle but unmistakable” across a field of 90° or more, not discernible under about 60°; most airline pilots say they cannot see it. | 38 px (0.935 %) / 35 px (0.872 %) | 0.0 px |
| 15,240 m | B-57 (D. Gutierrez): the curvature “does not become readily sensible until about 50,000 ft”. | 45 px (1.12 %) / 42 px (1.04 %) | 0.0 px |
| 15,787 m | Piccard and Kipfer's balloon, 1931: the first sighting of the curvature, as widely attributed. | 46 px (1.14 %) / 43 px (1.06 %) | 0.0 px |
| 18,288 m | 60,000 ft: “obvious” (Gutierrez); Concorde passengers “routinely marveled” at it. | 49 px (1.23 %) / 46 px (1.14 %) | 0.0 px |
| 22,066 m | Explorer II balloon, 1935: the first photographs of the curvature. | 54 px (1.35 %) / 51 px (1.26 %) | 0.0 px |

Two cases worth working through. An airline pilot photographs the horizon from 35,000 ft with an iPhone 16 Pro at 1× (24 mm equivalent[6], 71.6° across). With the horizon through the centre, the globe predicts a sagitta of 35 px on a 4,032-pixel-wide photo (0.872 % of the width) — measurable, and a little more than Lynch's frame; and since the phone corrects its lens, tilting it moves the horizon without bending it much. For balloon footage shot with an action camera, take the GoPro HERO7. GoPro publishes the horizontal, vertical and diagonal field of each mode, but not the projection law[8]; this page takes the family r = tan(kθ)/k (k = 1 is an ordinary lens, k → 0 the equidistant fish-eye) and fixes k = 0.372 from the three published angles of the Wide 4:3 photo mode. The 16:9 video mode played no part in that fit; the same law predicts its diagonal at 133.9°, against the published 133.6°. From 30 km, horizon centred, the globe's sagitta in Wide 4:3 is 2.69 % of the width; a perfectly flat horizon placed halfway between the centre and the top edge bends by 278 px (6.95 %) — the lens alone. As a payload swings, the horizon travels across the frame and its bend grows, vanishes and reverses; only the frames where it crosses the centre say anything about the Earth.

Read the table with the reports in mind. The numbers say what a camera records, not what an eye notices. A person sees a field much wider than 60°, but judges straightness over a narrower part of it, often through a curved window or glasses, and from above a mile or so the horizon is not the sharp sea line any more but a low-contrast band in the haze.[1] Lynch could not convince himself he saw the curve from Mauna Kea or Haleakalā, although with the same camera the sagitta there is more than half an airliner's (the dip is √(4,205/10,668) ≈ 0.63 of it); the numbers alone do not explain that, and this page does not guess why.[1] This is why the calculator gives heights for a photograph and a measurement, not for a glance.

## The flat model at its best

On an infinite plane the horizon is the vanishing line of the ground: it lies exactly at eye level at every height, and an ordinary lens draws it perfectly straight, wherever it sits in the frame. The plane's sagitta is 0 — not small, zero — from the beach to the stratosphere. That is a clean prediction, and it does not match Lynch's 0.51°. To give the flat model its best chance, let the plane end where the eye stops seeing — a haze edge at some distance D. That edge is a ring around the observer as well, at the depression atan(h/D), and it sags in a photograph by the same formula as the globe's horizon. Tune D so that it matches the globe at 35,000 ft: D = 184 km. Lynch's sagitta is then reproduced. But one D cannot serve two heights: the haze edge's depression grows in proportion to h, the globe's dip as √h. At 2 m that edge would sit 2.2″ below eye level, against 2.7′ (2.5′ refr.) for the globe; from Explorer II, 6.83° against 4.76° (4.44° refr.). The curvature of the horizon in a photograph is the dip spread across the frame — any ring at a depression δ around the observer gives the same sagitta — so the real test is the dip itself and how it grows with height, which the [Dip](/ai/dip.md) tab measures directly. What the sagitta adds is a way to read the dip from a single photograph, without a level.

> **Verdict rule, stated in advance.** *Globe:* a sharp horizon through the centre of an ordinary or calibrated lens sags by the amount the calculator gives — from 35,000 ft across 62.7°, 0.53° with standard refraction and 0.57° without — and the sagitta grows like the dip, as √h. *Plane:* the horizon stays at eye level and straight, sagitta 0.0 at every height. The flat model is vindicated if calibrated photographs from 10 km and higher, horizon on the optical axis, repeatedly show no sagitta to within 2 pixels where the globe predicts a dozen or more. The globe is refuted if the measured sagitta does not follow the dip — for instance if it stays the same from 3 km and from 20 km with the same camera.

**Limits of this tab.** There is one published measurement of this kind, from one flight, and its author placed the horizon on the axis to within a few arcminutes.[1] From high altitude the visible horizon is not the hard edge of the sea: it forms in the atmosphere, where a sightline becomes opaque several kilometres above the surface, and its contrast is less than a tenth of the sea horizon's.[1] The measured 0.51° lies 0.02° under the refracted value; one photograph cannot say whether that comes from the soft edge, the lens or the air. Real lenses keep some distortion even when sold as rectilinear; a sagitta of a few pixels means nothing unless the lens has been calibrated. And refraction near the ground varies with the weather: k = 0.13 is an average, not a constant.[4]

# The sky is lit for an hour before sunrise — and on a plane there is nothing above you for the Sun to light

> Tab "Twilight" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-twi. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Dawn & twilight · the light that arrives before the Sun does*

- Ceiling of the Earth's shadow over your head, from h = R(sec θ − 1) with R = 6,371 km: **35 km** at 6° · **142 km** at 12° · **328 km** at 18°. The left panel is at true scale, which is why the 6° shell is barely a line — that thinness is the point, not a drawing fault.

*Figure caption:* **Why there is light overhead and none underfoot.** Drawn **at true scale with no exaggeration at all** — none is needed, and the thinness of the lit shell is itself the finding. Note what the picture does *not* contain: any assumption about how bright the scattering is. The claim is only that a boundary exists and that its height is set by R.

Long before the Sun clears the horizon the sky is already bright, and long after it has gone the sky stays bright a while longer. That is not the question this tab asks. The question is sharper and much harder for a flat model to answer: why is it bright *up there* while it is dark *down here*?

A lit sky over an unlit ground is an asymmetry, and an asymmetry needs an edge. An edge needs a shadow. A shadow needs a body big enough and round enough to cast one. On a plane the Sun is above the plane at every hour of the day and night, so there is nothing anywhere that can be in shade while the air above it is in sunlight.

$$h = R\left(\sec\theta - 1\right) \approx \frac{R\theta^2}{2}$$
θ = the Sun's depression below the horizon

When the Sun is θ below your horizon, the last ray that grazes the Earth's surface passes over your head at a height h. Below h you are in the planet's shadow; above h the air is still in full sunlight and scatters some of it down to you. That single line is the whole of twilight, and it contains R — so twilight is a *measurement of the radius*, not merely a consequence of it. Put θ = 6°, 12° and 18° into it and out come 35 km, 142 km and 328 km, which is the table further down.

## Three twilights, and why they stop where they stop [evidence: prediction]

The three stages are defined by the Sun's geometric depression and by nothing else: civil twilight runs from sunset to 6° below, nautical from 6° to 12°, astronomical from 12° to 18°.[1]

The names record what a person could still do. Through civil twilight you can carry on outdoors without a lamp and the horizon stays crisp. Through nautical twilight the sea horizon is still visible while the brighter stars are out, which is exactly the window in which a sextant sight works and is why sailors named it. By the end of astronomical twilight the sky no longer adds measurable light to a telescope's field.

Those are human conventions, chosen for human tasks. What is *not* a convention is the height each one corresponds to. The formula above turns each threshold into a height above your head, and the answers land on the structure of the atmosphere without having been aimed at it. The table computes them; nothing in it is typed in by hand.

**Each twilight threshold, turned into the height of the shadow's ceiling over the observer — computed from h = R(sec θ − 1) with R = 6,371 km**

| Stage ends at | Sun's depression θ | Shadow ceiling h | h as a fraction of R | What is still in sunlight up there |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sunset / sunrise | 0° | **0.0 km** | 0.00 % | nothing: the ceiling is at your feet. This is sunset. |
| Civil twilight | 6° | **35 km** | 0.55 % | mid-stratosphere, above the ozone peak — about 99% of the atmosphere's mass is already below it |
| Nautical twilight | 12° | **142 km** | 2.23 % | thermosphere — the height auroras are seen at, and where meteors burn up |
| Astronomical twilight | 18° | **328 km** | 5.15 % | the altitude the space station orbits at — there is essentially nothing left up there to scatter light |

> **How much of that is an argument, and how much is a coincidence.** Be careful here, because the temptation is to claim more than the geometry gives. The 6/12/18 thresholds were fixed by what people can do, not derived from air density, so the correspondence in the last column is a *consistency check*, not a derivation. What the geometry does give, with no wiggle room, is the mapping itself: an 18° Sun puts the shadow ceiling at 328 km and a 6° Sun puts it at 35 km, and those follow from R alone. The interesting part is that the point where a human stops being able to see the sky glow lands where the air runs out — and that the same R which fixes the horizon in the dip tab, the star altitudes in the navigation tab and the arrival times in the seismology tab also fixes this.

## What the inverse-square law actually predicts on a plane [evidence: prediction]

Now the flat model, taken seriously and given its best case. Put a Sun at height H above an infinite plane, let it be as small and as close as you like, and let its light fall off as the inverse square of distance — which is the correct law for a compact source and is the law flat-earth accounts appeal to when they explain sunset as the Sun becoming distant and dim. An observer at ground distance d from the point directly under it is at slant range r = √(H² + d²), and the light lands on the ground obliquely, at an angle whose cosine is H/r.

$$E(d) = \frac{I H}{\left(H^2 + d^2\right)^{3/2}}$$
$$\vartheta(d) = \frac{D}{\sqrt{H^2 + d^2}}$$

E is the illuminance on level ground — the quantity a light meter pointed at the sky measures, and the quantity the published twilight measurements report. ϑ is the Sun's apparent diameter, with D its real diameter. Both are elementary and both hold on a plane for any H, any D and any brightness I.

Divide each by its value at noon, when the observer stands directly under the Sun, and something useful happens: every free parameter cancels. H disappears. D disappears. The Sun's brightness disappears. What is left is a relation between two things you can measure with a phone.

$$\frac{E(d)}{E(0)} = \left(\frac{H}{r}\right)^3 = \left(\frac{\vartheta(d)}{\vartheta(0)}\right)^{3}$$

On a plane, the ground can only get dark to the exact extent that the Sun gets *small*. Dim it by a thousand and it must have shrunk tenfold. That is not a claim about any particular flat map, or any particular Sun height, or any particular disc diameter — it is inverse-square geometry with the nuisance parameters divided out, in the same way the reciprocal zenith angles in the elevation tab cancel the two station heights. If you prefer the illuminance measured face-on to the rays rather than on level ground, drop the obliquity factor and the exponent becomes 2 instead of 3. It changes none of what follows.

So the flat model owes two numbers that must agree, and both have been measured to death. The measured day-to-night ratio of downwelling light is about **one hundred million**: a recent open-data study spanned it with two spectrometers precisely because no single instrument covers a factor of 10^8.[2] Full sun is of order 100,000 lux; a clear moonless night sky is of order 0.001 lux.[2][10]

And the Sun's apparent diameter runs between 31.6′ and 32.7′ over a whole year, a 3% swing caused by the Earth's orbital eccentricity, and is constant to far better than a percent across any one day.[7]

**The flat model's own arithmetic, with the Sun at three heights that have been proposed — all computed, none fitted**

| Sun height H | Distance d at "midnight" | Predicted brightness drop | Predicted disc shrinks to | Measured drop | Short by a factor of |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1,000 km | 20,000 km | 1 / 8,030 | 1.6′ | 1 / 100,000,000 | 12,453 × |
| 3,000 km | 20,000 km | 1 / 306 | 4.7′ | 1 / 100,000,000 | 326,422 × |
| 5,000 km | 20,000 km | 1 / 70 | 7.8′ | 1 / 100,000,000 | 1,426,680 × |
| 10,000 km | 20,000 km | 1 / 11 | 14.3′ | 1 / 100,000,000 | 8,944,272 × |
| **43 km** — forced | 20,000 km | 1 / 100,000,000 | 4.1″ | 1 / 100,000,000 | **matches — at the cost of the disc** |

> **The steel-man, and why it eats itself.** H is the flat model's free parameter, so tune it in the flat model's favour: pick whatever H makes the night as dark as the night actually is. The answer is H ≈ 43 km on a 20,000 km disc — the Sun would have to be lower than a weather balloon's ceiling. But the relation above is a package deal. Buying a factor of 10^8 in brightness means buying a factor of 464 in apparent size, so that Sun would cross the sky shrinking from 32′ at noon to 4″ at midnight, from a disc to a star. Nobody has ever recorded that, and a mobile phone with a solar filter rules it out in an afternoon.

> **Tune it back the other way, and it eats itself.** Push H back up to keep the disc the right size and the night gets bright again: at the usual 5,000 km the model's midnight is **one seventieth** of noon, about the difference between direct sun and a dull overcast afternoon, not the difference between noon and starlight. There is no H that does both jobs, because the exponent linking them is fixed by geometry.

*Figure caption:* **Eight orders of magnitude, and where the flat curves stop.** The vertical axis is the light on level ground relative to noon, on a log scale, so each gridline is a factor of ten; the horizontal axis is ground distance.

The gap is not a discrepancy that better numbers might close. The flat curves flatten out because a source at finite height never gets far away compared with itself, while the measurement falls off a cliff. On a globe there is no curve to draw at all past the terminator — the direct beam is geometrically zero there, and every photon that reaches you has been scattered down out of the sunlit shell above.

## The two models side by side, in motion [evidence: prediction]

Everything above compares one place at one moment. This panel puts the whole planet under both models at the same instant, because the disagreement is not really about how bright the sky is — it is about the *shape* of the lit region, and shape is the thing you can check without owning a light meter. On the left, a globe shaded by the Sun's altitude, with the three twilight thresholds drawn as the small circles they actually are. On the right, the same instant on the standard flat map, in two versions.

The second of those versions is the one that matters, and it is worth being clear about why it is not a straw man. Suppose everything is granted: forget the inverse square, forget the Sun's height, and assume only that brightness on a plane is *some* decreasing function of your distance from the point beneath the Sun. What that function is does not matter. Because it decreases, its contours are **circles centred on the subsolar point** — for every such function, without exception.

So a flat Earth is committed to a circular day–night boundary whatever its photometry turns out to be, and the single remaining number, the radius, is then tuned *in the flat model's favour*: each ring is pinned so that the plane is exactly right at 45° N at that instant. It touches the truth at one latitude, by construction, and misses everywhere else. The dashed teal curve is where sunset is really happening, which is not a claim of this page but the content of the sunrise and sunset tables printed for every city on Earth.

- Day 189 of the year, **11:15 UTC**. Sun overhead at **22.5° N, 12.5° E**; the middle of the night is at **22.5° S, 167.5° W**. **Dashed teal** = the real day–night edge at this instant, the line the published sunrise and sunset tables trace out. Its short ticks point into the night side, so the loop encloses the night rather than the day — worth checking at the December preset, where it closes around the pole. **Hollow dot** = that morning's sunrise at 45° N, **solid dot** = that evening's sunset. Both sit at the same map distance from the Sun, so one calibration pins the rings through both; any decreasing law gives rings, so only their radii were free and they have been spent there.

*Figure caption:* **One instant, two geometries.** The teal curve is not this page's assertion: it is the published rise and set tables, drawn as a line. One calibration pins both amber dots and every ring passes through them, so the plane is exact there *by construction* — the comparison is everywhere else. The globe's zone boundaries are computed, not traced; its daylight ramp is Lambert's cosine, but the ramp *through* twilight is interpolated, and schematic, because this page owns no scattering model.

Watch the ticks reverse. In July the day–night curve hugs the lit region and they face outwards; in December it closes around the pole and they face in, because in December the pole is the part in darkness. That reversal is not a drawing choice — it is what a tilted planet does.

The two halves do not animate alike, and it is worth knowing which. On the globe the viewpoint is fixed relative to the Sun, so the terminator holds still and the coastlines slide through it. On the flat map the coastlines are held still, in the orientation flat maps are always drawn in, and the lit patch sweeps across them instead. Both show the same rotation; they differ only in what they nail down. The right-hand panel offers two shadings: **1/r²** shades the plane by E/E₀ = (H/r)³ with the Sun 5,000 km up, and **Fitted** instead draws the circular contours that any decreasing law is forced to produce.

Switch the right-hand panel to **1/r²** and an obvious question arises: if the plane never goes dark on this map, then where does it go dark? The formula answers it. Solving E(d)/E(0) = 10^−8 for the distance, with the Sun 5,000 km up, puts real night **2,320,800 km** from the point beneath it — a hundred and sixteen times the radius of the whole flat map, and six times the distance to the Moon.

Even a mere thousandfold dimming, which is still a bright overcast afternoon rather than night, does not arrive until 49,700 km, two and a half times the rim. Lowering the Sun does not rescue this: at 1,000 km, about the lowest anyone has proposed, night still needs 464,000 km, twenty-three times the map. The plane is simply too small for its own light to fall off across it, and that is not a defect of one flat map but of the inverse-square law applied to a source hanging a few thousand kilometres above a surface you can walk on.

> **The day almost nobody is in the dark.** Set the panel to 8 July, 11:15 UTC and look at where the night is. Combining their solar data with a gridded population dataset, timeanddate found that at that moment it is night for just under 80 million people — so roughly **99% of humanity** is receiving some sunlight at once, about 83% in full daylight and 16% somewhere in twilight.[11]

> **What that number does and does not say.** They are careful, and so is this page: around 3% of that total, some 257 million people, are in astronomical twilight, which is not distinguishable from night by eye, so the honest figure for *perceptible* light is nearer 96%.[11] It is also not unique to one date — it holds on about sixty days around the June solstice, with the daily peak falling between 11:00 and 11:03 UTC.[12] This page ships no population grid and does not recompute those percentages; it quotes them, and they are checkable against the sources.

Why is that an argument rather than a curiosity? Because the number is a *census of who is standing inside the shadow*, and the shadow's shape is precisely what the two models disagree about.

It comes out that high because the middle of the night, on that date at that hour, sits in the emptiest part of the Pacific, while the tilt keeps the whole northern half of the planet — where most of humanity lives — in daylight at the same time. That is not a coincidence anybody arranged; it falls out of a tilted sphere turning once a day, and you can watch it fall out by pressing play.

Then switch the right-hand panel between its two versions and ask which landmasses each one puts in the dark. They are not the same landmasses, and only one of the two answers agrees with the sunrise and sunset times published for those cities on that date.

## The duration of twilight is the test with no radius in it [evidence: prediction]

Everything so far has used R. This section does not, and that makes it the counterpart on this tab of the magnetism tab's dip law: a constraint on *shape* that survives any rescaling. Twilight lasts as long as the Sun takes to travel from the horizon down to 18° below it, and how long that takes depends on the angle at which the Sun's daily circle meets your horizon. At the equator it comes down almost vertically and the whole business is over in a little over an hour. At 50° north it slants, and in June it slants so much that the Sun never gets 18° down at all.

$$\cos H = \frac{\sin h - \sin\varphi\sin\delta}{\cos\varphi\cos\delta}$$
$$h_{\min} = \left|\varphi + \delta\right| - 90^\circ$$

The first line is the hour angle at which the Sun stands at altitude h, for latitude φ and declination δ; the duration of a stage is the difference of two hour angles divided by 15.041° per hour. The second line is the Sun's altitude at local midnight, and it is the one that decides everything: if h_min never reaches −18°, there is no astronomical night at that place on that date, however long you wait. Notice that neither line contains R, or any distance at all, and an independent implementation of the same formulae is published by a different institution in a different country's service.[9] These are statements about a sphere's shape and its tilt, and they would read the same for a planet twice the size.

Set h_min = −18° and the condition falls out: astronomical night disappears above latitude 90° − 18° − δ. At the June solstice, with δ = 23.44°, that is **48.6°**. Nautical night goes at **54.6°** and civil night — the genuine white nights — at **60.6°**. Those are three sharp latitudes, predicted from the obliquity of the ecliptic and nothing else, and every one of them can be checked by looking up a published almanac[8] or by going outside in June.

Paris sits at 48.86°, a fifth of a degree past the first threshold, which is why Paris has no astronomical night for about two months either side of midsummer and Nice, 5° further south, has one every night of the year.

**Length of each twilight stage, computed from latitude and declination alone — sunrise taken at the standard −0°50′ for the centre of the disc**

| Place | Latitude | Date | Civil | Nautical | Astronomical | Sun's altitude at midnight |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quito | −0.22° | date-equinox | 21 min | 24 min | 24 min | −89.8° |
|  |  | date-june | 22 min | 26 min | 26 min | −66.8° |
| Nice | 43.70° | date-equinox | 29 min | 34 min | 34 min | −46.3° |
|  |  | date-june | 36 min | 47 min | 60 min | −22.9° |
| Paris | 48.86° | date-equinox | 31 min | 37 min | 38 min | −41.1° |
|  |  | date-june | 43 min | 61 min | *all night* | **−17.7°** |
| London | 51.51° | date-equinox | 33 min | 39 min | 41 min | −38.5° |
|  |  | date-june | 48 min | 74 min | *all night* | **−15.0°** |
| Copenhagen | 55.68° | date-equinox | 37 min | 44 min | 46 min | −34.3° |
|  |  | date-june | 61 min | *all night* | *all night* | **−10.9°** |
| Saint Petersburg | 59.94° | date-equinox | 41 min | 50 min | 54 min | −30.1° |
|  |  | date-june | 105 min | *all night* | *all night* | **−6.6°** |
