*Figure caption:* **Twilight length against latitude, and the three places it becomes infinite.** All three curves are at midsummer — June in the north, December in the south — so the axis is latitude without a sign and Ushuaia is plotted at its own midsummer rather than pretended to be northern. The three latitudes are 48.6° for astronomical, 54.6° for nautical, 60.6° for civil.

A flat model has no counterpart for any of this. Its Sun is above the plane at every instant, it never crosses a horizon, and nothing in an inverse-square falloff produces a latitude past which a stage takes infinitely long in June and eighty minutes in December.

> **This is a sign test, not a near miss.** The page prefers these wherever it can get them, for the reason set out in the elevation tab: a disagreement of a few percent can always be blamed on the instrument, but a question with a yes and a no cannot. Does astronomical night occur at your latitude in the third week of June? At 48° the answer is yes and at 49° it is no, and the almanac agreed with the calculation for a century before anyone thought to argue about it. The flat model does not give a different answer here. It gives no answer, because it has no quantity whose sign could flip.

## The Earth's shadow is an object, and you can photograph it

On a clear evening, turn your back on the sunset and look east about ten minutes after the Sun has gone. There is a dark blue-grey band lying along the horizon, with a soft pink band above it, and the boundary between them is straight enough to measure and slightly curved if you take in enough sky. The pink is sunlight reddened by its long passage through the lower atmosphere and back-scattered towards you — it has been called the Belt of Venus for a long time. The dark band under it is the Earth's own shadow, projected onto the air, seen edge-on.[6]

It behaves exactly as a shadow should. It appears opposite the Sun, centred on the antisolar point to within the accuracy anyone can hold a camera. Its top rises as the Sun sinks, at the Sun's own rate, so that its elevation above the eastern horizon tracks the Sun's depression below the western one. It is wider than the Sun because the Sun is not a point. And it fades out as it climbs, for the plainest of reasons: it is being projected onto air that is thinning as it goes up, so by the time the shadow's edge is 20° high there is nothing left up there to catch it.

*Figure caption:* **The eastern sky at three moments after sunset.** The dark segment is the geometric shadow of the Earth, drawn at the elevation the Sun's depression puts it, with the reddened band immediately above it. This is a schematic: the colours are indicative and the fading is drawn, not computed from a scattering model. What *is* computed is the height of the boundary in each frame, and that is the whole falsifiable content — an edge exists, it sits opposite the Sun, and its elevation equals the Sun's depression. The flat model predicts no edge at all in the eastern sky, because there is no body between the observer and the Sun to cast one and the Sun is never below the plane.

## Four objections, and what each one costs

Refraction is real and this page models it everywhere, so before the objections, here is its size: at the horizon it lifts an object by about 34′, a little over half a degree, and that is the reason sunrise is reckoned with the Sun's centre at −0°50′ rather than at zero.

### 1. "It is just perspective — the Sun goes too far away to see."

Perspective moves things towards a vanishing point; it does not switch them off, and it certainly does not switch off the ground while leaving the sky lit. If the Sun were merely far, its light would still be falling on your street at the same fraction of noon as on the air 200 km above your street, because both are essentially the same distance from it. The asymmetry is the whole phenomenon and perspective has nothing to say about it. Perspective also cannot make an edge: the shadow in the eastern sky has a boundary you can put a protractor on.

### 2. "The Sun is a spotlight and its beam has a limited reach."

This is the stronger version, and it is worth taking seriously because it does at least produce a boundary. But it produces the wrong one. A spotlight on a plane illuminates a circle, and the edge of that circle is at a fixed distance from the sub-solar point, so the time your location spends in the fade is set by how fast that edge sweeps past — which is nearly the same everywhere and in every season. The measured twilight lasts 68 minutes at the equator, 107 minutes at Paris in March and never ends at Paris in June. A beam of fixed reach cannot do that. It also cannot put the fade boundary in the sky *opposite* the Sun rather than in the direction the beam is going.

### 3. "Refraction explains it."

Its size is priced above: about 34′ at the horizon, against the 1,080′ that twilight runs to — thirty times larger, and refraction shrinks rapidly as you move away from the horizon. There is also no free parameter left to spend: the refraction tab prices the flat limit k = 1 at a sustained inversion of +12.9 °C per 100 m, and radiosondes have been failing to find one since 1905.

### 4. "The air simply gets dimmer as the light travels further through it."

Extinction along a long slant path is real too, and it is why the setting Sun is red and dim enough to look at. But extinction is a smooth, monotonic, exponential attenuation with air mass. It gives no threshold, no edge, and no dependence on the *direction* you look — whereas the observed twilight sky is bright in the west and dark in the east by an amount that tracks a single angle. And extinction cannot produce the latitude thresholds of the previous section, because the air mass along the path is a function of the Sun's altitude, and the whole point of that section is that the Sun's altitude at midnight is fixed by φ and δ in a way no atmospheric effect can touch.

Experiment 1f · dawn and twilight

Time first light against the clock, twice a year, from your own doorstep

This one costs nothing and needs no instrument beyond a phone and a clear horizon. Pick a spot with an open view east, go out well before sunrise on a clear morning near an equinox, and write down the clock time at which you can first make out the horizon line and the time the Sun's upper edge appears. Then do it again within a few days of the June solstice from the same spot. The interval is civil dawn, and the calculator below predicts both lengths from your latitude and the date alone, with no fitting and no free parameter. If you are north of about 48.6°, the more dramatic version is available to you: on the June nights the sky never goes properly dark at all, and the almanac will print a dash where the end of astronomical twilight should be.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **date**, and therefore the Sun's declination. Two dates two months apart are enough at mid-latitudes; equinox against solstice is the sharpest pair. Changing your **latitude** instead works just as well if you are travelling.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the **number of minutes** between first light and sunrise. A clock and your own eyes. No angles, no instruments, no trust in anyone else's data.

**Hold constant:** the site, the direction you face, and the criterion you use for "first light" — pick one and stick to it, because the criterion is worth several minutes and the effect you are after is tens of minutes. Clear sky both times; cloud on one morning and not the other ruins the comparison.
**Kit:** a phone. If you want the version with a number in it rather than a judgement call, point the phone's camera east on a tripod, shoot at fixed exposure every thirty seconds, and read the frame brightness afterwards — the curve is the twilight curve and its knee is unmistakable.
**The tell:** at 45° north the interval grows by roughly a quarter between March and June; at the equator it barely moves at all; north of 48.6° astronomical night vanishes outright in June. A flat Sun that dims by distance has no mechanism that makes the fade take longer in one month than another at the same place.

**Civil** 43 min · **Nautical** 61 min · **Astronomical** never ends
Total sunset → −18°: **never ends**. Sun's altitude at local midnight: **−17.70°**.
Astronomical night vanishes above latitude 48.6° · nautical above 54.6° · civil above 60.6°.

**Verdict rule.** At 48.86° with the Sun at 23.44°, the globe says there is **no astronomical night at all** on this date, because the Sun bottoms out at −17.70° and never reaches −18°. Look up the almanac for these coordinates: it should print a dash. If it prints a time — if the sky does go fully dark here on this date — the geometry on this tab is wrong and you should say so.

## How high the shadow stands — and why it climbs faster than the Sun sinks [evidence: prediction]

The table above gives the shadow's ceiling *over your head*, in kilometres. What you actually look at in the east is an angle, and the two are not the same number. Getting from one to the other takes no new physics, only the same formula applied twice. A patch of air lying angular distance ψ from you *towards* the antisolar point has the Sun that much further below its own horizon, at depression θ + ψ, so it is lit only if it clears its own ceiling: R(sec(θ + ψ) − 1). Follow a line of sight leaving your eye at altitude *a*, ask where along it that condition is first met, and the trigonometry collapses to one line.

> **Sunlit at distance s along a sight line at altitude a, when the Sun is θ below the horizon:** s · sin(a − θ) > R (1 − cos θ). **Two consequences arrive with no free parameter whatever.** First, if a ≤ θ the left-hand side is never positive, however far you look — so **the top of the shadow always stands higher than the antisolar point**, at every depression, above any atmosphere, on any sphere. It cannot be at or below it. Second, the whole sky goes shadowed once the ceiling rises past the layer that does the scattering, that is at cos θ_z = 1 / (1 + H/R) — which is the ceiling formula read backwards.

Only one quantity there has to be supplied from outside: H, the effective top of the scattering layer, which is not a sharp surface — air density falls off smoothly, so the shadow's edge is a gradient rather than a line. Rather than pick a value, the table prints three and lets you see how little the interesting behaviour depends on the choice. What does not depend on it at all is the shape: the shadow rises *faster* than the Sun sinks, the ratio grows without bound, and the sky is fully shadowed at a depression of a very few degrees.

**Altitude of the top of the dark segment in the east, computed from s · sin(a − θ) = R(1 − cos θ) with R = 6,371 km — three values of the scattering-layer top H, none of them fitted to anything**

| Sun's depression θ | H = 10 km | H = 15 km | H = 20 km | Rise ratio at H = 15 km |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0.5° | **0.55°** | **0.54°** | **0.53°** | × 1.07 |
| 1.0° | **1.23°** | **1.17°** | **1.14°** | × 1.17 |
| 1.5° | **2.16°** | **1.96°** | **1.87°** | × 1.31 |
| 2.0° | **3.65°** | **3.03°** | **2.79°** | × 1.52 |
| 2.5° | **6.88°** | **4.68°** | **4.03°** | × 1.87 |
| 3.0° | **23.25°** | **7.80°** | **5.91°** | × 2.60 |
| 3.5° | *whole sky* | **17.27°** | **9.34°** | × 4.93 |
| 4.0° | *whole sky* | *whole sky* | **18.32°** | — |

*Figure caption:* Depression at which the shadow reaches the zenith and the dark segment covers the sky: H = 10 km → **θ_z = 3.21°** · H = 15 km → **θ_z = 3.93°** · H = 20 km → **θ_z = 4.53°**. Note what that means for an observer: the **angle** is the same everywhere on Earth, in every season — but the **clock time** it takes to get there is not, and runs from about thirteen minutes near the equator to three quarters of an hour at high latitude in spring.

Experiment 1f-b · time the Earth's own shadow

Turn your back on the sunset and photograph the east — a phone, a wall to rest it on, twenty minutes

Ten minutes after sunset there is a dark blue-grey band along the eastern horizon with a pink one above it: the planet's own shadow, cast on its own air, with the Belt of Venus along its top edge.[6] Rest a phone on a wall, frame the eastern horizon with something vertical of known height in shot — a lamp post, a door frame, a distant mast — and shoot one fixed-exposure frame every minute from sunset until the band has climbed out of frame. Afterwards, convert the band's top edge into an angle using the object of known height and its distance. You will have the shadow's altitude against the clock, and the clock converts to the Sun's depression.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **time since sunset**, and therefore the Sun's depression θ, which an almanac gives you for your position to the minute.[1] Nothing else moves. If you can repeat it from a very different latitude, or six months later, do — that is where the sharper version lives.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the **altitude of the shadow's upper edge**, in degrees, frame by frame. One angle per photograph, read off against a foreground object whose height and distance you know.

**Hold constant:** the camera position, the focal length and the exposure — an automatic exposure will chase the fading sky and move the very edge you are trying to follow. Pick one criterion for the top edge, the colour boundary rather than the brightness one, and keep it. Face the antisolar azimuth, not simply east: ten minutes after sunset the two differ by several degrees.
**Kit:** a phone, a wall, and a foreground object. If you want the angle without trigonometry, hold a ruler at arm's length — a centimetre at 57 cm subtends one degree, near enough for a two-degree effect.
**The tells, stated in advance:** the shadow's top is **never below the antisolar point**, at any moment, which the derivation above gives with no adjustable quantity; it **accelerates**, the ratio in the last column growing from about 1.1 to beyond 5 within twenty minutes; and the sky is fully shadowed at a **depression of three to four and a half degrees** — the same angle in Quito and in Reykjavík, though one takes a quarter of the time the other does.

**What this experiment cannot do, said plainly.** It does not measure R. The single free quantity H is degenerate with the radius here — a bigger planet with a shallower atmosphere gives a similar curve — so anyone claiming a radius from a sunset photograph is claiming too much, and this page will not. Nor is the top edge sharp: air thins gradually, so two careful observers will disagree by something like half a degree, which is a few kilometres of H. What the experiment does settle is *shape*, and shape is what the two models disagree about.
**The verdict rule, symmetric.** The sphere fails if the shadow's top is ever measured at or below the antisolar point, if it climbs at a constant ratio rather than an accelerating one, or if the depression at which it reaches the zenith turns out to depend on where you stand or on the season. The flat model fails if a boundary it must explain as distance and haze instead behaves as a shadow does: an arc curved about the antisolar point, rising at an accelerating angular rate, closing over the sky at one fixed solar depression that is the same for every observer on the planet while the clock time is not.

Caveats this page owes you. Four, and the first is the one that matters. The heights in the first table are the *geometric* ceiling of the shadow; they are not a brightness model. Real twilight brightness involves multiple scattering, ozone absorption in the Chappuis band and aerosol loading, and the classical treatments are Hulburt's and Rozenberg's, not a one-line formula.[3][4][5] Second, the durations here use the mean Sun and a spherical Earth, with sunrise at the conventional −0°50′; published almanacs will differ from them by a minute or two, and a mountain horizon by rather more. Third, the measured 10^8 day-to-night ratio is downwelling irradiance at one dark rural site, and the same study measures a factor of 100 between that site and a city — the number is a scale, not a constant. Fourth, the anti-twilight figure is a schematic, and its colours are drawn rather than computed. None of the four moves an argument that turns on eight orders of magnitude against fewer than two, and on a stage length that goes to infinity at a latitude you can point to on a map.

The through-line. The dip tab measures how far the horizon falls below level; this tab measures how far the *shadow* rises above it, which is the same geometry read upwards instead of downwards, and it arrives at the same R. Then the duration section drops R entirely and constrains the shape on its own, the way the magnetism tab does. And the inverse-square section is the page's method in miniature: take the flat model's own physics, divide out its free parameters until nothing adjustable is left, and see what it is then obliged to predict. Here it is obliged to predict that the night is seventy times darker than the day. Go outside and see whether it is.

Ask for twilight rather than sunrise, and ask for a latitude above 48.6° in June to see the dashes.

It is also the source of the honest qualification quoted above, that roughly 3% of the total is in astronomical twilight and would call it night.
12. [12] [EarthSky, *99% of the world's population in sunlight July 8 … and other dates*](https://earthsky.org/earth/99-percent-worlds-population-receive-sunlight/) — the follow-up showing that the effect is not a one-day curiosity: the share stays above 98% for roughly two months around the June solstice, and the daily maximum falls between 11:00 and 11:03 UTC on almost every one of the top thirty days.

# Point at the Sun. You are pointing at a place on Earth.

> Tab "Azimuth" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-azim. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Azimuth · the bearing that forgets how far away the Sun is*

*Figure caption:* **The two angles of a direction.** From where you stand, a body in the sky has an altitude h above your horizontal plane and an azimuth A, counted clockwise from north. This tab tests the azimuth alone, and the azimuth does not depend on how far away the body is. Angles drawn arbitrary.

Every other solar panel on this page argues from a *time* — sunrise, the length of twilight, where a shadow falls. This one argues from a **direction**, which is cheaper to measure: a stick, its shadow, and a way of finding true north. The claim tested is not that the Sun is far or near, large or small. It is that the bearing you turn to when you face the Sun is the bearing of a particular *place* — the place with the Sun straight overhead at that instant — whatever the Sun's distance turns out to be.

> **The result the whole tab rests on.** The azimuth of any celestial body, measured from true north, is exactly the initial great-circle bearing to its **sub-body point**: the point on Earth that has the body at the zenith. Not approximately, and with no dependence whatever on how far away the body is. Two lines of proof: the sub-body point, the Earth's centre and the body are collinear, by the definition of the sub-body point. The observer's vertical also passes through the centre. So the vertical plane that contains the observer and the body contains the centre, therefore contains the whole line centre-to-body, therefore contains the sub-body point. Same vertical plane, same azimuth.

Two consequences are worth stating before anything is drawn, because both of them close doors that would otherwise be argued through. **First, the distance cancels completely.** This is the kind of quantity rule 5 of this page's own method asks for: the Sun at 150 million kilometres and the Moon at 384,000 obey the same rule, and so would a lamp at 5,000 km. Arguing about the Sun's distance cannot touch the azimuth.

**Second, parallax moves a body along the vertical circle**, toward the zenith — it changes the altitude and not the bearing. That is the objection an informed reader will make about the Moon, whose parallax reaches a whole degree, so it is answered here and not in a footnote; the numbers are further down.

## Three formulas, no free parameters [evidence: prediction]

$$\phi_{\text{sub}} = \delta \qquad \lambda_{\text{sub}} = \alpha - \text{GMST}$$

The sub-body point, from an almanac and a clock. Its latitude is the body's declination; its longitude is the right ascension minus Greenwich mean sidereal time, which is the same statement as −GHA. The USNO publishes GHA and declination for the Sun, the Moon and the navigational stars for any instant you ask for[2], so this line needs nothing from this page. Both quantities here are *geocentric*, and that matters for the Moon: the theorem points at the geocentric sub-point, which is why parallax leaves the bearing alone.

$$A = \text{atan2}\left( \sin\Delta\lambda \cos\phi_2 ,\ \cos\phi_1 \sin\phi_2 - \sin\phi_1 \cos\phi_2 \cos\Delta\lambda \right)$$

The sphere's prediction: the initial great-circle bearing from the observer (φ₁, λ₁) to the sub-body point (φ₂, λ₂). Standard spherical trigonometry, the same formula the distances tab uses, with nothing adjustable in it. Feed it a place, an instant and an almanac and it returns one number.

$$\rho = 90^\circ - \phi \qquad \theta = \lambda \qquad \text{north} = \text{toward the centre}$$

The flat model's prediction, and it needs the map to be *named* before it can have one at all. “The flat Earth” has no azimuths; a projection does. The one used here is the north-polar azimuthal equidistant map[6] — the standard flat-Earth map, the one Gleason patented in 1892[5], and the same map the distances and seismology tabs already run the flat model on. A point sits at radius 90° − φ from the centre at polar angle λ, and an observer's local north is the direction of the map's centre. That is a complete model: given a place and a sub-solar point it returns a bearing, with no height, no lamp size and no fitted constant anywhere in it.

A different projection would give different bearings, and that has to be stated, or the tab would be testing a straw man. What it does not buy is an escape, and the reason is the thesis of the whole page rather than of this tab: a projection that repaired the bearings would have to break the distances, which the distances tab measures, or the shadow zone, which the seismology tab measures. The claim is never “no flat map gets this right”; it is that no single flat map gets two of these right at once.

## One instant, seven observatories, two predictions [evidence: prediction]

The seven places below are Global Seismographic Network stations. Their coordinates are already published[4] and this page already uses them in the seismology tab — no new list, and no place picked to flatter an answer. Three instants are offered, all fixed in advance, and nothing here is adjustable; the play button is there to show there is no favourable moment, not to find one. Every row in the table can be checked without trusting this page, against the USNO's altitude and azimuth table[1] or NOAA's solar calculator[8].

### Where the seven places and the three instants come from

The three instants are two round solstice-week times and the moment of greatest eclipse on 12 August 2026, published to a tenth of a second[3]. At every one of them the sphere's bearing is the bearing to the sub-solar point exactly, and the flat map's is whatever its geometry forces. The play button runs the clock on from whichever instant you picked, for the same reason the magnetism tab has a latitude slider. Every frame satisfies the theorem on the sphere, and every frame leaves the flat map's lines missing each other. The **Moon** button does the whole thing again for the Moon, which is the interesting case.

- **instant** 21 Dec 2026, 12:00:00 UTC documented, and not adjustable
- **Sun overhead at** 23.44° S 0.48° W geocentric sub-solar point
- **stations that can see it** 4 of 7 hollow dots cannot, and carry no ray
- **flat-map error triangle** 37,174 km on its longest side KONO, PMSA, SBA — vertices off the map
- **KONO** 189.3° flat 193.7°
- **SUR** 290.1° flat 292.0°
- **PMSA** 76.3° flat 44.2°
- **SBA** 191.9° flat 354.9°

*Figure caption:* **The globe from the side, rays drawn.** The rays are parallel because they are computed from the body's real distance, not drawn that way. A side view shows only the near face, so a station round the limb is missing here; the strip above and the map beside carry all seven.

### Parallel to within how much

*Figure caption:* Every ray and sight line in this panel is computed from the body's real distance — about 23,000 Earth radii for the Sun, 60 for the Moon. Across the whole planet the Sun's sight lines close on each other by at most about 18″ (0.005°), far below one pixel. The Moon's close by up to about 2°, and at the tips you can see them converge. Switch bodies and watch: that visible difference is the distance, drawn to scale.

*Figure caption:* **The same instant on the flat map.** North-polar azimuthal equidistant, north pole at the centre, in the orientation flat maps are always printed in. Each half-line uses this map's own definition of north — the direction of its centre — at a bearing anyone can check against the USNO. On a correct map they would all run into the body. Press play: the disagreement moves, it does not resolve.

The picture carries the whole theorem. Rays arriving from the body are parallel, and orthographic projection preserves parallelism exactly — so they are parallel on your screen for the same reason they are parallel in space, not because they were drawn that way. Follow them in. At exactly one point the ray runs straight down the radius, and the dashed line continues it through the centre: ray, sub-point and centre are one line.

Nobody looks along a curve, and nobody is being asked to. Each coloured arc is where a station's vertical plane meets the ground; the dotted line leaving that station is the look direction inside the same plane. Every dotted line is parallel to every other, because there is one body and one direction in space. What changes from station to station is the local horizon that direction is measured against, and that alone is why one Sun hands every observer a different bearing.

**Bearing to the Sun at the selected instant: what the sphere predicts, what the flat map predicts**

| Station | Sun's altitude | Globe | Flat map | Disagreement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **KONO** Kongsberg, Norway | 6.5° | 189.30° | 193.72° | **+4.42°** |
| **HRV** Harvard, Massachusetts | -2.8° — below the horizon | 119.66° | 84.30° | **−35.36°** |
| **ANMO** Albuquerque, New Mexico | -25.8° — below the horizon | 101.62° | 51.65° | **−49.97°** |
| **CTAO** Charters Towers, Australia | -35.7° — below the horizon | 218.31° | 343.11° | **+124.80°** |
| **SUR** Sutherland, South Africa | 69.2° | 290.10° | 292.05° | **+1.95°** |
| **PMSA** Palmer Station, Antarctica | 32.3° | 76.33° | 44.25° | **−32.08°** |
| **SBA** Scott Base, Antarctica | 11.6° | 191.94° | 354.86° | **+162.92°** |

Read the last column rather than the first four. In the far north the two models very nearly agree — the flat map is least wrong near its own centre, which is exactly where its makers live and exactly where the objection “it works fine” comes from. Go south and the disagreement does not merely grow: it **changes sign**, and then passes 90°, and at the December instant a station on the Ross Ice Shelf is told to look almost due north for a Sun that is almost due south. That is not a three-per-cent discrepancy anyone can wave at refraction. It is the difference between turning left and turning right.

## The eclipse: a published bearing, and nobody's word for it [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the published eclipse bearing comes from an ephemeris that places the observer on the ellipsoid.]

Everything above is this page computing its own answers, which is worth exactly as much as your trust in this page. So here is one row this page did not compute. For the total solar eclipse of 12 August 2026, Fred Espenak publishes the instant of greatest eclipse, the place on Earth it happens, and the Sun's altitude and azimuth there — computed independently, from the JPL DE405 ephemeris[3]. The table below sets that published azimuth beside this page's own, and beside the great-circle bearing to the sub-solar point, which is the quantity the theorem says must equal it.

**Greatest eclipse, 12 August 2026, 17:45:53.3 UT1, at 65° 13.4′ N 25° 13.7′ W**

| Quantity | Published | This page | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sun's declination | +14.8013° | +14.8024° | 4.2″ |
| Moon's declination | +15.6162° | +15.6154° | 3.0″ |
| Sun's altitude there | 25.8° | 25.763° | 0.037° |
| **Sun's azimuth there** | **248.4°** | **248.366°** | **0.034°** |
| Bearing to the sub-solar point | — not published | 248.366° | 0.0000° from the azimuth above |
| Sun's and Moon's sub-points | — not published | 99 km apart | which is what an eclipse is |
| ΔT used | 72.4 s | 75.5 s | 3.1 s — under 1″ of Sun |

The agreement is not the interesting part — two correct calculations of the same sphere ought to agree. The interesting part is the third row: the bearing to the sub-solar point comes out equal to the azimuth to every decimal the page prints, which is the theorem being obeyed rather than assumed.

And the eclipse itself is the theorem at its most literal. An eclipse is the moment the Sun's sub-point and the Moon's sub-point nearly coincide; at greatest eclipse these two places are under a hundred kilometres apart on a planet forty thousand kilometres around, which is why one small patch of Iceland has the Moon exactly in front of the Sun. Two bodies, one at 384,000 km and one at 150 million, produce the same bearing from the same spot because their sub-points are in the same place. *Distance does not enter.*

The next total eclipse visible from Europe, on 2 August 2027, has a tab of its own: [Eclipses](/ai/ecl.md) computes its path, its local times and durations from NASA's Besselian elements, and asks a flat model to do the same.

One honest note on the arithmetic: this page's own ΔT model gives 75.5 s where the eclipse prediction uses 72.4 s, a three-second disagreement about the Earth's rotation rate that moves the Sun by well under an arcsecond and the Moon by under two.

## The Moon, and why being close does not rescue anything

The Moon is the one body where a reader can reasonably expect the distance to matter, because its parallax is not a rounding error: seen from the surface rather than from the centre of the Earth, the Moon shifts by up to a degree — twice its own diameter. The shift is **radial**, along the line from the zenith through the body, so it takes the Moon down the vertical circle it is already on. Altitude changes. Bearing does not. The table puts numbers on both, at the same instant and at the same seven stations.

**The Moon at the selected instant: what parallax does to the altitude, and what it does to the bearing**

| Station | Altitude shift | Bearing shift | Bearing to sub-lunar point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **KONO** Kongsberg, Norway | -1.000° = -60.0′ | −8.2″ | 44.552° |
| **HRV** Harvard, Massachusetts — Moon below the horizon | -0.947° = -56.8′ | +7.1″ | 330.011° |
| **ANMO** Albuquerque, New Mexico — Moon below the horizon | -0.996° = -59.8′ | +15.2″ | 302.800° |
| **CTAO** Charters Towers, Australia | -0.706° = -42.3′ | −1.6″ | 351.390° |
| **SUR** Sutherland, South Africa — Moon below the horizon | -0.803° = -48.2′ | +4.8″ | 82.829° |
| **PMSA** Palmer Station, Antarctica — Moon below the horizon | -0.684° = -41.1′ | −7.0″ | 212.131° |
| **SBA** Scott Base, Antarctica — Moon below the horizon | -0.972° = -58.3′ | −2.2″ | 334.718° |

The bearing shifts are arcseconds against a degree of altitude shift, and this page owes you an account of why they are not exactly zero. On a sphere they would be. They are not zero here because the topocentric correction used for the Moon is the standard one[9], which places the observer on an *ellipsoid*: the local vertical of a geodetic latitude does not quite pass through the centre, missing it by up to about 11.5′ of latitude, and the theorem's one hypothesis fails by exactly that much.

So the residue in the third column is the Earth's flattening, not the Moon's proximity — which is a strange thing to have to admit on a page that elsewhere declares the ellipsoid out of scope, and it is admitted rather than rounded away.

## Parallax as a ruler [evidence: prediction]

Up to here parallax has been set aside: it is radial, so it slides the Moon along the vertical circle it is already on, so the bearing does not care and this tab may set it aside. All of that is true, and it throws away the best thing in the section. The altitude that parallax shifts is the oldest measurement of the Moon's distance there is. So the same two observations yield two independent results, and they are not in competition: the bearing is the quantity the distance **vanishes from**, and the difference in altitude is the quantity that is **nothing but** the distance.

> **What parallax measures, and what it does not.** Two observers a known distance apart see the Moon in front of different stars. The angle between their two sight lines gives the Moon's distance **in Earth radii**, and in nothing else. Turning that into kilometres needs R, and R does not come from the sky: it comes from the surveying, distances and horizon-dip tabs, and from every other radius measurement on this page. This is the thesis of the whole page applied to a single body — the measurement constrains *d/R*, never *d* on its own.

$$\sin \pi = \frac{R}{d} \qquad \frac{d}{R} = \frac{1}{\sin \pi}$$

The classical form. π is the *horizontal parallax*: the angle the Earth's radius subtends as seen from the body, which is the same thing as how far the body shifts between being seen overhead and being seen on the horizon. It is published for the Moon every day[2]. One published number, and the distance in Earth radii follows with no other input whatever. The symbol is the astronomer's, not the circle constant: here π is the name of an angle — about 57′ (0.95°) for the Moon — so sin π ≈ 0.0166, and d ≈ 60 R.

$$\frac{d}{R} = \frac{b}{R \sin \theta}$$

The two-observer form, which is the one you could actually carry out. *b* is the part of the line joining the two observers that lies *across* the direction of the Moon, and θ is the angle between their two sight lines — which is exactly how far the Moon appears to move against the background stars between the two places. Nothing else enters it: no horizon, no height above sea level, no clock beyond agreeing on the instant.

**Measuring the Moon's distance from two of the stations above, at the selected instant**

| Quantity | At this instant | Where the number comes from |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The pair | KONO ↔ CTAO | the two stations that can both see the Moon and whose sight lines open widest — chosen by that rule, not by hand |
| Distance between them | 14,445 km along the surface | great circle, from the published station coordinates |
| Baseline across the line of sight | 1.683 R | the part of the straight line between them lying across the direction of the Moon: *b* in the formula |
| Shift of the Moon against the stars | 101.6′ = 1.693° | θ: computed here, measured by nobody — the angle between the two sight lines |
| **Distance reconstructed** | **56.98 Earth radii** | **b / (R sin θ), and nothing else whatever** |
| From the horizontal parallax alone | 57.13 R | 1 / sin π, with π = 60.2′: one published number, the classical form |
| This page's ephemeris, for comparison | 364,379 km = 57.19 R | Meeus — what the two reconstructions are checked against, not what they are derived from |
| The same measurement on the Sun | 17.5″ across 17,828 km | the widest opening the Sun gives anywhere on this planet: the negative witness |

Two things in that table are better said out loud than left for a careful reader to catch. **The two reconstructions do not agree exactly**, and they are not meant to. Part of the gap is fixed and exactly known: horizontal parallax is defined against the Earth's *equatorial* radius of 6,378.14 km, while the row below it is quoted in mean radii of 6,371 km, so those two lines differ by that ratio — 0.112 per cent — before anything else has happened.

The rest of the gap moves with the geometry, and it is the flattening again, exactly as in the bearing column further up: it is smallest when the two stations lie squarely across the line of sight, and largest when the baseline is badly foreshortened or the Moon is low in one of the two skies. On a sphere both parts would be zero. Watch it change as the clock runs, because a page that had quietly fitted something would not let you.

**And the same measurement fails on the Sun**, which is why the last row is there. Across the whole width of the planet the Sun shifts by some sixteen arcseconds — under a hundredth of the Moon's shift, and far below anything the equipment this experiment asks for could see. That failure is what shows the method is not manufacturing its answer: an instrument that returned a distance for everything you pointed it at would be measuring itself.

**The flat model given its best chance: a lamp at a fixed height above the disc, and the altitudes it would require**

| Station | Lamp 3,000 km up | 5,000 km up | 8,000 km up | The Moon, really |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **KONO** Kongsberg, Norway | 16.9° | 26.8° | 38.9° | 1.7° |
| **HRV** Harvard, Massachusetts | 13.8° | 22.3° | 33.2° | -18.8° — set |
| **ANMO** Albuquerque, New Mexico | 14.8° | 23.8° | 35.2° | -5.2° — set |
| **CTAO** Charters Towers, Australia | 31.1° | 45.1° | 58.1° | 45.1° |
| **SUR** Sutherland, South Africa | 9.3° | 15.2° | 23.6° | -36.9° — set |
| **PMSA** Palmer Station, Antarctica | 7.1° | 11.7° | 18.3° | -46.7° — set |
| **SBA** Scott Base, Antarctica | 13.4° | 21.7° | 32.5° | -13.7° — set |

The lamp's height is the flat model's one free parameter here, and rule 2 of this page's method says to spend it in the flat model's favour rather than to caricature it — so the table sweeps it instead of picking one. Choose whichever column comes closest at one station and it is wrong at the next; there is no height, inside that range or outside it, that produces the last column.

Then notice what happens at the places where the Moon has set. A lamp hanging over a plane is above the horizon from *everywhere* on that plane, always, at every height — its altitude is the arctangent of a positive number and cannot be anything else. The Moon is below the horizon at several of these places at the same moment. That is not a disagreement of a few degrees to be haggled over: it is a change of sign, and no choice of height touches it.

## Who did this before you

None of this is a modern measurement, and pretending otherwise would sell it short. Hipparchus, in the second century BC, got the Moon's distance out of a solar eclipse that was total at the Hellespont and about four fifths covered at Alexandria — two places, one instant, one angle. The figure usually reconstructed for him is around 67 Earth radii, with a spread of roughly 62 to 73[10], and the eclipse is most probably the one astronomers label −189, which is 190 BC[11]. Those are reconstructions from later summaries and they differ between scholars, so a range is the only honest form to give them in.

Ptolemy, three centuries after that, measured the parallax *directly*, with an instrument built for the purpose, in Book V of the *Almagest*[12] — a different geometry from the eclipse method, and the two are routinely run together by people retelling the story. His lunar model was also badly wrong about how much the distance varies, implying a swing from about 34 to 64 Earth radii[10] where the truth is about 56 to 64: a useful reminder that having the right order of magnitude is not the same as being right.

And in 1751 the thing was finally done properly. Lacaille observed the Moon from the Cape of Good Hope while Lalande, nineteen years old and sent in his teacher's place, observed it from Berlin on very nearly the same meridian[13]: two people ten thousand kilometres apart, agreeing on a minute. What the young Lalande then argued about with that teacher, in front of a commission of the Paris Academy, was how much to allow for the Earth not being a perfect sphere — which is the same correction that puts the tenth of a per cent into the table above.

## What could spoil your measurement

**Magnetic north is not north.** This is the one that will ruin the experiment if it is not taken seriously, because the error is the same size as the effect: the declination runs to 10–20° across western Europe and much more elsewhere, and it drifts. Either correct it with the official model[7] or, better, avoid the compass entirely — at true solar noon the shadow of a vertical stick is at its shortest and lies exactly along the north–south line, so one observation removes magnetic declination from the problem altogether.

**The clock matters more than it looks.** The sub-solar point travels 15° of longitude per hour; an hour of error is an hour of wrong answer, and everything on this tab is stated in UTC for that reason.

**Refraction is almost innocent here**, and that is not luck: like parallax, atmospheric refraction lifts a body along its vertical circle, so in a spherically stratified atmosphere it changes the altitude by up to 34′ near the horizon and the azimuth by nothing at all. Only a horizontally structured atmosphere bends a bearing, and by arcminutes.

**And the projection is a choice**, restated once more because it is the honest weak point: the numbers in the flat column are the azimuthal equidistant map's numbers, not a proof about every conceivable flat map.

Experiment 9 · where is the Sun for you?

A stick, its shadow, and one agreed minute — with a friend far away, if you can

Stand a stick vertically on level ground. At an agreed UTC minute, mark the shadow. The Sun's azimuth is the shadow's direction plus 180°. Measure that angle from **true** north — see above for why the compass will not do — with a printed protractor and a piece of string, or by taking a second mark at local solar noon to establish the north–south line first.

Independent variable
**What you change:** your **place**. The sharp version needs two observers far apart in latitude, ideally one in each hemisphere, at the same UTC minute; the weaker but still decisive version is one observer and the published bearing for their own coordinates.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the Sun's **azimuth** in degrees from true north. One angle. Not a duration, not a brightness, not a horizon.

At **21 Dec 2026, 12:00:00 UTC**, the widest disagreement among these stations is at **Scott Base, Antarctica**: the Sun is **191.9°** from true north, and the flat map says **354.9°** — a gap of **162.9°**. The narrowest is **Sutherland, South Africa**, where the gap is only **2.0°**, which a protractor and a string will not resolve.

**Verdict rule.** At SBA the two models do not differ in size but in **direction**: one sends you 163° round the horizon from the other. Measure the bearing to ±5° and one of them is finished. If it agrees with the flat map, the globe prediction is refuted; if it agrees with the great-circle bearing to the published sub-point, no choice of lamp height rescues the disc, because the disc's bearing has no lamp height in it.

Experiment 9b · the Moon against the stars

One photograph each, two places, one agreed second — and the sky is the ruler

Agree an instant, to the second, with someone far away from you in latitude. At that instant each of you photographs the Moon with a star close beside it in the same frame. Then measure how far the Moon sits from that star, in arcminutes, in each photograph, and take the difference. That difference is the parallax. You are deliberately *not* measuring a height above a horizon: an angle inside a single frame needs no level, no horizon and no calibration, and refraction lifts the Moon and the star beside it by almost the same amount, so most of it cancels instead of having to be modelled.

Independent variable
**What you change:** your **place**, at a fixed instant. Two observers as far apart in latitude as you can arrange; a few thousand kilometres is already plenty. Without a second observer, the published topocentric position for your own coordinates does the same job rather less convincingly.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the Moon's **angular distance from a nearby star**, in arcminutes. One angle inside one photograph. Not an altitude, not a time, not a horizon.

At **21 Dec 2026, 12:00:00 UTC**, **Kongsberg, Norway** and **Charters Towers, Australia** lie 14,445 km apart and both have the Moon above the horizon. Between those two viewpoints the Moon stands **101.6′** apart against the background stars — 3.1 times its own diameter, so a single photograph from each place settles it. That one angle gives **56.98 Earth radii**, against 57.19 from this page's ephemeris, and it needed no distance, no horizon and no clock beyond the agreed instant. The same two sight lines to the **Sun** open by only 17.5″, which is why this experiment does not work on the Sun.

**Verdict rule.** The globe fails if your measured shift does not put d/R within your own uncertainty of the almanac's, or if the answer changes when you turn the baseline. The flat model fails on the table above: the kindest of the three lamp heights at this instant is 3,000 km, and even that one misses some station's altitude by **53.8°** — and at 5 of these 7 places the Moon is below the horizon right now, where a lamp hung over a plane is above it from everywhere, at every height.

**See also**[Sun](/ai/sun.md)[Twilight](/ai/twi.md)[Magnetism](/ai/mag.md)[Cel. nav.](/ai/cnav.md)[Distances](/ai/dist.md)[Surveying](/ai/surv.md)[Observation](/ai/obs.md)

# An eclipse is an appointment published years in advance

> Tab "Eclipses" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-ecl. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Eclipses · predicted to the second, on a sphere*

The total solar eclipse of **2 August 2027** is already on the calendar. Totality touches down over the Atlantic at sunrise, crosses southern Spain, Gibraltar and northern Morocco, runs the length of North Africa, and is longest — **6 min 23.2 s** — near Luxor at **10:00:21 UT**, with the Sun 81° high.[1][2] The path table gives the edges of the shadow every two minutes, to a tenth of an arcminute, together with the Sun's altitude, its azimuth and how long totality lasts on the centre line.[1] None of it is observed yet. All of it is computed.

> **The objection this tab answers.** “Eclipses are predicted from the saros cycle, a pattern the Babylonians found in tables — nobody needs a globe to predict them.” The saros is real and this tab shows it: after 223 lunations, 18 years 11 days and about 8 hours, the Sun, the Moon and the Moon's node line up again almost exactly.[3] But a repeating pattern says *when* a similar eclipse comes back. It does not say *where* its shadow falls, at what time it reaches a given town, how high the Sun stands there or how long totality lasts — and the saros itself puts the next member of the series a third of the world further west[4], which is a statement about a turning planet.

Those numbers come from the **Besselian elements**: six short polynomials in time that describe the Moon's shadow on a *fundamental plane through the centre of the Earth*, perpendicular to the shadow's axis.[2][5] To turn them into a time and a place, the method needs the observer's position *as seen from the Earth's centre* — the quantities ρ sin φ′ and ρ cos φ′ of a point on an ellipsoid of 6,378 km equatorial radius and 1/298 flattening. There is no version of the calculation without that ellipsoid. This tab recomputes the published centre line of 2027 from the published elements and lands on it to the thousandth of a degree; that check runs every time the page's tests do.

$$H = \mu + \lambda$$
$$\xi = \rho\cos\varphi\prime\sin H,\quad \eta = \rho\sin\varphi\prime\cos d - \rho\cos\varphi\prime\cos H\sin d,\quad \zeta = \rho\sin\varphi\prime\sin d + \rho\cos\varphi\prime\cos H\cos d$$
$$\text{total} \iff \sqrt{(x-\xi)^2 + (y-\eta)^2} < |l_2 - \zeta\tan f_2|$$

x, y, d, μ, l_1, l_2: NASA's six polynomials in time (tan f_1, tan f_2: two constants) · λ: the observer's longitude, east positive · ρ sin φ′, ρ cos φ′: the observer's position on the ellipsoid, seen from the Earth's centre · ξ, η, ζ: the observer projected onto the fundamental plane · partial when the distance is below l_1 − ζ tan f_1; each contact is an instant when the distance equals one of the two radii

*Figure caption:* **What the Besselian elements describe.** The Moon's shadow — the wide penumbra and the narrow umbra — crosses a plane through the *centre* of the Earth, perpendicular to the shadow's axis. x and y place the axis on that plane, l₁ and l₂ are the radii of the two shadows there, and six polynomials in time give all of them[2]. To know whether one place is in the shadow, the method projects that place onto the plane — ξ, η, and its height ζ above it — from its position on the ellipsoid[5]. Schematic, not to scale.

## Why an eclipse does not happen every month

Every month the Moon passes between the Earth and the Sun. If its orbit lay in the Earth's plane, every new moon would be a solar eclipse and every full moon a lunar one. It is tilted by **5.145°**[6], so most months the shadow passes above or below the Earth. The tilted orbit crosses the Earth's plane at two **nodes**; an eclipse needs a new or full moon close to one — in Meeus's test, |sin F| under 0.36, F being the Moon's distance along its orbit from the ascending node[7]. The node line points at the Sun only twice a year: the two **eclipse seasons**. It also turns backwards once in 18.6 years[6], so the seasons come about 19 days earlier each year.

- Sun–node-line angle **22°**off season: the shadow passes above or belownext: lunar eclipse 22 Janclick: pause · drag: turn

*Figure caption:* **2027, day by day, not to scale.** Sun, Earth and the Moon's tilted orbit, with the node line in amber; sizes and distances squeezed to fit, the Moon's tilt drawn three times too steep — the stamp says so. The dates, phases, distance from the node and the node's backward turn come from Meeus's mean elements[6]; the verdict at each new and full moon is Meeus's test with the true 5.145°[7]. In the strip below (rings: new moons, dots: full moons, coloured: eclipses) it finds the annular eclipse of 6 February and the total of 2 August, and the lunar eclipses of 20 February, 18 July and 17 August — all in NASA's catalogue[10]. It also flags 22 January (|sin F| = 0.34, just inside the limit), where NASA lists none: a mean-element model may err at the edge, which is why the local circumstances further down are computed properly.

$$|\sin F| < 0.36 \text{ at new or full moon} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{eclipse possible}$$
$$F = 93.272^\circ + 483\,202.0175^\circ\,T,\qquad \Omega = 125.045^\circ - 1934.136^\circ\,T$$

F: the Moon's angle along its orbit from the ascending node · Ω: the longitude of that node, which turns backwards once in 18.6 years · T: Julian centuries from 1 January 2000 · Meeus's mean elements and test

## The saros: why eclipses repeat, and why somewhere else

Three of the Moon's rhythms happen to fall into step. A new moon comes back every synodic month; the Moon returns to the same node every draconic month; it returns to its closest point to the Earth every anomalistic month. Wait 223 synodic months and the other two have almost exactly caught up:[3]

| Cycle | Length | vs 223 lunations |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 223 synodic months (new moon → new moon) | 6,585.3223 d | — |
| 242 draconic months (node → node) | 6,585.3575 d | +0.8 h |
| 239 anomalistic months (perigee → perigee) | 6,585.5375 d | +5.2 h |

After one **saros** — 18 years, 11 days and **7 h 43 min** — Sun, Moon and node line up again at nearly the same distance, and an eclipse of nearly the same kind comes back. That is about orbits, and it gives the *date* whatever shape the ground has. It does not put the shadow in the same place: in those extra 7 h 43 min the Earth turns about 116°, so the next eclipse of the series lands that much further west. NASA rounds it to “~120° westward”[3]; the series catalogue gives **about 111°** from one member to the next[4]. The eclipse of 2 August 2027 is member 38 of 71 of saros 136; the previous one crossed India and China on 22 July 2009[8], the next will cross the United States on 12 August 2045[9].

- 22 Jul 2009 · 24.2° 144.1° E · shift -110.7°2 Aug 2027 · 25.5° 33.2° E · shift -110.9°12 Aug 2045 · 25.9° 78.5° W · shift -111.7°

*Figure caption:* **Three members of one series, as published.** Each band is NASA's path of totality[1][8][9]; the grey dots are the points of greatest eclipse of all 71 members of saros 136, pale for the oldest[4]. The camera follows the point of greatest eclipse from one member to the next, and that westward turn — about 111° — is the extra 7 h 43 min of rotation. The page computes nothing here; it only turns a globe. Three saroses later (an *exeligmos*, 54 years 34 days) the extra time is 23 h 09 min, nearly a whole turn, and the series comes back close to where it was: 5.6° E on 30 June 1973, 33.2° E on 2 August 2027, 53.6° E on 3 September 2081[4].

$$223 \times 29.530589\ \text{d} = 6585.32\ \text{d} \approx 242 \times 27.212221\ \text{d} \approx 239 \times 27.554550\ \text{d}$$
$$0.3213\ \text{d} \times 360^\circ \approx 116^\circ \text{ westward}$$

synodic, draconic and anomalistic months · 0.3213 d: the 7 h 43 min left over beyond whole days, during which the Earth turns under the Sun at 15° per hour

> **What the saros settles, and what it cannot.** A flat-earth reading can use the saros too: it is a calendar of the Sun and the Moon, and the date comes out the same on any ground. It cannot use the shift. A cycle that leaves every eclipse a third of the way round the world further west, by the amount of rotation the extra hours imply, is the calendar of a spinning body — and to draw the band itself, town by town, one needs the Besselian elements and the ellipsoid of the first section. The next sections compute that band and ask a flat model to draw the same one.

## Where and when: the eclipse at any place [evidence: prediction]

Pick a place and the page computes what it will see on 2 August 2027: when the Moon first bites the Sun, when totality begins and ends, how long it lasts, how deep the partial phase gets and where the Sun stands. It does it the way the published predictions are made — from NASA's Besselian elements[2] with Meeus's method[5], the observer placed on the ellipsoid by ρ sin φ′ and ρ cos φ′. The first line under the controls is not a claim: it is the same calculation run, as the page loads, on every point of NASA's published centre line[1], and it reports how far from the published time, duration, altitude and azimuth it lands.

- Checked now, against NASA's centre line (101 points):time of maximum ≤ **0.2 s**duration ≤ **0.18 s**Sun's altitude ≤ **0.49°**azimuth ≤ **0.51°**limits of totality, computed (dashed on the map) ≤ **1.6 km**the table gives altitude and azimuth to the whole degree

| --- | --- |
| second contact (totality begins) | 08:45:05 |
| maximum | 08:47:24 · magnitude 1.025 |
| third contact (totality ends) | 08:49:44 |
| fourth contact (partial ends) | 10:00:41 |
| duration of totality | **4 min 38.8 s** |

- Second route, the site's own Sun and Moon:maximum **08:47:24** (+0 s)totality with the Moon's size seen from the Earth's centre **226 s**…seen from this place **278 s** (Besselian 279 s)

*Figure caption:* **Two routes, both on a globe.** The table comes from the published Besselian elements. The last line redoes the same place with nothing from NASA: the site's own Sun and Moon[6], seen from that exact place, and the moment their centres come closest. The two agree on the time of maximum to a few seconds. The duration agrees only once the Moon is drawn at its size *from that place*: near the zenith the observer is some 6,000 km closer to it than the Earth's centre, the Moon looks about 1.6 % larger, and at Luxor that is worth over a minute of totality. The remaining few seconds are this simpler Moon's own error. On a plane there is no centre of the Earth to be closer to.

## The same shadow on a flat Earth, given every advantage

A flat model gets the best terms this page can offer. Its map is the usual azimuthal equidistant one, North Pole at the centre. Its Sun and Moon are local lamps, each hanging over the *real* point beneath the real Sun and Moon at every minute, from the same ephemeris as the globe[6]. The Moon at height H☾ is lit by the Sun at height H☉, and its shadow falls along the line from the lamp through the Moon. Only the ratio of the two heights moves that shadow, so it is tuned by least squares to follow NASA's published centre line as closely as possible[1]; the Sun's height is then tuned, separately, to the Sun's published altitudes along the path. Two free parameters, each set in the flat model's favour.

- published shadow (NASA)flat shadow, best fit: **8,393 km** awaySun over the published shadow: published **8°** · flat lamp **30°**f = 36.1 · H☉ 6,080 km · H☾ 5,911 km

*Figure caption:* **The flat model's own map, 08:26 to 11:46 UT.** Teal: NASA's path of totality, carried over onto this map as it falls, with the published position of the shadow's centre[1]. Amber: the flat model's shadow, on the best-fitting heights, with its lamp and the Moon's point beneath. The band as drawn here is stretched and bent — that is this map's distortion, not the shadow's; the published path is a smooth arc on the globe.

$$P = S + f\,(M - S),\qquad f = \frac{H_{\text{☉}}}{H_{\text{☉}} - H_{\text{Moon}}}$$
$$f \text{ chosen to minimise } \sum_t |P(t) - C(t)|^2$$

S, M: the points beneath the Sun and Moon lamps on the flat map · H_☉, H_Moon: their heights · P: where the line from the Sun lamp through the Moon meets the ground · C(t): NASA's published centre line · only the ratio of the heights moves P, so it is fitted, in the flat model's favour

The result, computed on this page: the best-fitting flat shadow stays on average **3,950 km** from the published centre line, **8,400 km** at worst. It moves the wrong way — ten degrees of longitude *westward*, following its lamp, while the published shadow sweeps over a hundred degrees *eastward*, from the Atlantic at sunrise to the Indian Ocean at sunset. Tuned to the published altitudes, its Sun is off by only about 6° on average, but at the two ends, where NASA's Sun is rising and setting, the flat lamp stands 28° and 24° high. And given the published width of the shadow for free, at its own speed totality would last 376 to 880 seconds along the path, against the published 255 to 383.

## The Earth's own shadow: eclipses of the Moon

The oldest argument on this page is an eclipse of the Moon. Aristotle, fourth century BC: “in eclipses the outline is always curved: and, since it is the interposition of the earth that makes the eclipse, the form of this line will be caused by the form of the earth's surface, which is therefore spherical.”[11] It can be sharpened. The Earth's shadow on the Moon is an arc of the *same* circle whether the Moon is rising, high or setting — a disc casts a round shadow only when lit square on, and a straight-edged one when lit along its edge. And its size is not free: from the published sizes and distances of the Sun, the Earth and the Moon, the page computes the Earth's shadow at the Moon's distance as about 2.7 times the Moon's radius, the value the photographs show.

$$r_{\text{shadow}} = 1.02\left[R_{\text{⊕}} - d_{\text{Moon}}\,\frac{R_{\text{☉}} - R_{\text{⊕}}}{d_{\text{☉}}}\right]$$

R_⊕, R_☉: radii of the Earth and the Sun · d_Moon, d_☉: distances of the Moon and the Sun · the Earth's shadow is a cone that narrows as it recedes; at the Moon it is about 2.7 Moon radii · 1.02: the customary enlargement for the atmosphere

*Figure caption:* **One circle, three moments, and what a disc would give.** The partial phase of a lunar eclipse seen at moonrise, at its highest and at moonset: the dark edge is an arc of the same circle each time, only turned with respect to the horizon. The last panel is the shadow of a disc lit along its edge. Schematic; the shadow's radius is computed from the Sun's, Earth's and Moon's radii and distances, with the customary 2 % enlargement for the Earth's atmosphere.

A flat model has no Earth to put between the Sun and the Moon: both hang above the disc. Flat-earth writers who address lunar eclipses invoke another, unseen body; none gives its size, its distance or its path, so none says when the next eclipse will come or who will see it. The published calendar does. The three lunar eclipses of 2027 are all penumbral — the Moon only grazes the Earth's outer shadow — and the next total ones visible from Europe fall on **31 December 2028**, **26 June 2029** and **20 December 2029**[10]. Each was computed decades ago, from the same kind of elements as the solar eclipse above.

## The Sun setting while the eclipsed Moon rises, and the shadow on the “wrong side” [evidence: prediction]

> **The objection.** “In an eclipse of the Moon the Earth stands between the Sun and the Moon. Yet the eclipsed Moon has been seen above the horizon while the Sun was still up on the other side. With the Earth in between, that is impossible — so it is not the Earth's shadow.” And its more common form: “On photographs of the eclipsed Moon the dark part is often on top, while the Sun that casts the shadow is below the horizon. The Earth's shadow would come from below.”

The “impossible” eclipse has a name, the **selenelion** or horizontal eclipse, and it is old news: Cleomedes reported it nearly two thousand years ago and put it down to the air.[12] It has been photographed, at sunrise over Minneapolis on 8 October 2014 for one.[13] On a globe it is a matter of a few arcminutes. Standing on the line between day and night, you are on the edge of the Earth as seen from the Sun: your horizon plane points straight at the Sun on one side and straight down the Earth's shadow on the other. The Sun and the centre of the shadow are both on your horizon, 180° apart. Three things move them by less than a degree. The Moon, 60 Earth radii away, seen from the surface instead of the centre, sits about 1° lower: its parallax π. Inside the shadow, 0.7° in radius, it may sit above or below the centre: δ. And a body is in sight as soon as its upper edge is, half a disc, s, above its centre. The air then lifts both edges by about half a degree each: ρ.

- **16:25 UT** · Moon, total eclipse
- Brest, Sun, upper edge: **+53′** (without air +28′)
- Brest, Moon, upper edge: **+3′** (without air −31′)
- **both in the sky, the Moon in the Earth's shadow**
- Adelaide: Moon **+26°**, Sun **-28°**
- Earth's shadow on the Moon, zenith up: Brest **from below**, Adelaide **from above**
- its angle from celestial north, the same for both: **154°** · **154°**

*Figure caption:* **One instant, two places.** Top: the Sun's rays, the Earth, its shadow and the Moon at one true scale, in the plane through the Sun, the Earth's centre and the first observer (white dot, on the line between day and night); Adelaide, which is not in that plane, is projected onto it (blue dot), with its line of sight to the Moon (blue dots); the box enlarges the Moon's surroundings uniformly, by the factor printed. Dashed: the observer's horizon plane; orange: the lowest ray that still reaches the eye through the standard atmosphere. Bottom: the eclipsed Moon at the same instant from two places, zenith up: on the left the place of the selenelion, the Moon on its sea horizon (1° bar); on the right Adelaide, a wider field so that its horizon is in the picture (10° bar), the Moon high in a night sky and shown again in a box enlarged uniformly to the scale of the left view (factor printed). The red arrow points from the Moon's centre to the centre of the Earth's shadow, the side the shadow comes from; the disc at the bottom right is the shadow as each place sees it, with the Moon's path during the animation. In each small yellow frame, the Sun for that place at that instant, looking towards it, horizon across the middle, at its own uniform scale (bar): above the horizon at the selenelion, far below it at Adelaide. Filled discs: with standard refraction, each point of the edge lifted by its own amount; dashed outlines: the same discs without air. The Moon's colouring is the Earth's umbra and penumbra, computed. Sea-level observers. Click to pause.

$$(h_{\text{☉}} + s_{\text{☉}} + \rho_{\text{☉}}) + (h_{\text{☾}} + s_{\text{☾}} + \rho_{\text{☾}}) = -\pi + \delta + s_{\text{☉}} + s_{\text{☾}} + \rho_{\text{☉}} + \rho_{\text{☾}}$$

the heights of the two upper edges above a sea horizon, added at the moment they are equal · h: height of each centre · π: the Moon's parallax in height, about 58′ · δ: how far the Moon, seen from the Earth's centre, stands above the shadow's axis · s: half-diameters, about 16′ each · ρ: refraction at the horizon, about 29′ each · the two can be seen together only if the sum is above zero; from a height, add twice the dip of the horizon

Computed on this page for **Brest** (48.39° N, 4.49° W) on **31 December 2028**: the Moon is totally eclipsed from 16:16 to 17:28 UT — NASA lists 1 h 11 min of totality[10] — and from a sea horizon the setting Sun and the rising, totally eclipsed Moon are both above it from **16:25 to 16:33 UT**, the Sun in the south-west at azimuth 234°, the Moon in the north-east at 54°. Without air, the same two edges would each miss the horizon by 2′: at sea level this selenelion needs the atmosphere, but only just. An eye 1.2 m above a sea horizon gains 2′ of dip on each side and would see both without any air. Refraction is the margin, not the explanation; the explanation is that the horizon of someone standing on the edge of a ball points at both. For Minneapolis on 8 October 2014, with the Moon partly eclipsed and high in the shadow, the page finds both above the horizon from 12:20 to 12:29 UT, possible even without air: the morning of the photograph.[13] Near the horizon refraction changes from one evening to the next by several arcminutes, with the temperature of the air near the ground, so the ends of each window are uncertain by a minute or two; a hill on the horizon shuts it.

**The shadow on the “wrong side”.** The second form of the objection is not about the selenelion: it is about which way is up. Seen from the Moon, the centre of the Earth's shadow lies in one direction among the stars, the same for everyone at a given instant. “Up” is each observer's zenith, and it turns from one place to the next. The figure shows one instant from two places 16,600 km apart. At Brest the Moon is on the horizon and the shadow comes from below. At **Adelaide** (34.93° S, 138.60° E) the same Moon is 26° high in the north-north-west, the Sun 27° below the opposite horizon, and the shadow comes from above: south of the equator the Moon is seen upside down compared with Brest. Measured from the celestial north instead of the zenith, the two directions agree to within 0.4°, and that small difference is the parallax between the two places. In the Minneapolis case Adelaide sees it from above as well, the Moon 37° high, to within 0.2°. A dark part on top while the Sun is below the horizon is what a ball predicts wherever the Moon is high and the observer's zenith lies on the shadow's side of the Moon.

> **The globe is sunk** if, on 31 December 2028, from a sea horizon at Brest, the Moon that appears in the north-east around 16:25 UT is not totally eclipsed; or if, anywhere and at any eclipse, the Sun and the eclipsed Moon are seen together with their upper edges adding up to more than **2°** above a sea horizon. Parallax, the shadow's size and the two half-discs allow at most about half a degree, standard refraction about one more, and the 2° leaves room for unusual air. It is also sunk if two observers, photographing the same eclipse at the same minute, find the shadow's centre at directions from the celestial north that differ by more than 5°: the parallax between any two places moves it by less than half a degree in both cases on this page.

> **A flat model** has both bodies above the plane at all times, so a selenelion costs it nothing — and explains nothing: with no Earth between them it has no shadow, no reason for the Moon to darken only when it stands opposite the Sun, and no time for the Brest window. A flat model that names its shadow-casting body, with a size, a height and a path, is welcome to state its own Brest time before the day.

## What would refute each model, stated before 2 August 2027 [evidence: prediction]

> **The globe is sunk** if, at **Tarifa** (36.013° N, 5.605° W, at the shore), totality does not begin within 15 s of **08:45:05 UT** or does not last **4 min 39 s** to within 10 s, with the Sun 38° high in the east; if **Luxor** sees totality at any time other than **10:02–10:08 UT**, lasting 6 min 20 s to within 10 s; or if **Marseille** sees totality at all — the globe gives it a partial eclipse, magnitude 0.77, deepest at 09:02:56 UT. These are the figures of the “Where and when” section, computed on this page from NASA's elements[2], which reproduce NASA's own centre line to within a second. The tolerances cover what the predictions leave out: the Moon's mountains and valleys at its edge, which move the contacts by a few seconds[2].

> **The flat model above is sunk** — on the heights that suit it best — if Tarifa sees a total eclipse at all: its shadow never comes closer than about 4,300 km. And it is sunk if Luxor's totality comes near 10:05 UT: its shadow passes 80 km from Luxor at about **06:09 UT**, four hours earlier, under a lamp that would then be high in Luxor's morning sky. A different flat model is welcome to state its own Tarifa and Luxor numbers before the day; this page will run it through the same test.
