# Grasse fires a laser at the Moon, and the Earth's radius comes back

> Tab "Moon" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-moon. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*The Moon as a ruler · lasers, parallax and shadow*

Seventy kilometres from Marseille, on the Calern plateau, a telescope fires laser pulses at a reflector left on the Moon by Apollo 15 and times their return to a fraction of a nanosecond. Over a night the time of flight changes by tens of milliseconds, and most of that change is the observatory itself being carried around the Earth's axis. The size of that circle is the Earth's radius.

## Laser ranges from Grasse: the radius from times of flight [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the Moon's direction (declination, hour angle) comes from a lunar theory, and the station's geocentric latitude uses the ellipsoid's flattening.]

**Each point is a time of flight, about 2.5 s there and back,** and the archive gives 55 passes of six hours or more from Grasse between 2015 and 2025[1][2]. The distance from the Earth's centre to the reflector changes smoothly over a night. The distance from the observatory does not: it carries the observatory's own circle around the axis. For a trial radius R, subtract the observatory's part and see how smooth what is left is. One value makes it smooth to a metre.

$$\rho = \tfrac12\,c\,\tau,\qquad \rho^2 = D^2 - 2DR\cos Z + R^2$$
$$\cos Z = \sin\psi\sin\delta + \cos\psi\cos\delta\cos H,\qquad {R:\ D(t)\ \text{smoothest}}$$

τ is the measured time of flight, ρ the distance from the observatory to the reflector, D the distance from the Earth's centre, Z the angle between the observatory's direction from the centre and the Moon's. ψ is the observatory's geocentric latitude, δ and H the Moon's declination and hour angle, from a lunar theory[3]: that is where a model enters, so this section is a check. For each pass, R is the value that makes D(t) closest to a cubic.

- 55 passes, GrasseR = 6,365.8 km (quartiles 6,364.5–6,368.0)station at rest: 10.0 km off

*Figure caption:* Top: for the first pass in the archive, how smooth the Moon's distance from the centre comes out for each trial radius (residual from a cubic, log scale). Bottom: the radius from each of the passes. The geocentric radius of the observatory on the reference ellipsoid, 6,369.3 km, is drawn for comparison.

> **The flat model, at its best.** On a plane the observatory does not move, so the range is the distance from a fixed point to a Moon that may follow any smooth path: set R = 0 and let the cubic do everything. The residual is then 10.0 km in the median pass, against 0.55 m with the observatory carried on a circle of radius R. **What would vindicate it:** passes whose ranges are as smooth with R = 0 as with any other value.

**Limits.** The radius found is the distance from the Earth's centre to the observatory, 6,365.8 km in the median, 3.4 km below the reference ellipsoid's value there, and the quartiles span 3.5 km. The Moon's direction comes from an abridged lunar theory good to about 10″; its errors and the observatory's latitude are the main source of the spread.

## The Moon's parallax, Kepler and a pendulum [evidence: prediction]

**A measurement to make with a camera.** Through a night the Moon shifts against the stars by up to a degree more than its orbit alone would carry it, because the observer is carried around the axis: the horizontal parallax π, about 57′, the angle the Earth's radius subtends from the Moon. Kepler's third law with g = GM/R² then gives R itself, with no distance on the ground.

$$\sin\pi = \frac{R}{D},\qquad n^2 D^3 = gR^2\left(1+\frac{m}{M}\right)$$
$${R = \frac{g\,\sin^3\pi\,(1+m/M)}{n^2}}$$

g is measured with a pendulum, n = 2π / (27.32 days) is the Moon's motion against the stars, m/M ≈ 1/81 the Moon-to-Earth mass ratio. With π = 57.04′ and g = 9.80 m/s², R ≈ 6,395 km. An error of 1 % in π is 3 % in R.

Experiment · the Moon against the stars

Photograph the Moon among the same stars at moonrise, transit and moonset

A camera on a tripod, a fixed focal length, the same stars in every frame.

**You measure** the Moon's position among catalogue stars at three times

**You get** its parallax π, then R from g and the month

Separate the parallax from the orbital motion with a second night, or by fitting the motion as a straight line across the night.

Prediction: π between 54′ and 61′ depending on the Moon's distance that week.

R = **6,399 km**

1 % on π moves R by 3 %: 6,209–6,593 km for ±1 %

## The Earth's shadow on the Moon (Aristarchus) [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the distances of the Moon and the Sun in km come from an ephemeris (DE440), and the catalogue kept only the timings whose layer height, computed from the Earth's radius, lies between −50 and +250 km.]

**During a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow crosses the Moon, and its edge is an arc of a circle about 2.6 Moon-widths across.** A crater timing is the instant that edge crosses a crater. It is the same for every observer, wherever they stand, so one timing puts one point on the edge of the shadow. Observers with small telescopes timed 22,539 of them at 94 eclipses between 1842 and 2011[4][5]. We reduced the 12,729 that mark the middle of a crater or a contact with the Moon's limb ourselves: the instant at the Moon, the crater placed on the Moon by its selenographic latitude and longitude[6] and the Moon's orientation[8], the shadow's axis from the Sun through the Earth's centre[7]. σ, the shadow's angular radius, is the angle between the two seen from the Earth's centre. Our reduction agrees with the catalogue authors' own, timing by timing (correlation 0.96).

$${\sigma + s_\odot = \pi_M + \pi_\odot}$$
$${R_s = \frac{\sigma + s_\odot}{1/D_M + 1/D_\odot}}$$

σ is the shadow's angular radius at the Moon, measured at each eclipse (41′ to 46′ as the Moon's distance changes), s☉ the Sun's angular radius, π = R/D the parallaxes, D☾ and D☉ the distances of that instant[7]. Aristarchus' relation holds for a ball without air; R_s is then the radius of whatever casts the edge of the umbra: **6,473 ± 1 km** over the 69 eclipses with 20 timings or more, 2.3 % more than an airless Earth would give. The Earth plus the lowest, opaque layer of its air, about 100 km thick[4].

*Figure caption:* The radius of the body that casts the umbra's edge, from the median σ of each eclipse with 20 timings or more, 1842-2011. Every eclipse lands above the Earth's mean radius: the shadow is cast by the Earth and the bottom of its air, and how thick that bottom is changes from one eclipse to the next.

**Limits, and where the radius enters.** A visual timing is good to 25 or 30 seconds, a few tenths of a percent of σ, and the enlargement changes from one eclipse to the next with the air along the Earth's edge. Julius Schmidt's clocks of 1842-1879 were corrected by the catalogue's compilers against modern ephemerides[5]. The catalogue kept only the timings whose layer height, which its authors computed from the Earth's radius, lies between −50 and +250 km: a selection that touched the radius, and the distances come from an ephemeris. That makes this radius a check, not a measurement. The parallax experiment of the previous section has not been done yet and stays a prediction.

## The shadow is round from every side: 12,700 timings [evidence: measurement]

**Aristotle's argument, with numbers.** The Earth's shadow on the Moon is always an arc of a circle; only a ball casts a round shadow whichever way it is lit[9]. Divide each timing's σ by the median σ of its own eclipse: no radius and no distance enter, only angles. The latitude β on the shadow says which side of the Earth cast that piece of the edge: ±90° the polar regions, 0° the equator. A round shadow gives 1 at every β.

$${\frac{\sigma(\beta)}{\sigma_0} \approx 1 - f_s \sin^2\beta}$$
$${\frac{\sigma(\beta)}{\sigma_0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\cos^2\beta + \sin^2\beta / \sin^2\delta_\odot}}}$$

Top line, a ball: f_s is the flattening of its shadow, fitted to the 12,729 timings: **0.0029 ± 0.0002**, against 0.0034 for the Earth's own shape. Bottom line, a flat disc with the Earth's axis as its normal: lit from the Sun's direction, its shadow is an ellipse whose height is sin δ☉ of its width, δ☉ the Sun's declination at the eclipse, between −23.4° and +23.4°.

*Figure caption:* Every timing's σ divided by its eclipse's median, against the latitude on the shadow. Top, the whole scale: the timings, counted in cells of 2° by 0.5 %, form one thin band at 1; the dashed curves are the best flat disc's shadow for the Sun at 3°, 12° and 23° of declination. Bottom, the band magnified a hundred times: ten-degree averages with two standard errors, the fitted flattening and the Earth's.

> **The flat model, at its best.** A flat Earth that casts a shadow on the Moon at all already borrows the globe's geometry; give it that, with the Earth's axis as the disc's normal and the best radius at each eclipse. The timings then scatter 27 % around the best disc's ellipse, in the median eclipse, against 0.67 % around a circle. Only a disc turned to face the Sun at every eclipse, whatever the season, would cast a round shadow every time, and a body whose shadow is round from every direction is a ball. **What would vindicate it:** a shadow whose radius changes with β the way a disc's does, or a shadow stretched along the equator.

**Limits.** The latitudes on the shadow are not evenly covered: the craters are on the near side, and the Moon crosses the shadow north or south of its centre depending on the eclipse. One eclipse's own flattening is uncertain by a few thousandths; it is the 12,729 timings together that fix it. The fitted flattening is a little below the Earth's: the air that enlarges the shadow is not the same over the poles and over the equator. Timings more than three standard deviations from the rest of their eclipse are set aside, the site's usual rule.

**See also**[Eclipses](/ai/ecl.md)[Azimuth](/ai/azim.md)[Gravity](/ai/grav.md)[Rotation](/ai/rot.md)

# Two equal segments — until you flatten the Earth

> Tab "Distances" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-dist. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Map ≠ territory · the azimuthal equidistant trap*

*Figure caption:* **The same two points, three geometries.** Schematics of the algebra, not scale drawings: no distance in them is to scale, and none is used for any number on this page.

Take a diagonal segment in the northern hemisphere — one that cuts across parallels and meridians — and its exact mirror image across the equator. On the globe the two are *identical in length* by symmetry. Now flatten the Earth, keep the coordinates, and measure with a ruler: the mirror twins stop agreeing, and how they disagree depends on which flat map you chose. Two pairs are shown, in different directions and regions.

Globe: great‑circle arc
$$(\lambda,\ \varphi)$$
Polar map (AE): straight chord on the disk

One pair of endpoints, three rulers — each model measured *its own way*: the sphere's shortest path on the globe, and honest straight ruler lines on both flat maps. Only the globe's answer matches odometers, flight times, and surveyed distances; the polar disk is the azimuthal equidistant *projection* of the globe, centred on the north pole.

## The three rulers, written out [evidence: prediction]

Each model is asked the same question — how far apart are these two coordinate pairs? — and each answers in its own geometry. These are the three formulas the page actually evaluates for the table above, with nothing hidden inside a function name.

$$\cos\sigma = \sin\varphi_1\sin\varphi_2 + \cos\varphi_1\cos\varphi_2\cos\Delta\lambda$$
$${d_{\text{globe}} = R\,\sigma}$$

The spherical law of cosines, the oldest formula on this page.[1] σ is the angle the two points subtend at the Earth's centre, so the distance is nothing but R times an angle. The code evaluates the equivalent dot product of two unit vectors. For legs of a few kilometres the arccosine is ill-conditioned and the haversine form is the right one to use;[4] at the thousands of kilometres compared here it makes no visible difference.

$$x = R\lambda,\quad y = R\varphi$$
$${d_{\text{cart}} = R\sqrt{\Delta\varphi^2 + \Delta\lambda^2}}$$

The plate carrée, or equidistant cylindrical projection: latitude and longitude read straight off as y and x.[3] Pythagoras then prices every degree of longitude at its equatorial length wherever you happen to be, inflating the answer by roughly 1/cos φ. It stays symmetric across the equator, which is exactly why this map hides the asymmetry while still disagreeing with every odometer.

$$r = R\left(\pi/2 - \varphi\right),\quad \theta = \lambda$$
$${d_{\text{AE}} = \sqrt{r_1^2 + r_2^2 - 2r_1r_2\cos\Delta\lambda}}$$

The azimuthal equidistant projection centred on the north pole, with a straight ruler line laid across it.[3] This is the flat-earth disk, and the record is explicit: the Boston Public Library catalogues Gleason's 1892 original as the globe flattened into a circular plane, and his own patent claim is filed on a projection.[5] Distances on it are true along the radii — any line through the pole — and along nothing else.

## Why the mirror test works, and where the disk's error comes from [evidence: prediction]

$$\text{globe: }\cos\sigma(-\varphi_1, -\varphi_2, \Delta\lambda) = \cos\sigma(\varphi_1, \varphi_2, \Delta\lambda)$$
$$\text{disk: }r(-\varphi) = R(\pi/2 + \varphi) \neq r(\varphi)$$

This is the whole tab in two lines. Flip both latitudes and the spherical formula is unchanged: sin(−φ) appears twice so the two minus signs cancel, and cos(−φ) = cos φ. Mirror-image segments are therefore exactly equal on a globe — not approximately, exactly, and for every value of R. The disk's radius is simply not an even function of latitude, so its answer has to change. No choice of disk size, scale or centring repairs that, because the disagreement is about shape, not size.

$$\text{along a parallel} \quad\text{globe: } d = R\cos\varphi\,\Delta\lambda$$
$$\text{disk: } d = R(\pi/2 - \varphi)\,\Delta\lambda$$
$${\text{ratio} = \frac{\pi/2 - \varphi}{\cos\varphi}}$$

Take the simplest leg there is, due east along a parallel, and both models close into elementary form. R divides out of the ratio, which makes this a radius-free test like the magnetism tab: it constrains the shape alone, whatever the size. The ratio equals 1 only at the pole and rises without bound going south — 1.11 at 45° N, 1.57 at the equator, 3.33 at 45° S, 17.1 at 80° S.

*Figure caption:* **The stretch factor, plotted.** The curve is the ratio above; the teal line at ×1 is what vehicles actually log. The disk never reads short, and never reads true except at the pole. At ±45° the two halves of a mirror pair differ by a factor of three, which is the discrepancy the experiment below asks you to go and settle.

> **One honesty note about that last pair.** A leg flown due east along a parallel is a rhumb line, not the shortest path: between 45° N 0° and 45° N 60° E the parallel measures 4,718 km and the great circle 4,605 km, 2.4% shorter. That approximation is real, and it is not what is being tested — both models are asked for the same parallel-following leg, so the ratio between them is unaffected. The table at the top of this tab avoids the issue entirely by giving the globe its true great-circle answer and the flat maps their own straight ruler lines, and it reaches the same verdict.

## Two legs the globe calls equal — and each flat map breaks a different one [evidence: prediction]

The mirror pairs above leave the cartesian map a way out: its grid is symmetric across the equator, so it keeps mirror twins equal and only inflates them both. This pair closes that door. Two legs, each exactly 60° of arc, chosen so the sphere makes them identical to the kilometre. Neither flat map can hold them equal, and — this is the part worth sitting with — they fail in opposite directions.

$$\text{polar leg: } 60^\circ\text{N } 0^\circ \to 60^\circ\text{N } 180^\circ$$
$$\text{equator leg: } 0^\circ\ 30^\circ\text{W} \to 0^\circ\ 30^\circ\text{E}$$
$${\sigma = 60^\circ \text{ for both} \implies d = 6,672\,\text{km}}$$

Both equalities are exact, not fitted. For the polar leg, cos σ = sin²60° + cos²60°·cos 180° = 0.75 − 0.25 = 0.5, so σ = 60°: the great circle runs straight over the pole, 30° down each side. For the equator leg cos σ = cos 60° directly. Same central angle, therefore the same distance, and R does not need to be known for the two to be equal — only for the 6,672 km. Any route planner returns both numbers.[2]

*Figure caption:* **The same pair under three rulers.** Panel A shows each leg on the great circle that carries it, seen face-on: two identical 60° arcs, which is the whole point — the sphere has no way to distinguish them. Panels B and C are drawn to scale within themselves, so the lengths you see are the lengths each model claims; there is no exaggeration factor anywhere in this figure, and none is needed.

**Equal on the globe by construction; each flat map preserves one leg exactly and breaks the other**

| Segment (endpoints) | Globe great‑circle | Flat cartesian ruler | Flat polar (AE) ruler |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| polar 60°N 0° → 60°N 180° | 6,672 km | 20,015 km (+200%) | 6,672 km (0%) |
| equator 0° 30°W → 0° 30°E | 6,672 km | 6,672 km (0%) | 10,007 km (+50%) |

> **Verdict rule, stated in advance.** Go and measure both legs — flight time × ground speed, a GPS track, or published great-circle tables. If they come out equal, the sphere survives and both flat maps are refuted, each by a different leg. If the polar leg really is three times the equator leg, the cartesian map survives and the sphere is refuted. If the equator leg really is one and a half times the polar one, the polar disk survives instead. The three models make three different predictions here, so this single measurement can eliminate at least two of them — and note that no flat map can be rescued by rescaling, since each is already exactly right on one of the two legs.

## See it in 3D · click & drag to orbit [evidence: prediction]

*Figure caption:* **Globe.** Pair A (blue / orange) and pair B (teal / violet): each southern segment is the mirror of its northern twin, so within each pair the great‑circle lengths are **exactly equal**. The arcs look curved because on a sphere the shortest path *is* an arc.

*Figure caption:* **Polar map (the flat‑earth disk).** The same endpoints plotted at r = 90°−φ, θ = λ, joined by *straight ruler lines* — how anyone measures a flat map. Each southern segment comes out far longer than its identical northern mirror, and the two pairs are distorted by different amounts.

**Same endpoints, three rulers — flat maps measured with straight lines, as a ruler would**

| Segment (endpoints) | Globe great‑circle | Flat cartesian ruler | Flat polar (AE) ruler |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A·N 50°N 40°W → 30°N 10°E | 4 692 km | 5 988 km (+28%) | 5 113 km (+9%) |
| A·S 50°S 40°W → 30°S 10°E | 4 692 km | 5 988 km (+28%) | 12 383 km (+164%) |
| B·N 10°N 60°E → 35°N 100°E | 4 909 km | 5 245 km (+7%) | 5 761 km (+17%) |
| B·S 10°S 60°E → 35°S 100°E | 4 909 km | 5 245 km (+7%) | 8 947 km (+82%) |
| C·N 33°N 71°W → 34°N 151°E | 11 369 km | 15 345 km (+35%) | 11 731 km (+3%) |
| C·S 33°S 71°W → 34°S 151°E | 11 369 km | 15 345 km (+35%) | 25 641 km (+126%) |

Experiment 3 · distances

The same east–west trip, north and south

Pick an east–west leg spanning a fixed number of degrees of longitude, and measure how long it really is. Then do the mirror-image leg in the other hemisphere. Book the flights, or read the published great-circle distances and flight times.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **latitude** of the leg — try +45°, then −45°. You choose which parallel to travel along.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the **ground distance actually covered** — odometer, GPS track, or flight time × cruising speed.

IV latitude 45° , span Δλ = 60°
DV globe: this leg 4 718 km · mirror leg 4 718 km → **equal**
DV flat disc: this leg 5 240 km · mirror leg 15 720 km → ratio 3.00×

**Verdict rule:** if the two mirror legs measure the same, the globe survives. If the southern one is really 3.0× the northern one, the disc survives. Airlines settle this daily: Sydney–Santiago is about 11,400 km and is flown non-stop in roughly 12½ hours, which no aircraft could do if it were the ~25,000 km the disc requires.

> **The confusion, named.** The flat‑earth disk (the “Gleason map”) is the azimuthal equidistant projection of the globe. It preserves distances *only along straight lines through the pole*; every east–west distance is stretched by (90°−φ)/cos φ — a factor of 1.11 at 45° N but **3.33 at 45° S**. Treating that projection as the territory forces the southern hemisphere to be three times wider than it measures. Real ships and aircraft cross it anyway: Sydney–Santiago is ~11,400 km and is flown non‑stop in ~12½ hours; on the disk it would be ~25,000 km, longer than any airliner's range.

Why the cartesian ruler also fails. Reading latitude/longitude as x‑y coordinates (a plate‑carrée grid) at least keeps north and south symmetric — but it prices every east–west degree at its equatorial length, inflating both segments by 1/cos φ (+41% at 45°). It hides the asymmetry while still disagreeing with every odometer. Coordinates are *addresses on a sphere*, not distances; the only ruler that returns what vehicles actually log is R·cos φ·Δλ — spherical geometry.

The through‑line. This is the third appearance of the same R: it curves the sightlines in the Simulator, sets k = 1/R in Celestial navigation, and here converts coordinate differences into the distances the world actually measures. One sphere explains all three; each flat model must fail at least one.

**See also**[Cel. nav.](/ai/cnav.md)[Surveying](/ai/surv.md)[GPS](/ai/gps.md)[Seismology](/ai/seis.md)[Azimuth](/ai/azim.md)

# A spirit level does not find a plane — and a gravimeter in a lift measures the radius of the Earth

> Tab "Gravity" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-grav. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Gravity and level · what a bubble is really finding*

*Figure caption:* **Where "down" points, in each model.** On the globe every vertical is a radius, so no two are parallel. On an infinite slab — the flat model at its strongest for this measurement — every vertical is perpendicular and every bubble is centred. Directions are exact; the bobs' heights are schematic.

“Water always finds its level” is the oldest argument there is, and it is *true*. It is also empty until someone says what **level** means. Level is not a geometrical idea: it is whatever a plumb line and a bubble say it is, and both of them are instruments that measure **gravity**.[1] So the question is not whether water is level — it is — but what shape a surface has when it is everywhere perpendicular to the local vertical. That is a question with an answer you can measure, in three separate ways, without ever looking at the horizon.

> **What both models agree on, stated first.** Still water sits perpendicular to gravity. A bubble level shows no slope on it. A plumb line hangs at right angles to it. None of that is in dispute here, and nothing on this page contradicts it. The disagreement is about three measurable consequences: whether the local vertical points the *same way* in two places, whether gravity gets *weaker* as you climb, and whether it has the *same strength* at every latitude. A flat world and a round one give different answers to all three, and the instruments are cheap.

## 01 · Down is a direction, and it is not the same direction twice [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: meridian arcs published after reduction on the spheroid.]

Hang a plumb bob in Marseille and another in Lille and ask the only question that matters: are the two strings **parallel**? On a plane they must be — “down” is one fixed direction for the whole world, so every vertical is a copy of every other. On a sphere they cannot be: each one points at the centre, so two of them separated by **d** along the ground make an angle **d/R** between them, which is 1° for every 111.2 km you travel. Both statements are testable, because the direction of a plumb line can be compared with the stars, and that comparison is exactly what *astronomic latitude* is.

$${\frac{d}{R}}$$
$$1^\circ$$
$${0.000^\circ}$$

This is Eratosthenes' measurement stated in modern words. He compared two shadows, which is the same as comparing two verticals against the same distant light. Every ship's noon sight, every star transit recorded by a zenith telescope, and every levelling network re-measures it.

*Figure caption:* Globe. Six plumb lines, six bubble levels, each perpendicular to its own radius. Directions are exact; the observers' heights are schematic.

*Figure caption:* Flat, at its strongest. An infinite slab holds every vertical perpendicular; a disc with a rim cannot, and section 02 weighs it.

**Angle between two plumb lines, as a function of how far apart they hang**

| Separation along the ground | Globe, R = 6,371 km | Flat: infinite plane | Flat: disc, from its centre | Measured (1° per 111.2 km) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0 km | 0.5′ | 0.000° | 0.1′ | **0.5′** |
| 10 km | 5.4′ | 0.000° | 0.9′ | **5.4′** |
| 111 km | 1.00° | 0.000° | 10.5′ | **1.00°** |
| 500 km | 4.50° | 0.000° | 47.4′ | **4.50°** |
| 1000 km | 8.99° | 0.000° | 1.58° | **8.99°** |
| 4572 km | 41.12° | 0.000° | 7.35° | **41.12°** |

The last column is not a model output: it is the measured rate at which astronomic latitude changes with northward travel, which is how every degree of every meridian arc has been surveyed since Picard in 1670. The fourth column is computed below, by integrating the gravity of the disc itself.

## 02 · Give the flat model the best gravity it can have

A flat earth is not obliged to have no gravity. Take the strongest version available and it is a good one: an **infinite uniform slab** of matter. By Gauss's law the field above such a slab is **2πGσ** — perpendicular to the surface, and exactly the same everywhere on it, forever. Water is level, plumb lines are parallel, nothing tilts. That model passes section 01 outright, and this page will not pretend otherwise. What it cannot do is survive being weighed.

$$g = {2\pi G\sigma}$$
at Earth's mean density that is **4,241 km** of matter under every square metre, and no edge

σ is mass per square metre of surface. The number is forced: to feel 9.81 m/s² you need that much matter under every square metre, spread out to infinity in every direction. Give the slab an edge and the argument collapses — the missing matter beyond the rim stops pulling sideways, and everything near the rim tilts.

So take the map the flat model actually publishes: a disc with the north pole at the centre and the rim 20,000 km out, the same disc the magnetism tab uses. Give it Earth's own mean density and make it thick enough to produce 9.81 m/s² at the pole. Now integrate its gravity at points across its face. The vertical component stays near 9.8 — but a **horizontal** component appears and grows with distance from the centre, because there is more disc on one side of you than the other. The local vertical tilts inward, and so does every level surface.

*Figure caption:* Tilt of the local vertical across a disc of radius 20,000 km and Earth's mean density, computed by integrating the disc's own gravity. It is zero at exactly one point — the centre. A spirit level is level nowhere else on it.

**The disc weighed against itself: tilt of the local vertical, computed by integrating the disc's own gravity**

| Place on the flat map | Distance from the centre | Tilt of the vertical | Slope water would run down | Observed slope |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| North Pole | 0 km | 0.00° | 0% | 0% |
| Reykjavík | 2,878 km | 4.58° | 8% | 0% |
| Paris | 4,572 km | 7.35° | 13% | 0% |
| Cairo | 6,667 km | 10.94° | 19% | 0% |
| Equator | 10,000 km | 17.30° | 31% | 0% |
| Sydney | 13,767 km | 26.41° | 50% | 0% |
| Ushuaia | 16,089 km | 34.17° | 68% | 0% |

Computed, not asserted: the disc is 20,000 km in radius and **4812 km** thick at Earth's mean density of 5514 kg/m³, which is what it takes to feel 9.807 m/s² at its centre. Making it thinner and denser barely helps — the tilt at the latitude of Paris only moves between about 7° and 9° across every thickness from 1,000 km to 40,000 km, because it is set by the position of the *rim*, not by how the mass is stacked. The last column is the slope a bubble level actually shows, which is zero to within a few arcseconds everywhere on Earth.

> **The flat model cannot have it both ways.** To keep water level everywhere it needs a field perpendicular to the disc everywhere, which requires the disc to be infinite — no rim, no ice wall, no edge, and infinite mass. To keep its own map it needs a rim at 20,000 km, and then the field tilts by the amounts in the table above: about 7° at the latitude of Paris and 26° at the latitude of Sydney. A 7° slope is a 12% grade. Rivers would all run north, seas would pile against the pole, and a bubble level would be visibly off in every building in Europe. Nobody measures that, on either side of the argument.

## 03 · Gravity weakens as you climb — and the rate *is* the radius [evidence: prediction]

Here is the measurement that separates the two models with no map, no horizon and no sightline. Above a sphere, g falls off as **1/(R+h)²**. Above an infinite slab it does not fall off at all: Gauss's law makes the field of an infinite plane independent of height, exactly, at every altitude. So one model predicts a definite gradient and the other predicts **zero**. This is a rule‑4 test: not a small difference, a presence against an absence.

$$\frac{dg}{dh} = {-\frac{2g}{R}}$$

Read it right to left and it stops being a correction and becomes an instrument. Every gravity survey on Earth applies the **free‑air correction**, 0.3086 mGal per metre of elevation[2], before anything else — and that constant, inverted, hands back the radius of the planet to a fraction of a percent. Geophysicists are not measuring the Earth's size when they apply it; they are using it, every day, and it works.

*Figure caption:* Loss of gravity with height. True scale, no exaggeration. The teal curve is g₀R²/(R+h)²; the amber line is Gauss's law for an infinite slab, which is height-independent exactly. A field gravimeter resolves 0.01 mGal, so the gap is measurable inside a building.

**How much gravity you lose by climbing, and whether an instrument can see it**

| Height above the surface | Globe: change in g | Infinite plane: change in g | Times the noise of a field gravimeter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 3.0 m one floor of a building | −0.92 mGal | 0.00 mGal | **92×** |
| 276 m Eiffel Tower, top platform | −85.0 mGal | 0.00 mGal | **8,496×** |
| 828 m Burj Khalifa | −254.9 mGal | 0.00 mGal | **25,485×** |
| 4,808 m Mont Blanc | −1478.5 mGal | 0.00 mGal | **147,848×** |
| 11,000 m airliner at cruise | −3377.6 mGal | 0.00 mGal | **337,763×** |

A relative gravimeter reads to about 0.01 mGal in the field and a laboratory absolute meter to a few microgal, so the difference between the pavement and the first floor of a building is already dozens of times the noise. The effect has been mapped up a real hillside with a portable atom interferometer[4], and airborne surveys apply it routinely at 11 km[3].

## 03b · Gravity measured up a 562 m tower [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the prediction each reading is compared with is built from a normal gravity field that contains the Earth's radius, and the paper publishes only the differences.]

**In the late 1980s a gravimeter was carried up a television tower in North Carolina and read at twelve heights.** Going up 562 m, gravity fell by about 173 mGal, 0.018 % of g: what a globe's free-air gradient of 0.3086 mGal per metre predicts. The test was of Newton's law at the scale of hundreds of metres, so the prediction for each height was built from 77 gravity stations on the ground around the tower and data to 220 km; the observed values stayed within 0.55 mGal of it all the way up[10]. A plane of any thickness, infinitely wide, predicts no change at all with height.

$$\Delta g(h) \approx -\frac{2g}{R}\,h = -0.3086\ \text{mGal/m} \times h$$
$${\Delta g(562\ \text{m}) \approx -173.5\ \text{mGal}},\qquad \text{observed} - \text{predicted} = -0.55\ \text{mGal}$$

The first line is the globe's normal gradient; the second, the drop it predicts over the tower and how far the measurement departed from the full prediction, which also carried the local terrain. The paper gives only the departures, not the readings, and its prediction used a normal gravity field built with the Earth's radius: a check.

> **The flat model's only escape is a gradient of its own.** An infinite slab has none; a finite disc has one only near its edge or its centre of mass, and none of the order of 2g/R under North Carolina. **What would vindicate it:** a gravimeter carried up a tall structure that reads the same at the top as at the bottom.

## 04 · Richer's clock, 1672: g is not the same at every latitude [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: compared with a reference gravity formula of the GRS80 family.]

Jean Richer took a pendulum clock to Cayenne, 5° from the equator, and found it running **2 min 28 s per day slow**[5] against the stars, having kept perfect time in Paris. A pendulum's period depends only on its length and on g, so the clock was a gravimeter: gravity is weaker near the equator. Newton and Huygens both seized on it, for different reasons, and the modern reference formula[3] reproduces it. An infinite slab predicts one value of g everywhere; a disc accelerating upward predicts one value of g everywhere; a rotating sphere predicts a systematic **sin²φ** pattern of about half a percent, pole to equator.

$$T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g} \;\Rightarrow\; g_{\text{Cayenne}} = g_{\text{Paris}}\left(1 - \frac{\Delta t}{86\,400\ \text{s}}\right)^2$$
$$g(\varphi) = 9.7803\,\frac{1 + 0.001932\sin^2\varphi}{\sqrt{1 - 0.006694\sin^2\varphi}}\ \text{m/s}^2$$

T: period of a pendulum of length L · Δt: time the clock loses per day, 148 s for Richer, so g is 0.34 % weaker at Cayenne than in Paris · g(φ): the reference formula for a rotating, flattened Earth, which gives 0.30 % between the two · on a slab or an accelerating disc, g is the same everywhere and Δt = 0

*Figure caption:* Gravity against latitude. Teal: the international reference formula, fitted to worldwide gravimetry. Grey dashed: what rotation alone would do to a sphere — about two thirds of the observed spread; the rest is the equatorial bulge. Amber: every flat model, which predicts one number everywhere. The black dot is Richer's 1672 clock rate converted to g, the only observation plotted.

**Standard gravity by latitude, and what a pendulum clock does about it**

| Latitude | g, international formula | Difference from the pole | Clock rate vs Paris | Any flat model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 90° | 9.83219 | 0.0 mm/s² | +99 s | no change |
| 60° | 9.81918 | -13.0 mm/s² | +42 s | no change |
| 48.85° Paris | 9.80967 | -22.5 mm/s² | −0 s | no change |
| 30° | 9.79325 | -38.9 mm/s² | −72 s | no change |
| 4.94° Cayenne | 9.78071 | -51.5 mm/s² | −128 s | no change |
| 0° | 9.78033 | -51.9 mm/s² | −129 s | no change |

Richer's clock lost **2 min 28 s** = 148 s per day at Cayenne. The formula above predicts **128 s** for that pair of latitudes, so he was 16% high — an overshoot his contemporaries already blamed on the tropical heat lengthening the pendulum rod, since brass expands about 19 parts per million per degree. The direction, the size and the sign are right, from an instrument built in 1671. Every flat model on offer predicts that the clock keeps perfect time in Cayenne.

> **The limit of a sphere, admitted.** Rotation alone accounts for about two thirds of the pole‑to‑equator difference: ω²R at the equator is 0.0339 m/s² against a measured 0.0519[3]. The missing third comes from the equatorial bulge, which this page does not model — everywhere else the sphere is good enough, and here it is not. That residual is not an embarrassment, it is Newton's prediction: a rotating self‑gravitating fluid must flatten, by roughly 1 part in 300, and the Lapland and Peru arc expeditions of the 1730s went out to measure precisely that. A flat model has no residual to explain because it predicts no variation at all.

## 05 · Mass attracts mass, and you can watch a mountain prove it [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the Earth's mass computed with its radius.]

In 1774 Nevil Maskelyne parked two observatories on the north and south flanks of Schiehallion and measured the vertical against the stars from each. The plumb lines leaned *toward the mountain*, by a total of **11.6″**[6]. That single number does three jobs at once. It shows gravity is not a fixed downward direction but an attraction toward matter. It gave Charles Hutton the Earth's mean density, about 4.5 times water, later refined to **5.51**[8]. And it is why the flat model's field has to be produced by something: a field that simply *points down*, with no matter making it, is not a physical theory, and the moment matter makes it, a disc's rim starts pulling sideways[7].

Cavendish closed the loop in 1798[9] by measuring the attraction between lead balls in a room, which fixes **G**. With G in hand, g and R give the mass of the planet directly:**5.96 × 10²⁴ kg**, and a mean density of**5,506 kg/m³** — twice the density of surface rock. Something denser is inside. The seismology tab finds that same something independently, from the shadow zone of P waves, and puts its boundary at 2,891 km. Two completely unrelated measurements, one object.

$$m g = \frac{G M m}{R^2} \;\Rightarrow\; M = \frac{g R^2}{G},\qquad \bar\rho = \frac{M}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3} = \frac{3g}{4\pi G R}$$

G: the gravitational constant, measured by Cavendish in a room · g: gravity at the surface · R: the Earth's radius, from the surveyors · with g = 9.81 m/s², R = 6,371 km and G = 6.674 × 10^−11: M = 5.97 × 10^24 kg and ρ̄ = 5.5 g/cm³, twice surface rock

## 06 · “Things fall because of density, not gravity”

This is the usual alternative and it deserves a straight answer. Buoyancy is real and it is Archimedes' law: the upward force on a body in a fluid is **ρ_fluid V g**. The g is inside the formula. Density decides which way a thing moves *through* a fluid; it cannot supply the field that defines “down”, and it says nothing at all in a vacuum, where a feather and a hammer fall together. The serious flat proposal is the other one — the disc accelerating upward at 9.8 m/s² — and it is a real theory, so it can be priced.

**Three flat proposals against three measurements. A cross is a prediction the measurement contradicts**

| Model | Vertical tilts with position? | g falls with height? | g varies with latitude? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Globe, radius 6,371 km | yes, d/R ✓ | yes, 2g/R ✓ | yes, sin²φ ✓ |
| Flat: infinite slab of matter | no ✗ | no ✗ | no ✗ |
| Flat: disc, rim at 20,000 km | yes, but wrong way ✗ | weakly, wrong sign ✗ | no ✗ |
| Flat: disc accelerating at 9.8 m/s² | no ✗ | no ✗ | no ✗ |
| Density and buoyancy only | no prediction | no prediction | no prediction |

> **Where the accelerating disc dies.** Constant proper acceleration reproduces free fall perfectly — that is Einstein's equivalence principle and it is not a joke. But an accelerating floor accelerates *all* of itself equally: the same 9.8 m/s² at the pole and at the rim, in the cellar and at the top of the Burj Khalifa. It therefore predicts a free‑air gradient of exactly zero and a latitude variation of exactly zero, and both are measured, daily, by people whose surveys would not close if they ignored them. It also has to explain why the whole disc has been accelerating for the age of the universe without arriving anywhere.

Experiment 1f · gravity and level

Weigh the same object in two cities, or time a pendulum in both

Every flat model on the table predicts that g is one number, the same everywhere. The globe predicts a specific difference between any two latitudes, set by rotation and the bulge. Two ways to see it: a pendulum, whose period goes as 1/√g, or a good spring‑type balance carrying a heavy mass. Pick your two places, and the calculator tells you in advance how big the effect is and whether your kit can resolve it.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **latitude** at which you make the measurement. Nothing else — same instrument, same mass, same pendulum, carried between the two places.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the **period** of the pendulum, or the **reading** of the balance. Both are proxies for g and the world decides them.

Globe: g = 9.80466 at 43.3° and 9.81124 m/s² at 50.6° → Δg = **657.6 mGal** (0.0671%)

Every flat model: Δg = 0.0 mGal, at both places, exactly

Pendulum of 2.00 m: period 2.83778 s vs 2.83683 s → **0.10 s** apart over 100 swings

10.0 kg on a force-reading balance: **6.7 g** difference

**Verdict rule.** If the two places really do differ, you will see it: 0.10 s over 100 swings is within reach of a phone timing the swings, and 6.7 g is readable on a 0.1 g balance. Measure a *difference of zero*, repeatably, with an instrument that can resolve this much, and the flat models win this test outright — no amount of curvature elsewhere would save the prediction.

## 07 · Two tides a day: what the Moon's pull does to a ball [evidence: prediction]

The usual flat answer for the tide is that the Moon pulls the water up under it. That gives **one** high water a day, while the Moon is overhead. Most coasts have **two**, 12 h 25 min apart, and the second comes when the Moon is on the other side of the Earth, under your feet. The far side bulges too, and the reason takes one idea: the whole Earth is falling towards the Moon, so what moves the water is not the Moon's pull but how much that pull *differs* from the pull at the Earth's centre.

*Figure caption:* **Six steps, from one fall to two tides.** 1: the Earth and the Moon at true scale, each falling round their common centre, which lies inside the Earth. 2: the Moon's pull at twelve points (black), then each minus the pull at the centre (blue, drawn 20 times longer): outward on both sides along the line to the Moon, inward across it. 3: the water those differences pile up, seen from above the North Pole, and a port carried round by the Earth's turn: two high waters every 24 h 50 min. 4: the Sun's pair of bulges, 0.46 times as strong, turns once a month against the Moon's: spring tides at new and full moon, neap tides at the quarters. 5: with the Moon 28° from the equator the bulges are tilted and a port at 45° N gets one big and one small tide a day. 6: the flat model's best case, a Moon 5,000 km above a plane: one hump, one tide a day. The water heights are drawn millions of times higher than they are, and the factor is written on each picture. This is the *equilibrium* tide, the shape the water would take if it had time to follow; real seas answer it with delays and resonances (next section). Click to pause.

$$a_{\text{axis}} = \frac{GM}{(d-r)^2} - \frac{GM}{d^2} \approx +\frac{2GMr}{d^3},\qquad a_{\text{across}} \approx -\frac{GMr}{d^3}$$
$${h(\theta) = \frac{M_\mathrm{L}}{M_\mathrm{T}}\left(\frac{R}{d}\right)^{3} R\,\frac{3\cos^2\theta - 1}{2}}$$

M is the Moon's mass, d its distance, r the distance of a point from the Earth's centre along the line to the Moon. The near side is pulled harder than the centre and the far side less hard; both differences point away from the centre, with the same size, 2GMr/d³. Across the line the pull converges and squeezes inward, half as hard. The height h the water would take is the potential of that difference divided by g: θ is the angle from the point under the Moon, M_L/M_T = 1/81.3 the Moon's mass over the Earth's, R the Earth's radius. With d = 60.3 R it is 0.36 m at θ = 0 and at θ = 180°, two bulges; −0.18 m round the ring between them.[12]

$$\frac{GM}{d^3} = \left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^2$$
$${\frac\mathrm{Sun}\mathrm{Moon} = \left(\frac{T_\mathrm{L}}{T_{\odot}}\right)^{2}\left(1 + \frac{M_\mathrm{T}}{M_\mathrm{L}}\right) = \left(\frac{27.32}{365.26}\right)^{2} \times 82.3 = 0.46}$$
$$\frac{N_2}{M_2} = \frac{7e}{2} = 0.19$$

Both tides go as GM/d³, and Kepler's third law gives exactly that quantity from a period: the year for the Sun, the sidereal month for the Moon, of which the Moon's own share is M_L/(M_T + M_L), 1 part in 82.3[13]. No distance in kilometres is needed: the Sun's tide is 0.46 of the Moon's, a little under half. The potential's own coefficients give S2/M2 = 0.465[12]. Kepler's first law gives another line: the Moon's orbit is an ellipse of eccentricity e = 0.0549[13], so its pull swells at perigee every 27.55 days; the tide it raises splits off a line called N2, 7e/2 = 0.19 of the main one, M2.

> **The flat model at its best.** Give it the most favourable Moon there is: as heavy and as low as it likes, circling over the disc once every 24 h 50 min. Water climbs towards a pull, and on a plane every point is on the same side of the Moon, so the water gathers in one hump under it and the level only falls as one moves away (last scene, *h* ∝ 1/√(*x*² + *H*²) for a Moon at height *H*). That is one high water a day. A second hump on the far side needs the ground itself to fall towards the Moon faster than the far water does, which is what a free body in orbit does and a plane held still does not. A flat model can still decree two humps, by choosing a rule for the water as a function of the Moon's direction; then it also has to choose the 14.77-day spring tides, the Sun's 0.46 and the 13.66-day cycle of the diurnal tides one by one, where the globe gets all three from the periods above.

## 07b · What the tide gauges record [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: nowhere: the records are compared with the tide that gravity on a globe and Kepler's laws predict; only the harmonic analysis takes the frequencies of its lines from the Moon's and Sun's motions, and the periods read off the records use the clock alone.]

Five gauges, one year each, a reading every hour: the research-quality records of the University of Hawaii Sea Level Center for 2018[11]. They were chosen for their differences: Brest has big tides twice a day; Marseille has almost none; Pensacola, in the Gulf of Mexico, has one a day; Manila mixes both; Fremantle, in the southern hemisphere, has small daily ones. Each record is read three ways. Two use nothing but the gauge's clock: the strongest periods in the record, and the period at which the daily range swells and shrinks. The third, the harmonic analysis that tide tables are made from, takes the frequency of each line from the motions of the Moon and the Sun and fits its height and its delay[15].

*Figure caption:* **The lines in a year of sea level.** The amplitude of the best sine wave at each frequency (the periodogram), each gauge scaled to its own highest line, whose height is written on the left. Dashes: the frequencies of the five largest lines of the tide-generating potential. Every record has its energy at those frequencies and nowhere else in the band. Read off the records themselves, the strongest twice-daily line is at **12.421–12.421 h** at all five gauges; the Moon's half-day is 12.4206 h. Brest's M2 is 2.06 m; Pensacola's twice-daily lines almost vanish under its daily ones.

*Figure caption:* **March 2018, hour by hour.** Top: Brest, two tides a day whose range swells after each new and full moon (blue dashes) and shrinks after the quarters. Middle: Pensacola, one tide a day, largest when the Moon is farthest from the equator (bottom curve, its declination) and almost gone when it crosses it. The Moon's phases and declination are computed with the page's ephemeris (Meeus); the sea level is the gauge's, less its running 25-hour mean (the weather's slow part).

| Gauge | Kind (F) | Line read off the record | Range beats | N2/M2 | S2/M2 | K1/O1 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Brest | semidiurnal (0.05) | 12.421 h | 14.74 d | 0.20 | 0.36 | 1.03 |
| Marseille | mixed, mainly semidiurnal (0.61) | 12.421 h | 14.76 d | 0.22 | 0.37 | 1.70 |
| Pensacola | diurnal (10.89) | 12.421 h | 13.64 d | 0.19 | 0.34 | 1.02 |
| Manila | mixed, mainly diurnal (2.26) | 12.421 h | 13.63 d | 0.20 | 0.35 | 1.10 |
| Fremantle | mixed, mainly diurnal (2.88) | 12.421 h | 13.60 d | 0.26 | 0.89 | 1.37 |
| Globe and Kepler |  | 12.421 h (M2) | 14.77 / 13.66 d | 0.19 | 0.46 | 1.41 |

*Figure caption:* **Five gauges against the globe and Kepler.** Kind: the form factor F = (K1 + O1)/(M2 + S2) of the harmonic analysis[14]. Line: the strongest twice-daily period read off the record. Range beats: the period at which the range of each lunar day swells and shrinks, also read off the record: 14.77 days where the twice-daily tide leads (the Moon's and Sun's bulges falling in and out of step), 13.66 days where the daily tide leads (the Moon's declination, twice a month). Ratios: heights of the lines from the harmonic analysis; last row, what the globe and Kepler give (N2/M2 = 7e/2, S2/M2 from the periods, K1/O1 from the potential[12]).

> **What fits and what does not.** The periods fit everywhere, to the second, and the beats to a few hours: those come from the sky alone. The heights do not follow the equilibrium tide, and should not: the sea needs hours to move and each basin rings at its own periods, so the tide turns around points where it vanishes and reaches several metres in funnels like the Channel[14]. Neighbouring lines are answered alike, so their ratios survive best: N2/M2, the trace of the Moon's ellipse, is 0.20 at Brest against 0.19. Lines further apart fare worse: S2/M2 is 0.36 at Brest, not 0.46, and 0.89 at Fremantle, where the twice-daily tide is small and the local response odd. Spring tides come 1.6 days after new and full moon at Brest (the age of the tide). At Marseille the fit explains only 40 % of the variance: the tide is a few centimetres and the weather moves the sea more.

**What would count for the flat model.** A gauge with one high water per lunar day and no line at 12 h 25 min anywhere along a coast, or a spring-neap cycle that does not follow the phases of the Moon. Pensacola has one high water a day, but its record still has the 12 h 25 min line, and its range follows the Moon's declination at 13.66 days, as the tilted bulges of the fifth scene predict.

## 07c · The tide globe: the pull and the real tides together [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: nowhere: the records are compared with the tide that gravity on a globe and Kepler's laws predict; only the harmonic analysis takes the frequencies of its lines from the Moon's and Sun's motions, and the periods read off the records use the clock alone.]

The two sections above take the pull and the gauges apart. This one puts them together: the surface the Moon and the Sun would give a still ocean, and the tide that more than six hundred gauges actually measure, on one turning Earth, at the same instant and the same scale. Each gauge's tide is computed from the constants TICON-3 fitted to its own record[16], eight lines that carry most of the tide; on our five gauges they agree with our own analysis above, once a quarter-cycle difference of convention in the daily lines is taken out.

*Figure caption:* **The pull and the real tides on one globe.** Shading and blue outline: the surface the Moon's and the Sun's pull would give a still ocean at that instant (the equilibrium tide, their positions from the page's ephemeris). Spikes: 613 tide gauges of TICON-3, one per 2° cell[16]; each spike is the tide that gauge's own measured constants give for that instant, blue above its mean, red below, at the same scale as the outline. The camera follows the Moon, 90° from it, so its two bulges sit on the left and right edges and the Earth turns under them. Scene 1: two days from the new moon of 17 March 2018. Scene 2: the Moon's twice-daily line M2 alone (and the Moon held on the equator). Scene 3: a month seen once every lunar day, 24 h 50 min, so the twice-daily rhythm stands still and only spring and neap remain. What to look at: the spikes rise and fall with the bulges' clock, but not under them; the North Atlantic is high while the Indian Ocean is low, and some gauges hardly move. That is the ocean's answer to the pull, set by its basins, not a failure of the pull: the periods are the same everywhere. Spikes longer than 2.3 m are cut and ringed. Click to pause.

## 07d · Why small seas have almost no tide [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: nowhere: the records are compared with the tide that gravity on a globe and Kepler's laws predict; only the harmonic analysis takes the frequencies of its lines from the Moon's and Sun's motions, and the periods read off the records use the clock alone.]

The tide is not water lifted where it stands. Over the open ocean the bulges travel round the Earth once every 24 h 50 min, and the water rises because it is carried in from far away. A closed lake cannot be fed: the pull can only tilt its surface, raising one end as the other falls, and the tilt is the slope of the equilibrium surface over the lake's length. That slope is A/R at most per unit length, with A = 0.24 m the Moon's twice-daily equilibrium tide at the equator[14], so a basin of length L can have a tide of at most A·L/R: under a millimetre for a lake of 20 km, a few centimetres for a sea a thousand kilometres long.

$$\eta \le A\,\frac{L}{R},\qquad A = 0.24\ \text{m}$$
$${T_{\text{bay}} = \frac{4L}{\sqrt{gh}}}$$

η: the tide of a closed basin of length L; R the Earth's radius. Lake Geneva, 73 km: 3 mm at most. Lake Superior, 560 km: 2 cm at most, and the NOAA gives under 5 cm for its spring tide, all lines together[17]. The Black Sea, 1,150 km: 4 cm at most, 2 cm measured. T_bay: the natural period of a bay open at one end, of length L and depth h (Merian's formula, the wave goes in and back twice); when it is near 12 h 25 min, each tide adds to the last. The Bay of Fundy with the Gulf of Maine rings at about 13 hours[18], which is why M2 alone reaches 4.9 m at the head of the bay[16].

*Figure caption:* **The twice-daily tide, sea by sea.** The M2 amplitude of every coastal gauge of TICON-3 inside a box round each sea[16] (number of gauges in brackets): the bar covers the middle half, the dot is the median, on a logarithmic scale. Rings: the most a closed basin of that length could have, A·L/R (lengths rounded, along each sea's main axis). The enclosed seas all sit below their ring; the Baltic far below, since it has its own points of no tide. The Mediterranean is not closed: Gibraltar lets in a little of the Atlantic tide, and resonant corners (the gulf of Gabès, the north Adriatic) reach 33 cm. The open coasts are a hundred times higher, and Fundy higher still, by resonance.

> **The flat model and the lakes.** A Moon a few thousand kilometres up lifting the water beneath it would lift a lake as surely as an ocean: the pull on each litre does not depend on how much water is around it. The lakes of the world should then have tides like the coasts. They have millimetres to centimetres, in proportion to their length, as the tilt of a globe's equilibrium surface predicts; and the seas behind narrow straits have less than the ocean outside. What would count for the flat model: a closed lake with a tide of the same size as the open coast nearby.

The through‑line. “Level” is the hinge this whole page turns on. The horizon‑dip tab measures how far the horizon sits below level; the surveying tab shows the curvature correction that a levelled sightline needs; the hidden‑height tab counts what a level surface hides. All three assume that level means perpendicular to gravity — and this tab is where that assumption is cashed out and measured. The same R comes back a fourth way here, out of a gravimeter, with no light involved at all.

# Earthquakes measure the distance between every pair of points on Earth, and no flat map survives the result

> Tab "Seismology" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-seis. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Seismology · the planet is scanned a hundred times a day*

*Figure caption:* **The travel-time curve, the way a seismologist checks it.** Arrival time against distance, every station plotted twice: once at its great-circle distance, once at its flat-map distance. This is the plot the experiment card asks you to reproduce from real traces.

Somewhere on Earth a magnitude-5 earthquake happens roughly every hour. Each one sends a pulse across the surface and through the interior, and a few thousand instruments write down when it arrives. That is a distance measurement between two points on the planet — thousands of them a day, over every pair of continents, made by institutions in dozens of countries that give the raw traces away for free. This tab is about what that pile of arrival times says about the shape of the surface, and then about what the *missing* arrivals say about what is underneath it.

*[Figure: Animation: the P wave of the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake lighting real stations on a globe; a trial centre sliding until the arrival times fall on one curve; the residuals of every large shallow earthquake under one curve, narrow for the globe and wide for the best flat map; one dot per earthquake above the line of equality; a map of every flat-map centre tried; the share of stations with a direct P wave against distance; the radius from every surface-wave arrival; a summary]*

*Figure caption:* **The whole tab in under a minute.** The P wave of the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake lighting real stations at their recorded times; the four kinds of waves told apart by how they move the ground; our own centre, found from the times alone; all 261 large shallow earthquakes under one curve, globe against the best flat map; the same, earthquake by earthquake; every flat-map centre tried; the shadow of the core at 368,987 stations; the radius from 13,586 surface-wave arrivals. Every number is the page's own. Click to pause.

$$t = \frac{R\Delta}{v}$$
Δ = great-circle angle
$$v \approx 3.8\ \text{km}/\text{s}$$

A surface-wave arrival time is the great-circle distance divided by the group velocity — one function of the angular separation Δ, the same in every azimuth and on every continent. That is a strong claim, and it is the one the flat model cannot match: on a plane the distance between two points is whatever the map says, and no flat map can reproduce the distances a sphere has. Not "no flat map yet" — no flat map ever, as a theorem.

## Why this is a shape measurement and not a geology lesson

Gauss proved in 1827 that a surface's curvature is fixed by distances measured *within* the surface alone — the *Theorema Egregium*. Its brutal corollary is that a sphere cannot be flattened onto a plane without changing distances. Every world map you have ever seen is therefore lying about something; the only question is which distances it wrecks and by how much. A seismic network measures exactly the quantity the theorem is about: surface distance between pairs of points, tens of thousands of pairs, continuously, for over a century.

So the test does not require believing any particular story about the Earth's interior. Take the arrival times, ask what surface geometry makes them consistent, and the answer comes back a sphere of radius 6,371 km — the same radius the other tabs get from horizons, from star altitudes and from satellites. Then, as a bonus no flat model has any analogue for, the pattern of the arrivals that are *absent* hands you a map of the inside.

> **How to read the figures below.** A page cannot ship a hundred megabytes of seismograms, so the arrival times drawn here are *computed* from the spherical model. What they show needs no data at all: for ordinary station pairs the two models' distances disagree by tens of minutes to over an hour of travel time. Whether real traces follow the globe column or the flat one is yours to settle — the experiment card at the bottom does it with free public data and about twenty lines of Python. Take this tab's word for the geometry, not for the arrivals.

- Sumatra 2004
- t = **0 min**
- front at **0 km** = **0°**
- reached **0/19** real stations, real recorded time
- reached **0/19** flat map, computed

*[Figure: The same seismic wave on a globe: a circle that grows from the epicentre and closes on the antipode]*

*Figure caption:* **Real epicentres, real stations, real recorded arrival times.** The background is the north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection — the standard flat-earth map, on which distance from the north pole is correct and nothing else is. The two wavefronts are still computed geometry, exactly like the rest of this tab's animation; what is new is that each dot switches on at that station's *own recorded* arrival time from the ISC bulletin, not a computed one. Pick any of the nine real earthquakes used further below.

## Telling the waves apart: by how they move, not only by when they arrive [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the kinds of waves and the direction each P wave came from are read off the records alone, with each sensor's orientation; the epicentres the directions are compared with are the ISC's, located with travel-time tables built for a spherical Earth.]

The sections below use readings the ISC names P, Pdif or PKP, and say each time that this is where a globe model enters: the ISC gives these names by comparing each arrival time with tables built for a spherical Earth.[5] But a seismometer records more than a time. It records the ground's motion in three directions, up, north and east, and each kind of wave moves the ground its own way.[20] That can be read off the record with no Earth model at all.

- **P**, the first to arrive: a push and pull *along* the ray. At a distant station the ray comes up steeply, so the motion is mostly vertical, with a small horizontal part pointing straight away from the earthquake.
- **S**: a shear *across* the ray, either horizontal and transverse to the path (SH) or in the vertical plane of the path (SV).
- **Love**: horizontal and transverse, like SH, but at long periods and after S.
- **Rayleigh**, the slowest and largest: the ground rolls on an ellipse in the vertical plane of the path, backwards at the top (retrograde).
- And the period: P and S shake at a few seconds, surface waves at tens of seconds, and surface waves are dispersed, their long periods arriving first.[15]

$$C = \frac{1}{N}\sum_i (\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})(\mathbf{x}_i - \bar{\mathbf{x}})^{T}, \qquad L = 1 - \frac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}$$
λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ λ₃ and u₁, u₂, u₃: the eigenvalues and directions of C. L near 1: the ground moves on a line (P, S, Love), along u₁. L small and λ₃ small: an ellipse in the plane normal to u₃ (Rayleigh).

Over a window of a few seconds to two minutes, the three components give a cloud of ground positions. Its covariance says how the cloud is spread: along one line, in one plane, or in every direction.[21][22] For the P wave, u₁ also says where the wave came from: its horizontal part points away from the source when its vertical part points up. Here the P onset is found by the ratio of a short to a long running mean of the energy,[23] the P direction is read from the first seconds after it, and the two horizontals are turned into R, away from the source along that measured direction, and T, across it. No travel time, no origin time and no Earth model is used.

- ANMO: the P wave came from 306° (measured from its motion)great circle to the epicentre: 312°straight line on the North Pole map: 327°period: P 10 s, Rayleigh 40 s

Station

*[Figure: The three components of ground motion at one station during the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake, vertical, radial and transverse, with two coloured bands underneath classifying each window by the shape of the motion]*

*Figure caption:* **Tōhoku 2011, three components at one station.** Real records from the Global Seismograph Network[24], ground velocity, 2 to 100 s, the horizontals turned to R and T with the direction the P wave itself gave. The coloured bands underneath classify each window from the motion alone: blue, a line in the vertical plane of the path (P, SV); violet, a line across the path (SH, Love); magenta, a retrograde ellipse in the vertical plane of the path (Rayleigh); grey, mixed. Top band: 20 s windows at 2–20 s periods; bottom band: 2 min windows at 25–100 s. The boxes mark the four windows of the next figure, found from the records alone: the P onset, the first strong transverse onset two minutes or more later, and the strongest minute of long-period transverse, then vertical, motion.

*[Figure: The path of the ground in four windows: a nearly vertical line for P, a line across the path for S and for Love, a retrograde ellipse in the vertical plane for Rayleigh]*

*Figure caption:* **The ground's path in the four windows.** P and Rayleigh in the vertical plane of the path (R across, Z up); S and Love seen from above (R across, T up). The arrow shows the sense of motion halfway through the window.

At the 4 stations shown, the P motion is a line (L from 0.96 to 1.00), in the vertical plane of the path, 20–29° from the vertical, at periods of 8–10 s. The first strong onset on the transverse component comes 7–10 minutes later at periods of 8–20 s. Then the long-period transverse motion (Love, transverse share 0.84 or more, 40–80 s), and after it the Rayleigh ellipse (24–48 s), retrograde at every station. The order and the shapes are exactly what the list above says, read off the records without a single travel time.

The P wave also says where it came from, and that is a test of the shape. Directions on the ground are angles: the direction of the epicentre from a station follows from latitudes and longitudes alone. On the globe it is the start of the great circle; on a flat map, the straight line on the map. The same was done for three great earthquakes, Tōhoku 2011, Maule 2010 and Nias 2005, at the same fourteen stations wherever they recorded a clear P: 38 records (4 without data or without a clear onset).

*[Figure: For each record, the measured direction of the P wave minus the predicted direction of the epicentre: tight around zero for the globe, spread over tens of degrees for the flat maps]*

*Figure caption:* **Where the P wave came from, against where each model puts the epicentre.** One dot per record, coloured by earthquake: the direction measured from the P motion minus the predicted direction. Top: the globe, no parameter. Middle: the North Pole flat map. Bottom: the one flat map, out of every centre, whose straight lines fit all 38 measured directions best.

**The P wave's direction against the predicted direction of the epicentre (rms difference)**

| Earthquake | Records | Globe | Flat, North Pole map | Flat, one best map | Flat, that earthquake's own map |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tōhoku 2011 | 14 | 9.9° | 24.5° | 12.5° | 9.2° |
| Maule 2010 | 13 | 15.1° | 60.6° | 45.1° | 14.0° |
| Nias 2005 | 11 | 7.2° | 34.5° | 41.5° | 7.3° |
| all three (rms) | 38 | 11.3° | 42.7° | 35.4° |  |

On the globe the measured directions differ from the great circle by 11.3° rms, 3.6° median. On the North Pole map, by 42.7° rms (30.1° median). The flat model's best case is its best map: the centre near 30° N, 152° W fits all three earthquakes best, and it still misses by 35.4° rms (22.3° median), 3 times the globe. As in the relocation sections, a flat map centred near one earthquake does nearly as well as the globe for that earthquake (7–14° rms, last column), because an azimuthal equidistant map keeps the lines through its centre straight; a flat Earth is one map, not three. The globe's 11.3° is not zero, and the largest single miss is kept: Maule 2010 at SBA in Antarctica, where the P motion comes out almost horizontal (89° from the vertical) and its direction, 83°, against 127° on the globe, changes by over a hundred degrees with the window length.

> **The flat model, stated before the measurement.** What would vindicate the plane: a P wave arriving from the direction of the straight line to the epicentre on one flat map, at all stations and for all earthquakes, as well as from the great-circle direction, even with the map's centre left free, a parameter the globe does not get. The best single map misses 3 times as much as the globe.

> **What this does and does not use.** (1) The epicentres are the ISC's, located with travel-time tables built for a spherical Earth; the measured directions themselves use only the records and the orientation of each sensor from the station metadata. An orientation error would turn every direction at that station by the same angle, globe and flat alike. (2) The amplitudes are scaled by one gain per channel, not by the full instrument response; it is enough for the shapes, which compare components of the same sensor. (3) The classes are a rule of thumb: thresholds on L, on the transverse share and on the flatness of the ellipse. Windows where waves overlap come out grey, as they should.

## Seven stations, one earthquake, two geometries [evidence: prediction]

These are real instruments of the Global Seismographic Network at their published coordinates. For each one the table gives the great-circle distance from the Sumatra–Andaman epicentre and the flat map's distance between the same two dots, then turns both into a Rayleigh-wave arrival time. Nothing is fitted: the inputs are seven pairs of coordinates and one wave speed.

**Arrival of the 3.8 km/s surface wave — both distances computed from the same coordinates, neither fitted**
