# Satellites in the Doppler: their orbits, the Earth's mass and the shape of the ground

> Tab "Satellites" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-sat. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Satellites · one day of Doppler from 80 receivers*

A navigation receiver counts the carrier cycles of every satellite it hears; the rate of the count is the Doppler shift, the speed at which the satellite comes closer or moves away. On 10 April 2025, 79 receivers of the International GNSS Service, on every continent, recorded it for 78 GPS, Galileo and GLONASS satellites[1]. This tab fits the orbits, the receivers' positions, the Earth's GM and its rotation to those speeds and to nothing else, starting with the receivers laid out on a flat map.

## What one day of satellite Doppler gives [evidence: measurement]

**Every number in the second column comes from the measured speeds, clocks and carrier frequencies alone, with the receivers started on a flat map. The third column is for comparison only and was never used[8][9]. How each is obtained is explained in the next sections.**

| Quantity | From the Doppler alone | Accepted value | Difference |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Earth's GM (×10¹⁴ m³/s²) | **3.9860157** | 3.986004418 | +2.83 ppm |
| Rotation Ω (×10⁻⁵ rad/s) | **7.2921155** | 7.292115 | +0.07 ppm |
| One turn (sidereal day) | **23 h 56 min 4.09 s** | 23 h 56 min 4.10 s | −0.006 s |
| Equatorial radius (km) | **6,378.8** | 6,378.137 | +0.6 km |
| Flattening, from the receivers' positions | **1/291** | 1/298.26 |  |
| Flattening, from the orbits (J₂ and Clairaut) | **1/299** | 1/298.26 |  |
| J₂ (×10⁻³) | **1.0773** | 1.08263 | −0.49 % |
| Kepler III: GM from GLONASS, GPS, Galileo | **agree to 10.5 ppm** | one GM |  |
| Speeds left unexplained: receivers free / held on a plane | **2.6 mm/s / 131 m/s** | — | × 50,000 |

**How to read it.** GM is the Earth's mass times the constant of gravitation: what sets the satellites' periods. Ω is how fast the ground turns with respect to the orbits; one turn is the sidereal day. The radius and the flattening describe the surface on which the receivers end up; the flattening is found twice, from where the receivers sit and from how the satellites move. The last row is the test: the receivers left free explain the speeds to millimetres per second, held on a plane they miss by more than a hundred metres per second.

## The Doppler shift of a passing satellite

**A GPS satellite broadcasts on 1575.42 MHz, a wavelength of 19.03 cm.** Coming closer at 800 m/s it is heard 4.2 kHz higher; moving away, 4.2 kHz lower[3]. The receiver does not only measure the shift: it counts the cycles of the carrier, and the count changes by one each time the satellite's distance changes by one wavelength[2]. Here the count is read every 5 minutes over one minute, on two carrier frequencies so that the ionosphere, which slows the two differently, drops out[3][4][5]. At Wettzell, in Bavaria, the satellites approach and recede at up to 682 m/s: each rises closing in, passes its nearest point, and sets moving away.

*Figure caption:* **A satellite's Doppler shift records its motion.** Left: a GPS satellite on its orbit passing over a receiver, the line of sight and the satellite's velocity, with its part along the line of sight (thick arrow): toward the receiver while it rises, away while it sets. The Earth and the orbit are to scale with each other; the receiver is carried round by the rotation. Right: one day of measurements at Wettzell for the six satellites tracked longest, each point the speed over one minute every five minutes, and the curve of the fitted solution. Click to pause.

$$\dot\rho = -\lambda\,D = \lambda\,\frac{L(t+30\,\text{s}) - L(t-30\,\text{s})}{60\,\text{s}}$$
$${\dot\rho_{\text{IF}} = \frac{f_1^2\,\dot\rho_1 - f_2^2\,\dot\rho_2}{f_1^2 - f_2^2}}$$

ρ̇ is the range rate (how fast the distance to the satellite changes), λ = c/f the carrier's wavelength, D the Doppler shift and L the count of carrier cycles. The ionosphere delays a carrier by an amount proportional to 1/f², so the combination of two frequencies f₁ and f₂ in the second line cancels it. Nothing in this uses a position or a distance on the ground.

**This is how satellite navigation began.** In October 1957 William Guier and George Weiffenbach, at the Applied Physics Laboratory of Johns Hopkins, recorded the Doppler shift of Sputnik's 20 MHz beacon and found that one pass, from one station, was enough to work out its orbit. Their colleague Frank McClure turned the problem round: if the orbit is known, the Doppler gives the station's position. That became Transit, the US Navy's satellite navigation system from 1964[7]. This tab does both at once, with no orbit and no station known in advance.

## How speeds give the Earth's mass and its rotation

**Step 1: one satellite gives GM from its speed and its period.** The Doppler gives speeds, in metres per second, and the clocks give times. Watched through the day, a GPS satellite goes round in 11 h 58 min: its angular rate is n = 2π/T = 1.4586 × 10⁻⁴ rad/s. Its speed along the orbit is v = 3.874 km/s. A body going round at speed v with angular rate n is on a circle of radius a = v/n = 26,560 km: the size of the orbit, in kilometres, without any ruler. Newton's law for a circular orbit, v²/a = GM/a², then gives GM = v²a = v³/n = 3.9860 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². That is all GM is here: how fast a satellite must go to keep falling around at the distance its period implies (Orbit tab).

$$a = \frac{v}{n},\qquad \frac{v^2}{a} = \frac{GM}{a^2}$$
$${GM = v^2 a = \frac{v^3}{n}}$$

v is the satellite's speed, n = 2π/T its angular rate and T its period, a the radius of its orbit. For GPS: v = 3.874 km/s and T = 11 h 58 min give a = 26,560 km and GM = 3.9860 × 10¹⁴ m³/s². The real orbits are slightly elliptical and pulled by the Earth's bulge, the Sun and the Moon; the fit uses the full motion, but the idea is this one.

**Step 2: many receivers give each satellite's whole velocity.** A receiver measures only the part of the satellite's velocity along its line of sight, like a radar. Three receivers looking from different directions at the same moment measure three different parts, and together they fix the velocity in space; with dozens of receivers through the day, each satellite's whole orbit is pinned down, and each receiver's position with it, since a line of sight starts at the receiver. Each receiver's clock adds the same small error to every satellite it hears at that moment; comparing the satellites it hears removes it.

$$\dot\rho_k = \mathbf{u}_k\cdot\mathbf{v}_s - \mathbf{u}_k\cdot\mathbf{v}_k + \delta\dot t_k,\qquad k = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$
$${\text{three directions } \mathbf{u}_k \Rightarrow \mathbf{v}_s}$$

ρ̇_k is the speed measured by receiver k, u_k the direction from it to the satellite, v_s the satellite's velocity, v_k the receiver's own velocity and δṫ_k its clock error, the same for every satellite it hears at that moment. One equation per receiver and satellite every five minutes: 467,192 of them for a few hundred unknowns.

**Step 3: the rotation shows in the receivers' own speed.** Every receiver is carried around the axis: at the equator at 465 m/s, at Wettzell (49.0° N) at 305 m/s. That velocity enters every speed the receiver measures, and its direction turns through the day, coming back after one turn. The satellites, meanwhile, follow Newton's laws in a frame that does not turn. The fit therefore needs one axis and one rate Ω that turn every receiver's position consistently against the orbits; it finds Ω = 7.292116 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, one turn in 23 h 56 min 4.09 s, the sidereal day a clock and a star give (Rotation tab). A ground at rest would be Ω = 0; free to take any value, the fit settles on this one.

$$\mathbf{v}_k = \Omega\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{p}_k,\qquad |\mathbf{v}_k| = \Omega\,r_k\cos\varphi_k$$
$${T_\text{turn} = \frac{2\pi}{\Omega}}$$

p_k is receiver k's position from the centre, r_k its distance and φ_k its latitude, ẑ the axis. The receiver's speed is Ω times its distance from the axis, r cos φ. With Ω = 7.292116 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, T_turn = 23 h 56 min 4.09 s.

**Step 4: everything at once.** The steps above are how the numbers can be read; the fit does them all together, because each unknown leans on the others: the orbits need the receivers' positions, the positions need the orbits, and both need GM and Ω. Least squares adjusts the few hundred unknowns until the 467,192 predicted speeds match the measured ones; the next section gives the full model and how it starts.

## Orbits, the Earth's mass and its rotation from the Doppler alone [evidence: measurement]

**Everything is unknown at the start except the clocks and the carrier frequencies.** Each satellite gets a position and a velocity at noon, moved by Newton's gravity: a point mass GM, a term for a flattened body, and the pull of the Sun and the Moon, which enters through their periods and a mass ratio, not their distances in kilometres[6]. Each receiver gets a position fixed on a body turning at a rate Ω about an axis. GM, Ω, the flattening term, 874 unknowns in all, are adjusted until the predicted speeds match the 467,192 measured ones. Each receiver's own clock rate is a free unknown at every epoch. **The receivers start on a flat map**, an azimuthal projection through the North Pole with GM 25 % too small; each receiver is placed on that map by its latitude and longitude, taken as angles from its file; the satellites start from the orbits they broadcast, the one input a globe model made. The restarts in the table below show what the start decides and what it does not.

*Figure caption:* **From a flat map to a ball, by the Doppler alone.** Left: the 80 receivers, iteration by iteration of the fit, in a tilted view that turns about the rotation axis (dashed), with the centre the orbits go round (cross). They start on a flat azimuthal map 6,371 km above the centre (orange disc); each iteration moves them to where the measured speeds put them, and they end on a ball. The wire sphere is drawn at 6,371 km for reference, not fitted; the view zooms as the network shrinks (scale bar). Right: each receiver's distance from the centre against its latitude: spread over thousands of kilometres at the start, all in the band 6,357–6,381 km at the end. Blue north, orange south. Click to pause.

$$\ddot{\mathbf{r}} = -\frac{GM}{r^3}\,\mathbf{r} + \mathbf{a}_{J_2} + \mathbf{a}_\odot + \mathbf{a}_{\text{Moon}},\qquad \mathbf{p}(t) = R_z(\Omega t)\,\mathbf{p}_0$$
$${\dot\rho\,\left(1 + \frac{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}_s}{c}\right) = \mathbf{u}\cdot(\mathbf{v}_s - \mathbf{v}_p)} + \delta\dot t_k$$

r is a satellite's position from the centre of attraction, p a receiver's, turned by the rotation R_z(Ωt) about the axis; u is the unit vector from receiver to satellite along the line of sight, v_s and v_p their velocities, the satellite's taken one light time earlier; δṫ_k is receiver k's clock rate at that epoch. The fit also carries the slant air delay's rate (one zenith delay per receiver, a flat layer), each satellite clock's offset and its relativistic drift −2 r·v/c².

*Figure caption:* The fit from its flat start: the speeds left unexplained (logarithmic, m/s) and the spread of the receivers' distances from the centre of the orbits, at each accepted iteration, before any point is rejected.

**The same points fitted from other starts. Δ is the difference with the main solution: GM and Ω in parts per billion, the largest displacement of any receiver in metres.**

| Start | rms (mm/s) | ΔGM (ppb) | ΔΩ (ppb) | Largest receiver shift |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| receivers at their catalogue positions, GM and J₂ accepted | 2.6 | -27.0 | -0.0 | 0.01 m |
| every receiver on a 3,000 km ball, GM 25 % low | 2.6 | -8.6 | -0.0 | 0.00 m |
| every satellite 5 % too high, receivers on the flat map | 2.6 | -9.5 | 0.0 | 0.00 m |
| every satellite 5 % too high, receivers at their catalogue positions | 2.6 | -7.0 | -0.0 | 0.00 m |
| every receiver at a random place on the flat map | 42,078.3 | — | — | another minimum |
| the Moon 10 % farther (GM/d³ kept) | 2.6 | -980.9 | 13.5 | 3.57 m |

- 467,192 speedsGM 3.986016 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² (+2.8 ppm)Ω 7.292116 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s (+71 ppb)rms 2.6 mm/sbest plane: 131 m/s

**The result.** The speeds are reproduced to 2.6 mm/s rms over 467,192 points, out of a signal of hundreds of m/s. The Earth's GM comes out at 3.986016 × 10¹⁴ m³/s², +2.8 ppm from the value adopted by the IERS, 3.986004418 × 10¹⁴[8]; the rotation at Ω = 7.292116 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s, one turn in 23 h 56 min 4.09 s, +71 ppb from the IERS value 7.292115 × 10⁻⁵[8]. The formal uncertainties are ±542 parts per billion on GM and ±17 on Ω; they assume independent errors. GM departs from the adopted value by 5 of them and Ω by 4: more than the formal uncertainties allow, a measure of what one day and the truncated forces leave out (see Limits). The receivers end 29 m from the positions in their files (median), positions this fit never read.

## The receivers sit on a ball, flattened at the poles [evidence: measurement]

**Every receiver ends between 6,357.6 and 6,380.6 km from the point the satellites orbit.** The nearest are in Antarctica and the Arctic, the farthest near the equator and on the high plateaus of the Andes and of Ethiopia. Laid on an ellipse, the distances give an equatorial radius of 6,378.8 km and a flattening of 1/291[9]; what is left, 0.70 km rms, is mostly the receivers' heights above sea level. The best plane through the same receivers misses them by 3,417 km rms.

$${r(\varphi) \approx a\,(1 - f\,\sin^2\varphi)},\qquad f = \frac{a-b}{a}$$

r is a receiver's distance from the centre, φ its geocentric latitude (the angle at the centre, from the fitted position), a and b the equatorial and polar radii. Fitted on the 79 receivers: a = 6,378.8 km, 1/f = 291.

*Figure caption:* Each receiver's distance from the centre of the orbits against its latitude (dots), and the fitted ellipse (line). Excluded receivers in grey. The vertical axis starts at 6,350 km; the best plane through the receivers would put them thousands of kilometres off this axis.

$$J_2 = \frac{\mu_J}{GM\,a^2},\qquad q = \frac{\Omega^2 a^3}{GM}$$
$${f \approx \tfrac32 J_2 + \tfrac12 q}$$

μ_J is the oblateness term of the satellites' force, fitted with the rest (1.7473 × 10²⁵ m⁵/s²); J₂ = 1.0773 × 10⁻³ and q = 3.462 × 10⁻³, the ratio of the spin's push to gravity at the equator. Clairaut's relation for a fluid body in equilibrium[10] turns them into a flattening of 1/299: the same flattening seen a second way, in the satellites' motion rather than in the receivers' positions.

## Kepler's third law at three heights [evidence: measurement]

**Above, one GM was shared by every satellite: Kepler's third law was assumed.** Given its own GM, each satellite tests it: from its period and the size of its orbit, n²a³. GLONASS orbits at 25,507 km, GPS at 26,560 km, Galileo at 29,600 km, with periods from 11 h 16 min to 14 h 05 min. The 78 satellites give the same GM to 21 parts per million (standard deviation), and the three constellations' medians agree to 10.5 ppm. The Moon, 15 times farther out (Orbit tab), gives the same law.

*Figure caption:* **Three orbits, one GM, and how an orbit is checked.** Left, to scale: the Earth and the median orbits of GLONASS, GPS and Galileo found by the fit. Each satellite turns at the period its own constellation's GM gives, T = 2π√(a³/GM): the higher orbit is the slower, and n²a³ comes out the same for the three. Right, validating an orbit: from the fitted orbit of GPS satellite G32 and the receiver's place, the speed of the satellite toward Wettzell is computed for every five minutes of the day (blue line, drawn in advance); the measured speeds arrive as the day goes by (dots). Below, their difference in millimetres per second, against speeds of several hundred metres per second: an orbit is accepted when it predicts the next measurements this closely, at every receiver that sees the satellite. One day is played in 24 seconds. Click to pause.

$${GM_j = n_j^2\,a_j^3},\qquad n_j = \frac{2\pi}{T_j}$$

n_j is satellite j's mean motion, T_j its period and a_j its semi-major axis, all fitted to its own Doppler; the J₂ and Sun–Moon terms are kept in the motion, so GM_j is the point mass that each orbit needs.

*Figure caption:* GM from each satellite's own orbit, against its semi-major axis: GLONASS, GPS and Galileo. The vertical axis is in parts per million around the shared solution. A failure of the third law would tilt the three groups or separate them.

## The flat model, steel-manned

**The same points, the same satellites, the same freedoms, and one constraint: every receiver on one plane.** The plane's tilt and height and each receiver's position on it are free; the satellites keep Newtonian orbits around a centre that the fit may put anywhere above or below the plane; GM, Ω, the clocks and the air are as free as on the globe. It is generous: a flat model has no orbits to offer, and is given these. The fit is started twice, from the plane that best fits the globe's receivers and from the classic disc, the receivers on an azimuthal map perpendicular to the axis, and the better result is kept.

> **The best plane leaves 131 m/s unexplained**, against 2.6 mm/s for the receivers left free: 50,000 times more. Half of its residuals exceed 69 m/s and one in a hundred 407 m/s; the plane it settles on is tilted 92° from the rotation axis. **What would vindicate the flat model:** receivers held on a plane fitting the Doppler as well as free ones, to a few millimetres per second; or satellites needing different GM for their periods.

*Figure caption:* One satellite over Wettzell through the day: the measured speeds (dots), the globe solution (blue) and the best flat solution (orange). The receiver's clock rate is taken out of the points as each model estimates it.

## Limits

**One day, 80 receivers, every five minutes.** 1 receiver (BRMG) and 1 satellite (E04) are left out because their residuals lie more than 3 standard deviations from the others', and 14,057 single points (2.5 %) for the same reason, the rule of this site. The forces are truncated: no higher terms of the Earth's field and no pressure of sunlight, which is why 2.6 mm/s remains instead of a millimetre. The Doppler cannot tell north from south, since the mirror image of the whole solution fits as well; the first receiver's longitude, an angle, only turns the drawing. The satellites' first guess is the broadcast orbit, made with a globe model; the restarts show it does not decide the answer: every satellite started 5 % too high still lands on the same solution when the receivers start from their catalogue positions, but not when they also start on the flat map, where the fit ends in another minimum, at 49 m/s. With every receiver dropped at a random place on the flat map, it also ends in another minimum, at 117 m/s: the fit needs the receivers' rough directions to find its way, and the solution it then finds is the one with by far the smallest residual. Changing the Moon's distance in kilometres by 10 %, with GM/d³ kept as its period gives it, moves GM by 0.8 ppm and the receivers by 3.5 m.

**See also**[Orbit](/ai/orb.md)[GPS](/ai/gps.md)[Rotation](/ai/rot.md)[Moon](/ai/moon.md)[Gravity](/ai/grav.md)

# How fast, how far: a clock of the Earth's motions, and the distance scale

> Tab "Scale" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-scale. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Scale · the Earth's motions on one clock, and the distances*

The Earth turns, goes round the Sun, its axis and its orbit slowly swing, and the Sun itself goes round the Galaxy. The clock below shows all five at once, each hand at its true angle now and turning at its true speed: nothing is sped up. Then the distances, from the Earth's radius to the next galaxy, each measured with the step before it.

## A clock of the Earth's motions

**Five hands, five periods.** The first is the Earth's rotation relative to the stars, one turn in 23 h 56 min 4.1 s: the Earth Rotation Angle of the IERS, the same angle the ring lasers and the satellites measure in the Rotation and Satellites tabs[1]. The second is the Earth going round the Sun, one turn in 365.256 days[2]. The third is the slow turn of the Earth's axis, the precession of the equinoxes that Hipparchus found by comparing star positions, one turn in 25,770 years[3]. The fourth is the slow turn of the orbit itself, its long axis swinging round in 111,360 years[2]. The fifth is the Sun going round the centre of the Galaxy: the radio source Sgr A*, at the centre, seems to slide along the Milky Way by 6.411 thousandths of an arcsecond a year, the reflection of our own motion, one turn in 202 million years[4].

*Figure caption:* **The Earth's motions, at their true speeds.** Left: each hand at its true angle at this moment, on the computer's clock, counted counterclockwise as seen from the north. Even the fastest hand, the rotation, turns only a quarter of a degree a minute, so the dial seems still. Right: for each hand, its angle now, with enough decimals that the last ones change as you watch; how far it has turned since the page opened; and a tape graduated in the hand's own angle (arcseconds, or millionths of an arcsecond for the slow ones), sliding at the hand's true rate. The graduation and its rate are printed: nothing is sped up. Click to show one frame a second.

$${\theta(t) = \theta_0 + 360^\circ\,\frac{t - t_0}{T}},\qquad \omega = \frac{360^\circ}{T}$$

θ is a hand's angle, θ₀ its angle at t₀ = 1 January 2000 at noon (J2000), T its period and t the time on your computer. That is the whole program: each hand is a straight line in time. Its code is a few lines in `src/tabs/scale/logic.js` (function `armAngle`), with the five values of T and θ₀ and their sources. Open the page twice an hour apart: the rotation hand has turned 15.04°, the orbit hand 0.041°.

**The five hands: their period, how fast their angle changes, and the speed of travel it means where it applies (v = ω r: at the equator, on the Earth's orbit, around the Galaxy)[5][6][7].**

| Hand | One turn | Angular speed | Speed of travel |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The Earth's rotation | 23 h 56 min 4.1 s | 15.04″/s | 0.465 km/s |
| The Earth around the Sun | 365.256 days | 0.0411″/s | 29.78 km/s |
| Precession of the axis | 25,770 years | 1.594 µas/s | — |
| Precession of the orbit | 111,360 years | 0.369 µas/s | — |
| The Sun around the Galaxy | 202 million years | 0.203 nas/s | ~251 km/s |

$${v = \omega\,r = \frac{2\pi r}{T}}$$
$$v_\text{orbit} = \frac{2\pi\,(1\ \text{AU})}{1\ \text{year}},\qquad v_\odot = 4.74\,\mu\,R_0$$

r is the radius of the circle: the Earth's equatorial radius, the astronomical unit, or the Sun's distance from the Galactic centre R₀ = 8.275 kpc[7]. μ is Sgr A*'s apparent motion in milliarcseconds per year and 4.74 converts mas/yr × kpc into km/s. You are moving at 0.465 km/s around the axis (at the equator), 29.78 km/s around the Sun and about 251 km/s around the Galaxy.

**In one minute** you are carried 1,787 km around the Sun and about 15,100 km around the Galaxy. None of it is felt, because the motions are almost perfectly smooth: what the body feels is acceleration, and the largest here, toward the Earth's axis at the equator, is 0.034 m/s², a third of a percent of gravity.

> **On a flat model,** the first hand belongs to the sky, which turns over a ground at rest, and the other four have no counterpart: the Sun circles above the disc every day, and nothing goes round anything over a year. The ring lasers of the Rotation tab, which feel a rotation without looking at the sky, and the satellites, which see the receivers turn under their orbits, are where the two pictures part.

## The distance scale

**Each step is measured with the one before it.** The Earth's radius comes from angles and lengths on the ground (Results tab). The Moon's distance follows from its parallax seen from opposite sides of the Earth, and now from laser echoes timed to a fraction of a nanosecond (Moon tab). The Sun's distance, the astronomical unit, comes from light time, aberration and Doppler shifts (Orbit tab), and radar echoes from the planets[6]. With the Earth's orbit as a baseline, the nearest stars shift back and forth each year: their parallax gives their distance, Proxima Centauri's 0.768″ puts it at 4.25 light-years[9]. The orbits of the stars around the Galactic centre, followed in position and in Doppler velocity, give its distance[7]; and stars whose brightness is known from their pulsation period, calibrated on parallaxes, give the distance of the next galaxy[10].

*Figure caption:* The distance scale on a logarithmic axis, each tick ten times the one before. Blue: the distances measured, each from the step before it. Orange: where the flat models put the Sun, a few thousand kilometres up (the best flat lamp of the Orbit tab, fitted to the Sun's Doppler shift); the measured Sun is fifteen thousand times farther.

**The steps of the scale, the time light takes to cross them, and how they are measured[6][7][8][9][10].**

| Object | Distance | Light time | Measured by | Tab |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Earth (radius) | 6,371 km | 0.02 s | angles and lengths on the ground | [Results](/ai/results.md) |
| Moon | 384,400 km | 1.28 s | parallax; laser echoes | [Moon](/ai/moon.md) |
| Sun | 149.6 million km | 8 min 19 s | light time, aberration, Doppler; radar | [Orbit](/ai/orb.md) |
| Neptune | 4,515.0 million km | 4.2 h | Kepler's third law with its period; spacecraft | [Orbit](/ai/orb.md) |
| Proxima Centauri | 4.25 light-years | 4.25 light-years | parallax (Gaia) | [Orbit](/ai/orb.md) |
| Galactic centre | 26,990 light-years | 26,989.64 light-years | orbits of the stars around Sgr A* | [Satellites](/ai/sat.md) |
| Andromeda galaxy | 2,482,076 light-years | 2,482,068 light-years | Cepheids calibrated on parallaxes | [Results](/ai/results.md) |

*Figure caption:* **Powers of ten, from the Earth to Andromeda.** The Earth stays at the centre; the field of view widens tenfold about every second and a half, from 20,000 km to four million light-years. Each object sits at its true distance from us, in its own direction, with its distance circle drawn once it can be seen; every frame has its scale bar, and the bottom of the frame names the last object passed and the next one: the empty frames are empty because space is. Objects too small to see at the scale of the frame are drawn as dots. Click to pause.

$${d = \frac{1\ \text{AU}}{\tan p}},\qquad 1\ \text{pc} = \frac{1\ \text{AU}}{\tan 1\text{″}} = 206\,265\ \text{AU}$$

p is the star's parallax, half its yearly back-and-forth shift against more distant stars, and the parsec the distance at which p = 1″. Proxima Centauri: p = 0.768″, d = 1.302 pc = 4.25 light-years.

$${d = c\,t},\qquad c = 299\,792.458\ \text{km/s}$$

t is the one-way light time: the laser echo from the Moon comes back after 2.56 s, the Sun's light is 8 min 19 s old when it arrives, Proxima's 4.25 light-years, Andromeda's 2.48 million years.

> **The flat models' distances.** On a plane, two observers far apart see the Sun at different heights only if it is close: triangulated from a plane, the Sun comes out a few thousand kilometres up, and so does the Moon. Those distances are not measured from the Sun or the Moon themselves: the Sun's Doppler shift, its unchanging size through the day and the Moon's laser echoes all give the large ones. **What would vindicate the flat model here:** a laser echo from the Moon after a few hundredths of a second instead of 2.56 s, or a Sun whose apparent size grows by a large factor between sunset and noon.

**See also**[Rotation](/ai/rot.md)[Orbit](/ai/orb.md)[Satellites](/ai/sat.md)[Moon](/ai/moon.md)[Results](/ai/results.md)

# How far is the Sun? Ask a moon of Jupiter

> Tab "Sun" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-sun. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*The Sun · distance, motion & the analemma*

*Figure caption:* **Globe.** Both panels are what a level camera aimed at the year's mean Sun would frame. The 8 is one rigid curve on the celestial sphere, the same for every observer at every hour, so its drawn shape never changes — slide φ and it only turns with you.

*Figure caption:* **Flat disc, steel-manned.** The Sun circles above the disc at exactly the height that makes the equinox noon altitude correct for *your* latitude — the model is given its best free parameter, not a straw one.

Move to mid-latitudes and it breaks. Solstice altitudes miss by 10–16° at φ = 45–60°, and — unlike the globe's rigid celestial curve — **the flat 8's very shape morphs as you travel**, from 65°×16° at the equator down to 29°×11° by φ = 60°. Slide φ and watch it deform: no analemma photograph has ever shown that.

And the Sun's altitude never reaches zero. On a flat disc **the horizon can never cut the 8** — no sunset at any latitude, and no polar night at any pole, where six months of measured darkness are the plainest fact of Arctic life. The Sun can only shrink into the distance; it measurably does not.

The Sun's distance was pinned down by several completely independent routes — triangulating a planet from two points on Earth, timing Venus crossing the Sun's face from opposite hemispheres, and, most elegantly, using light itself as a ruler. Then, once a year of noon Suns is photographed from one spot, the sky draws a figure-8 — the **analemma** — whose exact shape is a fingerprint of the geometry producing it.

## A brief history of the distance (simplified)

**Each method independent of the last · values rounded**

| When | Who / method | Result (million km) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ~270 BC | Aristarchus — angle Sun–Earth–Moon at half moon; right idea, the angle (89.85°) was too fine for naked eyes | ~8 (20× too small) |
| 1672 | Cassini & Richer — Mars triangulated simultaneously from Paris and Cayenne, 7,000 km apart | ~140 |
| 1761 / 1769 | Transits of Venus — Halley's 1716 plan; worldwide expeditions incl. Cook at Tahiti; Encke's combined solution | ~153 (2.5% high) |
| 1849–62 | Fizeau & Foucault measure *c* on the ground — combined with Io's eclipse delays (below), light itself becomes the ruler | ~148–154 |
| 1961+ | Radar echoes off Venus + Kepler's third law | 149.598 |
| 2012 | IAU Resolution B2 — the au fixed by definition | 149.597 870 700 exactly[4] |

The routes share no assumptions: parallax needs only a baseline on Earth and simultaneous angles; the transit method needs timing; the light-time method needs a stopwatch and a terrestrial measurement of *c*. They agree to a fraction of a percent. One number, many roads.

## Rømer's clock, run in reverse [evidence: prediction]

In 1676 at the Paris Observatory, Ole Rømer noticed that the eclipses of Jupiter's moon **Io** — a natural clock ticking every 42.5 h — ran *late* when Earth was far from Jupiter and *early* when near, and he predicted the 9 November eclipse would arrive 10 minutes behind Cassini's tables[1]. It did. Light, he concluded, takes time to travel: about 22 minutes (his estimate) across Earth's orbit. Huygens turned that into the first speed of light.

**Now run it backwards.** By 1849 Fizeau had measured *c* on the ground — a toothed wheel and a mirror 8.6 km apart in Paris, no astronomy involved — and Foucault refined it to ~298,000 km/s[2]. Feed that *c* into Io's timings: the eclipse delay swings by **≈16.6 minutes** between Jupiter's opposition and conjunction, and the only distance that swing can correspond to is the *diameter of Earth's orbit*: 2 AU = c × ~998 s ⇒ **1 AU ≈ 149.6 million km**. Note what is *not* assumed: Jupiter's distance comes free from its 11.86-year period via Kepler's third law, which needs only angles; the relative map of the solar system was already known — Io's lag simply sets its absolute scale[3].

*Figure caption:* **Left:** the Earth and Jupiter round the Sun, to scale in astronomical units (orbits drawn circular and coplanar: the real eccentricities move the swing by a few percent). The dashes are the light leaving Jupiter for the Earth, with its time of flight. In the medallion, Jupiter up close and to its own scale: its shadow points away from the Sun, and Io (enlarged, and slowed down about thirty times) goes into it once a turn. **Right:** the light time over the last two years, one dot per few eclipses seen; it swings by about 16.6 minutes every 399 days.

$$\Delta t = \frac{D}{c} \implies 2\,\text{au} = c\cdot\Delta t_{\text{max}} \approx 299,792\ \text{km}/\text{s}\times 998\ \text{s}$$

The flat model has no account of this at all: a lamp a few thousand kilometres up gives Earth–Sun and Earth–Jupiter distance variations of a few thousand km — light-time wobbles of *hundredths of a second*, not sixteen minutes ticked out by a moon on schedule.

## Rømer's clock in every eclipse of Io timed since 1652 [evidence: measurement]

*[Figure: Animation: Io going round Jupiter and into its shadow every 42.5 hours; the Earth going round the Sun while the light from Jupiter takes 35 to 52 minutes to reach it; the eclipses timed from 1652 to 1983 and Harvard's photometric timings on the light-time curve; the delay against the Earth-Jupiter distance, one straight line giving the astronomical unit; the flat model's free curve landing on the globe's prediction; Europa making Io run early or late every 437.6 days]*

*Figure caption:* **The whole section in forty-five seconds.** Io going into Jupiter's shadow every 42.5 hours; the eclipses seen late by the light's time of flight, a swing of 16 minutes every 399 days; the eclipses timed from 1652 to 1983, and Harvard's on the light-time curve; the delay against the distance, one straight line whose slope is the astronomical unit; the flat model's best free curve, landing on the globe's prediction; and the wobble Europa gives Io, every 437.6 days. Click to pause.

**Three centuries of eclipses, in one file.** J. H. Lieske gathered 16,802 timings of eclipses of Jupiter's four large moons, from the manuscripts Delisle collected in Paris and Pingré's annals of the seventeenth century — Delambre's collection, long thought lost — to the observatories' publications of 1983[9][10]. 8,822 of them are of Io, from 401 observatories. Each line is one time: the instant Io faded into Jupiter's shadow (a disappearance) or came out of it (a reappearance), mostly by eye, and at Harvard from 1878 to 1903 with a photometer (439 timings).

**What is fitted, era by era.** Io's clock (its rate and a slow drift); where the shadow points, which is where the Sun is seen from Jupiter (an angle); the half-width of the shadow, which Io crosses off its centre as Jupiter's seasons turn; the 437.6-day wobble that Europa forces on Io's orbit[13]; one offset per observatory; and one more number: how many seconds the light takes per astronomical unit of Earth–Jupiter distance, A/c. The distances are in astronomical units only. The orbits are angles[11], and Jupiter's distance from the Sun, 5.203 AU, comes from Kepler's third law and the two periods, 11.86 years against one. Kilometres enter once, at the very end, through the velocity of light measured in laboratories[2]. Times are turned into the uniform time of the orbits with ΔT[12].

$$t_{\text{obs}} = t_{J} + \frac{A}{c}\,d$$
**A/c = 502.7 ± 1.7 s** ⇒ **A = 150.7 ± 0.5 million km**

t_obs is the time written in the logbook, t_J the instant Io crossed the shadow's edge, d the Earth–Jupiter distance in AU, A the astronomical unit and c the velocity of light. The figure: the eclipses' delay, averaged by distance in each of the six eras (one colour each), against the distance. Every era's points lie on one line, whose slope is A/c: about 8.4 minutes per astronomical unit. Its zero is not measured (Io's clock absorbs a constant): only the rise is.

*Figure caption:* Every photometric eclipse timed at Harvard, 1878 to 1903 (433 kept), as a dot: its delay against the date. The line is the light time from Jupiter, computed from the orbits with the A/c of these timings alone, 492.6 ± 3.0 s. The swing of about sixteen minutes comes back every 399 days, when the Earth passes between Jupiter and the Sun.

**The six eras, each fitted on its own; the error of A/c is a bootstrap over whole oppositions**

| years | eclipses | opp. | A/c (s) | check: DE440 (s) | no free year term (s) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ● 1660–1709 | 1,199 | 40 | **501.4 ± 3.3** | 499.6 ± 3.5 | 514.8 |
| ● 1710–1759 | 1,148 | 40 | **500.5 ± 4.3** | 497.1 ± 4.0 | 495.8 |
| ● 1760–1809 | 1,955 | 43 | **508.0 ± 2.9** | 506.0 ± 2.7 | 503.2 |
| ● 1810–1869 | 1,182 | 49 | **507.9 ± 3.4** | 509.6 ± 2.9 | 525.9 |
| ● 1870–1919 | 1,686 | 47 | **501.1 ± 2.0** | 501.9 ± 2.2 | 518.3 |
| ● 1920–1983 | 1,453 | 51 | **497.0 ± 3.5** | 498.8 ± 2.9 | 507.9 |

**The six eras together:** A/c = 502.7 ± 1.7 s, so **A = 150.7 ± 0.5 million km**. The adopted value, 149.6 million km[4], is 499.0 s: ours is 0.7 % long, 2.2 times its error. One fit of all 8,675 eclipses at once gives 504.6 ± 1.6 s; Harvard's photometry alone, 492.6 ± 3.0 s (-1.3 %). Europa's wobble comes out at 199–212 s in every era, 3.4 minutes.

**Limits.** The eras disagree more than their errors allow (χ² = 9.3 for 5 degrees of freedom; 497–508 s), so the error of the mean is widened by the Birge ratio[16]. The orbits are approximate elements, wrong on Jupiter by a few hundredths of a degree with the period of its year; a free term of Jupiter's year takes that up, so only the 399-day swing measures the light time. Without that term the eras range over 496–526 s; with the shapes of the orbits of JPL's DE440[14] instead (a check: DE440 rests in part on radar ranging), 497–510 s. Most timings are by eye, and a small telescope loses a fainter Io a little earlier: a drift with distance, of opposite sign for disappearances and reappearances, is fitted. Lieske reduced the local times to universal time and corrected the longitudes of some observatories from the residuals of an ephemeris[10]; a longitude moves every timing of an observatory by the same amount, and each observatory has its own free offset, so no such correction can reach the light time. 147 eclipses more than three standard deviations from the fit of the others are left out.

> **What would have vindicated the flat model:** Io's clock alone fitting the eclipses as well as the light time does, or a delay that does not follow the Earth–Jupiter distance. Io's clock alone leaves 210 s of scatter; with the light time, 52.9 s.

## The flat model's best curve for Io's delay

**A flat Earth has no distance to Jupiter that changes by two astronomical units in a year,** so nothing in it predicts a delay. Give it the best chance anyway: let Io's clock carry a free curve that repeats with Jupiter's synodic cycle, two harmonics, four free numbers, its phase φ read from Jupiter's place against the Sun in the sky; and a free term of Jupiter's 11.86-year year, two more, the same as the globe was given. Six free numbers where the globe has one.

$${\delta(\varphi) = a_1\cos\varphi + b_1\sin\varphi + a_2\cos 2\varphi + b_2\sin 2\varphi}$$
$${\delta = \frac{A}{c}\sqrt{a_J^2 + 1 - 2a_J\cos\varphi}}$$

φ is the angle between the Earth and Jupiter seen from the Sun (0 at opposition, when Jupiter is opposite the Sun in the sky), a₁, b₁, a₂, b₂ the flat curve's free numbers, a_J = 5.203 AU. The figure: the flat curve fitted to the 330 years (dashed) over the curve one astronomical unit predicts (thick), and Io's clock alone (the flat line). The two curves lie on top of each other.

**The flat curve's free numbers (as a phase of Io's clock: a delay counts negative), and what one astronomical unit predicts for them**

| term | flat model, fitted | one AU predicts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a₁ | 493.5 ± 2.0 s | 497.2 s |
| b₁ | 11.6 ± 2.1 s | -1.2 s |
| a₂ | 30.2 ± 1.2 s | 27.5 s |
| b₂ | 0.5 ± 1.2 s | 0.4 s |

**The free curve fits exactly as well as the globe** (rms 52.8 s against 52.9 s, with three more free numbers), **and its numbers fall where one astronomical unit puts them:** a swing of 493.5 ± 2.0 s against 497.2 s predicted, a second harmonic of 30.2 ± 1.2 s against 27.5 s. The flat model can copy the delay; it cannot say why the copy has the size and the lopsided shape of light crossing the Earth's orbit, nor why the same number comes out of every century. One term does not fit either model: b₁, 11.6 ± 2.1 s against -1.2 s, a difference between the months before and after opposition, when disappearances and reappearances are timed — the observers' habits, which neither model explains.

## An objection: Rømer's method with modern ephemerides

AlanSpaceAudits (Aether Cosmology Research Group) has published a careful null test of Rømer's method[15]: the times of eclipses of Io, Europa, Ganymede, Callisto, Rhea and Titan over 2023–2025, found from the positions of JPL's Horizons, each fitted with a constant period, and what is left compared with the Earth–moon distance. The slopes do not give the velocity of light back: 460,005 km/s from Io, 116,235 km/s from Europa, a negative value from Callisto. The residuals of Io and Europa keep a period near 436 days, which he reads as tied to the Earth. He writes plainly that he does not claim the Earth acts on Io, nor that c has another value. His question is a fair one: if Rømer's delay is light time, why does the method not return c?

**Our answer is the 437.6-day term of the fit above.** Europa pulls Io into a slightly eccentric orbit whose nearest point to Jupiter turns with their conjunctions (the Laplace resonance[13]). Seen at each eclipse, where the shadow points away from the Sun, Io runs early or late by about 3.4 minutes over 437.6 days — measured here in every era, 199–212 s. Over three years that period sits between the year (365 days) and the synodic cycle (399 days) and cannot be told apart from them, so a fit with a constant period passes part of it into the slope. Europa, in the same resonance, swings far more. With that term in the model, three centuries of eclipses give the light time to 0.7 %, and we think his 436-day peak is the wobble itself; his code is public, and the test is easy to run there.

**Where we agree with him:** Rømer's own observations were few[1], and one to three years of eclipses cannot separate the light time from the satellites' own motions. That is why this section uses 330 years, and the error it gives comes from whole oppositions resampled, not from the scatter of single timings. Read with the IAU's astronomical unit, our A/c means c = 297,589 km/s.

## The analemma: a year of noon Suns, one exposure [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: noon altitudes from an almanac computed for positions on the globe.]

Photograph the Sun at the same clock time every few days for a year and it traces a lopsided figure-8: east–west spread from the **equation of time** (orbital eccentricity + axial tilt, ±16 minutes), north–south from the **declination** swing (±23.44°). Both models below are driven by the same equation-of-time and declination inputs — what differs is the geometry turning them into a sky position. The flat sun's height is tuned *in its favour* so the equinox noon altitude at your latitude is exact.

**Noon Sun at your latitude — measured (any almanac / NOAA calculator)[6] vs the two geometries**

| Date | Measured noon altitude | Globe | Flat (tuned) | Flat error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Equinox (Mar 20) | **44.9°** | 44.9° | 44.9° | +0.0° |
| June solstice | **68.5°** | 68.5° | 64.4° | −4.1° |
| Dec solstice | **21.6°** | 21.6° | 33.3° | +11.7° |

The "measured" column is what any almanac, sextant, or the NOAA calculator returns — noon solar altitudes are among the oldest routinely tabulated measurements on Earth. The flat sun was granted its best possible height (5.0k km, equinox made exact) and still misses the other dates. Meanwhile its distance to you changes ~1.8× between noon and evening on a June day — so its disc should visibly shrink ~1.8× every afternoon. Measured variation: ±1.7% per YEAR.

> **Two more measured properties the flat sun cannot survive.** **(1) Angular size.** The real Sun's disc varies only ±1.7% over a *year* (perihelion in January — measured with any solar filter or pinhole), exactly matching a mildly elliptical orbit. A local sun a few thousand km up must swell and shrink by a factor of ~2–3 between noon and night, every single day (computed for your latitude in the table note above); it does not. **(2) Sunset.** The Sun crosses the horizon at a sharp, predictable time and is cut by the horizon *bottom first*, at full angular size. A receding lamp would dwindle to a dot near the horizon and never touch it. The analemma, the constancy of the disc, and sunset are three views of the same geometry — and each is a backyard measurement.

## The daily motion: one sky-clock, many observers [evidence: prediction]

What is actually measured, every day, everywhere: the Sun crosses the sky at a **constant angular speed** — 15.0°/h at the equinox, the equal spacing of the discs in any solar time-lapse, the reason sundial hour lines are evenly cut (corrected only by the ±16-min equation of time) — and at **constant angular size**. On the flat disc, a sun circling the pole at a uniform rate cannot produce either: it is close to you at your noon and far at your midnight, so its apparent speed across your sky must surge and slacken, and its disc must swell and shrink. The two panels are driven by the φ slider above; the equinox is used throughout.

$$\frac{d\psi}{dt} \approx {15^\circ/\text{h}}$$
flat, uniform spin: **varying**
flat, tuned for you: **wrong for everyone else**

The flat model's only escape is to make the sun itself accelerate and decelerate along its track so that *your* sky-rate comes out constant. But the sun is one object, shared in real time: the speed schedule that flattens your curve is simultaneously measured by an observer at another latitude — and for them it is worse than the uniform case. There is no schedule that works for two observers at once; the globe needs none, because a rotating sphere gives every observer the same 15°/h for free.

*Figure caption:* **One equinox day, whole-sky chart** (zenith at centre, horizon = outer circle, dots every hour). The globe's path is one arc of a perfect circle about the celestial pole — the same circle long-exposure sun- and star-trail photographs show — entering and leaving at the horizon with its hourly dots evenly spaced. The flat sun traces a lopsided loop whose shape changes with your latitude, with dots crowded on the far side and stretched on the near side — and the loop never touches the horizon.

*Figure caption:* **Apparent angular speed through the day.** Teal: measured (and the globe's prediction) — flat at 15°/h. Amber solid: the flat sun at uniform spin, as seen from your latitude. Amber dashed: what an observer at 10°S measures *at the same moments* if the sun's track speed is re-tuned to flatten **your** curve — the acceleration that fixes your sky breaks theirs. One sun cannot keep two skies uniform; a rotating Earth keeps them all uniform at once.

At φ = +45° the uniform flat sun sweeps your sky at 9–21°/h through the day — a 2.2× swing where clocks, sundials and time-lapses measure a constant 15. Re-time the sun's track to hide that from you, and observer B at 10°S — watching the same sun at the same moments — measures 7–18°/h. The tuning is not free: it is a physical acceleration of the one shared sun, and it must be wrong for everyone it wasn't tuned for. (Mean sun used here; the ±16-min equation of time is the same small correction in both models.)

## The sundial: a stick aimed at the axis [evidence: prediction]

Humanity's oldest clock is the hardware version of the last section. A sundial keeps time all year only if its shadow-caster — the **gnomon** — is set **parallel to Earth's rotation axis**, pointing at the celestial pole. Then the sun simply revolves around the stick at 15°/h, whatever the season, and the hour lines can be engraved once and trusted forever. The price of that trick is written on every dial ever made: the gnomon must lean above the ground by **exactly your latitude** — vertical at the pole, flat on the ground at the equator, 51.5° in London — which is why antique dials are cut for a stated latitude and mis-read when moved. Below, one distant sun held fixed at the left while the planet turns beneath it: drag to orbit, pause the day with the button.

*Figure caption:* **Five dials, one sun.** Seen from the side the gnomons lean at 65°, 35°, 0° and 30° south, each equal to its own latitude. The hour fans below all differ — splayed wide at 65°, tighter at 35°, running *anticlockwise* on the southern dial, and a horizontal dial fails outright at the equator, where the equatorial master dial takes over. Yet every shadow lands on the **same hour**, matching the readout on the globe, computed from one and the same shadow function: the agreement is geometry, not styling.

$${\varphi}$$
$${\tan\theta = \sin\varphi\cdot\tan H}$$
$${15^\circ/\text{h}}$$

All three follow from one fact: an axis-parallel stick sees the sun circle it uniformly. The flat model has no counterpart — under a nearby circling sun, no fixed stick orientation gives season-proof hour lines, the required "tilt" would not follow the simple tilt-equals-latitude law that dials from Egypt to China to Peru all obey, and a dial carried across the disc could not be corrected by latitude alone. Every garden sundial is a standing measurement of the axis it points at.

Watch the planet carry the dials through the fixed sunlight. The shadows sweep *together*, in lock-step, at 15°/h about every gnomon at once; dials crossing the terminator light up — sunrise, on camera — while the far side goes dark. That planet-wide synchrony is what makes "solar time ± longitude" work, and it is exactly what the flat model's surging, latitude-dependent shadow speeds cannot produce.

## The length of the day, measured at forty stations [evidence: measurement]

**The stations of the Baseline Surface Radiation Network record the sunlight every minute,** on instruments calibrated against one world standard, from 79° N to 69° S[8]. Count the minutes in which a horizontal pyranometer reads 5 W/m² or more and you have the length of the day as the instrument sees it. Here are March, June and December 2019 at 43 stations: 116 station-months. In June Ny-Ålesund had 24.0 h of light a day and Syowa, in Antarctica, 0.0 h; in December, 0.0 h and 24.0 h.

$${\cos H_0 = \frac{\sin(-0.833°) - \sin\varphi\sin\delta}{\cos\varphi\cos\delta}}$$
$${d(t) = \sqrt{r_s^2 + r^2 - 2 r_s r \cos\theta(t)} \le \rho}$$

Top line, the globe: H₀ is the hour angle at which the Sun's centre is 0.833° below the horizon (its radius and the refraction), φ the latitude, δ the Sun's declination; the day lasts 2H₀ at 15° an hour. The measured day is a little shorter, 18 min in the root mean square: a Sun just above the horizon does not yet give 5 W/m². Bottom line, the flat model at its best: on the azimuthal-equidistant map the point under the Sun turns around the pole on a circle of radius r, a station sits at r_s, and its day lasts as long as it is within ρ of that point.

> **The flat model, at its best.** Give the spotlight whatever reach suits each month: ρ = 11,029 km in March, 10,675 km in June, 11,367 km in December, fitted to all the stations at once. It still misses the measured days by 3.2 h in the root mean square, because on that map a southern station is far from the pole and the Sun's circle alike: it cannot have long days in December while a northern one has short ones, nor twelve hours everywhere in March. **What would vindicate it:** days of the same length north and south at the solstices, or a spotlight that fits them as well as the globe.

**Limits.** A pyranometer reads 5 W/m² only once the Sun has cleared the horizon by a little, later behind hills, so the measured day is shorter than sunrise to sunset by a few minutes in the tropics and by up to half an hour at high latitude, where the Sun rises slowly; thick cloud can shorten it further. A day counts only when at most an hour of readings is missing, and the stations are those whose data for 2019 are published.

Experiment 6 · the Sun with a pinhole

Measure the Sun's angular size and noon altitude — cardboard, tape measure, stick

A pinhole in foil projects a solar image whose diameter is the projection distance ÷ 107.5 — that ratio *is* the angular size (32′). A vertical stick's shadow at solar noon gives the altitude: alt = atan(stick ÷ shadow). Repeat at different hours and dates.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **time of day** and the **date** — morning vs noon vs just before sunset; equinox vs solstices. Set latitude above to see the predictions for your home.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the Sun's **angular diameter** and its **noon altitude**. The sky decides both.

**Hold constant:** the same pinhole and screen distance; never look at the Sun directly — project onto paper. **The tells, stated in advance:** a distant sun keeps the same 32′ disc from sunrise to sunset (±0.005%, far below your pinhole's precision) and its noon altitude follows the almanac column above; a nearby sun must change apparent size by whole factors through the day and can never reach the horizon at all.

At φ = +45°, June solstice:
globe → noon alt 68.5°, disc 31.5–32.5′ all day, sunset at a sharp time
flat → noon alt 64.4°, disc shrinking ~1.8× by evening, minimum altitude 15.8° — no sunset, ever

**Verdict rule:** if your pinhole shows the disc shrinking through the afternoon and the Sun gliding toward the horizon without reaching it, the near sun is vindicated. If the disc holds 32′ from morning to evening, noon altitudes match the almanac column, and the Sun is cut by the horizon bottom-first at the predicted minute, the distant sun on a rotating globe stands. The two predictions differ by whole factors, not margins.

Experiment 6b · who has daylight right now

Poll one instant across the world — no instrument at all, and the December version cannot be argued with

This is the cheapest experiment on the page: it needs no equipment, no clear sky and no patience. Pick one instant in UTC. Ask people in half a dozen widely separated places whether the Sun is above their horizon at that instant — a message each, or six public webcams, or six live-streamed city squares. Write down six yes/no answers against one clock reading. Both models predict that set of answers in advance, and they do not predict the same one.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **set of longitudes and latitudes** you poll, and the **date**. Spread the places as widely as you can in longitude; then repeat near a solstice, when the two models diverge most.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** a single **bit per location** — Sun up, or Sun down — all read at one agreed UTC minute. Not a length, not an angle, not a brightness. Nothing to calibrate and nothing to fudge.

**Hold constant:** the instant. Agree a UTC minute in writing beforehand and have everyone answer for that minute, not "when they get round to it"; an hour of drift is 15° of longitude and will smear the boundary you are trying to find. Take the Sun's *centre* on the horizon as the criterion, and ignore mountains — a valley floor loses several minutes.

**Kit:** none. A group chat, or the webcam pages that Antarctic stations, harbours and ski resorts publish for free. This is the one experiment on this page that a reader with no money, no sky and no daylight can run tonight.

**The tells, stated in advance.** On a sphere the lit region is *exactly half* the surface at every instant, and its boundary is a great circle, so your yes/no answers must sort cleanly on either side of one such line and no other. On the standard flat map — a disc with the north pole at its centre — the lit region is a spot cast by a Sun circling above the tropics, so it must be a compact patch, and places on opposite sides of the disc cannot both be lit.

**Then the December version, which is the one that ends it.** Between late October and mid-February the Sun never sets anywhere inside the Antarctic Circle. On a globe that region is a cap around one pole. On the flat map it is the *entire rim of the disc* — so the flat model must light the whole circumference at once, all 360° of it, while leaving the middle of the disc in darkness. There is no position for a spotlight that does that. Ask two Antarctic stations on opposite sides of the continent — say a Ross Sea station and one on the Atlantic side, some 150° of longitude apart[7] — on any January midnight, and the answers decide between the two geometries without a single number being measured.

**The verdict rule, symmetric.** The globe fails if your polled answers cannot be separated by any great circle — if two places 180° apart in longitude are both in daylight at the same instant while a place between them is dark, or if any Antarctic station reports a genuine night in January. The flat model fails if the lit set is consistently a hemisphere rather than a patch, and if stations spread right around the Antarctic coast all report continuous daylight at once. Both statements are checkable tonight, and only one of them survives.

## Further reading

Not cited above, and no claim on this tab rests on it — listed because it is what you would read next, or because it lets you redo the measurement on data this page did not choose.

- [« Démonstration touchant le mouvement de la lumière trouvé par M. Rœmer », *Journal des Sçavans*, 7 December 1676, pp. 233–236 — digitised by the Bibliothèque nationale de France](https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k56527v/f234.image). Four pages, in the original French, reporting Rømer's argument to the Académie: the eclipses of Io run late when Earth is receding and early when it is approaching, therefore light takes time. It is the first measurement of a solar-system distance scale that did not depend on the parallax expeditions, and you can read the original rather than an account of it.
- **Edmond Halley, "Methodus singularis quâ Solis Parallaxis sive distantia à Terra…", *Philosophical Transactions* 29 (1716), 454–464.** The proposal that sent the transit expeditions out: observe the transit of Venus from widely separated latitudes, time the contacts, and the difference gives the solar parallax. Halley knew he would be dead before the 1761 transit and wrote it for whoever came after.
- **IMCCE (Observatoire de Paris) and NASA JPL Horizons.** Two independent ephemeris services, one French, one American. Any number in this tab can be regenerated in either, from institutions with no stake in this page's argument.

# Two people watch the same sky turn opposite ways.

> Tab "Star trails" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-star. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Star trails · the one thing a rotation cannot fake*

*[Figure: Star motion at one place, globe and flat disc]*

- **Melbourne, Australia** 37.82° S · December solsticefixed point 37.8° due south, clockwisefixed point 19.4° due north, counter-clockwise30 min tail

*Figure caption:* **One sky, one place, two models.** The same 515 stars over Melbourne (37.8° S) at the December solstice, with 30-minute trails. Left, the globe, facing south: the stars turn clockwise about a fixed point due south, as high as the latitude. Right, the flat disc under its dome, facing north: the only fixed point is the northern one, low over the horizon, and the stars turn counter-clockwise about it. Real positions and colours, every Hipparcos star brighter than magnitude 4[7], gnomonic camera; on a narrow screen the globe is the upper panel; the readout above gives both fixed points.

Point a camera at the sky for an hour and the stars draw arcs. From Europe they turn counter-clockwise about a point in the north; from Chile they turn clockwise about a point in the south. That difference is not a matter of degree. It is a **sign**, and a sign is the hardest thing in this whole page for a model to get wrong quietly.

> **The result, and it is about the flat model alone.** The apparent sense of a rigid rotation is the sign of **ω · û**, where û is the direction you are looking. Reversing it means crossing the surface ω · û = 0; nothing else does it — not distance, not size, not speed. On a plane, everyone shares the same *up*. The dome turns about a vertical, so ω points up for every observer at once, and the fixed point sits at altitude atan(h/r), which is above the horizon everywhere on the disc whatever h is. So ω · û > 0 everywhere, and the sense is the same everywhere. The flat model does not get the sense wrong: it cannot produce a reversal at all, and no setting helps it.

Where the numbers come from, before any of them is used. The stars are the Yale Bright Star Catalogue, J2000, as published[1], checked line by line against Hipparcos: the largest disagreement is 2.4″, except α Centauri at 21″, which is its proper motion between the two catalogue epochs[2]. Precession to the date is applied — 0.36° by 2026, the same order as the precision claimed here — so Polaris sits 0.625° from the pole rather than the 0.736° of J2000. Proper motion is not applied; it is an order of magnitude below anything asserted. The twelve cities are Natural Earth, public domain[3], the same dataset as the coastlines elsewhere on this page.

$$\text{sense} = \operatorname{sign}(\omega\cdot\,û)$$

ω is the rotation vector — along the axis, by the right hand. û is the direction you are looking. The sense you see is the sign of their dot product, so reversing it means crossing the plane ω · û = 0 and nothing else does: not distance, not size, not speed. On a plane, ω points up for every observer at once and the fixed point is always above the horizon, so the sign never changes anywhere on the disc.

## The sky has a map: right ascension and declination

Measure the angle between two stars tonight, next month, from Paris or from Melbourne: it is the same angle, once the bending of light near the horizon is allowed for. The stars keep their places among themselves. Their **directions** can therefore be drawn once and for all on a sphere around the observer, as towns are drawn on a globe, and every star gets two numbers. That sphere is a map of directions only: it does not say how far any star is, and nothing on this tab needs to know.

*Figure caption:* **The celestial sphere, drawn as a glass ball seen from outside; we are at its centre.** The 960 stars brighter than magnitude 4.55 that have a position in the Hipparcos catalogue[7], at their J2000 places, with the Big Dipper, Cassiopeia, Orion and the Southern Cross joined up. Teal: the celestial equator, graduated in hours. Gold dashes: the ecliptic, the Sun's yearly path; it crosses the equator at 0 h. For six stars in turn, the amber arc is the right ascension and the blue arc the declination. The far side of the ball is the sky as it is seen from inside, so it is drawn brighter. Click to pause.

**Declination** (δ) is the latitude of that map: 0° on the celestial equator, +90° at the north celestial pole, −90° at the south one. The poles are the two fixed points the trails turn about. **Right ascension** (α) is its longitude, counted eastwards along the equator from the point where the Sun crosses it in March. It is given in hours because the sky is a clock: it turns once in 24 sidereal hours, so 1 h is 15°, and a star with one more hour of right ascension crosses the meridian one sidereal hour later. Sirius is at α = 6 h 45 min, δ = −16.7°; Vega at 18 h 37 min, +38.8°; Polaris at 2 h 32 min, +89.3°; Acrux, the foot of the Southern Cross, at 12 h 27 min, −63.1°.

$$\delta = a - (90° - \varphi)$$
$$\alpha = \text{sidereal time when the star crosses the meridian}$$

How the two numbers are measured, with a telescope that only swings along the meridian and a clock. a is the star's altitude as it crosses the meridian, φ the latitude of the observatory, 90° − φ the altitude of the celestial equator there (the formula is written for a star crossing on the equator's side of the zenith). The clock keeps sidereal time, 24 h for one turn of the sky, and reads 0 h when the March equinox point crosses. No distance and no model of the Earth's shape enters: two angles and a time.

## Fixed from one night to the next, not from one century to the next

From one night to the next the two numbers do not change by anything an eye or a camera can see. The whole grid slides by 0.14″ a night and the fastest star known, Barnard's, moves 0.03″ a night; the eye separates about 60″. Over centuries two slow motions add up. The first is **precession**: the axis the sky turns about is itself swinging, and it carries the grid with it, 50.3″ a year[8]. Hipparchus found it about 129 BC, by comparing his position of Spica with one measured 150 years before him[9].

*Figure caption:* **The stars stay, the grid moves.** The sky around the pole of the ecliptic (gold cross), 43° either way. The white ring is the celestial pole of the year; it travels along the gold dashed circle, 23.4° from the cross, and the grid of declination circles and hour lines (amber: 0 h) travels with it. The readout gives the nearest bright star to the pole and the coordinates of Polaris and Sirius in the grid of that year. The rate (50.288″ a year) and the tilt (23.439°) are held at their present values, which gives one turn in 25,772 years; in reality both drift a little, so dates far from today are good to a century or two, not to the year. Click to pause.

$$\Delta\alpha \approx (m + n\sin\alpha\tan\delta)\,t$$
$$\Delta\delta \approx n\cos\alpha\;t$$
$$m = p\cos\varepsilon = 46.1\,\text{″/yr},\quad n = p\sin\varepsilon = 20.0\,\text{″/yr}$$

p = 50.29″ a year is the rate at which the pole goes round its circle, ε = 23.44° the radius of that circle (the tilt of the equator on the ecliptic), t the number of years. The two lines hold for a few centuries and away from the poles; the animation and the tables turn the whole sphere instead. For Sirius (α = 101°) the second line gives −3.9″ a year: its declination was −16.58° in 1900 and is −16.75° in 2026, of which 0.04° is the star's own motion.

What it does to the numbers: Polaris was 12.4° from the pole in Hipparchus's time and is 0.63° from it in 2026; it will pass closest, 0.46°, about 2100. Thuban, in the Dragon, was the pole star about 2800 BC, and Vega will be within 4° of the pole about AD 13,700. Spica was 0.5° north of the equator for Hipparchus and is 11.3° south of it now. This is why every catalogue carries a date (B1950, J2000), and why the tables of this tab move the J2000 positions to the date before using them, by 0.36°. Precession does not separate the two models: a dome may be given a swinging axis as easily as a globe. It is here because the coordinates cannot be read without it.

The second motion is each star's own, its **proper motion**. Halley found it in 1718: Sirius and Arcturus stood more than half a degree south of where Ptolemy's catalogue had put them[10]. It is small, different for every star, and it slowly undoes the constellations.

*Figure caption:* **The Big Dipper from 100,000 years ago to 100,000 years ahead.** Each star is moved along a straight line at the proper motion Hipparcos measured[7]; the dashed outline is today's. Five of the seven stars travel together and keep their figure; Dubhe and Alkaid go another way, and the bowl opens. The motion towards or away from us is left out, so this is the right picture for the angles and not for the brightness. Click to pause.

$$\mu = \sqrt{\mu_{\alpha}^2 + \mu_{\delta}^2},\qquad \Delta \approx \mu\,t$$

μ_α and μ_δ are the two components the catalogue gives, in arcseconds a year (the first already multiplied by cos δ, so that both are angles on the sky); μ is the star's speed across the sky and Δ the angle it has covered after t years.

| Star | Proper motion, ″ per year | Years to move 0.5° (the Moon's width) | Moved since Hipparchus (129 BC) |

| Kapteyn's star | 8.67 | 208 | 5.19° |
| Groombridge 1830 | 7.06 | 255 | 4.22° |
| 61 Cygni | 5.28 | 341 | 3.16° |
| α Centauri | 3.71 | 485 | 2.22° |
| Arcturus | 2.28 | 790 | 1.36° |
| Sirius | 1.34 | 1,344 | 0.80° |
| Vega | 0.35 | 5,131 | 0.21° |
| Polaris | 0.05 | 39,368 | 0.03° |

*Figure caption:* Proper motions as published by Hipparcos[7], fastest first, then four well-known stars. The last line is the sliding of the grid, the same for every star: it is 5 to 1,000 times faster than any star's own motion, which is why a catalogue must be dated long before its stars have visibly moved.

## Southern stars from the north, northern stars from the south [evidence: prediction]

A star is called northern or southern by the sign of its declination, not by where one must stand to see it. On a globe, the horizon of latitude φ hides only the cap of sky within |φ| of the far pole; everything else rises. Sirius is a southern star (δ = −16.7°) and the brightest star of a Paris winter night, 24° up. Orion's belt lies on the celestial equator (Mintaka, δ = −0.3°) and is seen from every inhabited place. From Melbourne, Arcturus (δ = +19°) climbs to 33° and Vega (+38.8°) to 13°. From the equator the whole sphere passes overhead; only at a pole is one reduced to one's own half. And what stays hidden changes with latitude exactly as the cap says: Canopus never rises in Paris and culminates 7° above the horizon of Cairo. Aristotle already used it: stars are seen in Egypt and Cyprus that are not seen further north[11].

*Figure caption:* **Six places, north to south.** The same glass ball, positions of 2026. The white line is the observer's zenith and the white circle the horizon; they go round once a sidereal day, and the horizon sweeps everything except the red cap around the far pole, which never rises. The teal cap around the near pole never sets. For each place, three stars of the other half of the sky: teal if they rise there, red if they never do. Altitudes are geometric; near the horizon refraction lifts a star by about half a degree more. Click to pause.

$$a_{\max} = 90° - |\varphi - \delta|$$
$$\text{never rises: } |\varphi - \delta| \ge 90°,\qquad \text{never sets: } |\varphi + \delta| \ge 90°$$
$$f = \frac{1 + \cos\varphi}{2}$$

φ is the latitude and δ the declination, both positive to the north. a_max is the star's altitude when it crosses the meridian, its highest of the night. f is the share of the celestial sphere that rises at latitude φ: one half at a pole, 83 % in Paris, all of it at the equator. Same triangle as the trail formula above, taken on the meridian.

What would count for the flat model: Canopus or the Southern Cross seen from Paris, or Polaris from Melbourne, on any night. Check any cell against the USNO service[5].

## 1 · The fixed point, place by place [evidence: prediction]

- **Paris, France** 48.87° N2026-12-21, local mean midnight · 4 h exposure · facing the fixed point**globe** fixed point 48.87° N, counter-clockwise**flat** fixed point 47.57° N, counter-clockwise, dome 5,004 km

Nothing is fitted here. The globe puts the fixed point at the altitude of the pole — that is the celestial-navigation result, and it is argued there rather than again here[6]. The flat model puts it at atan(h/r), where r is the distance to the centre of the azimuthal-equidistant map. Read the table for what it is worth in both directions: at northern mid-latitudes the two models agree to about two degrees, and that half of the case is stated here rather than buried.

$$a = \arctan\left(h/d\right)$$
$$d = \sqrt{r^2 + \rho^2 - 2r\rho\cos\theta}$$

The flat model, edge-on and from above. h = height of the dome, r = your distance to the centre of the azimuthal-equidistant map, ρ = the radius of the circle the star's ground point travels, θ = how far round that circle it has got. a is what you would measure with a clinometer. Note that a is positive for every r, every ρ and every θ: on this model nothing ever sets.

**The flat dome is swept, never fitted. The break between the two models is not in the altitude — it is in the azimuth and in the sense, and both of them flip south of the equator without any value of h being involved.**
