Sphere, not ellipsoid: the WGS-84 geodesic differs by 0.3 %, which moves the Grand Mourre answer by 0.08′ out of a 12.7′ effect.[4]

## The crossing: one point that has to be in two places [evidence: prediction]

The strongest thing at this viewpoint is not a summit. It is the place where two ridges *touch*. Sweep left from Mourre Frey[5] and the near ridge at 16 km sinks; sweep right from Le Grand Mourre and the far ridge at 54 km rises to meet it. At azimuth **241.29°** the two silhouettes cross. Photograph that spot and you have measured nothing — you have only observed that two ridges touch — and yet the flat model is already finished.

> **The two points that meet are on opposite sides of the observer.** The near side of the crossing is ridge **C** in the table, sixteen metres from PeakFinder's point, at **1,683 m** on the IGN's LiDAR — seven metres *below* the viewpoint.[4] The far side, 54 km out, is at **1,809 m**, 119 m *above* it. On a plane only height enters the formula: lower than you is below eye level, higher is above, at every distance. So the two points cannot appear at the same height — and they do.
> On a sphere, at k = 0.13, curvature takes 200 m from the far ridge and 18 m from the near one, and both land near **−5′** (−6′ with straight rays), where the crossing is observed. Put the other way: a plane makes them coincide only for an observer at **1,629 m**, about **60 m** below the real 1,690 m — and no value of k can repair that, since a plane has no curvature to correct.

The cheapest test on the page: no instrument, no clock, no angle, not even a level — two measured altitudes, your own, and a photograph in which two ridges touch. **Its limit, stated plainly:** it works only because the viewpoint sits *between* 1,683 m and 1,809 m, and the lower margin is only **seven metres**. That margin is measured, not inferred — airborne LiDAR is good to about ten centimetres vertically, where the 90 m model used before was off by twenty metres on sharp ground — but two readings shave it. PeakFinder publishes the near point at 1,677 m, where the LiDAR reads 1,683 m at the crossing itself: the published figure is the one not to lean on. And the viewpoint is published at 1,690 m with ground at 1,686.9 m on the LiDAR, so a standing eye at about 1,688.5 m leaves nearer **six metres**. Know your altitude to a few metres — from a LiDAR spot height, not a phone's GPS — or the argument does not close; standing six metres lower would end it. The far margin, 119 m, is not in question.

## Why this viewpoint

The viewpoint is a documented spot at **44.09388° N, 6.92856° E, 1,690 m** in the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence.[1] Its interest is one summit: **Le Grand Mourre, 1,898 m**, 54.1 km away on a bearing of 241.2°. It stands **208 m higher than the observer** — and on a plane, a summit higher than you is above eye level at every distance, because on a plane only height counts. A sphere of R = 6,371 km costs it 231 m of curvature drop over that range, which is more than its 208 m of extra height, so it must sit *below* eye level. Refraction at k = 0.13 lifts it back to roughly level, and no further.

> **A 3°-wide window where the models disagree by 12.7′.** Ray-marching the IGN's LiDAR terrain out to 120 km,[4] the far ridge at 54 km is the skyline from azimuth **238.1°** to **241.2°**. Across that window a plane puts it **7′ to 15′ above** eye level; a globe keeps it within a couple of arcminutes of level (−7′ to +0.5′ with straight rays, −5′ to +2.4′ at k = 0.13). The sign does not flip at every azimuth — the older 90 m model said it did, wrongly — but the 12.7′ gap, 40 % of the solar disc, holds across the window. The Sun rides it on **24 November 2026**: first contact at **16:54:48 CET**, upper limb gone at **16:58:17**, for the standard atmosphere at the viewpoint[6][7]; plausible weather moves those by under ten seconds (the Atmosphere control shows how). Three and a half minutes, the neighbouring evenings nearly as good — one filtered video takes it.

The same kind of dated appointment, at the scale of a continent, is the total eclipse of 2 August 2027: the [Eclipses](/ai/ecl.md) tab states in advance when totality begins at Tarifa and at Luxor, and what a flat model would predict instead.

Two things the panel refuses to do. It does not treat the drawn skyline as evidence: both curves come from a terrain model, which cannot test the geometry that built it — they show *where* to point the camera. And named summits use their published heights, never the model's, so the terrain model never supplies the number a summit test turns on (the LiDAR happens to read Le Grand Mourre, Mourre de Chanier and Mourre Frey within a metre of them[4]). The crossing is the one exception: its two points have no published height good to a few metres, so both come from the LiDAR.

Experiment · photograph the sign change

One filtered camera, one synchronised clock, six minutes

Stand at the published viewpoint. Point a solar-filtered camera at azimuth 241°, start recording before 16:53 CET and stop after 17:00. Film a network-synchronised clock in shot, or note the timestamps. That is the entire apparatus.

Independent variable
**What you change:** the **instant**, and nothing else. The viewpoint, the azimuth and the target summit are all fixed and published in advance — you only choose when to read the frame.

Dependent variable
**What you measure:** the ridge's height above or below the Sun's centre, **in units of the solar disc**, read straight off that frame. The disc is 32.4′ wide, so the frame carries its own scale — you do not get to choose this, the photograph tells you.

**Hold constant:** one tripod, one clock synchronised to network time and filmed in shot. **The tells, stated in advance:** a plane requires Le Grand Mourre to stand **13.2′ above** eye level, a sphere with straight rays **1.4′ below**, a sphere with k = 0.13, **0.5′ above**. The spread between plane and sphere is **12.7′, or 39 % of the solar disc**, and it converts to about **83 seconds** of sunset timing at this latitude. **Read the limb, not the blaze:** a Sun photographed near the horizon is overexposed, and the white blob is wider than the real disc, so judging "half hidden" by eye runs early. Stop the exposure down until the disc has an edge before you time anything.

**Le Grand Mourre**, 54.13 km out and 208 m above eye height: a plane puts it **13.21′** above the horizontal, a globe **-1.40′** with straight rays. The two differ by **14.61′**, which is **45%** of the Sun's disc as drawn.

**Verdict rule.** The models disagree about the **sign** here, not the size: above eye level on a plane, below it on a globe. Photograph the summit against the disc. Above → the plane prediction holds and the globe's is refuted. Level or below → no k on a plane can produce that.

> **What would settle it for the plane.** If the ridge photographs 13′ above the Sun's centre at the stated minute — two fifths of a disc high, unmistakable at any zoom — the flat prediction holds and the globe's is refuted. If it photographs level with the Sun or below it, no value of k on a plane can produce that, because a plane has no curvature to correct for. The measurement is the same either way; only the answer differs.

## The arithmetic, in full [evidence: prediction]

Everything on this tab comes out of three formulas, and the argument is entirely about which symbols appear in them. Here they are, with nothing hidden.

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{\Delta h}{d}$$

Δh is the target's height above the observer's eye, d the distance between them. That is the complete formula. Notice what is **absent**: any length to compare d against. Double d and double Δh and α is unchanged, because a plane has no size. This is not a simplification of the flat model — it *is* the flat model, and it has no free parameter left to tune.

$$\tan\alpha = \frac{r_2\cos\gamma - r_1}{r_2\sin\gamma}$$

r₁ = R + h₁ and r₂ = R + h₂ are the two distances from the planet's centre, and γ is the angle the two radii open between them. **γ = d/R is where the whole disagreement lives.** The observer's horizontal is perpendicular to *his own* radius, and the target's vertical has swung away by γ, so the target has to be found lower than a plane would put it — by an amount that depends on **distance alone**. This is the exact form the page computes; it is not expanded or approximated.

$$\alpha \approx \frac{\Delta h}{d} - \frac{d}{2R}$$

Expand the sphere formula and the plane's answer falls out first, followed by a correction of **d/(2R)**. Everything this page argues is contained in that one term. Set R = ∞ and it vanishes and you are back on a plane — so a plane is not a rival model here, it is the **R → ∞ limit** of the same formula. Refraction does not remove the term, it only replaces R with R/(1−k), shrinking it by a factor (1−k). At the standard k = 0.13 that is a 13 % reduction. To cancel it outright you need **k = 1**, which makes the effective radius infinite — that is, k = 1 *is* the plane, and it would take a temperature rising 12.9 °C per hundred metres held over the whole sight line.

## Diagram: where d/R enters

*Figure caption:* Panel B's curvature is exaggerated ×90 by drawing a **smaller planet** and scaling the heights to match, then rendering both axes at one scale. Stretching the vertical axis instead would turn the globe into an ellipse and *reduce* the tilt between the two verticals, which is the very effect being shown. Panel C is at true scale and needs no exaggeration. This figure is generated by `make_fig_curvature.py`, shipped beside the page — edit the generator, never these coordinates.

> **And the flat model's own object.** The dashed outline is where a lamp circling above the disc would have to be. Its azimuth is the direction, on the azimuthal-equidistant map, from the viewpoint to the point the Sun stands over — **independent of the lamp's height**, so there is nothing to adjust and no refraction to appeal to, refraction being vertical. Its altitude does depend on the height, hence the slider: from 500 to 20,000 km the dashed disc never reaches the horizon; even at 500 km it stands 2.5° up while the real Sun touches the ridge.
> **Its size is fixed, not fitted:** the diameter that subtends the observed 32.4′ when overhead, 47 km at 5,000 km up. At sunset the lamp is 11,578 km away across the map, so it must look **12.8′ wide, 40 % of what the camera records**, whatever the height.
> **You will usually not see it in frame:** at the 24 November sunset it sits 40° from the real Sun, and an arrow at the border points to it; *Frame both* pulls back far enough to hold the two. That they cannot share a normal photograph *is* the finding.

## 10 January 2026: one sunset, four ways [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the ridge's distance from the terrain model, the Sun from an ephemeris.]

The same kind of appointment as the Celestial theodolite tab's 24 November, on the evening of 10 January 2026, when a P900 on a tripod was aimed in advance at the notch where the globe's Sun was due to set. The three drawn panels share that camera — direction, zoom, instant. **A**: the globe, the ephemeris Sun and the ridge with standard refraction. **B**: the same Sun over a plane, whose far ridge stands higher (the globe's ridge dashed). **C**: the plane with its own Sun, a lamp 5,000 km above the point under the real Sun — about 33° right of the frame and 23° up, never setting. **D**: the video itself. **E** and **F**: the same instant seen from above, as in the Azimuth tab — the globe with the point beneath the Sun and the great circle from this viewpoint to it, and the Gleason flat-earth map, where the Sun's bearing, laid off straight from the viewpoint, misses that point.

*Figure caption:* 17:11:06 CET

*Figure caption:* 17:12:37 CET

*Figure caption:* 17:12:40 CET

**What the camera saw, against a network clock.** Three phone photographs frame a website showing network time (NTP) beside the camera's screen, and so date the recording independently: at 17:11:06 the screen shows what the video shows at 17:11:07 by the camera's clock, and the recording counter drops by 91 s between 17:11:06 and 17:12:37, as the network clock does. At **17:11:06** the lower left edge of the Sun touches the shoulder where the ridge, rising to the left, levels off (azimuth 238.95°). The globe puts that contact at **17:11:05**, with the Sun about half hidden. The plane, with the same Sun over its higher ridge, puts it at 17:10:38, and at 17:11:06 has the Sun three quarters hidden, its edge cutting the ridge lower down the slope. The Sun is gone between **17:12:37 and 17:12:40**: the globe predicts the last light at 17:13:10, the plane at 17:11:29. The globe's lag of about 30 s is stated, not tuned away: the last sliver, seen through 54 km of low air, fades before the geometric contact, and the terrain model is bare ground, without the forest on the ridge (about 1.6′ at 54 km, some 12 s). All the times on this tab take the Sun's disc as it appears near the horizon, flattened by refraction (here 27.9′ tall for 32.5′ wide), each edge refracted at its own height.

**Eratosthenes, from one photograph.** The Sun's altitude needs no radius: it is 90° minus the angle between the viewpoint and the point beneath the Sun (90.44° at 17:11:06), plus the atmosphere's refraction. So when its edge touches the shoulder, the shoulder's elevation angle is measured: **1.5′** (0.9′ to 2.1′, depending on where along the edge the contact sits). The shoulder is 54.1 km away and 238 m above the eye on the LiDAR. On a plane its angle would be the slope alone, 15.2′; on a sphere, the slope minus a curvature term of about d/2R. Solving for R gives **about 5,900 km**, and 5,000 to 6,500 km across the uncertainties (the contact point, refraction k from 0.09 to 0.17, up to 20 m of forest on the ridge): the Earth's 6,371 km lies inside, as it did for Eratosthenes. A plane, an infinite radius, would need the shoulder at 15.2′, thirteen arcminutes above what was photographed: two fifths of the Sun's disc.

## 24 November, as a measurement: the Grand Mourre with a theodolite [evidence: prediction]

**The 24 November shot is a check, and can only be one.** The ridge's distance and height come from maps, and the Sun's position from an ephemeris that computes it for a latitude on a sphere. To turn the same line of sight into a measurement, the Sun has to be replaced by a level and the maps by a tape. A theodolite reads the angle α between the horizontal and the summit, face left then face right to cancel its index error. The distance s comes from a baseline of a kilometre or so measured on the ground with a wheel or a laser rangefinder, never a GPS, and the two horizontal angles from its ends to the summit. The height difference Δh comes from two recording barometers, one left at the viewpoint and one carried to the summit, with the temperatures at both ends.

$$s = \frac{b\,\sin B}{\sin(A+B)},\qquad \alpha = \frac{\Delta h}{s} - \frac{s\,(1-k)}{2R}$$
$${\frac{R}{1-k} = \frac{s^2}{2\,(\Delta h - s\,\alpha)}}$$

b is the measured baseline, A and B the horizontal angles at its ends. On a plane α = Δh/s, 13.2′ here; on a globe with standard refraction, about 0.5′. Without k, the result is the apparent radius, a bound on R as in the reciprocal-zenith-angle section of the Surveying tab; with a second observer on the summit reading back at the same moment, Δh drops out and the sum of the two angles exceeds 180° by about 25′ on a globe, against 0 or less on a plane.

**What each measurement costs in the result, with the map values used only to plan (54.1 km, 208 m). Planned precisions: α to 10″ (a used 5–20″ theodolite, two faces), s to 0.4 % (a 1 km baseline), Δh to 5 m (two barometers, temperatures logged).**

| Measurement | Planned precision | Effect on R/(1 − k) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| elevation angle α | ±10″ | ±1.3 % |
| distance s | ±0.4 % | ±0.8 % |
| height difference Δh | ±5 m | ±2.4 % |
| **together** |  | **±2.9 %** |

Experiment · the Grand Mourre, measured

Enter your own α, s and Δh

Nothing here comes from a map once these three are yours.

**You measure** α with the theodolite, s by triangulation, Δh with barometers

**You get** the apparent radius R/(1 − k), and the plane's α for the same s and Δh

Prediction before measuring: α ≈ 0.5′ on a globe with standard refraction, 13.2′ on a plane.

Best variant: a second observer on the summit, both theodolites read at the same instant (signal mirror by day, lamp at dusk).

R/(1 − k) = **7,324 km**

plane α = 13.2′ · globe α (k = 0.13) = 0.52′

> **What would vindicate the plane:** α within a minute of arc of Δh/s, about 13.2′ with today's map values. The globe needs α near 0.5′, and with no k at all, −1.4′. Twelve minutes of arc is forty times the planned uncertainty of the theodolite. This section is a prediction until the measurement is made.

Note that PeakFinder is itself a spherical calculation with refraction, so its panorama illustrates the globe prediction and cannot be used as a measurement of it.
2. [2] Jean Meeus, *Astronomical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., chapters 22 (nutation), 25 (solar position, ~0.01°), 40 (parallax) and 47 (lunar position, abridged ELP-2000/82). The implementation here was checked against [PyEphem/libastro](https://rhodesmill.org/pyephem/) on 42 dates spread over 2026–2027: worst disagreement 35″ for the Sun and 15″ for the Moon, against an effect of 12.7′.
3. [3] Astronomical refraction. Þ. Sæmundsson, *Sky & Telescope* 72 (1986), 1.02·cot(h + 10.3/(h + 5.11)), takes a **true** altitude and is what this page uses to predict where an object will appear. G. G. Bennett, "The calculation of astronomical refraction in marine navigation", *Journal of Navigation* 35 (1982), cot(h + 7.31/(h + 4.4)), takes an **apparent** altitude and is used the other way, to recover a true angle measured off a photograph. They are not inverses and are not interchangeable: swapping them overstates horizon refraction by 7.7′, a quarter of the solar disc. Checked against [libastro](https://rhodesmill.org/pyephem/), agreement is within 0.33′ from 40° down to the horizon. Below about −1° true altitude the formula is outside its range and the page's numbers there should not be trusted; the object has set in any case.
4. [4] Terrain from the IGN's [LiDAR HD](https://geoservices.ign.fr/lidarhd) digital terrain model (about 1 m; RGE ALTI where the LiDAR has a gap), read through the Géoplateforme WMS-R service by this project's `research/lidar_horizon.py`, EPSG:4326. Checked against the published heights at this viewpoint, highest ground within 40 m of each published point: Le Grand Mourre 1,898.8 m (published 1,898), Mourre de Chanier 1,930.3 m (1,930), Mourre Frey 2,025.4 m (2,025); ground at the viewpoint's own coordinates 1,686.9 m (published 1,690). Until September 2026 the tab used SRTM-derived 3 arc-second (≈90 m) data, which read those summits 22–23 m low.
5. [5] **Mourre Frey, 2,025 m — coordinates derived, not published.** PeakFinder's panel covers its coordinate line, so the summit was located in the elevation model of source [4] at the published bearing and range: the highest cell within 220 m of the projected point sits at 44.03250° N, 6.73333° E, which recovers 17.03 km at azimuth 246.44° against a published 17.1 km at 246.4°. The 90 m model read 2,016 m there; the LiDAR model of source [4] finds 2,025.4 m within 44 m of the point, against the published 2,025 m, which supports the derived position. The height used on this page is the published one; the position is this page's own and should be replaced when the published coordinates can be read.
6. [6] Jean Meeus, *Astronomical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., chapter 16 (Atmospheric Refraction): the formulas of source [3] assume 1010 millibars and 10 °C, and are to be multiplied by (P/1010)·(283/(273 + T)) for other conditions. At this viewpoint the factor is 0.836, which moves the predicted contacts about 35 s earlier than the sea-level value. The refraction coefficient *k* of the terrain sight lines, and the formula k = 503·P/T²·(0.0342 + dT/dh) the Atmosphere control uses, are set out with their own sources in the refraction tab.
7. [7] International Civil Aviation Organization, *Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere* (Doc 7488/3, 1993): at 1,690 m the standard atmosphere has a pressure of about 826 hPa and a temperature of about 4 °C, the default conditions of this tab. Real evenings differ; the Atmosphere control shows that plausible ones — a clear winter evening, a strong inversion, a summer afternoon — move the contacts by under ten seconds.

## Further reading

- **IGN — Géoportail and RGE ALTI.** The coordinates on this tab come from PeakFinder, a commercial application, and one summit's position had to be derived rather than read. The terrain on this tab now comes from the IGN's LiDAR HD model (source [4]), which also supports the derived position; the IGN's own geodetic points are where the coordinates themselves should come from next.
- [U.S. Naval Observatory — data services](https://aa.usno.navy.mil/data/index), for independent sunset times and solar altitude at the observing position. If the prediction on this tab is going to be tested against a photograph, the timing should come from somewhere other than this page.

# They swapped the theodolite for a clock. That part works.

> Tab "Theodolite" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-ct. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Celestial theodolite · someone else's experiment, taken seriously*

*Figure caption:* The instant that makes the measurement. The observer, the crest and the star lie on **one straight line**, so the star's altitude at that second is also the elevation angle of the crest. Nothing is measured with an instrument: the clock says *when*, and an almanac turns the when into an angle. The two angles marked at the ends of that one line are what the method turns on — on a plane they are equal. Elevation enlarged.

A flat-earth project called the **Celestial Theodolite** films a star being occulted by a mountain. The occultation puts the observer, the crest and the star on **one straight line**, and the claim is that on a plane, where every horizontal is parallel to every other, that one line must make the *same* angle at both ends. The clock supplies the angle: a star's altitude at a stated second is known to arcseconds. The published target list runs from 8.8 to 130.7 km and pays a bounty for recordings[1]; the method is argued in a recorded debate[2] and, as of the last check, in no methodology paper[3].

> **The idea is a good one, and this page has a rule about saying so.** Every reciprocal-angle test here levels an instrument with a bubble, and a bubble is gravity — the very thing under dispute. A star has no bubble. At 45° a star setting due west drops **10.6″ every second**, so a GPS-synchronised phone reads an angle to better than 0.2′. That is an order of magnitude finer than the difference between the two models over these distances. *The timing is not the weak part of this experiment.*

## 1 · What the clock buys

$$\frac{d\alpha}{dt} = 15.041″\,\mathrm{s}^{-1} \times \cos\varphi \times \sin A$$

How fast a star loses altitude. φ is your latitude, A is the star's azimuth counted from north, and the rate is fastest due east and due west and zero due north and due south. The sidereal rate 15.041° per hour is 15.041 arcseconds per second of clock[5], which is the coincidence that makes this method cheap: one second of clock error is a tenth of the effect at the shortest range on that list, and under a hundredth of it at the longest.

**Seconds of clock worth one arcminute of altitude. Read it as the timing precision you need: anywhere below about 60° of latitude, and on a star setting anywhere near west, a clock good to one second is already ten times better than the angle in dispute.**

| latitude φ | star due E or W | star 45° off E–W | clock worth 1′, due E or W |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0° | 15.04″/s | 10.64″/s | 4.0 s |
| 20° | 14.13″/s | 9.99″/s | 4.2 s |
| 45° | 10.64″/s | 7.52″/s | 5.6 s |
| 60° | 7.52″/s | 5.32″/s | 8.0 s |
| 70° | 5.14″/s | 3.64″/s | 11.7 s |

## 2 · What the two models predict [evidence: prediction]

Take the two ends of that line — the observer, and the crest the star is grazing — and ask each for the star's altitude at the same second. On a plane the two horizontals are parallel, so the difference is **0.000°, with no free parameter at all**. On a globe the two local verticals diverge by the central angle γ, so the same straight line makes two different angles, and the difference is γ. It is the surveying tab's reciprocal-angle test from the other direction: a prediction of exactly zero against one that grows with distance. A federal survey crew observed the same quantity over 70 to 93 km lines in 1977, though the report is a scan whose readings could not be recovered here[9].

$$\theta_{2} - \theta_{1} = 0 \quad \text{(plane, exactly)}$$
$$\theta_{2} - \theta_{1} = \gamma = s/R \quad \text{(globe)}$$

θ₁ is the star's altitude above the observer's horizontal, θ₂ its altitude above the crest's horizontal at the same instant, s the distance between them and R the radius. Neither height appears: the two heights cancel out of the difference, which is what makes this worth measuring. With refraction the globe's figure becomes γ(1 − k)[7]; the plane's stays exactly zero, because a plane has nothing to correct.

**Distances are the ones published on the project's target list[1]; γ is computed here, and the last column says how many seconds of star motion that angle is worth at latitude 45° due west. At 50.8 km γ is 27.4′ — the same 0°27′ the project's spreadsheet prints as the globe's slant, so this is not a disputed number. There is no measured column because no recording has been checked on this page, and a column headed *measured* stays empty until it can be filled from something published.**

| peak | s | plane | globe, γ = s/R | γ(1 − k) | worth, in clock | measured |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hound's Tooth | 8.8 km | 0.00′ (0.000°) | 4.75′ (0.079°) | 4.13′ (0.069°) | 27 s | — |
| Varley SE2, Squamish | 16.7 km | 0.00′ (0.000°) | 9.03′ (0.150°) | 7.85′ (0.131°) | 51 s | — |
| Blodgett Peak | 35.9 km | 0.00′ (0.000°) | 19.38′ (0.323°) | 16.86′ (0.281°) | 109 s | — |
| Cheyenne Mountain | 42.6 km | 0.00′ (0.000°) | 23.00′ (0.383°) | 20.01′ (0.334°) | 130 s | — |
| Pike's Peak | 50.8 km | 0.00′ (0.000°) | 27.40′ (0.457°) | 23.84′ (0.397°) | 155 s | — |
| North Peak | 130.7 km | 0.00′ (0.000°) | 70.52′ (1.175°) | 61.36′ (1.023°) | 398 s | — |

### How the clock column is worked out

Three lines of arithmetic, so the table above can be recomputed by hand for any peak and any latitude

Take γ from the column beside it, in arcminutes, and multiply by 60 to get arcseconds. Divide by the rate at which the star is losing altitude, 15.041 cos φ sin A arcseconds per second of clock — 10.635 at latitude 45° on a star setting due west, which is what the column assumes. The result is how much clock time that angle is worth: the size of the timing error that would be needed to fake it. Nothing else enters, and in particular no height, since the heights cancel out of a difference between two vantages.

## 3 · Where the execution decides the result

**The star is occulted by the skyline, not by the summit.** It comes down at an angle and vanishes wherever its path crosses the silhouette — a point on the ridge with its own height and distance. The instructions themselves say to aim for the summit where possible and to send daytime reference photographs[1]. In numbers: at 50 km, a crest height wrong by 30 m moves the angle by 2.1′, a thirteenth of the 27′ at stake — not fatal, but the crest must be identified before the arithmetic starts, not after.

**The refraction correction is switched off, and that is presented as the answer to refraction.** The method's own diagrams specify Stellarium with the refraction correction function *off at both vantages*[2]. But a checkbox in a program does not reach the air. Turning the correction off does not remove the bending; it removes it from the number, and leaves the observation uncorrected rather than unaffected. At the altitude in the worked case, 2°31′, astronomical refraction is 15.1′[6] — which is the 15 arcminutes printed in the same spreadsheet, so the size of the thing being switched off is not in dispute either.

**A switch with two positions and two places to apply it is a free parameter.** Off at both ends, off at one, on at one: those are four settings, and they move the answer by up to 15′ against a disagreement of 27′. This page allows itself exactly one refraction coefficient, announced in advance, applied to the globe only, with the uncorrected value printed beside the corrected one — and the reason for that rule is visible here. Whichever setting is chosen, it has to be chosen *before* the two angles are compared, and stated.

> **And refraction lifts a distant object; it does not lower it.** A ray through the lower atmosphere bends downward, toward the surface, so a summit is seen *higher* than bare geometry puts it and less of it is hidden — that is exactly what R_eff = R/(1 − k) means, an effective radius *larger* than the real one, curvature partly cancelled[7]. Any argument that reads the refraction literature as showing that summits sit *lower* has the sign backwards, and it matters: with the sign the right way round, refraction is a term that helps the flat model's numbers look closer, not a defect of the globe.

**And the second vantage is often not there at all.** The call for recordings asks for a single video from a single place[1]. With one end only, there is no pair of angles to difference, and the zero the plane predicts has nothing to be tested against: what remains is one measured altitude compared with a number the same software computed, which is where the next section starts.

## 4 · The simplest objection, and it is built from the method's own instrument

*Figure caption:* **Figure 1 — the rule.** One line of sight, three stations lying on it. On a plane every horizontal is parallel to every other, so the one line makes the same angle a at each of them.

*Figure caption:* **Figure 2 — the same rule, one direction later.** Same construction, one change: the line of sight is horizontal. That is the fixed point of the sky as an observer on the equator sees it, on the horizon, at 0°.

> The method carries an angle from one station to the next, and figure 1 is that rule. So carry it, in a direction whose angle is already known somewhere: the **fixed point of the sky**, which an observer on the equator sees at 0°. A direction horizontal at one station is horizontal at the next, the horizontals being parallel; apply it again and again — figure 2 — and the fixed point sits at 0° everywhere on Earth. **From Paris it is at 48.9°**, and Polaris marks it to 0.6°. No instrument, no second observer, no clock, no software — and the 2,930′ to explain is 86 times the biggest nuisance term the horizon has to offer.

**The two ways out, and there is no third: the instrument that supplies the measured angle assumes the very thing the conclusion has to deny.**

| If they keep | Then they lose |
| --- | --- |
| The distant sky of the ephemeris software — stars far enough away that their rays arrive parallel, which is what lets an altitude be tabulated at all. | The premise that horizontals are parallel, refuted by any observation of the pole from a mid-latitude. |
| A near sky — a dome a few thousand kilometres up, whose rays are not parallel, so the same direction can make different angles in different places. | The software, which computes altitudes on a globe with the stars at infinity. Without it there is no measured angle at all, and the method has nothing left to read. |

> **What this objection does not do.** It does not show that any recording is wrong, or that a timing is sloppy. It shows that the number the method calls *the measured angle* is defined by the globe, so a result cannot be read as evidence for a plane until someone publishes a flat star ephemeris — a dome height and a ground track per star — and recomputes the same occultations in it. That would be a real test, and this page would have to take it seriously. Nobody has published one.

## 5 · Which model fits the published readings [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: star altitudes from a planetarium program at positions on the globe.]

One number is measured: the second at which the star is cut by the crest. Everything else is computed. From that second an almanac gives the star's altitude; from the published coordinates, trigonometry gives the crest's elevation angle — **a different one for each model**. Subtract, and the leftover is the residual. This answers the obvious worry that the comparison must be circular: the star's altitude comes from the clock and does not know which model you hold, while the two crest angles differ by s/2R, which is 35′ at 131 km. The star altitude cannot sit on both.

$$\Delta = \theta_{\text{star}}(T) - \theta_{\text{crest}}$$
$$\theta_{\text{flat}} = \arctan\left(\frac{H - h}{s}\right)$$
$$\theta_{\text{globe}} = \arctan\left(\frac{H - h}{s}\right) - \frac{s}{2R}$$
$$\theta_{\text{flat}} - \theta_{\text{globe}} = \frac{s}{2R} = \frac{\gamma}{2}$$

**Why the half, when section 2 used the whole γ.** The chord joining observer and crest makes an angle γ/2 with the local horizontal at *each* end — that is the angle between a chord and the tangent. One end taken alone therefore sees half the central angle, and the pair sees all of it: γ/2 separates the two *models* at one vantage, γ separates the two *vantages* along one line. The calculator prints both under those names, *Central Angle (γ)* and *θGeo,Terrestrial,Drop (γ/2)*, in a ratio of exactly two[8]. H and h are the crest and observer heights, s the ground distance, R the radius, T the occultation second; θ_star(T) is the almanac's altitude, geometric when the software's refraction correction is off and apparent when it is on, and the crest angle must be taken the same way.

**One worked case from the project's published calculator, the North Peak sheet[8]. The heights, the distance and the four star altitudes are read from it; every angle below them is recomputed here and agrees with its cells to the arcsecond. The last three rows are the two-vantage test of section 2, run on those numbers.**

| Pikes Peak, 39 Aquarii, 2025-01-27 18:43:07 | value |
| --- | --- |
| crest and observer heights | 4300 m, 2073 m |
| ground distance s | 50.55 km |
| crest angle, plane — arctan(Δh/s) | 2.5225° |
| crest angle, globe — minus s/2R | 2.2952° |
| star altitude at the observer, geometric | 2.1024° |
| star altitude at the observer, apparent | 2.3256° |
| star altitude at the crest, geometric | 2.5562° |
| **difference between the two ends, measured** | **0.4538°** |
| **predicted: globe γ = s/R · plane 0** | **0.4546°** · **0.0000°** |
| residual on that difference | **−0.05′** · **+27.23′** |
| **their comparison: crest star − flat crest angle** | **+2.02′** |
| … which is the flat residual, plus the measured γ | −25.21′ plus +27.23′ |

*Figure caption:* The same case asked four ways: each model, with and without the almanac's refraction correction, and in each the crest angle reduced the same way as the star altitude. The bars are absolute residuals, so shorter is better, and the arithmetic is entirely from the sheet — only the subtraction is done here.

> **What the dataset returns.** Two questions can be put to it. The first compares the crest angle, worked out from maps and heights, against the almanac's star altitude — and that is the one that carries weight, because only one of its two terms comes from the software. The second is the two-vantage test the method itself advertises, where the plane predicts exactly zero. The figures below run both over every case, and the table under them gives the numbers. **The caveat travels with the result:** those star altitudes are Stellarium's, computed on a globe, so the second question is close to a check on the transcription rather than a measurement.

> **Why the sheet reports the plane as the closer of the two — worth following carefully.** The comparison it prints sets the star's altitude *at the crest* beside the flat crest angle *seen from the observer*: two different vantages. The gap comes out small — on the North Peak case the +13′35″ the sheet shows. But that subtraction contains the plane's residual at one vantage, **−56.5′**, plus the measured difference between the vantages, **+70.1′** — and that second term is γ, the quantity the flat model says is exactly zero. **The plane only comes close because it is credited with the globe's own measured curvature.** Hold the flat premise honestly — the star at the same altitude from both ends — and the flat residual is its worst score of the four.

*Figure caption:* Both studies over every case on file: the one-vantage residual at the top, the two-vantage residual below, each split between the models and each with refraction applied at both ends. The dots beyond the whiskers matter — they are the cases where both models miss together, which is the signature of a misidentified crest rather than of a curved or a flat Earth.

- Closest to their measured second**globe, refraction on** · median 2.08′next: plane, refraction on · 13.02′46 cases

**The same four series as numbers. Residuals are absolute, so smaller is closer to what was measured, and the median is the column to read first — one badly identified crest moves a mean and leaves a median alone.**

| series | median | mean | quartiles | beyond |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| one end · plane | **13.02′** | 17.42′ | 5.32–18.27′ | 1 |
| one end · globe | **2.08′** | 8.08′ | 0.77–3.69′ | 6 |
| two ends · plane | **22.50′** | 20.63′ | 3.68–27.26′ | 3 |
| two ends · globe | **0.03′** | 0.55′ | 0.00–0.40′ | 7 |

Which rows are in: every row of the *data_table* sheet carrying the seven numbers, less four kinds set aside **before the residuals were looked at** — rows the sheet labels *Test*, rows where the occulting body is the Moon, the four rows aimed at aircraft, and one row whose apparent altitude is below its true altitude, which cannot happen. Nothing else is dropped. Cases where **both** models miss stay in: at 1 and 7 km the two predictions are indistinguishable, so a joint miss is a misidentified crest, not a verdict, and removing them would flatter both. Adding the four aircraft rows would not change the direction — the globe wins all four, by more.

> **The short version.** Of the four ways of putting the question to the dataset, the globe with refraction at both ends sits closest to the recorded second, and not marginally; no arrangement of the flat model gets nearer. It comes with the limit that has followed this section from the start: the star altitudes come from software that computes on a globe, so this is the method's arithmetic checked against itself, not an independent measurement. **The independent version is old:** Canigou has been photographed from Allauch, 263 km off, cut out against the setting Sun since 1808, and the hidden-height tab shows what each model puts on the disc — a black mass taller than the Sun, or a notch an eighth of its width.

## 6 · The radius, recovered from the same data [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: crest angles from distances in km computed from coordinates and map heights.]

Every case can be run backwards. Instead of asking whether a radius of 6,371 km fits, solve for the radius each observation implies and see where they land. This is the page's unifying claim applied to flat-earth data: one R has to satisfy everything, and here it is being asked to emerge from a flat-earth dataset. **Only cases beyond 20 km are used**, and the threshold is geometric rather than chosen after the fact: below it the two models differ by under 5′, the denominator is the size of the crest error, and the division returns noise or a negative radius.

$$R_{\gamma} = \frac{s}{\theta_{\text{crest}} - \theta_{\text{obs}}}$$
$$R_{\text{raw}} = \frac{s}{2\left(G - \theta_{\text{obs}}\right)}$$
$$R_{\text{red}} = \frac{(1 - k)\,s}{2\left(G - \theta_{\text{obs,app}}\right)}$$

**Every symbol is a row of the case table above.** s is *ground distance s*; Δh is the difference of the two heights on the *crest and observer heights* row; G is *crest angle, plane — arctan(Δh/s)*, the only quantity here that comes from maps rather than from software. θ_obs is *star altitude at the observer, geometric* and θ_obs,app the *apparent* row beneath it; θ_crest is *star altitude at the crest*. Angles go in radians, so R comes out in the units of s. k is the terrestrial refraction coefficient implied by the sheet, 0.148 — that correction is written s/1,500,000 in degrees[8], which is that k and not the 0.13 the rest of this page uses. The three lines produce the three rows of the table below, in the same order.

- Radius from their data, reduced consistently**6380 km** · median of 28accepted value 6371 km

*Figure caption:* Three reductions, three answers. Same box plot as before — box between the quartiles, bar the median, whiskers to 1.5 interquartile ranges, dots past them — with the accepted radius drawn as a vertical line so the deviation is the distance to it.

**The same three as numbers, with the median's departure from 6,371 km in the last column.**

| reduction | cases | median R | quartiles | off 6371 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| γ · two ends | 28 | **6371 km** | 6353–6390 km | 0.0 % |
| one end · raw | 28 | **2942 km** | 2417–3457 km | -53.8 % |
| one end · reduced | 28 | **6380 km** | 6043–7281 km | 0.1 % |

> **Read the three lines in order; only the third means anything.** The first solves R from γ, the difference of two altitudes the software computed on a globe of 6,371 km — it lands on 6,371 by construction and only checks the transcription. The second uses the crest angle from maps and heights, genuinely independent of the software, but pairs it with a geometric star altitude when the occultation happened in the *apparent* direction; that mismatch, the method's default, returns a radius near 3,000 km — **not a plane and not the Earth, but a globe of the wrong size**. The third fixes the mismatch and nothing else. It is the one to argue with.

## 7 · What this page is doing about it

Criticising somebody else's observation is cheap unless you make one. The **observation** tab attempts the same experiment, pre-registered here, with three changes. The Sun stands in for the star, so the frame **carries its own angular scale** — the disc is 32.4′ wide — and no software turns a time into an angle. There are **two ridges**: a near crest at 16 km where the models barely differ, a control on the method, and a far one at 54 km where they differ in sign. And the prediction sits at **0°**, eye level, the one angle you can check without knowing where level is: the far ridge is either above the Sun's centre or below it, and the photograph says which.

The shot can be placed on these axes before it is taken, and that is worth doing because it uses **a different instrument**: a solar disc as the ruler, no clock, no star altitude read out of software. Beyond 20 km the plane's miss tracks (1 − k)s/2R — the curvature term itself, not a fitted line — with a correlation of 0.97, while the globe's misses stay flat with no trend at all. So the two boxes below are not just a summary: they are a prediction. The 24 November geometry, 208 m of height over 54.1 km, says where one more point has to fall on each of them, and arithmetic alone fixes it

- Flat residual against the curvature termr = 0.971 over 28 casesslope 1.28 against a predicted 1.00the 24 November shot must land at 12.4′

*Figure caption:* The same two boxes as section 6, restricted to the 28 cases beyond 20 km, with the 24 November shot marked on each. The mark on the orange box is the 12.4′ the plane will have to be out by; the mark on the teal box is the zero the globe will have to show. **If the plane is right instead, the two marks swap places** — that is the whole prediction, and the photograph puts the point on one row or the other.

*[Figure: The Sun sinking behind the ridge on 24 November 2026, through a solar filter, fixed camera]*

*Figure caption:* What a dense solar filter will show, minute by minute, from the viewpoint on 24 November — the disc, and the terrain only where it cuts into it, at true angular scale. The blue band is the extra ridge the plane requires; the black is the globe's silhouette. The profile is sampled every 0.1° of azimuth, which is the resolution of the terrain read and not a smoothing, so the facets are the data. Each frame is centred on the disc: it is the ridge that climbs through it.

> **Stated before the shot, which is the whole point.** Le Grand Mourre, 54.1 km away and 208 m taller than the viewpoint, must sit **13.2′ above** eye level on a plane, **1.4′ below** on a sphere with straight rays, and **0.5′ above** with k = 0.13. The spread is 12.7′, 39 % of the solar disc, and the Sun crosses that window on **24 November 2026 between 16:54:48 and 16:58:17 CET** (standard atmosphere at the viewpoint, 826 hPa; see the observation tab). Those numbers are computed, not observed: at the time of writing **no photograph exists**, and if it comes out against the globe this tab will say so — a verdict rule announced in advance binds whoever announced it.

**A first shot, 10 January 2026.** Before that date the same method was tried from the same viewpoint on a winter sunset, filmed by a camera aimed in advance with a network clock photographed beside its screen. At 17:11:06 the Sun's lower left edge touched the shoulder of the ridge, where the globe puts it at 17:11:05; the plane, with the same Sun over its higher ridge, puts it at 17:10:38, the Sun already three quarters hidden. Used like Eratosthenes' shadow, that single contact gives the Earth's radius: about 5,900 km, 5,000 to 6,500 km across the uncertainties. The last light came about 30 s before the globe's prediction, a gap stated rather than tuned away. The video, the photographs and the calculation are in the [observation tab](/ai/obs.md).

## Experiment 11 · time a star onto a ridge

**Independent variable:** the distance to the peak — the same summit recorded from several places, or several peaks at different ranges. **Dependent:** the second at which the star is cut by the skyline. **Held constant:** one clock discipline (GPS-synchronised), one star, the summit itself as the target rather than a shoulder. **Kit:** a camera that records a timestamp, published coordinates for both ends, and a published altitude for the star[4].

**Verdict rule, announced in advance and symmetric.** The globe fails if the two ends of the same line of sight return the same altitude — difference zero within your error, repeatably, at 9 km and at 131 km alike. The flat model fails if the difference grows in proportion to s, returning one radius near 6,371 km from peaks at three different ranges at once. Either way the refraction setting is stated before the recording and applied the same way at both ends, because a switch worth 15′ cannot be chosen after seeing a 27′ disagreement.

Deliberately left out: any claim about what the recordings show, since none has been checked here; the ellipsoid, which is orders of magnitude below the effect; and terrain models, since the argument is about the angle to a named point, not about a silhouette.

**See also**[Elevation angles](/ai/elev.md)[Refraction](/ai/ref.md)[Star trails](/ai/star.md)[Cel. nav.](/ai/cnav.md)[Surveying](/ai/surv.md)[Observation](/ai/obs.md)

# The air above us: why it stays, how it bends radio waves, why satellites do not melt

> Tab "Atmosphere" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-atmo. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Atmosphere · pressure, eruptions, radio waves, heat*

Three questions often asked as objections. How can the air sit next to the vacuum of space with no container? How can a radio amateur talk to someone beyond the horizon? How can a satellite survive in a layer of air at a thousand degrees? Each has a measured answer, and the same physics works on any shape of Earth: the shape shows up only in the details, which this page points out. The air also carries a measurement of its own: the pressure waves of two volcanic eruptions, Hunga Tonga in 2022 and Krakatoa in 1883, timed on ordinary barometers, give the Earth's radius.

## Why the air stays without a lid: the pressure gradient

**Gravity is the container.** Every molecule is pulled down; molecules collide and push on each other; each layer of air carries the weight of all the air above it. So the pressure falls with height, smoothly, with no edge: half the sea-level pressure at 5.5 km, a tenth at 16 km, a hundredth at 31 km, a millionth near 100 km[1]. At the top, molecules move at about a kilometre per second, far below the 11 km/s needed to leave the Earth; thrown up, they fall back like a ball.

*Figure caption:* **No lid, and the air still stays.** Seven hundred molecules thrown about with the speeds of a gas at a given temperature, pulled down by gravity, bouncing off the ground; there is no ceiling, and the ones that leave the frame come back. On the right, how many are found in each slice of height (bars), against the exponential law e^−h/H (orange): the profile holds by itself. The left axis gives the true scale for air at 15 °C, one scale height H = 8.4 km; the pressures on the right are those of the 1976 standard atmosphere at those heights. Click to pause.

$$\frac{dp}{dh} = -\rho\,g,\qquad p = n\,k\,T$$
$${p(h) = p_0\,e^{-h/H}},\qquad H = \frac{k\,T}{m\,g}$$

p is the pressure, ρ the density and n the number of molecules per m³, g the acceleration of gravity, k Boltzmann's constant, T the temperature and m the mass of a molecule. The first line says that a thin layer of air is held up by the difference of pressure between its bottom and its top; with a constant temperature, it gives the exponential of the second line. H, the scale height, is 8.4 km for air at 15 °C: every 8.4 km up, the pressure is divided by e = 2.718.

*Figure caption:* The 1976 standard atmosphere from the ground to 500 km: the pressure on a logarithmic axis (blue), falling smoothly over a dozen powers of ten with no edge, and the temperature (orange), which falls in the troposphere, rises in the stratosphere, falls again in the mesosphere and climbs to about 1,000 K in the thermosphere.

> **The objection** says that a gas next to a vacuum must spread out, so the air needs a wall, and a dome. It would, without gravity. With it, the same molecules form a column whose pressure falls exponentially and never meets a wall: that is what barometers carried up mountains, weather balloons and rockets have measured since the seventeenth century. **What would vindicate a container:** an atmosphere whose pressure stays nearly constant with height and then drops to zero at a definite altitude, where a wall would be.

## The air rang too: Hunga Tonga's pressure wave on 102 barometers [evidence: measurement]

*[Figure: Animation: the Hunga Tonga pressure wave lighting 102 US barometers at their recorded times; their band-passed traces side by side, two bands of pulses crossing; the short way and the long way around the globe adding up to one lap, and the radius from each barometer; the best flat-map predictions against the same traces; the Krakatoa barographs of 1883 lighting at each of up to seven passes; the three wave trains of the 1961 explosion at eight Japanese microbarographs, with the lap between the first and the third; every lap of the three events on one ruler and the radius from all of them; a summary]*

*Figure caption:* **Three explosions in under a minute.** The Hunga Tonga pressure wave lighting 102 barometers at their recorded times; their traces side by side, the pulse passing twice; the short way and the long way adding up to one lap, and the radius from each barometer with no distance and no map; the best flat-map predictions against the same traces; the Krakatoa barographs of 1883 lighting at each pass; the three wave trains of the 1961 Novaya Zemlya explosion in Japan, a lap from the first to the third; every lap of the three events on one ruler, and the radius from all of them. Every number is the page's own. Click to pause.

On 15 January 2022 at 04:14:45 UTC the Hunga Tonga–Hunga Ha'apai volcano exploded.[11] The blast sent a pressure pulse through the whole depth of the atmosphere, a Lamb wave, which instruments all over the world recorded circling the planet four times.[14] Every US airport weather station (ASOS) logs its barometer once a minute, and the logs are open.[10] This section uses 102 of them: two per state, plus Alaska, Hawaii and Puerto Rico. The pulse is typically 0.6–0.75 hPa high. The background before it is about 0.1 hPa.

Each record is filtered (a 5-minute mean minus a 2-hour mean). Then two arrivals are picked without any model of the Earth. t₁ is the largest pulse between 2 and 20 hours after the eruption, and t₂ the largest between t₁ + 6 h and 40 h. The windows are wide on purpose, so they cannot carry the answer. Each station's angle θ from the volcano is computed from its coordinates only afterwards.

$$t_1 = \dfrac{R\,\theta}{v}, \qquad t_2 = \dfrac{R\,(2\pi - \theta)}{v}$$
$$t_1 + t_2 = \dfrac{2\pi R}{v} \quad\Rightarrow\quad R = \dfrac{v\,(t_1 + t_2)}{2\pi}$$
$$v \approx 310\ \text{m}/\text{s}$$

On a sphere the wave reaches every station twice, once each way round, and the two paths add up to one circumference. So t₁ + t₂ is the same at every station, whatever its θ. On a plane the pulse is a circle growing from the volcano: it crosses each station once, and nothing comes back from the other side. To produce a second arrival the flat model needs an extra ingredient: an echo off a rim, or a bounce off a dome overhead. Both are tried below, in its favour.

- 102 barometers, 90 with both passagesbest plane, first passage: 3.2× the globe's scatter

R = 6,382 ± 73 km

95% confidence: 6,240 – 6,525 km · the mean radius, 6,371 km, lies 0.16 σ away

statistical ± 5 km (64 stations) · systematic ± 73 km, mostly the wave's speed (the two eruptions differ by 1.1 %)

flat models, tuned in their favour: no radius, and a scatter 9× the globe's (best: a dome 22,111 km high)

*Figure caption:* **The radius found, and how sure it is.** The dot is the median of the 64 stations that saw both passages. The dark bar is the statistical uncertainty alone, a few kilometres. The pale bands are the total uncertainty, at one standard deviation and at 95%. Almost all of it is systematic: it is measured by redoing the calculation with each of the other reductions this section shows (each passage alone, the start time left free) and with the speed the 1883 eruption needs, 1.1% lower (the small ticks). The speed measured during this event is not used: it was measured with globe distances. The mean radius, 6,371 km, falls inside the band. This is the value carried to the home page's table of radii.

*Figure caption:* **The V: 102 barometers, sorted by their angle from the volcano.** Each thin line is one station's filtered pressure. The first band of pulses arrives later the farther away the station. The second band arrives *earlier* the farther away the station, because the stations farthest from Tonga are the closest to it the long way round. The blue dashes are the globe with nothing fitted (R = 6,371 km, v = 310 m/s, start at the eruption). The orange dots are the plane's best fit to the first band, with its speed and start time both free. There is no orange second band: an expanding circle does not come back. The orange open circles are the second flat model, a bounce off a dome at its best height. At that height the bounced path is almost the same length everywhere, so they barely slope at all, and the little slope they have goes the wrong way: later the farther the station.

*Figure caption:* **One radius per station.** Open circles: R = v t₁ / θ, from the first passage. Dots: R = v t₂ / (2π − θ), from the second. Grey: excluded, more than 3 standard deviations from the others. The second passage, the cleaner of the two, puts every kept station within a few tens of kilometres of 6,371 km. Both sets drift slightly downward with θ, by about 1.3 km per degree (some 100 km across the United States). That drift is real and is left in; it is explained below.

**The radius three ways from the same picks, then with the start time left free**

| Reduction | Stations kept | Mean R | Spread | Off 6,371 km |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first passage, R = v t₁ / θ | 80 / 96 | 6,392 km | ± 89 km | +0.3 % |
| second passage, R = v t₂ / (2π − θ) | 76 / 90 | 6,380 km | ± 21 km | +0.1 % |
| both, R = v (t₁ + t₂) / 2π | 64 / 90 | 6,383 km | ± 33 km | +0.2 % |
| both on one line, t₀ left free | 157 / 186 | 6,373 km | ± 7 km (fit) | +0.0 % |

$$L = \sqrt{d^2 + 4h^2}, \qquad \dfrac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}d} = \dfrac{d}{\sqrt{d^2 + 4h^2}} > 0$$

The second flat model. The pulse goes up, bounces off a dome and comes down. Over the region the vault is taken as a ceiling at height h, and in a mirror the bounce becomes a straight line from the volcano's image, 2h up. Whatever h, that path grows with distance, so the echo would reach the farther stations *later*. The real second passage reaches them *earlier*, by 0.76 h per 1,000 km of map. That is a sign, not a size, and no height flips it. A dome posed on the map's edge adds nothing new: its shortest path runs along its foot, which is the rim echo in the table below.

**How closely each model's best line follows all 186 picks**

| Model | Free parameters | Speed | Start | Scatter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| globe, nothing fitted (R = 6,371 km, v = 310 m/s) | 0 | 310 m/s | 0 h | 7 min |
| globe, v and t₀ free | 2 | 310 m/s | +0.0 h | 7 min |
| plane, first passage only | 2 | 427 m/s | +1.5 h | 27 min |
| plane, second passage as an echo off a rim at 20,015 km (the map's edge) | 3 | 270 m/s | −3.0 h | 111 min |
| plane, second passage as an echo off a rim at 25,000 km | 3 | 435 m/s | +1.8 h | 89 min |
| plane, second passage as an echo off a rim at 40,000 km | 3 | 937 m/s | +6.1 h | 88 min |
| plane, second passage as an echo off a rim at 60,000 km | 3 | 1,620 m/s | +7.7 h | 89 min |
| plane, second passage as an echo off a rim at 100,000 km | 3 | 3,002 m/s | +8.8 h | 80 min |
| plane, second passage bounced off a dome 22,111 km high (best height) | 3 | 581 m/s | +3.8 h | 65 min |

> **The flat model, tuned in its favour, still misses by hours.** With its own speed and start time, the plane fits the first band with a scatter of 27 minutes. On the same band the globe, with nothing fitted at all, scatters by 8 minutes. The plane's fit also needs the wave to travel at 427 m/s, 38% faster than the 310 m/s the air's temperature allows.[12] For the second band the plane has no path at all. It was offered an echo off a rim, at any radius from the map's edge (20,015 km) out to 100,000 km. Its best line then scatters by 80 to 111 minutes. It also has to start the wave between three hours before and almost nine hours after the eruption, whose time is measured. That echo comes off the nearest stretch of the rim, so it arrives later the farther the station, roughly parallel to the first band. An echo off the far side of the rim would slope the right way, but every station would first have heard the near-rim echo, and no trace shows it. The dome does a little better and still fails: at its best height, 22,111 km, it scatters by 65 minutes, needs 581 m/s, and starts the wave 3.8 h after the eruption.

> **What this measurement cannot do.** R is proportional to v. The 310 m/s comes from the physics of the air.[12][13] But the speed measured during this very event was 318 ± 6 m/s,[15] and with it every radius here would be 2.6% larger (about 6,550 km). That speed was itself measured with globe distances, so using it to compute R, or even to size the uncertainty, would be circular: it is quoted and nothing more. The uncertainty takes instead the speed the Krakatoa wave of 1883 needs, 1.1% lower, a ratio of lap times with no radius in it. That is about 70 km, far more than the spread between stations. A second limit: all the stations are in the United States, between 45° and 116° from Tonga. That is too short a lever to fit the start time and the radius together. Left free, the first band alone gives 6,193 km and the second alone 6,691 km, with a start 1.3 h before the eruption. The two disagree, and only the measured eruption time reconciles them. The slow drift of R with θ is the same problem seen another way. A speed that differs slightly from one path to another, or an effective start slightly off the explosion, would each produce it, and US stations alone cannot tell the two apart. What survives all of this needs no speed at all: two bands sloping opposite ways, the V.

## Before any of it: Krakatoa, 1883, on the barographs of the Victorian world [evidence: measurement]

On 27 August 1883 Krakatoa, a volcano in the Sunda Strait between Java and Sumatra, blew itself apart. Its pressure wave was traced by the self-recording barometers of observatories from Melbourne to Toronto, and the Royal Society's Krakatoa committee gathered the traces. Lieutenant-General Strachey, of the Meteorological Office, read up to seven passages of the same wave on them, and printed the times station by station in Greenwich Mean Time.[16] This section uses nothing else: 47 stations, typed in from the scanned tables. They were also checked against the report's own table of intervals between passages: all 175 agree to the minute.

The method needs even less than Tonga's. At any one station, passage III is passage I one full turn of the Earth later, and IV is II one turn later in the other direction. Subtracting two readings of the same barograph's clock gives the time of one lap. That needs neither the station's position nor the moment of the explosion, which nobody measured: Strachey had to work it out from the waves themselves. The wind speeds up the wave one way round and slows it the other (Strachey's own explanation[16]), so one lap in each direction is averaged.

$$T_{\to} = t_{\text{III}} - t_{\text{I}}, \qquad T_{\leftarrow} = t_{\text{IV}} - t_{\text{II}}$$
$$R = \dfrac{v\,(T_{\to} + T_{\leftarrow})}{4\pi}$$
$$v \approx 310\ \text{m}/\text{s}$$

Each lap is the difference between two readings of one clock, so a clock set wrong cancels out, and so does the station's position. On a plane there is no lap. A circle growing from the volcano crosses each station once; to get later passages the plane needs echoes, off a rim or off a dome, and their delays depend on where the station sits. The real laps do not: from Calcutta, 33° from Krakatoa, to Washington, 147°, they take about 36 hours one way round and 35 the other.

- 47 barographs of 1883, 29 with a lap each waylaps: 36.2 h towards the antipodes, 34.7 h coming back

R = 6,310 ± 137 km

95% confidence: 6,042 – 6,578 km · the mean radius, 6,371 km, lies 0.45 σ away

statistical ± 8 km (29 stations) · systematic ± 136 km: the gap fit and the wave's speed (the two eruptions differ by 1.1 %)

flat models, tuned in their favour: no lap at all, and on the first interval a scatter 4× the globe's

*Figure caption:* **The radius from 1883, and how sure it is.** The dot is the median of the 29 stations with a clean lap in each direction (times Strachey marked with a “?” left out). The dark bar is the statistical uncertainty alone. The pale bands are the total uncertainty, at one standard deviation and at 95%. As for Tonga, almost all of it is systematic: the small ticks redo the calculation with every lap, with the queried times kept, from the interval between the first two passages, and with the speed the 2022 eruption needs, 1.1% higher. The speed measured in 2022 is not used: it was measured with globe distances. The mean radius, 6,371 km, falls inside the band. This value is carried to the home page's table of radii.

*Figure caption:* **One lap of the Earth, at every station.** Each point is the time between two passages of the same wave over one barograph, spread out by the station's angle from Krakatoa, which is not used to compute it. Dots: laps towards the antipodes (III − I, V − III, VII − V), about 36.2 h. Open circles: laps coming back (IV − II, VI − IV), about 34.7 h. The gap between the two is the wind Strachey described. The dashed line is the globe with nothing fitted, 6,371 km at 310 m/s: 35.9 h. The North American stations (θ ≈ 142–147°) split the most, both ways. Their waves passed close to the poles, and Strachey called their speeds “peculiar”. They are kept.
