*Figure caption:* **The first interval, passage I to passage II, against the angle from the volcano.** On a globe it is the time to go on to the antipodes and come back, (2π − 2θ) R / v: a straight line, 28 h near Krakatoa, 7 h near its antipodes. Black dots: the 40 stations with both times unqueried. Blue dashes: the globe with nothing fitted. Orange: the plane at its best, with its own speed. The dots are a single echo off a rim at the map's edge. The open circles are a bounce off a dome at the best height. Neither follows the measured points.

**How closely each model follows the 40 intervals I → II**

| Model | Free parameters | Speed | Scatter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| globe, nothing fitted (R = 6,371 km, v = 310 m/s) | 0 | 310 m/s | 50 min |
| globe, R/v free | 1 | 320 m/s | 37 min |
| plane, II as an echo off a rim at 20,015 km (the map's edge) | 1 | 295 m/s | 446 min |
| plane, II as an echo off a rim at 25,000 km | 1 | 454 m/s | 403 min |
| plane, II as an echo off a rim at 40,000 km | 1 | 946 m/s | 362 min |
| plane, II as an echo off a rim at 60,000 km | 1 | 1,609 m/s | 347 min |
| plane, II as an echo off a rim at 100,000 km | 1 | 2,941 m/s | 338 min |
| plane, II bounced off a dome 5,012 km high (best height) | 2 | 62 m/s | 200 min |

> **The flat model, tuned in its favour.** The test uses only the interval between the first two passages, which a plane can at least attempt: the wave goes out once, and an echo comes back once. The intervals need no explosion time, so the only free parameter is the plane's speed. With an echo off a rim, at any radius from the map's edge (20,015 km) out to 100,000 km, its best line scatters by 5.6 to 7.4 hours, and it needs 295 to 2,941 m/s. The globe, with nothing fitted, scatters by 50 minutes. With a bounce off a dome, the best height is 5,012 km: the scatter is 3.3 hours and the wave would have to travel at 62 m/s, a fifth of the speed of sound. The later passages, five more at many stations, are not modelled for the plane: each would need yet another echo. **What would have vindicated the plane:** laps that change with the station's position, as any echo would make them, or no regular passages after the first two.

> **What this measurement cannot do.** As with Tonga, R is proportional to the speed v. With the speed measured in 2022 (318 m/s[15]), the radius would become 6,477 km, but that speed was measured with globe distances and is quoted only, never used in the uncertainty. The two eruptions also differ from each other at equal speed. 1883 gives 6,310 km and 2022 gives 6,382 km, 1.1% apart: one wave crossed an August atmosphere, the other a January one, and the Lamb wave's speed depends on the air's temperature. Strachey had to choose which wiggle of each trace counts as “the” passage. He states his reading errors to be well within thirty minutes,[16] which is 1.4% of a lap. One direction alone gives 6,468 km (out) or 6,187 km (back): the wind is not small, and only the average cancels it. The North American and Australian stations sit low (6,202–6,252 km) and are kept. The interval I → II, fitted against θ, gives 6,173 km: it mixes the two directions unevenly, and it needs the station's position. None of these limits touches the shape of the result: a lap of the same length wherever the barograph stood.

## Every lap together: two eruptions and a bomb, one size [evidence: measurement]

The same pressure wave has now been timed three times, by three generations of instruments: Krakatoa in 1883 on paper barographs, the Soviet test of 30 October 1961 at Novaya Zemlya (the "Tsar Bomba") on Japanese microbarographs, and Hunga Tonga in 2022 on airport barometers. Each lap timed at one station gives R = vT/2π on its own, with no position, no map and no distance. Here every lap goes into one measurement, as the earthquakes do in the seismology tab: 147 laps from four sets give **6,388 km ± 43 km**.

R = 6,388 ± 43 km

95% confidence: 6,305 – 6,472 km · the mean radius, 6,371 km, lies 0.41 σ away

statistical ± 6 km (147 laps) · systematic ± 42 km: how far the result moves when the sets are combined other ways

*Figure caption:* **Every lap, one ruler.** Each dot is one station's lap turned into a radius at 310 m/s; the black tick is the set's median. Blue sets time the wave both ways round, which cancels the wind; violet sets time one way only. Each set is tight, and the sets sit within 2.9 % of each other: the wave's speed changes with each route's wind and temperature. Combined other ways (each set weighing the same, one set left out at a time, only the sets timed both ways), the result moves by at most 42 km: that is its systematic uncertainty, and it dominates. The bottom row is all the laps together, with its bands at one standard deviation and at 95%. This value is carried to the home page's table of radii.

**The four sets of laps and the result**

| Set | Lap | Directions | Laps kept | Median R | Off 6,371 km |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hunga Tonga 2022, t₁ + t₂ | t₁ + t₂ (eruption time measured) | both ways | 64 | 6,382 km | +0.2 % |
| Hunga Tonga 2022, lap A4 − A2 | A4 − A2, same station | one way | 50 | 6,418 km | +0.7 % |
| Krakatoa 1883, laps both ways | (III − I + IV − II) / 2, same station | both ways | 29 | 6,310 km | −1.0 % |
| Novaya Zemlya 1961, lap III − I | III − I, same station | one way | 4 | 6,234 km | −2.1 % |
| **all together** | median of every lap |  | 147 | **6,388 km** | +0.3 % |

**Novaya Zemlya, 1961.** N. Murayama of the Japan Meteorological Agency tabulated three passages of the wave at eight microbarographs: the first by the short way, the second by the antipodal way, and the third, the first one back after a full circuit.[17] The third minus the first, at one station, is a lap: 35.08–35.13 h at 4 of the 5 stations whose times he did not mark as uncertain (the fifth, 9 minutes shorter, falls more than three standard deviations from the others and is set aside by the rule used everywhere on this site). To check our transcription, each velocity he printed is found again from his distance and his time; his distances used the radius of 1962, so they serve only that check. **Hunga Tonga, seven days.** The wave went round four times one way and three the other.[14] With the same barometers over seven days, each passage's return was looked for 24 to 48 hours later, a window as wide as a sphere of 4,260 to 8,520 km. The long-way passage came back after 36.13 h at 50 of 86 stations, within 4 min of each other. The other returns did not stand out of the weather: their picks spread over the whole window (5–7 h of scatter), so they are left out rather than forced.

> **What this measurement cannot do.** All four sets share the speed of 310 m/s, computed from the air's temperature and fixed in advance.[12] A different speed scales the result in proportion. The sets disagree with each other by more than their own scatter: the 1961 lap and the 2022 long-way lap were timed one way round only, so the wind along their route stays in them, and Krakatoa shows how much that can be. Pooling does not hide that disagreement: the systematic uncertainty is how far the answer moves when the sets are combined differently, and it is most of the total. Pooling only stops one event from deciding the answer alone. What the pooling does show is the shape: whatever the year, the instrument and the route, a lap at one station lasts the same 35 to 36 hours.

## Radio waves and the ionosphere

**Above 60 km, sunlight strips electrons off the air.** The free electrons form layers: D (60–90 km, by day only), E (around 110 km) and F (150–500 km, densest near 300 km). A radio wave entering this electron gas is turned back where its frequency equals the local plasma frequency, which grows with the number of electrons[3]. Long waves (below 1 MHz) mostly creep along the ground and, by day, are absorbed by the D layer. Short waves (3–30 MHz) are bent back to the ground, beyond the horizon, and can go round the world in several hops; between the ground wave and the first return lies a skip zone where nothing is heard[4]. Above 30–50 MHz the waves go through: FM radio and television reach only to the horizon, and satellites, GPS among them at 1.2–1.6 GHz, use frequencies the ionosphere cannot stop. At night the D layer vanishes and the F layer thins: lower frequencies travel far, which is why distant medium-wave stations come in after dark.

*Figure caption:* **Which waves the ionosphere sends back.** A section of the Earth at true scale, a transmitter on the left, the D, E and F layers at their heights with their critical frequencies, by day then by night. Every few seconds another frequency: 500 kHz follows the ground and fades; 3.5 MHz is absorbed by day and bounces at night; 7 to 28 MHz bounce in hops beyond the horizon, leaving a skip zone (orange dots); 144 MHz goes straight through to space. Each ray leaves at a different elevation and is reflected only if its frequency is below the critical frequency times the secant of its angle on the layer. Click to pause.

$$f_p = 8.98\,\sqrt{N_e}\ \text{Hz}$$
$${f \le f_{oF2}\,\sec\varphi}\ \Rightarrow\ \text{reflected}$$

N_e is the number of free electrons per m³, f_p the plasma frequency, f_oF2 the critical frequency at the peak of the F layer and φ the angle at which the wave meets the layer. With 10¹² electrons per m³ (a sunny day), f_oF2 = 9.0 MHz: a wave sent straight up at 14 MHz goes through, but the same wave sent low over the horizon meets the layer at a grazing angle and comes back[3].

$${d_{\max} = 2R\,\arccos\frac{R}{R+h}}$$

R is the Earth's radius and h the height of the reflecting layer. The longest single hop is the one that leaves and returns grazing the ground: for the F layer at 300 km, d_max = 3,836 km, which is why HF predictions count F2 hops of up to about 4,000 km and longer paths in several hops[4]. A flat ground under a flat mirror would put no limit on the length of one hop.

**The radio bands and what the ionosphere does to them[3][4].**

| Band | Frequencies | What happens | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LF / MF | 30 kHz – 3 MHz | ground wave; absorbed by the D layer in daytime, reflected at night | long and medium-wave broadcasting, navigation beacons |
| HF | 3 – 30 MHz | reflected by the E and F layers, in hops beyond the horizon; skip zone | short-wave broadcasting, radio amateurs, aircraft over oceans |
| VHF | 30 – 300 MHz | goes through (except rare E-layer clouds): line of sight | FM radio, aircraft and marine radio |
| UHF / SHF | 300 MHz – 30 GHz | goes straight through: line of sight and space | television, mobile phones, GPS, satellite links |

> **The objection** says that radio contacts thousands of kilometres away, beyond the horizon, prove a flat Earth. They happen at short wave, not at VHF or microwave frequencies, and their reach changes with the hour, the season and the Sun's activity exactly as the ionosphere does: they are reflections. **What would vindicate the flat model here:** VHF and microwave links routinely working far beyond the line of sight with no satellite and no relay, or single short-wave hops much longer than 4,000 km.

## Why satellites do not melt in the thermosphere

**Temperature is not heat.** The two words answer two different questions. **Temperature** says how hard *each* molecule hits: it measures the energy of one molecule, that is how fast it moves, whatever their number. **Heat** says how much energy *reaches* a body each second: the energy of one hit times the number of hits. A gas can therefore be very hot and bring almost no heat, if its molecules are few.

**An everyday example.** In a sauna the air is at 90 °C and one sits in it for minutes; water at 90 °C scalds in a second. Same temperature, so each molecule hits just as hard; but the same volume of water holds over a thousand times more molecules, so a thousand times more hits. In the same way the hand stands the air of an oven at 200 °C for a moment, not its metal tray, and a sparkler's sparks are over a thousand degrees but so small that they do not burn the hand. The thermosphere is the extreme case: a very high temperature, and almost nothing there to bring it.

**The numbers at 400 km.** The temperature there is about 996 K: each molecule is very fast[1]. But at that height, where the International Space Station flies[7], there are 1.06 × 10¹⁴ molecules per cubic metre, 241 billion times fewer than at sea level. Their impacts on a surface at room temperature bring 0.58 mW per square metre[2]. The same gas at sea-level density would bring 105 MW per square metre and melt anything.

*Figure caption:* **The same 1,000 K, two very different heats.** The same box on both sides, a cube of one micrometre resting on one square micrometre of wall at 300 K, watched for the same 100 microseconds. Left: a gas at 1,000 K as dense as the air at sea level: 25 million molecules in the cube, far too many to draw, and some 5 × 10¹¹ impacts on the wall in 100 µs. Right: the thermosphere at 400 km, also at 1,000 K: one molecule for every 9,500 such cubes; the three molecules that strike the wall in those 100 µs are drawn one by one, at the times a random draw at the true rate gives. The counters of impacts and energy follow the true rates. Below, on a logarithmic scale, what reaches or leaves a square metre of satellite: sunlight dominates, the gas of the thermosphere is two million times weaker. Click to pause.

$$\Phi = \frac{n\,\bar v}{4},\qquad {q = \Phi\cdot 2k\,(T_{\text{gas}} - T_{\text{wall}})}$$
$$q_{\text{ram}} = \tfrac12\,\rho\,v^3$$

Φ is the number of molecules striking a square metre each second, v̄ their mean speed, n their number per m³; each brings 2kT of energy on average and leaves with the wall's temperature. At 400 km, Φ = 3.03 × 10¹⁶ per m² per second and q = 0.58 mW. The satellite's own speed, 7.7 km/s, makes the molecules strike its front much harder: ½ρv³ = 0.63 W/m², still two thousand times less than sunlight.

**What sets a satellite's temperature is sunlight, and how well it radiates.** In the Sun, a surface absorbs up to 1,361 W/m²[5]; it gets rid of heat only by radiating, as σT⁴. A black ball in sunlight at the Earth's distance settles where the two balance: 278 K, about 5 °C. Satellites are painted, insulated and fitted with radiators to stay in a comfortable range; the thousand degrees of the thin gas around them hardly enter the budget.

$$\alpha\,S\,\pi r^2 = \varepsilon\,\sigma\,T^4\,4\pi r^2\ \Rightarrow\ {T = \left(\frac{\alpha\,S}{4\,\varepsilon\,\sigma}\right)^{1/4}}$$

S is the sunlight per square metre, α the fraction absorbed, ε how well the surface radiates (both 1 for a black body), σ the Stefan–Boltzmann constant and r the ball's radius: it catches sunlight on πr² and radiates from 4πr². T = 278 K[5][6].

**From radiation to energy to temperature.** Light carries energy: 1,361 W on every square metre facing the Sun[5]. A body that absorbs it does not jump to its final temperature: the energy piles up in its matter, and the temperature is that stored energy divided by the body's heat capacity C, its mass times its specific heat. Take a black aluminium plate of 1 m² and 2 mm, facing the Sun at 400 km: 5.4 kg, C = 4,844 J/K[8]. Cold, it gains 1,361 joules each second and warms by 17 K a minute. The warmer it gets, the more it radiates, as σT⁴ from each of its two faces[6], so the rise slows and stops at 331 K (58 °C), where what comes in equals what goes out. An orbit at 400 km lasts 92.4 minutes[9], of which up to 36 in the Earth's shadow: there nothing comes in, the plate keeps radiating and cools, to 177 K (-96 °C) before sunrise. That swing, not the thermosphere, is what satellite designers fight.

*Figure caption:* **Radiation in, energy stored, temperature, radiation out.** The black plate of 1 m² × 2 mm on an orbit at 400 km, the Sun in the plane of the orbit. Top: the four steps with their values at each moment (the energy gained is counted from the coldest moment, just before sunrise), and the balance C dT/dt = P_in − P_out. Left: where the plate is (the Earth's shadow in grey), its colour following its temperature, the yellow arrows (sunlight absorbed) and the red ones (heat radiated from each face) drawn in proportion to their power. Right: the temperature over one orbit of 92.4 minutes, from 177 K to 331 K, and the balance it reaches in sunlight. One orbit is played in 24 seconds. Click to pause.

$$C\,\frac{dT}{dt} = P_{\text{in}} - P_{\text{out}} = \alpha\,S\,A - 2\,\varepsilon\,\sigma\,A\,T^4$$
$${T_{\text{eq}} = \left(\frac{\alpha\,S}{2\,\varepsilon\,\sigma}\right)^{1/4}}$$

C is the heat capacity (mass × specific heat, 4,844 J/K for the plate), A its area, facing the Sun on one side and radiating from both; α and ε are 1 for a black surface. The left side is the energy stored each second; when it is zero, the temperature no longer moves: T_eq = 331 K. The animation integrates this equation step by step over the orbit, with P_in = 0 in the shadow. The 2 mm of aluminium carry heat across so fast that both faces are taken at the same temperature; the Earth's own reflected light and infrared, which add a little, are left out.

> **The objection** says that satellites cannot exist, since the thermosphere at 1,000–2,000 °C would melt them. It takes the temperature of a gas for the heat it delivers. **What would vindicate it:** a thermosphere dense enough to bring watts per square centimetre; but such a gas would also brake every satellite to the ground within days, and satellites stay up for years at these heights.

# Rockets: what pushes a rocket when there is nothing to push against

> Tab "Rockets" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-rocket. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Rockets · what pushes in empty space*

“A rocket cannot work in space: there is nothing to push against.” “A gas next to a vacuum has no pressure, it just flies apart.” “Free expansion does no work, so the exhaust cannot push anything.” These are the usual reasons given for saying that nothing has ever reached orbit, which would also mean that the satellites of the [Satellites](/ai/sat.md) and [GPS](/ai/gps.md) tabs are not there. This tab answers them with the same balls as the [Atmosphere](/ai/atmo.md) tab: molecules flying about and hitting walls. Every push in the animations below is *measured*, by adding up the hits of the balls on each wall; nothing is drawn from a formula. Nothing here is about the shape of the Earth. It is about whether a rocket can push itself, and the answer, measured since 1916, is that the air only gets in the way.

*[Figure: Animation: gas balls hitting the walls of a closed box, then of a box with a hole, then of a rocket chamber kept full by a fire; the push on the rocket equals the momentum of the jet; the same rocket loses thrust in air; in empty space the centre of mass of rocket and fuel never moves]*

*Figure caption:* **The whole tab in forty-five seconds.** A closed box of gas, whose pushes cancel; the same box with a hole, pushed until it is empty; a chamber kept full by a fire; the push on the rocket, equal to the momentum the jet carries off; the same rocket in air, which pushes less; and a rocket free in space, whose centre of mass, with all its fuel, never moves. The balls are enlarged and much fewer than real molecules. Click to pause.

## Pressure is molecules hitting the walls

**A gas is not a fog that fills space; it is a crowd of molecules flying in straight lines.** Each one bounces off a wall like a ball, and each bounce gives the wall a small kick. Daniel Bernoulli explained pressure this way in 1738, and Maxwell worked out the speeds in 1860[4][5]. At sea level, about 2.9 × 10²³ molecules of air hit each square centimetre every second, each at a few hundred metres per second[6]. The kicks are so many that they add up to a steady push: 10 tonnes on every square metre. In a closed box, every wall is kicked as hard as the wall opposite, so the pushes cancel and the box goes nowhere, however high the pressure. Heat the gas and every molecule goes faster: each kick is harder, and kicks come more often, but they still cancel.

*Figure caption:* **A closed box of gas.** 400 balls fly in straight lines and bounce off the walls. The green arrows are the pushes *measured* on each wall, the total of 2 m v per hit, averaged over a second and a half: 100 on each wall at the start. Halfway, every ball is made √2 times faster, which doubles the temperature: each hit is √2 times harder and √2 times more frequent, and every push doubles. The sum of the four stays at zero, give or take the randomness of the hits. Click to pause.

$${\Delta p = 2 m v_\perp},\qquad p = n\,k\,T = \tfrac{1}{3}\,\rho\,\langle v^2 \rangle$$

**One hit, then billions.** A molecule of mass m hitting a wall at speed v⊥ across it comes back at −v⊥: its momentum changes by 2 m v⊥, and the wall gets the opposite, by Newton's third law[3]. Add up the hits on a square metre for a second and you get the pressure p: n molecules per cubic metre, at temperature T, give p = n k T, with k Boltzmann's constant[15]; ρ is the density and ⟨v²⟩ the mean squared speed. In the RS-25, the main engine of the Space Shuttle, the gas in the chamber is at 206 bar, 204 times the air's pressure, and up to about 3,300 °C[8][10]: 4.2 × 10²⁶ molecules per cubic metre, 16 times as many as in the air we breathe, each much faster. (In the animations the gas is two-dimensional: p = n m ⟨v²⟩/2, a force per unit length.)

## A hole: one wall loses its partner

**Now cut a hole in the bottom.** The molecules that would have hit that piece of the bottom fly out instead. The top is still hit as often as before, but the patch of bottom opposite it is gone. The pushes no longer cancel: the box is pushed upwards, with a force of the order of the pressure times the area of the hole. Nothing outside the box takes part, so there is no difference between a hole in air and a hole in empty space, except that in air some outside molecules come in through the hole and push back. This is a balloon let go: the push lasts as long as there is gas inside. A rocket keeps the gas coming.

*Figure caption:* **The same box, in empty space, with a hole.** After two and a half seconds, the middle 36 % of the bottom is removed. The bottom's measured push drops, the top's does not, and the net push (black arrow, same scale) points up. The balls that leave take that much momentum downward with them: the total kick received by the box and what the balls that left carry off come together. With every ball that leaves, the box empties and the push fades. Click to pause.

$${\vec F = \oint p\,\vec n\,dA}\quad\Rightarrow\quad F = C_F\,p\,A$$

**Add up the pushes all round.** n is the outward direction of each piece of wall dA, and p the pressure on it. Over a closed box the sum is zero: each piece has an opposite piece. Take away a piece of area A at the bottom and the piece of top opposite it is left unbalanced: the box is pushed up by C_F p A, where the factor C_F depends on how the gas flows out. It is ½ for a gas as thin as the animation's, because fewer molecules are left near the hole; about 1.3 for a dense gas leaving at the speed of sound; and up to about 2 with a well-shaped nozzle in a vacuum[7]. That is what nozzles are for.

## Keeping the pressure: fire in, throat out

> **What the videos say.** “Pressure cannot exist next to a vacuum. The vacuum of space would suck the gas out of the chamber at once, so there is never any pressure to push with.”

**A vacuum does not suck.** Empty space has no molecules, so it cannot pull on anything; it only fails to push back. A molecule leaves the chamber when its own flight happens to take it through the opening, and not before. How many leave each second depends on how many there are inside, how fast they go and how large the opening is, never on what lies outside. So the fire makes new gas, the narrow throat lets some out, and the amount inside rises until as much leaves as is made. Then the pressure holds, as the level of a bath holds when the tap fills it as fast as the drain empties it. In a real engine the gas goes through the throat at the speed of sound; nothing that happens downstream can then travel back up to change the chamber at all[7].

*Figure caption:* **A rocket chamber in empty space, starting empty.** The fire (orange band) makes 60 balls a second, in pairs flying in opposite directions, so that burning the fuel adds no push of its own. The curve is the number of balls in the chamber. At first more are made than leave, and it rises; once as many leave as are made, it stays put. After 18 seconds the fire goes out and the chamber empties. The chamber walls are rough: a ball bounces off them in a random direction, which is what collisions with other molecules do in a real gas; the nozzle is smooth. Click to pause.

$${\frac{dN}{dt} = \dot N_{\text{in}} - \frac{N}{\tau}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad N \to \dot N_{\text{in}}\,\tau,\qquad p_c = \frac{\dot m\,c^*}{A_t}$$

**A bath with the tap on.** N is the number of molecules in the chamber, Ṅ_in the number the fire makes each second, and N/τ the number leaving: each molecule has a chance 1/τ per second of finding the opening. N rises until the two match, at Ṅ_in τ. For a real engine the same balance reads p_c = ṁ c*/A_t: the chamber pressure p_c is the mass flow ṁ times a speed c* set by the propellants, divided by the throat area A_t[7]. For the RS-25, 206 bar, 514 kg/s and a throat 0.26 m across give c* ≈ 2.2 km/s[10]. Double the flow and the pressure doubles; the outside pressure appears nowhere.

## The push: Newton's third law, one hit at a time

> **What the videos say.** “Newton's third law needs something to push against. On the ground the exhaust pushes on the air, or on the launch pad. In space there is nothing, so a rocket can do nothing.”

**The rocket pushes on its own gas, and its gas pushes back on the rocket.** That is the pair of forces of the third law[3]: every hit of a molecule on the top of the chamber is a push up on the rocket and an equal push down on the molecule, which then flies down and out. The rocket does not need to push on anything else, any more than a gun needs air to recoil, or a person on a skateboard needs a wall to roll back when they throw a heavy ball. Each second, the rocket gains as much upward momentum as its jet takes downward. The animation adds up both, exactly, from the start.

*Figure caption:* **Where the push comes from.** A rocket held on a stand in empty space, its chamber kept full by the fire. Green arrows: the push measured on each part of the wall, averaged since the start; the top of the chamber is pushed up, the converging walls are pushed down, the two sides push outwards and cancel. Their sum, the black arrow, points up. On the right, that push and the momentum the jet carries off each second through the nozzle exit: the same number, within the scatter of the hits. Below, the exact account since the start: what the rocket received, plus what the balls inside carry, plus what the balls that left carry, is zero, to the last digit, because every bounce gives the wall exactly what it takes from the ball. Click to pause.

$${F = \dot m\,v_e + (p_e - p_a)\,A_e}$$

**The thrust equation of every engine data sheet.** ṁ is the mass of gas leaving each second, vₑ its speed at the nozzle exit, pₑ its pressure there, Aₑ the exit area and pₐ the pressure of the air outside[7]. The first term is the momentum the jet carries off each second; the second is the pressure left over at the exit. The air appears in one place only, with a minus sign: pₐ Aₑ is the air pushing on the outside of the rocket, everywhere except over the exit, where the jet is. In empty space pₐ = 0 and the thrust is largest.

## The air only gets in the way

**If rockets pushed on the air, they would push harder in thicker air.** They do the opposite. Robert Goddard tested it in 1915–1916 at Clark University: he burnt smokeless powder in a small steel chamber with a nozzle, first in air, then inside a tank pumped down to between 1/100 and 1/1,520 of an atmosphere, and read the speed of the gas from the recoil of the chamber[11]. He found “a general tendency for the velocities in vacuo to be larger than those in air”, up to 22 % larger, and concluded that the push “is really a jet of gas having an extremely high velocity, and is not merely an effect of reaction against the air”. When he published in 1919, the *New York Times* wrote that he did not know “the need to have something better than a vacuum against which to react”[1]. The paper printed its correction on 17 July 1969, the day after Apollo 11 left for the Moon: “The Times regrets the error”[2].

*Figure caption:* **The same rocket, the same fire, twice.** Left, in empty space; right, in air (grey balls, cooler and thinner than the gas in the chamber). The air hits the outside of the rocket from every side except over the nozzle exit, where the jet keeps it out, so on balance it pushes the rocket down. The bars give the measured pushes, averaged since the start (over a few seconds the randomness of the hits is as large as the effect), and the prediction of the thrust equation, the push in empty space minus the air pressure times the width of the exit. Because these balls do not collide with each other, the dashed line across the exit stands for the jet: it turns the air back, and what it receives is not counted on the rocket. The air's pressure is 1/37 of the chamber's, chosen so that the loss is like the RS-25's; in the RS-25 it is 1/204. Click to pause.

$${F_{\text{vac}} - F_{\text{sea}} = p_a\,A_e}$$

**The check on a real engine.** NASA gives the RS-25 at full power 2,279 kN of thrust in a vacuum and 1,852 kN at sea level[8]: 23 % more where there is no air. The thrust equation says the difference is only the air's push on the exit area. 427 kN divided by the sea-level pressure, 101.3 kPa, is 4.21 m², a circle 2.32 m across; the nozzle exit of the RS-25 is 2.30 m across[10]. The specific impulses tell the same story: 4.44 km/s of effective exhaust speed in vacuum, 3.59 km/s at sea level[9]. The same engines have run for more than a million seconds on test stands and in flight[8], and upper stages are fired in vacuum chambers built for the purpose, such as NASA's 38-foot In-Space Propulsion Facility in Ohio[14].

**What would have vindicated the objection, stated in advance:** a rocket that gives less push, or none, when the air is pumped away. Every test since Goddard's gives more. The animations are honest about their own limits too: their gas is so thin that the balls never meet, which is why a rough chamber wall and a line across the exit stand in for collisions; a real jet leaves faster and better aligned than these balls do. What does not depend on collisions is the bookkeeping, hit by hit, and that is exact.

## “Free expansion does no work”

> **What the videos say.** “A gas expanding into a vacuum does no work: this is Joule's free expansion, in every thermodynamics textbook. The exhaust leaving a rocket in space is a free expansion, so it can do no work, and the rocket cannot gain any energy from it.”

**Joule's experiment is real, and it says something else.** In 1845 Joule connected a vessel of compressed air to an empty one and opened the tap: the air spread into both, and since nothing outside moved, no work was done on anything outside[12]. Work is a force times a distance moved by the thing pushed. In a free expansion there is no piston, nothing for the gas to push on that moves. A rocket is exactly the piston that free expansion lacks: the gas pushes on the top of the chamber, and the chamber moves. The gas gives the rocket energy before it leaves; once it has left, it does expand freely into space, and that last part indeed pushes nothing. Even at rest on a test stand, where it does no work at all, the rocket still feels its thrust, measured on the stand: force needs no work, only momentum.

$${W = \int p\,dV_{\text{moving}}}:\quad W_{\text{Joule}} = 0,\qquad W_{\text{rocket}} = F\,\Delta x$$

**Work counts only the walls that move.** dV_moving is the volume swept by a wall that moves while the gas pushes on it. Joule's vessels are fixed, so W = 0. The top of a rocket chamber is pushed by the gas with the force F and moves by Δx: the gas does the work F Δx on the rocket. The second law of thermodynamics is not involved: the hot gas becomes a fast, cold jet in the nozzle, which is how every engine turns heat into motion.

## In empty space: the centre of mass never moves

**Throwing mass backwards is enough.** Free in space, a rocket and its fuel start at rest together. Each throw of fuel backwards gives the rocket the opposite momentum: their common centre of mass stays where it was, forever, as Newton showed for any bodies that act only on one another[3]. The rocket goes forward because its fuel goes back, and nothing else is needed. Since the rocket gets lighter with every throw, each throw speeds it up a little more than the last. Tsiolkovsky worked out the total in 1903[13].

*Figure caption:* **A rocket free in space.** It weighs 1 and throws 0.75 of fuel backwards, in 48 throws, each at the same speed u relative to the rocket; then it coasts. The frame is that of the launch. The green cross, the centre of mass of the rocket and of every ball thrown, stays where it was. The speed, computed throw by throw, follows Tsiolkovsky's curve. The last balls, thrown once the rocket goes faster than u, move forward too in this frame, more slowly than the rocket: the rocket does not push on them from behind, it pushes them backward from its own speed. Click to pause.

$${\Delta v = u\,\ln\frac{m_0}{m_1}}$$

**Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation.** u is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket, m₀ its mass full and m₁ its mass empty. Each small throw dm at speed u gives the rocket dv = u dm/m; adding them up gives the logarithm. A rocket with three quarters of its mass as fuel reaches ln 4 = 1.39 u; in 48 separate throws, as in the animation, a little less, 1.36 u. At the RS-25's 4.44 km/s, the 7.9 km/s of a low orbit ([Orbit](/ai/orb.md)) needs m₀/m₁ = 5.9: a rocket 83 % fuel, before counting the air and the climb against gravity, which is why rockets are built in stages that drop their empty tanks.

## The recurring arguments, one by one

**Each argument, the physics that answers it, and what was measured.**

| The argument | The answer | Measured |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nothing to push against in space | The rocket pushes on its own gas, the gas on the rocket: the third law[3] | Goddard's chamber recoils faster in a vacuum[11] |
| Rockets push on the air | The air pushes the rocket back by pₐ Aₑ[7] | RS-25: 2,279 kN in vacuum, 1,852 kN at sea level[8] |
| No pressure next to a vacuum | A vacuum does not pull; the gas leaves through the throat only as fast as it reaches it | Engines hold 206 bar in their chambers[10] |
| Free expansion does no work | Work needs a moving wall: the rocket is that wall[12] | A thrust is felt even on a fixed test stand[8] |
| So nothing reaches orbit | Δv = u ln(m₀/m₁)[13]: about 83 % fuel for 7.9 km/s | Upper stages fired in vacuum chambers[14] |

**In one sentence:** pressure is molecules hitting walls; a closed chamber cancels its pushes, an opening leaves one push unbalanced, a fire keeps it going, and the gas carries off backwards exactly the momentum the rocket gains forwards. The air adds nothing but a push the wrong way. What rockets have put into orbit is measured in the [Satellites](/ai/sat.md) tab, from the Doppler shift of their signals.

**See also**[Basics](/ai/phys.md)[Atmosphere](/ai/atmo.md)[Orbit](/ai/orb.md)[Satellites](/ai/sat.md)[GPS](/ai/gps.md)[Results](/ai/results.md)

# Every flat map of the world is a picture of a globe — the flat-earth map included

> Tab "Maps" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-map. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Maps · history and projections*

For most of history a map was flat because it was small, and it was right to be. A town, a valley, even a kingdom fits on a sheet of paper with errors smaller than anyone could pace. The trouble starts with the whole world. Since Ptolemy, about 150 CE, every world map has been drawn from a ball, with rules for spreading its curved grid on a plane, and every set of rules has to give something up. The map used today to illustrate a flat Earth is one of those rules: the azimuthal equidistant projection, centred on the North Pole. This tab is history and geometry, not a measurement; the measurements that decide between the models are in the other tabs.

## Small maps are flat, and rightly so

**The oldest map of the world we have is a disc.** A clay tablet from Sippar, a Neo-Babylonian copy of an older original, shows Babylon on the Euphrates inside a ring of “bitter river”, with triangular regions beyond it[1]. It is a diagram of the known world, not a survey. Practical maps were local: Roman itineraries listed roads and stages, medieval portolan charts drew the Mediterranean coast from compass bearings and sailing days[2]. Treating the ground as a plane cost them nothing, because over a small region the plane and the sphere disagree by far less than their measurements could see.

*Figure caption:* The Babylonian map of the world, redrawn as a schematic: the disc of Mesopotamia inside a ring of ocean, regions beyond it as triangles. It is a picture of what was known, drawn as a disc because the known world surrounded the place that drew it.

How much do they disagree? Draw the best possible flat map of a region around its centre: every distance from the centre exact, every direction from the centre exact. A circle at ground distance d from the centre is then drawn 2πd long, but on a sphere of radius R the circle that is everywhere d from a point is only 2πR sin(d/R) long. The map must stretch it, and that stretch is the smallest error any flat map of the region can have[3].

$$C_{\text{sphere}} = 2\pi R\sin\frac{d}{R},\qquad C_{\text{map}} = 2\pi d$$
$${k = \frac{c}{\sin c} \approx 1 + \frac{c^2}{6},\quad c = \frac{d}{R}}$$

c is the distance from the centre as an angle at the Earth's centre. The error grows as the square of the region's size: 0.004 % at 100 km, 0.41 % at 1,000 km, and it reaches 1 % only 1,560 km from the centre.

*Figure caption:* The smallest error of a flat map against the size of the region it covers, on logarithmic scales. A town map is wrong by less than a millionth; a kingdom by a fraction of a percent; a map of the whole Mediterranean by a few percent, about what a careful sailing chart could notice. The world cannot be drawn this way without errors of tens of percent.

> **The flat model's best case is real.** Within a few hundred kilometres a flat map is not an approximation anyone can catch with a tape, a chain or a compass: it is the right working tool, and surveyors still use it (the last section). The flat intuition comes from here, and it is sound at this scale. It stops being sound when one map has to hold the whole world, which is what the other tabs test with distances, angles and times.

## The Greeks: a sphere, then its size

**By the fourth century BCE the sphere was argued from observation.** Aristotle gives two reasons: the Earth's shadow on the Moon during an eclipse always has a curved edge, and travelling north or south changes which stars rise and set[4]. About a century later Eratosthenes measured its size. At Syene the noon Sun at the solstice was overhead; at Alexandria, to the north, a gnomon's shadow showed it 1/50 of a circle from the vertical. The two places, 5,000 stadia apart, are therefore 1/50 of the way around[5]. Hipparchus then proposed fixing places by latitude and longitude, angles on the sphere, rather than by itineraries[2].

*Figure caption:* **Aristotle** 384–322 BCE
[Marble bust, a Roman copy of a Greek bronze by Lysippos, c. 330 BCE (Palazzo Altemps, Rome)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Aristotle_Altemps_Inv8575.jpg)

*Figure caption:* **Eratosthenes** c. 276–194 BCE
[Imagined: no likeness of him survives (engraving, date unknown)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Eratosthenes.jpg)

$${C = \frac{360°}{\alpha}\,s}$$

α is the Sun's angle from the vertical at the second place when it is overhead at the first, s the distance between them along the meridian. α = 7.2° and s = 5,000 stadia give C = 250,000 stadia. The length of the stadion he used is uncertain, so the result in kilometres is too; the method is what lasted. The tabs on celestial navigation and dip repeat it with modern instruments.

## Ptolemy: a map that knows it is drawn from a ball

**Ptolemy's *Geography*, about 150 CE, is a list and a method.** The list gives some 8,000 places by latitude and longitude; the method tells how to draw them on a plane[6]. He starts by criticising his predecessor Marinus of Tyre, who drew meridians and parallels as a rectangular grid. Marinus had at least spaced his meridians correctly at one latitude, that of Rhodes, 36°, where a degree of longitude is shorter than a degree of latitude in the ratio cos 36°. Ptolemy gives that ratio as 93 to 115[6][7].

*Figure caption:* **Claudius Ptolemy** c. 100–170
[Imagined: no likeness survives (Justus van Gent, c. 1475, Louvre)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Claudio_Ptolomeo.png)

$$x = R\,\lambda\cos\varphi_1,\qquad y = R\,\varphi$$
$${\frac{\text{parallel}}{\text{equator}} = \cos\varphi:\quad \cos 36° = 0.809 \approx \frac{93}{115}}$$

λ is longitude and φ latitude, in radians. The length of a parallel shrinks as cos φ because the parallel is a circle of radius R cos φ: that ratio only exists on a sphere. Ptolemy's 93/115 is 0.8087, cos 36° is 0.8090; his 52/115 for Thule, 63°, is 0.4522 against 0.4540.

*Figure caption:* **Marinus's rectangular grid, with modern coastlines.** Degrees of longitude are drawn cos 36° as long as degrees of latitude, so lengths are true along the parallel of Rhodes (orange) and along every meridian, and too long east–west north of it, too short south of it. The dashed frame is the region Ptolemy's list covered, in modern longitudes.

**Ptolemy's own first projection** curves the parallels into concentric arcs and makes the meridians straight lines meeting at a point above the pole, as if a cone had been set over the globe and unrolled. He chose it so that the parallels of Rhodes and Thule keep their true length relative to the meridians, 93 and 52 parts for 115 at the equator[6][7]. In modern terms it is an equidistant conic projection with two standard parallels, written down again by Snyder in 1987[3].

$$n = \frac{\cos\varphi_1 - \cos\varphi_2}{\varphi_2 - \varphi_1},\qquad G = \frac{\cos\varphi_1}{n} + \varphi_1$$
$${\rho = R\,(G - \varphi),\quad \theta = n(\lambda - \lambda_0),\quad x = \rho\sin\theta,\ y = \rho_0 - \rho\cos\theta}$$

φ₁ = 36° and φ₂ = 63° give n = 0.753: the fan of meridians opens 136° for 180° of longitude. Distances along every meridian are true (ρ falls by R for each radian of latitude), and the two chosen parallels have exactly the length 2πR cos φ, which is the property Ptolemy asked for.

*Figure caption:* **Ptolemy's world computed from his own numbers, beside a map drawn from them.** Left: the 6,372 coordinates of his catalogue (brown dots), placed with his first projection inside his frame, 63° N to 16°25′ S over 180° of longitude east of the Fortunate Isles[6][17]. The parallels of Thule and Rhodes (orange) and every meridian are at true scale. Underneath, modern coastlines through the same projection, his zero meridian set on the Canaries. For 56 towns whose site is known, a line joins where he puts them (black) to where they are (blue)[19]: his latitudes are off by 0.4° on average (standard deviation 2.5°), but his longitudes grow 1.40 times too fast eastward. Right: the world map of the Byzantine manuscript Urbinas gr. 82, about 1300, drawn by hand on the same projection from the same lists[18].

> **Admitted limits.** Ptolemy's projection was right and his data were not. He adopted a circumference of 180,000 stadia, smaller than Eratosthenes', and longitudes estimated from travel times, so the known world spans 180° of longitude on his maps; the towns above put the same lands across about 128°[6]. The factor 1.40 is almost exactly 252,000 / 180,000 = 1.4: distances counted in stadia and turned into degrees at 500 stadia a degree instead of about 700 come out 1.4 times too many degrees. The method held; the numbers were corrected over the next fifteen centuries by exactly the kind of measurements this site collects.

## The Middle Ages kept the globe

**The round “T-O” maps of medieval manuscripts are diagrams, not claims about shape.** They split the inhabited quarter of the globe into Asia, Europe and Africa with a T of waters, east at the top, as a schema to remember the three parts of the world[2]. The scholars who copied them taught a spherical Earth: Bede in the eighth century, Sacrobosco's *De sphaera* in every university from the thirteenth. The story that medieval people thought the Earth flat, and that Columbus had to prove otherwise, was popularised in the nineteenth century, largely by Washington Irving's 1828 life of Columbus[8].

*Figure caption:* A T-O map, as a schematic: the ocean around the inhabited lands, the Mediterranean as the stem of the T, the Don and the Nile as its arms. It is to a world map what a metro diagram is to a street map.

Meanwhile the sailors' portolan charts, from the late thirteenth century, drew the Mediterranean and the Black Sea as a plane criss-crossed by compass lines, accurate enough for a basin about 3,000 km long[2]. Ptolemy's *Geography* came back to Western Europe in a Latin translation in the early 1400s and was printed with maps from 1477; Renaissance mapmakers inherited his projections along with his errors[2][9].

## Mercator, 1569: a map for steering

**A navigator wants a straight line on the chart to be a constant compass heading.** On the globe, meridians converge toward the poles; on a chart where they are drawn parallel, every parallel at latitude φ is stretched east–west by 1/cos φ. Gerardus Mercator's world map of 1569 stretched the north–south direction by the same factor at every latitude, so that small shapes and all angles stay true[10]. He did it graphically; Edward Wright computed the spacing of the parallels in 1599, by adding up sec φ degree by degree[11].

*Figure caption:* **Gerardus Mercator** 1512–1594
[Frans Hogenberg, 1574, at the age of 62](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Gerardus_Mercator2.jpg)

$$x = R\lambda,\qquad y = R\sum_{0}^{\varphi}\sec\varphi\,\Delta\varphi \to R\ln\tan\left(\frac{\pi}{4} + \frac{\varphi}{2}\right)$$
$${h = k = \sec\varphi,\qquad \text{area} \times \sec^2\varphi}$$

h and k are the scales along the meridian and the parallel. They are equal, so the map is conformal: angles and small shapes are true. Areas are not: at 72° N, Greenland's latitude, every area is drawn 10.5 times larger than at the equator, and the pole itself is infinitely far away[3].

*Figure caption:* **Mercator's projection with Tissot's circles.** Every blue circle is the same circle on the globe, 1,560 km across; on the map they keep their round shape and grow toward the poles. The orange line from Frankfurt to San Francisco is straight: a single compass heading, 10,540 km. The dashed curve is the great circle, the shortest route on the globe, 9,150 km, which airliners fly; on this map it bulges toward the pole.

> **The flat model and Mercator.** A flat Earth drawn as Mercator's rectangle would need the poles infinitely long and every route straight on it to be the shortest; neither is the case, and no flat-earth proposal uses it. A flat map with straight shortest routes has to be azimuthal, centred somewhere, which is where the rest of this tab goes.

## Gauss, 1827: no flat map can be true everywhere

**Every projection gives something up, and this is a theorem, not a lack of skill.** Carl Friedrich Gauss showed in 1827 that the curvature of a surface can be measured from inside it, from lengths alone, and is unchanged by any bending without stretching[12]. A sheet of paper has zero curvature and a sphere 1/R²; so no map of any part of a sphere keeps every length. In 1881 Nicolas Auguste Tissot published how to see what each map gives up: draw small equal circles on the globe and look at the ellipses they become[13].

*Figure caption:* **Carl Friedrich Gauss** 1777–1855
[Gottlieb Biermann after Christian Albrecht Jensen, 1840](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Carl_Friedrich_Gauss.jpg)

$$K_{\text{sphere}} = \frac{1}{R^2} \neq K_{\text{plane}} = 0$$
$${\text{conformal: } h = k,\qquad \text{equal-area: } h\,k = 1,\qquad \text{never } h = k = 1 \text{ everywhere}}$$

h and k are the scales of the map along the meridian and the parallel at a point; the small circle becomes an ellipse whose axes come from them. A map can keep shapes (Mercator, stereographic), or areas (Lambert, sinusoidal), or distances along one family of lines (Ptolemy's meridians, the azimuthal equidistant's lines from the centre), never all of them[3].

*Figure caption:* **The same circles on six maps.** Each blue patch is a circle 7° in radius on the globe, at the same places on every map. The equirectangular grid of Marinus keeps neither shape nor area; Mercator keeps shapes; Lambert's cylinder (1772) and the sinusoidal keep areas and squash shapes; the polar azimuthal equidistant keeps distances from the North Pole and stretches the south east–west; the orthographic is how a globe looks from far away, half of it hidden[9].

## The azimuthal equidistant: true from one point

**Put one place at the centre and draw every other place at its true distance and true direction from it.** That is the azimuthal equidistant projection. Mercator used it in 1569 for the inset of the Arctic on his world map, and Guillaume Postel for a map in 1581, which is why it is also called Postel's projection[10][9]. It is the right map for questions asked from one place: which way and how far to any city from here, as on radio amateurs' maps centred on their station[3]. The rim of the disc is a single point, the antipode of the centre, drawn as a circle.

*Figure caption:* **The centre travels, the map is redrawn.** From the North Pole to Paris, Mecca, Cape Town, the South Pole, Sydney and Honolulu, along great circles: the same coastlines, the same rule, a different flat map at every step. Any of them is a correct azimuthal equidistant map; none of them is more “flat” than the others. Click to pause.

$$\cos c = \sin\varphi_0\sin\varphi + \cos\varphi_0\cos\varphi\cos(\lambda - \lambda_0)$$
$${\rho = R\,c,\quad \theta = \text{azimuth from } (\varphi_0, \lambda_0);\qquad h = 1,\ k = \frac{c}{\sin c}}$$

(φ₀, λ₀) is the centre, c the angular distance to the point, θ its direction from the centre. Along lines from the centre the scale h is exactly 1; across them it is k = c/sin c, the stretch of the first section, which reaches π/2 = 1.57 at 90° from the centre and grows without bound toward the rim. The site draws all its flat maps with this one function, for any centre.

- Sydney – Santiagoon this map: 25,684 kmgreat circle: 11,347 kmmap / ground: ×2.26

*Figure caption:* **One globe, one rule, any centre.** The thin lines from the centre are true in length and direction; the dashed orange rings are 30° apart on the ground. The orange straight line joins Sydney and Santiago, and the reading below compares its length on this map with the great-circle distance (dashed blue). Change the centre: the line is right only when it passes through the centre, and the polar map, the one used for a flat Earth, more than doubles it.

## The flat-earth map is a globe map

**In 1892 Alexander Gleason of Buffalo published a “New Standard Map of the World”** on a north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection, drawn on the projection of J. S. Christopher; he patented it in 1893 as a time chart, and he wrote that it supported his belief that the round Earth was false[14]. Its grid is the polar map above, computed from latitudes and longitudes measured on a globe. The United Nations emblem, adopted in 1946, is the same projection centred on the North Pole and cut at 60° S[15]. Both are reproduced today as “the” flat Earth.

$$\rho = R\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \varphi\right),\qquad \text{parallel drawn } 2\pi R\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \varphi\right) \text{ vs } 2\pi R\cos\varphi$$
$${k_{E\text{–}W} = \frac{\pi/2 - \varphi}{\cos\varphi}}$$

On the polar map every parallel is a circle whose radius is its true distance from the pole, so its drawn length is 2πR(π/2 − φ) while its true length is 2πR cos φ. East–west distances are drawn 1.08 times too long at London's latitude, 1.57 at the equator, 2.60 at Sydney's, and without limit toward the rim.

*Figure caption:* **Gleason's map with Tissot's circles.** The same 7° circles as on the other maps: round near the North Pole, stretched east–west further south, 2.60 times too wide at the latitude of Sydney, Cape Town and Buenos Aires. The dashed orange circle is the edge of the UN emblem, 60° S. Antarctica, a continent, becomes the rim.

> **Steel-manning the flat map.** On the polar map, every distance from the North Pole and every north–south distance along a meridian is exactly right; a test along a meridian cannot tell it from the globe. Nor is the North Pole special: any centre gives an equally valid map, true from its centre and wrong elsewhere. The flat model therefore has a free parameter, the centre, and the dist tab tunes it in the model's favour: the best centre for a set of measured flight distances still misses the southern routes by thousands of kilometres. **What would vindicate it:** one centre for which measured east–west distances in the south, Sydney–Santiago or Johannesburg–Perth, match the map's straight lines.

## Today: flat again, one small piece at a time

**Modern surveying and every phone's map grid come back to the first section.** The Universal Transverse Mercator system cuts the globe into sixty zones 6° of longitude wide and maps each on its own cylinder, touching the globe along the zone's central meridian[16]. Inside a zone the ground is treated as a plane, with an error small enough to be ignored and a formula to correct it: the reason a flat map of a small region was fine for the Babylonians is the reason it is fine for a land surveyor, and the reason the zones have to stop after 6°[9].

$${k \approx k_0\left(1 + \frac{x^2}{2R^2}\right),\qquad k_0 = 0.9996}$$

x is the distance from the zone's central meridian. The scale is set slightly below 1 on the central meridian so that it is exactly 1 about 180 km either side and only 1.0010 at the zone's edge, 334 km away at the equator: a thousandth at most, the same c²/2 growth as the first section's c²/6, for the same reason[16].

Reading the history this way, nobody ever had to choose between a flat map and a globe. Flat sheets were always right for small places, and the sphere was always behind them as soon as the sheets had to join. The other tabs measure where the join shows: the horizon, the distances, the angles to the Sun and the stars.

**See also**[Distances](/ai/dist.md)[Cel. nav.](/ai/cnav.md)[Dip](/ai/dip.md)[Aviation](/ai/avia.md)[Surveying](/ai/surv.md)[GPS](/ai/gps.md)
