# The aether: how a medium for light was looked for, and why physics stopped needing it

> Tab "Aether" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-aether. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Aether · history, and the arguments built on it*

Flat-earth and geocentric videos often cite the same handful of nineteenth-century experiments: “Airy's failure”, Michelson–Morley, Sagnac, Michelson–Gale, Dayton Miller, and the claim that Lorentz and Einstein invented relativity to hide a motionless Earth. This tab tells the story in order, simply: what the aether was supposed to be, what each experiment measured, which ideas it ruled out, and how special relativity came out of it. Two things are worth knowing before starting. None of these experiments looks at the *shape* of the Earth: they are about motion, and give the same answer on a ball or on a disc. And the one kind of motion that light can detect without looking outside, rotation, has been found every time a loop of light was built to look for it.

*Figure caption:* Two hundred and fifty years in one line. Above the line, the ideas; below, the experiments that tested them. Blue: a result that fits the moving Earth; amber: a null result, which the videos read as a motionless Earth.

## Light is a wave. A wave in what?

**Sound is a wave in air, ripples a wave in water. So what does light wave in?** Huygens described light in 1690 as a disturbance spreading through a very fine matter that fills space[1]. Young made light interfere with itself in 1801–1804, bright and dark bands where two waves add or cancel, which particles cannot do[2]. Fresnel showed in the 1810s that the waves are transverse, shaking sideways like a rope, not back and forth like sound. A wave needs something to wave: the *luminiferous aether*, the “light-carrying air”, invisible, weightless, filling even the vacuum between the stars, and at rest.

$${c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\,\varepsilon_0}}}$$

**Maxwell's surprise.** μ₀ and ε₀ say how strongly currents attract and how strongly charges attract; both come from bench experiments with coils and charged plates, nothing to do with light. In 1862 Maxwell found that waves of electric and magnetic field must travel at 1/√(μ₀ε₀), worked it out from Weber and Kohlrausch's electrical measurements, 310,740 km/s, and set it beside Fizeau's measured speed of light, 314,858 km/s[4]. Light is an electromagnetic wave. With today's constants the formula gives 299,792 km/s. The aether became the medium of electric and magnetic fields too, and the speed c in Maxwell's equations seemed to be the speed *relative to the aether*. If the Earth moves through it, light should go faster one way than the other. Finding that difference became the goal of the century.

## 1727: the Earth's speed seen in the stars

**Bradley was looking for parallax and found something else.** In 1725–1728 he watched γ Draconis pass overhead near London. It swung north and south by about 20 seconds of arc over the year, but three months out of step with what parallax would give, and by the same angle as every other star in the same part of the sky, near or far. He found the cause on a boat: a vane on the mast changes direction when the boat turns, though the wind has not changed[5]. The telescope must be tipped forward into the light, as a walker tips an umbrella forward into vertical rain. The full measurement, with today's data, is in the [Orbit](/ai/orb.md) tab.

*Figure caption:* **Starlight on a moving telescope.** The light falls straight down at c while both telescopes move to the right at v. In the one pointed straight at the star, the back wall catches up with the light before it reaches the eye. The one tipped forward by α, with tan α = v/c, lets it through. The Earth's speed is drawn 3,500 times too large, so the angle is 19° instead of 20.5″. Click to pause.

$${\tan\alpha = \frac{v}{c}}$$

v is the Earth's speed across the line to the star, c the speed of light. With v = 29.78 km/s, α = 20.5″. The aether story starts easily here: a still aether, an Earth moving through it, light arriving in straight lines, and the telescope tipped by the ratio of the two speeds. The angle is the same for all stars in a given direction because it depends on *our* velocity, not on theirs.

## 1810–1851: does moving glass or water carry light along?

**Arago expected starlight to bend differently through a prism** when the Earth moved toward a star than away from it. In 1810 he found no difference at all[6]. Fresnel answered in 1818 with a precise guess: the aether stays still, but a transparent body carries along a fraction of it, just enough to hide the motion: the fraction 1 − 1/n², where n is its refractive index[3]. Nothing for air (n ≈ 1), 0.44 for water. In 1851 Fizeau sent two beams of light through water flowing in opposite directions and compared them: the light was dragged, and by Fresnel's fraction, not by the full speed of the water[7]. Michelson and Morley repeated it in 1886 and confirmed it[31].

$${u = \frac{c}{n} + v\left(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\right)}$$

u is the speed of light in the lab, c/n its speed in still water, v the water's speed. f = 1 − 1/n² = 0.437 for water. In Fizeau's tubes the water ran at about 7.06 m/s: light gained 3.09 m/s, not the full 7.06 m/s. At the time this was the strongest support for a still aether with a moving Earth. Fifty years later, relativity gave the same formula without any aether (below).

## 1871: “Airy's failure”, a telescope full of water

**The idea is Boscovich's, from 1766.** Light is slower in water. If the telescope moves and the light inside crawls along at c/n, it should take longer to cross the tube, and the tube should need more tilt: fill the telescope with water and the aberration should grow. Klinkerfues claimed in 1867 that it did. Airy built a zenith telescope with a tube of water at Greenwich and watched γ Draconis, Bradley's star, in the spring and autumn of 1871: the aberration was exactly the same as with air[8].

> **What the videos say.** “Airy proved that the telescope is not moving. If the Earth moved, water would have changed the aberration. Since it did not, it is the stars that move around a motionless Earth: *Airy's failure*.”

$$\alpha_{\text{in}} = \frac{\alpha}{n}\ \text{(Snell)}\qquad {\frac{v - f v}{c/n} = \frac{v}{n c} = \frac{\alpha}{n}}\ \text{(Fresnel)}$$

**Fresnel had predicted Airy's result 53 years before it was measured**[3][31]. Two angles inside the tube must agree. The first is where the light goes: entering the water at the angle α = v/c, it bends toward the axis to α/n (Snell's law). The second is where it must go to reach the eyepiece: the tube moves at v, the light is dragged at f v, so it drifts back relative to the tube at v − f v while crossing at c/n. With f = 1 − 1/n², both angles are α/n, 15.4″ for n = 1.333. The water changes nothing. Without Fresnel's drag the ray and the tube would disagree by 11.9″, which Airy would have seen. So Airy's null result is not a failure of the moving Earth: it is the predicted result of a moving Earth and Fresnel's drag, the same drag Fizeau had measured in running water twenty years before.

**Could the stars be the ones moving?** Kinematically, aberration only shows the *relative* velocity between the telescope and the light, and relativity agrees that a motionless Earth with everything else swinging around it is a possible description (the last section). But in a still aether, a star's own motion does not tip its light: the star is simply seen where it was when the light left it. Aberration is the same 20.5″ for every star, near or far, and every star swings in step with the Sun's year. The stars would have to move each on its own ellipse, sized to its own distance so that all the angles come out equal, all keeping time with the Sun. A moving Earth gives it with one number. The [Orbit](/ai/orb.md) tab adds the stars' Doppler shift, which swings by ±30 km/s with the same year. And none of this involves the shape of the ground: a flat Earth in a still aether would face Airy's question exactly as a round one.

## 1881–1887: Michelson and Morley look for the aether wind

**All the earlier experiments measured effects of order v/c, one part in ten thousand, and Fresnel's drag hid them all.** Maxwell pointed out that a round trip of light would still feel the motion, at order (v/c)², one part in a hundred million, far too small to measure, he thought[31]. Michelson built an instrument that could: split a beam in two, send the halves along two perpendicular arms to mirrors and back, and recombine them. Any difference in the two travel times moves the interference fringes. A swimmer explains why. Crossing a river and back takes less time than swimming the same distance upstream and back down, because what the current takes going up it does not fully give back coming down. If the Earth moves through the aether, the arm along the motion is the upstream swim.

*Figure caption:* **The race Michelson set up.** Left: the instrument as an aether supporter expected it, with the aether blowing past along one arm. Both pulses leave the half-silvered mirror together; the one along the wind goes up at c − v and back at c + v, the one across goes at √(c² − v²) both ways, and it comes back first. Right: what was measured, the two pulses back together, as if there were no wind. The wind is drawn at half the speed of light, 5,000 times the Earth's orbital speed, so that the delay can be seen. Click to pause.

$$t_{\text{∥}} = \frac{2L/c}{1 - v^2/c^2},\qquad t_{\text{⊥}} = \frac{2L/c}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}},\qquad {\Delta t \approx \frac{L}{c}\,\frac{v^2}{c^2}}$$

L is the length of each arm, v the speed of the aether wind. In 1887, mirrors folded the light path to L = 11 m; with v = 30 km/s, v²/c² = 0.99 × 10⁻⁸ and Δt = 0.36 × 10⁻¹⁵ s. Turning the instrument by 90° swaps the arms, so the fringes should move by 2(L/λ)(v/c)² = 0.39 of a fringe. Michelson and Morley saw less than a fortieth of that[10]. Their first attempt, at Potsdam in 1881, was already null, but with arms of 1.2 m it was too small to be sure[9]. They also measured at different times of day and planned to repeat it at different seasons: even if the Earth happened to stand still in the aether one day, six months later it would move at 60 km/s relative to that day.

> **What the videos say.** “Michelson–Morley found no motion of the Earth. The simplest explanation is that the Earth does not move. Scientists would not accept it, so they invented relativity.”

**What the experiment actually tested is motion through the aether, not motion around the Sun.** A motionless Earth would indeed give a null result, if the aether were also motionless around it. But then aberration, which needs the light and the Earth to move relative to each other by 30 km/s, swinging through the year, would have no cause; and if the aether swept past a fixed Earth at that speed to make aberration, Michelson would have measured the wind. A motionless Earth explains one of the two results, not both. The second point is that the interferometer cannot tell the shape of anything: the same arms on a disc give the same null result. And the third: rotation *is* visible to a loop of light, at Michelson's own hands in 1925 (below). A bench instrument with two straight arms, like his of 1887, encloses no area and is blind to it.

## 1889–1904: saving the aether, contraction and “local time”

**Physicists did not give the aether up after 1887; they tried to keep it.** Stokes had proposed in 1845 that the Earth drags the aether completely along at its surface, which would explain a null result, but Lorentz showed in 1886 that no smooth flow could both stick to the Earth and give the aberration[11]. FitzGerald in 1889, then Lorentz in 1892, suggested something stranger: a body moving through the aether shrinks along its motion, by exactly the amount that cancels Michelson's time difference[12]. Lorentz grounded it on the idea that the forces holding matter together are electromagnetic, and so are affected by motion through the aether as light is.

$${L_{\text{∥}} = L\,\sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad t_{\text{∥}} = \frac{2L/c}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = t_{\text{⊥}}$$

Shorten the arm along the motion by √(1 − v²/c²) and the two round trips take the same time at any speed: no fringe moves. For the Earth's 30 km/s, the shortening is 5 parts in a billion, 0.05 µm on Michelson's 11 m path. No ruler could see it, because the ruler shrinks too.

**Contraction alone was not enough.** Lorentz added in 1895 a “local time” for moving bodies, a mathematical device at first, and in 1904 wrote the full set of transformations between a frame at rest in the aether and a moving one; Larmor had found the slowing of moving clocks in 1897–1900[31]. Poincaré named them after Lorentz in 1905 and showed that they form a group, and that the principle of relativity holds exactly with them[13]. Lorentz kept his aether to the end of his life. His theory was the aether, at rest, but with every effect of moving through it exactly hidden.

> **What the videos say.** “Lorentz contraction is an *ad hoc* invention. It was made up to rescue the moving Earth from Michelson–Morley, and has never been seen.”

**It was ad hoc in 1889, and the honest account says so.** What changed is that it was then tested by experiments it was not designed for. Kennedy and Thorndike (1932) built an interferometer with arms of *unequal* length: contraction alone predicts a fringe shift that changes over the day and year, and none was seen; only contraction together with slowed clocks gives zero[16]. Ives and Stilwell (1938) measured the slowed clocks directly, as a shift in the light of fast-moving hydrogen ions[16]. The muons of the next section live 29 times longer than at rest, and a particle collider is built on these formulas. An idea that began as a patch became a predicted, measured effect. Nor did any of it have anything to do with the Earth's shape: the whole debate was about a flat bench with two arms on it.

## 1905: Einstein drops the aether

**Einstein started from two rules instead of a medium.** First, the principle of relativity: the laws of physics are the same in every frame moving uniformly, so no experiment inside a smoothly moving cabin can tell its speed; Galileo had said it for ships in 1632 ([Basics](/ai/phys.md)). Second, light in vacuum always goes at c, whatever the speed of its source. Together they seem to contradict each other, until one accepts that time and length depend on the frame. Lorentz's transformations then follow from the two rules, with no aether behind them, and Einstein wrote that the introduction of a “light aether” would prove superfluous[14]. The aether was not disproved by one experiment: it became undetectable by construction, and then unnecessary.

*Figure caption:* **Two identical light clocks.** Each tick is a round trip of light between two mirrors. The clock on the right passes at 0.6 c: its light, at the same speed c, runs along a longer zigzag, so each tick takes γ = 1.25 times longer. After ten ticks of the clock at rest, the moving one has ticked eight times. Click to pause.

$${\Delta t = \gamma\,\Delta\tau},\qquad \gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}},\qquad x^{\prime} = \gamma\,(x - v t),\quad t^{\prime} = \gamma\left(t - \frac{v x}{c^2}\right)$$

**The light clock.** A pulse bounces between two mirrors; each tick is a round trip. Seen from a frame where the clock moves at v, the pulse runs along a longer zigzag at the same speed c, so each tick lasts longer by γ: moving clocks run slow. τ is the time the clock itself shows. For the Earth's orbital speed γ − 1 = 4.9 × 10⁻⁹. Muons made by cosmic rays live 2.2 µs at rest; in CERN's storage ring at γ = 29.33 they lived 64.4 µs, against 64.4 µs predicted[17]. Atomic clocks flown around the world in 1971 gained and lost what was predicted[18].

$${u = \frac{u^{\prime} + v}{1 + u^{\prime} v / c^2}}\quad\Rightarrow\quad u^{\prime} = \frac{c}{n}:\ \ u \approx \frac{c}{n} + v\left(1 - \frac{1}{n^2}\right)$$

**Velocities no longer simply add.** u′ is a speed measured in a moving frame, v the frame's speed, u the result. At everyday speeds the denominator is 1 and u = u′ + v; near c the sum never passes c. Put in light in water, u′ = c/n, and the formula gives Fresnel's drag, coefficient and all, as von Laue showed in 1907[15]. Fizeau's and Airy's results, once the best evidence *for* an aether, are consequences of relativity with no aether at all.

$$\frac{\Delta f}{f} \approx -\frac{v^2}{2c^2} + \frac{GM}{c^2}\left(\frac{1}{R} - \frac{1}{r}\right)$$

**The same formulas in every phone.** A GPS satellite moves at 3.87 km/s at r = 26,560 km from the Earth's centre. Its speed slows its clock by 7.2 µs a day (special relativity); the weaker gravity up there speeds it up by +45.7 µs a day (general relativity). Net: +38.5 µs a day, which at the speed of light is about 11 km of range error a day. The clocks are tuned slow before launch to cancel it[19] ([GPS](/ai/gps.md)).

**Six ideas, six experiments.** The table puts the main hypotheses of the period against the experiments of this tab. Each row is a model of what light does; each column an experiment; a tick means the model gets that result without extra help.

**Which idea survives which experiment. Aberration: Bradley[5]; drag: Fizeau and Airy[7][8]; MM: Michelson–Morley[10]; KT: Kennedy–Thorndike[16]; rotation: Sagnac and Michelson–Gale[23][25]; binaries: light from double stars arrives together whatever the speed of its source[30].**

| Hypothesis | Aberration | Drag | MM | KT | Rotation | Binaries |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Still aether, no drag | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Still aether, Fresnel's drag (1818) | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Aether fully dragged by the Earth (Stokes, 1845) | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ |
| Motionless Earth in a motionless aether | ✗ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓* | ✓ |
| Light thrown from its source like a ball (Ritz, 1908) | ✓ | – | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Aether with contraction and local time (Lorentz, 1904) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Special relativity, no aether (Einstein, 1905) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| *** only if the aether, and the stars with it, turn around the Earth once a sidereal day (next section).** | | | | | | |

**Two rows survive everything, and the table says so honestly.** Lorentz's aether theory predicts exactly what special relativity predicts; it keeps a frame of absolute rest that no experiment can ever find. Physics chose Einstein's version because it says the same with fewer assumptions, not because Lorentz's was refuted. The motionless Earth fails on aberration, the first experiment of the list, and needs a rotating aether for the next section. None of the rows says anything about whether the ground is curved.

## 1913–1925: rotation, which light does see

**Uniform motion cannot be felt from inside; rotation can.** A merry-go-round pushes you outward with your eyes closed. Light feels it too. Send two beams round a closed loop in opposite directions: if the loop turns, the beam going with the turn has further to go before reaching the starting point, which has moved on, and arrives later. Sagnac did it on a turntable in 1913. He was an aether supporter, and titled his paper “the luminous aether demonstrated”[23]. But von Laue had already worked out the same effect from special relativity in 1911, two years before the experiment[24]: the result needs rotation relative to the local non-rotating frames, not an aether.

*Figure caption:* **Two pulses round a loop.** Both leave the splitter (black dot) together, one each way, at the speed of light. Left, the loop is at rest: they meet it again at the same moment. Right, the loop turns: the splitter moves on while they travel, the pulse going against the turn meets it early and the one going with the turn late, at 2πR/(c ∓ ωR). The rim is drawn turning at a quarter of the speed of light; the Earth's surface turns at most at 465 m/s. Click to pause.

$${\Delta t = \frac{4 A\,\Omega}{c^2}},\qquad \Delta N = \frac{4 A\,\Omega \sin\varphi}{\lambda\,c}$$

A is the area enclosed by the loop, Ω its rate of turn, λ the wavelength, φ the latitude: a loop lying flat on the ground feels only the part Ω sin φ of the Earth's rotation. In 1925, Michelson, Gale and Pearson laid pipes in a rectangle of 2010 × 1113 feet (20.8 hectares) at Clearing, Illinois, pumped the air out and sent light both ways round. With the Earth's sidereal rotation the formula gives 0.236 fringe; they measured 0.230 ± 0.005[25]. Today ring lasers a few metres across read the Earth's rotation continuously, down to small wobbles of its axis[26] ([Rotation](/ai/rot.md)).

> **What the videos say.** “Sagnac proved the aether exists. Michelson–Gale measured the aether turning around a motionless Earth. Michelson–Morley shows the Earth does not move, Michelson–Gale shows the sky does.”

**Sagnac's own reading lost, but his measurement stands.** Relativity predicts the same Δt = 4AΩ/c² without a medium, so the effect does not choose the aether. What Michelson–Gale measured is a rotation of Ω sin φ with Ω the sidereal rate: one turn in 23 h 56 min, relative to the stars, not to the Sun. The geocentric reading needs a universe, aether and stars included, turning around the Earth every 23 h 56 min, and dragging with it every other effect of rotation: the Foucault pendulum's turn ([Foucault](/ai/fou.md)), the gyroscopes of aircraft ([Aviation](/ai/avia.md)), the equatorial bulge and the weaker gravity at the equator ([Gravity](/ai/grav.md)), each with the right value at each latitude. One turning Earth gives all of them. And the two Michelson experiments do not contradict each other: the 1887 instrument had straight arms enclosing no area, blind to rotation by design and to uniform motion by relativity. **What would have changed the verdict:** a loop at rest on the ground reading zero. Every such loop since 1925 has read Ω sin φ.

## 1921–1933: Dayton Miller's aether wind, and what came after

**One physicist kept finding a wind.** Dayton Miller, who had worked with Morley, repeated the experiment for years, on Mount Wilson in the 1920s, and reported a small periodic fringe shift corresponding to a wind of about 9 to 10 km/s[27]. It is the result most often quoted against relativity. In 1955 Shankland and colleagues went through Miller's original sheets: the signal followed the temperature of the hut, warmed unevenly by the sun, and not the stars[28]; a 2006 reanalysis found that the instrument's own drift was larger than the signal[28]. Meanwhile every other repetition came out null, with better instruments: Joos in 1930 at Jena saw at most 0.002 fringe where 0.75 was expected[20].

*Figure caption:* How tightly the aether wind has been ruled out, as the largest difference allowed between the light's round-trip times along two directions, as a fraction of the time. The dashed line is what a 30 km/s wind would give. Interferometers 1881–1930[9][10][20]; rotating optical cavities 2009 and 2015[21][22]. Logarithmic scale: each step is a factor of ten.

**Today's versions are a hundred million times more sensitive than 1887.** Lasers locked to optical cavities of sapphire or glass, turned on a table, compare the light's speed along two directions to one part in 10¹⁸, and find no difference[21][22]. A Miller-sized wind would be ten billion times larger than the limit.

## “Either coordinate system with equal justification”: what relativity says about the Earth

> **What the videos say.** “Einstein himself admitted that you cannot tell whether the Earth moves around the Sun or the Sun around the Earth. So the heliocentric model is a choice, not a fact, and the globe with it.”

**The quotation is real.** Einstein and Infeld wrote in 1938, introducing general relativity, that if the laws of physics hold in every coordinate system, “the struggle, so violent in the early days of science, between the views of Ptolemy and Copernicus would then be quite meaningless. Either CS could be used with equal justification”[29]. It means one may *compute* in a frame where the Earth stands still. In that frame, though, the equations contain centrifugal and Coriolis terms, and a far-off universe sweeping round at enormous speeds; the pendulums, the bulge, the gyroscopes, the satellites come out exactly as in the other frame ([Basics](/ai/phys.md), frames of reference). Choosing a frame changes the velocities in the description; it does not change what instruments read.

$${\Delta D = D\left(1 - \sqrt{1 - \frac{v^2}{c^2}}\right) \approx D\,\frac{v^2}{2c^2}}$$

**A change of frame does not change a shape.** The distance between two points on the ground, measured with instruments resting on the ground, is the same whatever frame one uses to describe the Earth's motion. The one thing relativity changes is the Earth's length along its motion as described from the Sun's frame: D = 12,742 km and v = 30 km/s give 6.3 cm, five billionths of the diameter, invisible on any drawing and the same for a disc. No choice of coordinates makes a ball flat or a disc round; the shape is measured by the other tabs ([Results](/ai/results.md)).

## The recurring arguments, one by one

**Each argument, what the experiment measured, and what it says about the Earth's motion and its shape.**

| The argument | What was measured | Motion | Shape |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| “Airy's failure”: water did not change aberration, so the stars move | The same 20.5″ with water, as Fresnel predicted for a moving Earth in 1818[3][8] | fits the moving Earth; the alternative needs each star's own synchronised ellipse | nothing |
| Michelson–Morley found no motion | No difference along two arms, less than 1/40 of 0.4 fringe[10] | no detectable aether; aberration still needs relative motion of 30 km/s | nothing |
| Lorentz contraction is ad hoc | Later: Kennedy–Thorndike, Ives–Stilwell, muons, flying clocks, GPS[16][17][18][19] | the effects are measured, at the predicted size | 6 cm on the Earth's diameter, from the Sun's frame |
| Sagnac proved the aether | A rotating loop delays one beam by 4AΩ/c²[23] | predicted by relativity in 1911[24]; detects rotation, not a medium | nothing |
| Michelson–Gale measured the aether turning | 0.230 fringe against 0.236 for the Earth's sidereal rotation[25] | the Earth turns once in 23 h 56 min relative to the stars | nothing |
| Miller found an aether wind | A signal that followed the hut's temperature[28] | no wind, to 1 part in 10¹⁸ today[22] | nothing |
| Einstein said no frame is preferred | A statement about coordinates[29] | any frame can be used; the instruments read the same | a shape does not depend on the frame |

**In one sentence:** the aether was a reasonable idea, tested honestly for a century; the experiments that found nothing found nothing for any Earth, round or flat; the ones that found something found rotation and orbital motion; and relativity, which came out of them, is checked every day by the clocks that position a phone. Where the Earth's shape is actually measured, angles, distances, times and shadows, see the other tabs and [Results](/ai/results.md).

# Case studies

> Tab "Case studies" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-cases. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Case studies · claims examined with their own data*

Each section takes one published observation offered as evidence for a flat Earth, finds where and when it was made, and redoes it with the operators' own numbers and the open data of that day. Both models get the same inputs. The question is not whether the observers saw what they say, but what their own measurements allow anyone to conclude.

## Worthing–Brighton, February 2019: a laser across 15 km of sea [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the 15.2 km between the piers is computed from their coordinates on a sphere of radius R.]

**The claim.** On the evening of 23 February 2019 a group set up lasers and cameras on the beach at the end of Worthing Pier and at the foot of the West Pier ruins in Brighton, 15.2 km apart across the sea, each about 1 m above the water at low tide.[1] Each side saw the other's laser, blocked and released on command over a livestream; then the green laser at Worthing was lowered to about 0.5 m and 0.15 m above the water, and still seen from a camera 0.7 m up at Brighton. Their presentation concludes that no refraction occurred, since no mirage could be seen, and that no curvature lies between the piers. It also records an earlier attempt, on 2 February, when the laser could not be seen; that failure was put down to a "refraction zone" above the sea.[1]

**Where and when.** The slides give the piers and a map. On OpenStreetMap[7] the laser and camera at Worthing sit on the sand off the south end of the pier, about 50.807° N 0.369° W, and those at Brighton on the beach north-west of the West Pier ruin, about 50.820° N 0.153° W: 15.2 km apart (they give 15.3), all of it over the sea, half a kilometre to two kilometres off the coast. The tide was near its low; the Newhaven gauge[5] confirms the low water just after 20:00 UTC. That evening Shoreham Airport, halfway along the line, reported a clear sky and 3 to 4 knots of wind,[4] and ERA5 gives 1,033.9 hPa.[3]

$$H = \frac{\left(d - \sqrt{2Rh_c}\right)^2}{2R},\qquad R_{\text{eff}} = \frac{R}{1-k} \ge \frac{d^2}{2\left(\sqrt{h_s} + \sqrt{h_c}\right)^2}$$

d is the distance, h_c the camera's height and h_s the laser's above the water, R the Earth's radius. H is the height hidden behind the bulge for straight light: 10.7 m for their first trial, 8.9 m with the usual refraction k = 0.13, so their slides are right that a 1 m laser should be hidden from 1 m. It is seen if the air bends light enough to stretch the effective radius past d²/2(√h_s + √h_c)²: a uniform k of 0.78 for 1 m to 1 m, 0.92 for 0.15 m to 0.7 m. The bulge between the piers is 4.5 m.

*[Figure: Animation: the laser 1 m above the sea at Worthing seen from a camera 1 m up at Brighton, 15.2 km away, on a globe (top) and on a plane (bottom) in the same air, through four airs. On 2 February, in the cold air estimated from ERA5, the beam passes far above the camera on both. On 23 February, in the air measured at Worthing, the globe shows it directly and the plane by reflection; in the air measured at Brighton, the globe hides it and the plane shows it; in the weakest uniform air the globe needs, the globe shows it directly.]*

- **2 Feb 2019, air estimated from ERA5 and OISST (6.3 °C colder than the sea)**
- globe: hidden
- plane: hidden

*Figure caption:* **The same test, ray by ray, in four airs.** 81 rays of a 1 mrad beam fired level 1 m above the water, traced to a camera 1 m up, over the globe (top; the sea bulges 4.5 m between them) and over a plane (bottom), in the same air. 2 February, the air estimated from ERA5 and OISST, cold over a warm sea: the beam is thrown upward and passes far above the camera on both, as the laser was not seen. 23 February, the air measured at Worthing: the globe shows the beam directly, the plane only by reflection off the water (dashed after a first bounce). The air measured at Brighton: the globe hides it, the plane shows it. Last, the weakest uniform air in which the globe shows the laser: +0.17 °C over 2 m, less than their thermometers could resolve. The method is the Refraction tab's laser section. Click to pause.

| Trial | Laser → camera | Seen | Hidden, straight light | k needed | Warming needed over 2 m | In the air measured at Worthing: globe / plane | At Brighton: globe / plane |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Feb 2 | Worthing 1.00 m → Brighton 1.0 m | no | 10.7 m | 0.78 | 0.16 °C | no readings that night; air estimated from ERA5 and OISST: hidden / hidden |  |
| Feb 23 20:48 | Brighton 1.00 m → Worthing 1.0 m | yes | 10.7 m | 0.78 | 0.17 °C | seen, direct / by reflection | hidden / seen, direct |
| Feb 23 | Worthing 1.00 m → Brighton 1.0 m | yes | 10.7 m | 0.78 | 0.17 °C | seen, direct / by reflection | hidden / seen, direct |
| Feb 23 | Worthing 0.50 m → Brighton 0.7 m | yes | 11.8 m | 0.87 | 0.20 °C | by reflection / by reflection | hidden / seen, direct |
| Feb 23 | Worthing 0.15 m → Brighton 0.7 m | yes | 11.8 m | 0.92 | 0.21 °C | hidden / hidden | hidden / seen, direct |

*Figure caption:* **The five trials of the presentation.** Hidden height for straight light over a globe of 6,371 km; the uniform refraction coefficient that would let the camera see the laser; the same as a warming of the air with height at that evening's pressure and temperature. The last two columns trace 81 rays of a 1 mrad beam through the air measured at each end (thermometer A; B gives the same), over the globe and over a plane: *direct*, a ray reaches the camera without touching the water; *by reflection*, only rays that bounced off calm water arrive; *hidden*, none arrives. For 2 February, with no readings, the air is estimated from ERA5 and OISST with the usual logarithmic profile of the surface layer. The method is the Refraction tab's laser section.

**What their thermometers could see.** They read the air at several heights at both ends, with two thermometers good to ±0.25 °C, read to the half degree.[1] The refraction coefficient follows the vertical temperature gradient,[8] and the globe needs only 0.17 °C of warming between the water and 2 m for the first trial (0.21 °C for the lowest). At Worthing both thermometers show the air warming by 1.5 °C over 2 m, 0.77 °C per metre: 9 times what is needed, and at least 0.51 °C per metre within their stated precision. At Brighton the readings are flat between the water and 1.78 m, which their precision cannot tell from any gradient between −0.28 and 0.28 °C per metre, the needed one included. Their own conclusion, that the readings were "indistinguishable within the precision", is exactly why they cannot rule refraction out.

$$k = 503\cdot\frac{P}{T^2}\left(0.0342 + \frac{dT}{dh}\right)$$

P in hPa, T in K, dT/dh in K per metre: with that evening's 1,034 hPa and 8 °C, every 0.1 °C per metre of warming adds 0.66 to k. Air whose temperature does not change with height gives k ≈ 0.22; the standard atmosphere 0.13–0.17.

**Two evenings, two answers.** On 2 February, when the laser was not seen, ERA5 puts the air 2 m above the sea at 2.9 °C over a sea at 9.2 °C, with a wind of 34 km/h off the land.[3][6] Cold air over warmer water bends low rays upward, the hot-road mirage the slides describe; estimated with the usual logarithmic profile of the surface layer, it hides the laser on the globe and on the plane alike. On 23 February the air offshore was as warm as the sea (9.2 against 8.9 °C) under a light wind, and the water at Brighton, 7.0 °C, was no warmer than the air above it: the warm-over-cold layer their Worthing thermometers measured, in which the traced beam reaches the camera on the globe directly. The presentation accepts refraction when the laser disappears and rejects it when the laser appears. Both evenings follow the air; neither tests the shape.

*Figure caption:* The two evenings from ERA5 (air 2 m above the sea, sea cell 50.75° N 0.25° W) and OISST (the sea), 17 to 22 h UTC. 2 February: air 6 °C colder than the sea, wind 34 km/h from the north-north-west; the laser was not seen. 23 February: air as warm as the sea offshore, light wind; the laser was seen. The water at the beaches was colder than OISST's offshore cells: they measured 7.0 °C at Brighton.

**What the night pictures show.** The stills from Worthing show the laser at Brighton just below the lamps of King's Road and well below the British Airways i360, 162 m tall.[1][7] These cannot decide anything: the i360, the lamps and the laser are at the same distance, so the angle between them is the same whatever bends the light, 10.95 mrad between the i360's top light and the laser in straight air, 10.96 mrad with k = 0.78. And with the air it takes to see the laser at all, only about a metre stays hidden on the globe: the lamps 12 to 13 m above the water are seen in both models. "No mirage" proves no more: a steady gradient bends light without doubling any image; a mirage needs the gradient to change sharply with height.[9]

> **The flat model at its best, and the symmetric verdict.** In ordinary air the plane predicts the laser seen every time, from any height; the globe predicts it hidden by about 11 m. That is a clean test, but only if the air is ordinary, and nothing on these evenings showed that it was: on 2 February the laser vanished as it would over a globe in cold air, and on 23 February it appeared in air measured to be warming with height. **What would vindicate the plane:** a narrow beam seen again and again from 1 m at 15 km, by day and by night, while thermometers good to 0.05 °C at 0.25, 0.5, 1 and 2 m, at both ends and on a boat halfway, show the air not warming with height. **What would vindicate the globe:** the same beam hidden, under the same thermometers.

**How to make it decisive.** Their own list of improvements points the right way: measure at the same heights at both ends, and away from the body heat of the people taking the readings. Add the missing pieces: thermometers ten times finer, a reading halfway along the line, and the angle of the laser above or below the true level at the camera, read with a theodolite or a levelled camera. That is where the two models part by a sign: in the air it takes to see the laser, the globe puts it 0.26 mrad below the camera's horizontal, the plane 0.93 mrad above it (0.16 in ordinary air); a good theodolite reads a hundredth of that. Repeat from several heights, as the lasers were lowered here, and by day.

> **Limits.** The thermometer readings are the operators' own, at the beach, at low tide; nobody measured the air over the 15 km between. Each traced verdict applies one end's air to the whole path, which is why the lowest trial, 0.15 m, comes out hidden in Worthing's air for both models while it was seen: the air along the line was not Worthing's. The sites are placed from the slides' map to about 50 m; the distance from their coordinates uses the globe's radius, so the case is a check, not a measurement. The 2 February profile is estimated from ERA5 and OISST, not measured, and the time of that attempt is not given.

6. [6] [NOAA OISST v2.1](https://coastwatch.pfeg.noaa.gov/erddap/griddap/ncdcOisst21Agg_LonPM180.html), daily sea surface temperature (NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP), the two cells offshore of the line.
7. [7] [OpenStreetMap contributors](https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright) (Nominatim): Worthing Pier, the West Pier and the British Airways i360 (162 m), Brighton.
8. [8] S. Baselga & L. García-Asenjo, "Practical Formulas for the Refraction Coefficient", *Journal of Surveying Engineering* 140(2), 2014: k = 503·P/T²·(0.0342 + dT/dh).
9. [9] A. T. Young, [An Introduction to Mirages](https://aty.sdsu.edu/mirages/mirintro.html) (San Diego State University): what makes a mirage, and why a steady gradient does not.

*Contributions · observations sent to the site, measured in the open*

This tab collects observations sent by readers, including readers who think the Earth is flat. Each one is measured with open data, and both models get the same data, the same distances and the same freedom. The analysis is published as it stands, limits included, so that the contributor can check every number and every step.

## Bass Rock from East Lomond Hill, 40 km across the Firth of Forth [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the 39.9 km from the camera to Bass Rock, computed from coordinates (the camera placed on the Copernicus elevation model) on a sphere of radius R.]

**The photograph.** [KenRDKAB](https://x.com/KenRDKAB) sent this annotated picture, published here with his permission, taken at 5:28 am on 9 August 2023, just after sunrise, from 345 m up East Lomond Hill in Fife, Scotland. The caption gives Bass Rock as 112 m high and 39.9 km away, and St Abb's Head, on the right, as 75.9 km away. There is no original file and nothing else. The picture shows one thing clearly: the sea horizon passes *behind* Bass Rock, about two thirds of the way up, so the top of the rock stands against the sky although it is more than 230 m below the camera.

**What open data adds.** A first guess puts the camera on East Lomond's 345 m contour, on the Copernicus GLO-30 elevation model[4], where its distances to Bass Rock and to St Abb's Head[8] match the contributor's within 20 m. The photograph corrects it, by parallax. The rock is 40 km away and the coast of St Abb's Head 76 km, so a step of one metre sideways changes the angle between them by 12 µrad. The outline of St Abb's Head is read on the photograph, column by column, and the model's outline, seen over GLO-30 from the camera, is slid along it. From the first guess the model puts St Abb's Head 5.7 mrad (160 px) too far to the right, though once slid the two outlines agree within 0.9 px. Fitted with a free scale, the outline's own shape gives 27,700 px per radian, against 28,158 from the rock's height: the picture's scale is right, the camera stood elsewhere. The angle comes out right only along one line across the eastern flank of East Lomond, and where that line has a clear view of the sea its ground rises no higher than 336 m. The camera is put there, 466 m to the left of the first guess, 1.5 m above the ground: 337 m rather than the contributor's 345 m, at 56.2408° N, 3.2074° W. The two outlines then agree to 0.02 mrad. One thing fits less well: from there the near coast of Fife, at the bottom of the picture, comes out about 1.2 mrad (some 30 px) lower in the model than in the photograph. A camera near 310 m would fit it, but GLO-30 renders the trees and roofs along that coast only roughly, so the height is kept as close to the contributor's as the line allows. From there the rock is 39.5 km away (the contributor wrote 39.9) and St Abb's Head 75.5 km (75.9). Bass Rock rises to 107 m[5]; the contributor wrote 112 m, and GLO-30's 30 m cells round its summit down to 96 m. The photograph has its own estimate: its width there against the angle it spans from the camera gives the scale, and its height in pixels then gives 118 ± 9 m. The Leith tide gauge[6] has a gap from 03:00–05:30 UTC that morning. Four weeks of readings were fitted with 12 tidal constituents and the weather's surge interpolated across the gap; done the same way on every other window of that length, the method is off by 9 cm (root mean square). The sea was −0.02 m from its mean level, so the camera was 337 m above the water. The air comes from the ERA5 reanalysis[1], Open-Meteo's sea temperature[2] and the GFS model's levels up to 750 m[7], at three points along the line of sight.

*Figure caption:* **The globe and the plane side by side.** The header gives the date and time, a gauge of the tide at Leith that day (low water on the left, high on the right, in metres from the mean level; the triangle is the sea at the photograph's minute) and the camera's height above the water. From 337 m the tide barely matters: a metre of water moves the horizon on the rock by less than 1% of its height. The light is first straight: on the globe the horizon crosses the rock about half way up, on the plane it stands far above the summit (the sea is drawn out to 200 km). Then standard refraction, k = 0.13, then the refraction each model needs for the horizon of the photograph. Both panels then draw the same picture, and [KenRDKAB](https://x.com/KenRDKAB)'s photograph is laid over each, scaled by the rock's height and levelled on the horizon it shows (the camera was tilted by 0.55°). Each view is a little wider and taller than the photograph, so the picture sits whole inside it, the model continuing around it. The orange dashes mark the horizon measured on the photograph; the bar right of the rock shows f. The relief is Copernicus GLO-30 seen from the camera, the rock raised to its surveyed height. **Below each view**, the cross-section along the line of sight: the model's true surface (a sphere of radius R, or a plane), the ray that grazes the sea at the horizon with its own curvature, k/R, and in orange the part of the rock below it. Rule 1: heights and both curvatures are multiplied by the same printed factor in both panels. **The gauges**, far left for the globe and far right for the plane, show the same thing for both: the mean temperature gradient between 2 m and the camera, in kelvin per 100 m. The black bar is the GFS model's that morning, with the range of the three points and of the reanalysis' surface. The coloured triangle is the gradient the panel needs at that moment, from rays traced through the air with GFS's difference between the air and the sea. Once the photograph is laid, the coloured band gives both models the same margin: the air − sea differences of the models and their points (−7.0 to −3.4 K) and f plus or minus its uncertainty. The dotted lines are the dry adiabatic lapse rate (−0.98 K per 100 m) and the autoconvective one (−3.4 K per 100 m), below which air is denser at the top than at the bottom.

**Measuring the photograph.** Three edges are read on brightness profiles. The sea horizon, in 50 bands of 20 columns on both sides of the rock, is a straight line to 0.5 px; its slope is the camera's tilt, 0.55°. The rock's outline above it gives the summit, the lowest row of a 5-column running mean. The rock's foot at the water is the median over 100 columns, levelled with the tilt. The horizon cuts the rock at **f = 0.650 ± 0.008** of its height from the foot. That is a ratio of two lengths on the same picture: it needs no scale, no focal length and no time.

$$f = \frac{d}{H}\left[\frac{e}{d} + \frac{c\,d}{2R} - \sqrt{\frac{2ce}{R}}\right]$$
$${c_{\text{globe}} = 1 - k},\qquad c_{\text{plane}} = -k$$

e is the camera above the water, d and H the rock's distance and height, c the apparent curvature: straight light over a surface of radius R/c. The bracket is the horizon's dip below the rock's foot, as an angle, times d. As at Brighton, one picture fixes c and cannot tell the models apart; the photograph needs c = 0.82, so k = +0.18 on the globe and k = −0.82 on the plane.

$$k = 503\,\frac{P}{T^2}\left(0.0343 + \frac{dT}{dz}\right)$$

The refraction coefficient of air whose temperature changes with height at the rate dT/dz (K/m), at pressure P (hPa) and temperature T (K)[3]. In the standard atmosphere, −0.65 K per 100 m, k is about 0.17. Light bends upward (k < 0) only when the temperature falls faster than 3.43 K per 100 m: at that rate the air no longer gets thinner with height.

**What each model needs from the air.** In uniform air the globe's k = +0.18 means −0.6 K per 100 m, close to the standard atmosphere. The plane's k = −0.82 means −16.3 K per 100 m, through the whole 337 m the light crosses. The traced rays say the same with the morning's own layers. Near the sea the air was cold over a warm sea (11.7 °C against 15.5 °C), and above it the GFS model has the temperature almost flat up to 750 m: 0.0 (−0.3 … +0.4) K per 100 m on average. In that air the globe puts the horizon at f = 0.52, 0.58, with a dip of 32,832.2′, a little low. The difference comes from the lowest metres. GFS has the air at 2 m −6.1 K from the sea (ERA5 −3.8 K), and a sea warmer than the air bends the rays that graze it upward, which lowers the horizon. Keep the model's column and change only that difference: with air as warm as the sea the globe gives f = 0.68, and the photograph needs the air −1.0 K from the sea (−1.0 (−1.3 … −0.6)). Those differences come from model cells 25 km wide on a coast, where land cooled by the night can enter, and the wind blew from the land. Put as one gradient over the whole column instead, the same correction looks large, +2.1 (+0.8 … +2.5) K per 100 m or +7 K over the column, because a uniform change of the column is a weak lever on the lowest metres. Given the same freedom, the plane gains little: no air − sea difference alone moves it (f stays > 1.5–> 1.5), and with the column it needs −12.8 (−13.8 … −12.4) K per 100 m over the models' range, still −11.6 with the air − sea difference most favourable to it, −10 K: the camera's air −43 K colder than the sea's, and denser at the top than at the bottom over 337 m. Air like that overturns at once; it can only exist in a thin layer over hot ground.

> **Limits, stated plainly.** There is no original file: the picture is a 1920 × 1080 slide, resized and compressed, the time is the contributor's, the focal length unknown. At dawn the horizon may be a line of haze rather than the sea's true edge; a haze line nearer than the horizon would sit lower and favour neither model. The camera's height (±5 m) moves the globe's f by ±0.02 and the rock's height (±5 m) by ±0.03. The GFS model is a forecast on a 25 km grid, not a sounding, and the traced columns change its whole profile by one uniform gradient, which is only one of the ways the air can vary. The traced globe misses the photograph by 0.07–0.13 in f, about 6–10 pixels: the sea was about 1 K warmer than the air rather than the models' 4 to 6 K, or the air above had a mild inversion, or the other inputs are off by about their uncertainties. The drawing uses the GLO-30 outline of the rock raised to 107 m.

> **The flat model, steel-manned.** It gets the same camera, the same distance, the same rock, the same tide, and it may bend light as it likes. With k = −0.82 it reproduces the photograph exactly, as the animation shows. It cannot do it with straight light, nor with any light that bends down: over a plane, the sea beyond the rock (it runs on to St Abb's Head, 75.5 km away) is seen *above* the rock's summit, which is 230 m below the camera, so the summit would stand against the sea, never against the sky. That is a sign, not a size. **What would vindicate it:** the horizon at or above the summit of the rock from 337 m, with thermometers on the hill and at the shore showing the usual fall of about 0.65 K per 100 m. **What vindicates the globe**, by the same rule: the horizon crossing the rock about half to two thirds up in that ordinary air, as here.

**How to make it decisive.** Keep the original files, for their time and focal length. Photograph the rock from several heights within the hour, from the hilltop down to the shore. On the globe the formula above says where the horizon crosses the rock from each height: lowest on the rock from about 100 m, back up to the summit as the camera nears the water. On the plane, in ordinary air, the horizon stands above the summit from any height above the rock's. A thermometer on the hill and one at the shore give the gradient each model needs before the photograph is looked at.

## Horizon dips from airliner windows: a radius from eleven phone readings [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: the heights (transponder pressure altitudes placed in the GFS model's geopotential heights), the terrain at the horizon, found along each heading on a sphere of radius R, and the ground speeds (GNSS) behind the accelerations.]

**The readings.** [earthlyskeptic](https://x.com/earthlyskeptic) measured the dip of the horizon from airliner windows on two flights with Theodolite, an iPhone app that shows the elevation of its reticle from the phone's motion sensors[9]: the reticle set on the horizon, a screenshot each time, published here with his permission. The flights are AA 6322, Chicago to Des Moines on 5 September 2025 (seven readings: two at cruise over Illinois, five in the descent over Iowa), and AA 5255, Des Moines to Washington on 8 September (four, over West Virginia and Virginia). The dips run from 1.0° to 3.5°, read as they are, with no correction for refraction. Each file also holds the phone's GPS position and altitude, the camera's heading and the time, and the app's reading at the shutter, which can differ from the one on screen by a tenth or two of a degree.

**Where the aircraft was.** Both flights' transponders were logged by FlightAware every 15 to 30 seconds: time, position, course, ground speed and pressure altitude[10]. Matched by the phone's clock, the first flight agrees with the phone's GPS within seconds. On the second, the phone's position had frozen: it is where the aircraft had been 2.5 to 12.6 minutes before. The screenshot labelled 32,173 ft was taken in the descent at 19,825 ft, 6,310 m; the three labelled 15,6xx ft were taken in a holding pattern. Every height here is the transponder's pressure altitude placed in the day's air (the height where the model's air has that pressure[11]). On the first flight it agrees with the phone's GPS within 8–50 m. The heights go from 725 to 8,670 m.

**From a plane, the horizon is the ground.** Over land the line of sight grazes the terrain, not sea level, so the height that counts is the height above the terrain where it grazes, h′. Along each photograph's heading, the Copernicus GLO-90 surface model[12] gives the terrain out to one and a half times the horizon's distance, and the horizon is where the terrain stands highest in angle: 349–409 m under the first flight's horizons, 417–659 m under the second's, over the Appalachians. At low altitude this matters: 350 m of terrain is half the height of the lowest reading.

$$\cos\delta = \frac{R}{R + h\prime},\qquad \delta \approx \sqrt{\frac{2h\prime}{R}}$$
$$\cos\delta = \frac{n_t\,(R + z_t)}{n_e\,(R + h)}$$

δ is the dip, h the aircraft's height, z_t the terrain where the line of sight grazes it, h′ = h − z_t, R the radius. The first line is straight light. In air layered with height, n·r·cos θ keeps the same value all along a ray[13]: the second line is the dip through real air, n_e being the refractive index at the aircraft and n_t at the ground. On an infinite plane the horizon lies at eye level: δ = 0 at every height.

**The real refraction.** No standard coefficient here. The NOAA GFS model gives the air above each aircraft position and above each horizon at the photograph's time, at 21 levels from the ground to 16 km: temperature, humidity and height[11]. The line of sight is traced through that air, which the second formula sums up. The refractive index falls from 258–271 parts per million at the ground to 109–258 at the aircraft. Real air raises the globe's horizon by 0.05 to 0.18°, as a uniform k of 0.12–0.19 would: refraction makes the readings look *deeper* than the globe's, never shallower. The same air over a plane bends a ray from the aircraft back down to the ground whenever it leaves upward at less than a certain angle. An unbounded plane would put its horizon **above** eye level, by 0.8–1.3°.

$$\delta = \delta_{\text{read}} + \frac{a_u}{g}$$

The phone measures its tilt against apparent gravity. An aircraft that speeds up, slows down or turns tilts apparent gravity by a/g, 0.6° for every 0.1 m/s². a_u is the horizontal acceleration along the direction the camera looks, the Coriolis term 2Ω×v included[14]. A plane slowing down, seen forward, makes the horizon read deeper. A turn is a bank, and from a side window most of the bank falls along the view: a bank of 1° moves the reading by nearly 1°.

**The aircraft's accelerations.** They come from the two logged fixes around each photograph, the change of ground speed along the track and of course across it. They tilt the readings by −0.83° to +0.24°, each to about ±0.2° (the log rounds to 1 knot and 1°). The largest is at 3,047 ft, taken while the first flight levelled off and slowed down. Where the log shows a turn between two fixes, the steady side is used if the photograph is within 10 s of it; otherwise the reading would be left out of the corrected fits. A turn's start cannot be placed better than the log's spacing, and a bank of a degree or two can hide in it.

*Figure caption:* **The radius, read nine ways.** R is fitted to the dips by least squares; its range is that of 4,000 bootstrap resamples of the photographs. A reading more than three standard deviations from the fit of the others is set aside (“out”). “Offset”: a constant zero error of the instrument, fitted with R. The last six rows give each model its own free parameters: the globe its offset only, the plane a haze distance and an offset.

*[Figure: The dip of the horizon against the height above the terrain at the horizon, for eleven readings from two flights, each with the reading once the aircraft's acceleration is removed; the dip of a 6,371 km sphere with straight light and, for each photograph, through the day's air; the radius fitted at face value; and the plane's predictions: zero, above level in the day's air, or a haze edge plus a constant offset.]*

- Click a sightline or a point to see its photograph and its numbers.

*Figure caption:* **Dip against height.** Filled points: the readings on screen, with the app's resolution of 0.1°; rings: the readings stored at the shutter (EXIF); grey crosses: the reading once the aircraft's acceleration is removed, with its error. Blue: a sphere of 6,371 km, dashed with straight light; the blue ticks are its dip through the day's air at each photograph. Grey: the radius fitted at face value. Orange: the plane, 0° with straight light, the orange ticks above level its horizon in the day's air, and dashed its best case, a far edge lost in haze at a fixed distance plus a constant offset. To scale of its axes. **Click a point** for its photograph, its numbers and what each model predicts there.

**The surface the readings draw.** As in the dip tab, each reading becomes a sightline from its height on one vertical, tilted by its own dip, and no ground is drawn. Lines that agree on a radius are all tangent to one circle.

*[Figure: Eleven sightlines from heights on one vertical, each tilted down by its measured dip, with no ground drawn; a button shows the circle of 6,371 km and the circle of the radius fitted at face value.]*

*Figure caption:* **Eleven sightlines, no ground.** Each line starts at the reading's height above the terrain of its horizon and is tangent to the circle of the radius its own dip gives. Rule 1: heights are multiplied by the printed factor and the planet is divided by it, at the same scale in both directions, so a line tangent to the true sphere stays tangent to the drawn one. The readings were taken in different places and directions; they are put on one vertical because a dip depends only on the height. The second button subtracts from every reading the constant zero error fitted with the radius (straight light). The lines do not gather on one circle either way: alone, a reading gives a radius between 2,110 and 6,937 km, and between 4,567 and 17,988 km once the offset is subtracted. A single dip read to a tenth of a degree cannot fix a radius; only the trend over the heights can, which is what the fit uses. **Click a line** for its photograph.

**What the readings say.** As they are, with straight light and the true heights, they give R = 4,801 (4,273–5,295) km. That is about a quarter smaller than the surveyed 6,371 km, and smaller still through the day's air (4,309 (3,879–4,708) km). With the phone's GPS heights instead, the frozen 32,173 ft among them, the same fit gives 5,147 (4,780–5,485) km: a wrong height had been making the radius look closer to the truth. Every reading is deeper than the globe's through the day's air, by 0.1° to 1.2°, 0.4° in the median, at low altitude as at cruise. A reading deeper at every height by the same amount is what a zero error does, and removing the accelerations does not remove it. With a constant offset left free, the fit gives R = 5,866 (4,387–7,990) km (day's air, accelerations removed), with an offset of +0.31 (0.00 … +0.65)°. The globe at its surveyed radius then fits with an RMS of 0.29°, the plane's best case with 0.38°.

> **Limits, stated plainly.** The dips are the app's readings, set by eye on a hazy horizon through a cabin window, displayed to a tenth of a degree. The phone's tilt is measured against apparent gravity. The track log gives the aircraft's acceleration only every 15 to 30 s, so a brief bank or a change of speed between two fixes goes unseen, and a bank of 1° moves a side-window reading by nearly 1°. The phone's own zero error is unknown, and the constant offset stands for it. From cruise altitude the horizon may be the top of a cloud or haze layer rather than the ground; that raises it and reduces the dip. The heights rest on the transponder and the model's air, good to a few tens of metres. The terrain comes from a 90 m model along a single bearing, the camera's heading coming from the phone's compass inside a metal cabin. Eleven readings cannot pin down both a radius and an offset tightly, hence the wide range.

> **The flat model, steel-manned.** On a plane with straight light the horizon is at eye level and the dip is zero at every height. In the day's air the plane does worse: its horizon would stand 0.8–1.3° *above* level, the wrong sign. To produce dips of 1 to 3.5° it needs the far ground to vanish in haze at a fixed distance, seen below level, and it may have the same constant offset. Its best case, through the day's air with the accelerations removed, is D = 222 km with an offset of +1.24°. It fits nearly as well as the globe (RMS 0.38° against 0.29°): **these eleven readings alone do not separate a dip growing as √h′ from one growing as h′.** The plane needs 3 times the globe's zero error to do it, and the same haze distance from 700 m and from 8.7 km. **What would vindicate it:** readings with the instrument's zero removed that stay at zero, or grow in proportion to the height. **What vindicates the globe**: the same readings growing as the square root of the height above the horizon, with one radius for all.

**How to make it decisive.** Remove the zero error: take each reading twice, the second with the phone turned half a turn about the line of sight (screen to the window, then screen to the cabin), and keep the mean, as surveyors do with a theodolite's two faces. Read in level, steady cruise, not while climbing, descending, slowing or turning, and note the time to the second: the track log then says what the aircraft was doing. Check that the phone's GPS is live (its position changes from one screenshot to the next). Add readings from a few tens of metres over the sea, where the terrain is not in question and the √h′ curve is steepest. Note whether the horizon is ground, sea or a cloud deck.
