# Find where you are from the satellites' raw signals, then measure the Earth's radius with people far away

> Tab "Your own GPS" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-rx. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*Your own GPS · raw signals, solved in your browser*

The [GPS tab](/ai/gps.md) solved 80 reference stations from their raw signals and found a sphere of radius 6,371.2 ± 0.9 km through them. This tab does the same with **your** phone. Most Android phones since 2016 give applications the raw times of the satellite signals;[1] the page turns them into distances, solves your position from the centre of the coordinates with no shape assumed, and shows how far the result is from the surface the stations define. One phone is one point, and a sphere needs at least four: so each participant can share a short code, and a group spread over thousands of kilometres fits its own sphere. The tool comes first, then what the code contains and what it protects, then every equation with the same step written in Python, C or Go. **Everything is computed in this page. The files are not sent anywhere, nothing is stored, and the result is gone when the page is closed.**

**What you need.** An Android phone, outdoors, and an app that logs raw measurements: GPSTest or Google's GnssLogger[1] (raw logging on; the .txt log or a RINEX observation file both work). A few minutes are enough. Then the broadcast navigation file of the same day, from the open IGS archive:[7] the page tells you which folder once your log is read.

## ① Try it with your phone

Choose your log and the navigation file, together or one after the other; compressed `.gz` files can be chosen as they are. The page reads them, tells you which navigation file it needs if it is missing, solves every instant, then puts your phone among the 80 stations of the GPS tab. Your position is shown rounded to 0.1°. How each step is computed is in section ④.

*Figure caption:* **Your phone among the stations.** Left: where it solved itself, on a flat map (only to locate it). Right: its distance to the sphere fitted through the stations, against latitude, with the flattening curve the stations draw. Tiles: your distance to the centre of the coordinates, the sphere refitted with you added, your pseudorange residuals and the gap to the fix the phone computed itself (its GNSS fix only, never the network one). A phone on one frequency is good to a few metres or tens of metres; the stations' surface only to about a kilometre, because their heights differ. Limit: the orbits are written in the Earth-centred WGS84 frame,[6] so your distance to its centre is a consistency check, not a radius found from nothing; what can fail is the residuals, metres if the geometry is right, kilometres if it is not. *Would favour the flat plane: a phone whose pseudoranges only solve with kilometre residuals, or that lands kilometres away from the surface the stations define.*

## ② Your code, and the codes of the others

Once your log is solved, the page writes your code below. Copy it and send it yourself to the people you choose — a message, a forum, an e-mail; the site has no server and never sees it. Paste the codes of the others in the second box: a whole message is fine, the page finds the codes in it. With four participants or more it fits a sphere through the group alone, centre and radius free, with the same formula as for the stations, and the best plane beside it. Every page given the same codes finds the same numbers, since your own point enters by its rounded position too.

Solve your own log above to get your code.

*Figure caption:* **The group's own sphere.** Tiles: the radius of the sphere through the participants alone, with its uncertainty; what the best plane through the same points leaves; the largest distance in the group and the bulge the sphere predicts over it. Left: where the participants are, as their codes say (a flat map, only to locate them; you in orange). Right: each participant's height above the best plane through the group, against the distance from the sphere's axis; the curve is the fitted sphere, the dashed line the plane. A chart with its own scales, not a drawing. *Would favour the flat plane: participants lying on a plane, with no bulge, or groups in different places finding radii that disagree beyond their uncertainties and beyond what the flattening allows.*

## ③ What the code contains, and what it protects

The code is plain text, readable by anyone; nothing in it is hidden or encrypted. Its fields, with an example:

| Field | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `FOG1` | format and version |
| 2 | `Oslo` | a name, optional (20 characters at most) |
| 3 | `20261003` | the day of the log |
| 4 | `1000` | the rounding step q, in metres (1000, 10000, or 1 for exact) |
| 5–7 | `3150\|598\|5495` | x, y, z: the position in Earth-centred coordinates, divided by q and rounded (here 3,150 km, 598 km, 5,495 km) |
| 8 | `65` | rms of the pseudorange residuals, in decimetres (6.5 m) |
| 9 | `60` | number of instants solved |
| 10 | `GE` | systems used: G for GPS, E for Galileo |
| 11 | `brpax3` | check digits: FNV-1a hash of fields 1–10 in base 36; a copying error changes them |

**What stays with you, and what does not.** Your log, your exact position, the times of your measurements and your phone's model never leave this page. The code is the only thing that does, and only if you copy it. It is **not** just a radius or a centre: it carries your position, rounded to the step you chose, so whoever reads it knows where you were to within about a kilometre with the 1 km step (a district), about ten with 10 km (a town and its surroundings). The page writes the latitude and longitude it reveals before you copy it. Why not share less? A radius or a distance to the centre alone would hide more but measure nothing: every phone's distance is to the centre of the frame in which the orbits are written,[6] so it repeats the frame instead of measuring the bulge between people. The group's centre and radius are found *from* the points, so the points must be shared. What you control: whom you send it to, the rounding (10 km if 1 km is too precise; the figure in section 4.6 shows what it costs in precision), and the name, which can stay empty.

## ④ The calculation, equation by equation

Each formula below comes with its figure and the same step as code, in the language you choose. The pieces build on each other: the satellite's position serves the equation, which serves the solution. They are short versions of the page's own code (`src/tabs/rx/userlogic.js` and `grouplogic.js`), with the same numbers and constants; each was run, and gives the page's results on the same inputs to the millimetre.

## 4.1 What your phone records

A GPS satellite does not send a distance. It sends its own clock: every signal carries the time at which it left the satellite. Your phone notes when the signal arrived, on its own clock. The difference is the flight time, and times the speed of light it is a distance — a *pseudo*range, because the phone's clock is off by an unknown amount, which the calculation solves as one more unknown. Android gives the pieces separately: a hardware counter, its offset to GPS time, and the time read in the signal.[1]

$$t_{rx} = \text{TimeNanos} - (\text{FullBiasNanos} + \text{BiasNanos}) \quad \text{(modulo one week)}$$
$$\rho = c\cdot(t_{rx} - t_{tx})$$

TimeNanos: the phone's hardware counter · FullBiasNanos, BiasNanos: its offset to GPS time (about −1.5×10¹⁸ ns, too large for ordinary floating point: the page uses 64-bit integers) · t_tx = ReceivedSvTimeNanos: the emission time read in the signal · c = 299,792,458 m/s. A measurement is kept only if the phone has decoded the full time of week from the signal (otherwise t_tx is known modulo 1 ms or 100 ms), on the L1/E1 frequency, for GPS and Galileo.[1] The result lies between 20,189 km and 25,784 km for a satellite overhead or on the horizon.

## 4.2 Where the satellites were [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: satellite orbits broadcast in the WGS84 frame, whose scale was fixed by stations on the ellipsoid.]

Distances alone place you nowhere: you must know where each satellite was when it sent its signal, and how wrong its clock was. Every satellite broadcasts both, as a few dozen numbers — the elements of its orbit and a clock polynomial — refreshed every two hours or so.[2][3] Your phone decodes them for its own fix but does not hand them to applications; the IGS stations record and archive them, one file per day: the *navigation file* you add. Prefer `BRDC00IGS_R_…`, published the next day, which also carries the ionosphere coefficients; on the day itself, `BRDC00WRD_S_…` has the same orbits without them.[7] The page turns the elements into a position with the algorithm of the GPS specification, line by line:[2]

$$M = M_0 + \left(\sqrt{\mu/a^3} + \Delta n\right) t_k, \qquad E - e\sin E = M$$
$$r = a(1 - e\cos E), \qquad \Omega = \Omega_0 + (\text{Ω̇} - \Omega_E)\,t_k - \Omega_E\,t_{oe}$$

t_k: time since the reference epoch t_oe of the elements · M: mean anomaly, growing evenly with time · E: eccentric anomaly, from Kepler's equation · e, a: eccentricity and semi-major axis · μ: the Earth's GM as the message defines it · Ω: longitude of the node, turned by the Earth's rotation Ω_E so that the result is in the Earth-fixed frame. Six small harmonic terms correct the argument, the radius and the inclination. Galileo uses the same form with its own μ.[3] The elements chosen are those of the same satellite with the nearest t_oe, within four hours, and only if the satellite declares itself healthy.

## 4.3 The equation, every term

The [GPS tab](/ai/gps.md) writes the pseudorange as a distance plus the receiver's clock. A real calculation adds the satellite's clock, the Earth's turn while the signal flies,[8] and two delays in the atmosphere. The figure gives the size of each term: the corrections are metres on a distance of twenty thousand kilometres, and leaving one out shows up directly in the residuals.

$$\rho_i = \left\lvert R_z(\Omega_E\tau_i)\,\mathbf{s}_i(t - \tau_i) - \mathbf{x} \right\rvert + c\,\delta t_{sys} - c\,\delta t_i + T_i + I_i$$
$$\delta t_i = a_{f0} + a_{f1}\Delta t + a_{f2}\Delta t^2 - \frac{2\sqrt{\mu a}}{c^2}\,e\sin E - T_{GD}$$

x: your position (three unknowns) · δt_sys: your phone's clock, one unknown per system (GPS, Galileo) · τ_i: flight time; the satellite is taken where it was at emission, then turned by Ω_Eτ_i about the axis because the Earth turned meanwhile (up to 41 m)[8] · δt_i: the satellite's clock, broadcast polynomial (up to 300 km of range), relativistic term (14 m for e = 0.02) and group delay T_GD for a single frequency[2] (Galileo: its E1/E5b delay[3]) · T_i: troposphere, Saastamoinen[5] · I_i: ionosphere, Klobuchar's model when the navigation file has its coefficients;[4] otherwise left in, a few metres. Unlike the stations, a phone receives one frequency, so the ionosphere cannot be cancelled by combining two.

## 4.4 Solving from the centre of the Earth [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: satellite orbits broadcast in the WGS84 frame, whose scale was fixed by stations on the ellipsoid.]

The equation is not linear in x, so it is solved in steps. Start from the origin of the coordinates — the centre of the Earth, with no idea where the phone is — compute what each pseudorange should be, compare with the measured one, and move x and the clocks by the least-squares correction. The troposphere, the ionosphere and the 10° elevation mask enter from the fourth step, once x is close enough to have a local horizon. Each instant of your log is solved alone, from the origin again; instants whose residuals exceed 100 m rms are dropped, with no limit on where the position may land; the rest are averaged.

$$\mathbf{H}\,\delta\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y}, \qquad \delta\mathbf{x} = (\mathbf{H}^{T}\mathbf{H})^{-1}\mathbf{H}^{T}\mathbf{y}, \qquad \mathbf{x}_0 = (0,\ 0,\ 0)$$

y: measured minus computed pseudoranges · one row of H per satellite: the unit vector from the satellite towards x (changed sign), then 1 in the column of that satellite's system clock · δx: the move of x, y, z and the clocks · repeated until the move is below a millimetre. At least one satellite more than unknowns is required, so that the residuals say something. The figure runs the page's own code on a synthetic sky built from a real broadcast record: from the centre to the surface in a handful of steps.

## 4.5 Rounding your position

$$\hat{x} = q\cdot\text{round}(x/q), \qquad \sigma = q/\sqrt{12}$$

x: one coordinate of your solved position · q: the step you chose · x̂: what the code carries · σ: the standard deviation of a rounding error spread evenly over ±q/2, used to weight each participant in the group's fit. The check digits[9] catch a mistyped code; they do not stop anyone from inventing one.

## 4.6 The group's sphere [evidence: check — Where the radius enters: satellite orbits broadcast in the WGS84 frame, whose scale was fixed by stations on the ellipsoid.]

What makes the radius measurable is the bulge: over the distance L the surface rises above the straight line by s, at true scale in the figure. The sphere through the group is found in two steps — a linear first guess, then least squares on the true distances to the surface — and its uncertainty from the rounding and from the real scatter.

$$s = R - \sqrt{R^2 - (L/2)^2} \approx \frac{L^2}{8R}$$

L: the distance between the farthest participants · s: the height of the arc above its chord: 20 km over 1,000 km, 179 km over 3,000 km. A rounding error of q shifts a point by about q/√12; the radius is measured to roughly R·σ/s, so the farther apart the participants, the tighter it gets.

$$\text{Cov}(\mathbf{c}, R) = (\mathbf{J}^{T}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{J})^{-1}, \qquad w_j = 1/(q_j^2/12 + \sigma_{fix}^2)$$
$$s^2 = \sum_j \text{res}_j^2/(n - 4) \quad (n > 4)$$

J: one row per participant, the derivatives of its distance to the sphere with respect to the centre c and the radius R · w_j: its weight, from its rounding step q_j and a fix good to σ_fix ≈ 20 m · the first line gives the uncertainty the rounding alone would cause; with more than four participants the second uses the real residuals (different heights, the flattening). The page shows the larger of the two. With exactly four the sphere passes through every point and nothing measures the scatter: the page says so.

## 4.7 Which radius to expect [evidence: prediction]

$$M(\varphi) = \frac{a(1 - e^2)}{(1 - e^2\sin^2\varphi)^{3/2}}, \qquad N(\varphi) = \frac{a}{\sqrt{1 - e^2\sin^2\varphi}}$$

The Earth is slightly flattened, so a group spread over a few thousand kilometres measures the local curvature, which depends on where it is and in which direction it spreads: north–south M, from 6,335.4 km at the equator, east–west N, up to 6,399.6 km at the poles[6] (a, e: the WGS84 semi-major axis and eccentricity, a published model, compared and never fitted). “The same radius” means within this range and within the group's uncertainty. A group spanning continents measures something close to the stations' 6,371.2 ± 0.9 km.

## The flat model at its best

A flat model cannot use the broadcast orbits, which are written around a centre; it would need its own positions for the transmitters, and with a free height for each it could be tuned to match any one receiver. What it cannot do with one set of transmitters is to make phones everywhere solve to metres *and* make a group of them lie on a plane: the group's points come out of their own signals, and the bulge between them is either there or not.

> **Verdict rule, stated in advance.** *Globe:* each phone solves with residuals of metres, lands within about a kilometre of the stations' surface, and a group spread over thousands of kilometres finds a radius between 6,335.4 km and 6,399.6 km within its uncertainty, with the plane far behind. *Flat plane:* residuals of kilometres, or a group whose points lie on a plane, or groups whose radii disagree beyond their uncertainties.

**Limits of this tab.** The orbits are expressed in WGS84, so a single phone checks consistency rather than measuring the size from nothing; the independent part is the residuals and, for a group, the bulge between its own points. Without the ionosphere coefficients a few metres of error remain. A code can be invented, and the page cannot tell. Heights differ between participants by up to a kilometre or more, which the uncertainty of the group includes only from five participants on. GLONASS and BeiDou are not used, nor Hatanaka-compressed (.crx) or RINEX 2 observation files, nor the navigation messages some phones log themselves.

**See also**[GPS](/ai/gps.md)[Surveying](/ai/surv.md)[Distances](/ai/dist.md)

### The two results in detail

**Measurements only** (5 of 5 kept): weighted by the inverse of their variances, **R = 6,374 ± 3 km**, 1.2 standard errors from the mean radius of 6,371 km. χ² = 0.8 for 4 degrees of freedom (Birge ratio 0.46). The most precise, Satellite Doppler: receivers' distance from the centre of the orbits, carries 96 % of the weight; one vote per measurement would give 6,385 km. Set aside at more than 3 standard deviations from the others: none.

**Checks**, kept apart because the radius entered their data at some point, even when it was taken out again (5 of 8 counted): R = 6,365 ± 153 km, 0.0 standard errors from 6,371 km; χ² = 4.6 for 4 degrees of freedom. Shown but not counted: An aircraft's weight flying east and west (Eötvös) ; Laser ranges to the Moon from Grasse (station's distance from the centre) ; Doppler shift of the Sun, HARPS-N (local radius at 28.75° N). Set aside: none. This second result is never mixed into the first.

### Lines shown but not counted

An aircraft's weight flying east and west (Eötvös) ; Laser ranges to the Moon from Grasse (station's distance from the centre) ; Doppler shift of the Sun, HARPS-N (local radius at 28.75° N). The Eötvös line because its published data were corrected with the GRS80 radii (see the aviation tab). The lunar laser and the Sun's Doppler shift because each gives the distance of one station from the centre, which on a flattened Earth depends on latitude by up to 21 km, more than their few-km uncertainty.

### How the lines are combined

How each result is combined. Each line's uncertainty adds the statistical error of its median (from the scatter of its values and their number) to a systematic error measured in its own tab: the largest change produced by redoing it with the other reductions that tab presents. An alternative that itself used the radius, such as a wave speed measured with globe distances, is quoted in its tab but never used to size the uncertainty of a measurement. The lines of a group are weighted by the inverse of their variance; when they scatter more than their uncertainties say (Birge ratio above 1), the standard error is multiplied by that ratio, as the Particle Data Group does. A line is set aside when it lies more than three standard deviations from the weighted mean of the others, computed without it.

### Reading the spread

Read the spread honestly. Each method has its own biases, explained in its tab: seismic waves run at different speeds under oceans and continents, the pressure wave's radius scales with a speed taken from the physics of the air, surveyors must correct for refraction, airliners fly detours that make the Earth look bigger, the Eötvös reconstruction undoes a published correction, the lunar laser and the Sun's Doppler shift read a local radius through an ephemeris, and the author's two measurements, one photograph and one filmed sunset, depend on the bending of light on the day and on a few pixels. Al-Bīrūnī's value is quoted from the literature, not recomputed. None of them was tuned to land near 6,371 km, and none of them gives the flat Earth a radius: on a plane the surveying, theodolite and dip methods return an infinite radius, and the others find no distances that fit at all.

## Rotation and orbit, measured

The same rule as for the radius: a measurement is pure when the quantity it gives, here the rotation rate Ω or the astronomical unit, never entered its data; the checks are kept apart.

**Measurements:** Ω = 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s (the stars give 7.292 × 10⁻⁵); astronomical unit = 147.5 million km from light alone. **Checks:** 149.6 million km from Doppler shifts, the transits of Venus, radar echoes and pulsar timing. The accepted values are 7.292 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s and 149.6 million km.

*[Figure: The rotation and the size of the orbit measured by each method: every value as a dot and the median as a tick, on axes starting at zero, where the flat models' predictions lie]*

Orange: what the flat models predict, on the same axes: a plane at rest does not turn, and the flat model's Sun is a few thousand kilometres up. The ring lasers, the satellites and the sky agree to a few parts per thousand or better; the falling balls scatter, and the plot shows it.

### What the orbit measurements do not separate

A yearly swing common to all stars, a yearly Doppler shift and a light time that changes with the season all show the observer moving relative to the stars and the Sun. An Earth at rest under a sky that swings in step every year reproduces the angles exactly (Tycho's arrangement); only the dynamics, why the whole sky would do that, chooses. The rotation measurements have no such twin: a ring laser or a falling ball feels the turning of the ground it stands on.

# What would refute each model

> Tab "What would refute each model" of *Flat plane or Globe?*. Web page: /#tab-falsify. Generated from the rendered page: same text, same computed numbers and sources; drawings are replaced by their captions and descriptions, formulas are TeX. Licence: content and data CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/), Xyphophor (https://x.com/Xyphophor); source code MIT; third-party data keep the licence of their source, cited in each tab.

*The mirror of the front page*

Every tab on this page ends with a number you can go and check. This one collects the other half of each of them: the result that would refute the globe, and the one that would refute the flat model. Not a rhetorical concession — a stated threshold, decided before the measurement, with the precision an instrument has to reach for the answer to mean anything. If one of these results is produced, the model it targets is refuted, and the threshold is written down in advance rather than afterwards.

Writing this table exposed a gap. Nine tabs state what would refute them. Six did not: celestial navigation, horizon dip, gravity, the pendulum, magnetism and GPS carried the measurement and the numbers but never the threshold. Those six rules are written here for the first time, and they still have to be carried back into their own tabs. A page that asks to be checked has to state that line everywhere, not in most places.

Read a row from the middle out. The centre column is what a flat-earth measurement would have to show to end this page; the right column is what a globe measurement would have to show to end the flat model. Both are stated with the same care on purpose — a threshold that only ever fires one way is not a threshold.

**One row per line of evidence: the measurement, the result that would refute each model, and the precision it takes**

| tab | what you measure | what would refute the globe | what would refute the flat model | precision you need |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Elevation angles](/ai/elev.md) | The angle of a distant peak above the horizon. | A documented summit photographed at the angle the flat map predicts, repeatably, over a sightline long enough that the two models differ by more than your sighting error. | One radius fitting three sightlines of different lengths at once — the flat model needs a new correction for each. | ±2′ on the angle: a theodolite, or a phone clinometer on a levelled base. |
| [Hidden height](/ai/hh.md) | How much of a distant target is hidden. | A target of known height, at a measured distance, photographed from a measured eye height, with its whole height visible where the globe hides a slice. | Any hidden slice at all that zoom does not recover: a plane hides nothing, ever, at any distance. | Eye height to ±0.5 m, distance to ±1 %, and the time of day recorded. |
| [Cel. nav.](/ai/cnav.md) | The altitude of Polaris, from two places. | Polaris measured at an altitude that is not the latitude, or a rate that is not 1° per 111 km along a long north–south baseline. | A constant rate over a baseline of thousands of kilometres — the flat map requires that rate to change with distance from its centre. | ±10′ with a sextant; ±0.5° is already enough over 1,000 km. |
| [Star trails](/ai/star.md) | Which way the sky turns, and the shape of the trails. | A southern observer photographing arcs centred on Polaris, the same sense of rotation in both hemispheres, or a culmination mean that does not return the latitude. | Any reversal of sense between hemispheres at all: on a plane everyone shares one up, so the sense cannot change. | A phone on a wall, 30 minutes. | [Gravity](/ai/grav.md) | The weight of the same object at two latitudes. | g at the equator and near a pole agreeing to better than a few parts in ten thousand, or varying with latitude in a way that is not sin²φ. | Any latitude dependence of the observed size and sign — a plane gives no reason for one. | A pendulum timed over 1,000 swings reaches one part in 10⁴, which is the size of the effect. |
| [Foucault](/ai/fou.md) | Which way a long pendulum drifts, and how fast. | A precession rate that is not 15.041 sin φ degrees per hour, or one that fails to reverse when the pendulum crosses the equator. | Any reversal of the drift between hemispheres, or any dependence on latitude at all. | A 10 m pendulum, one hour, a chalk mark on the floor: the rate is ~11°/h at 45°. |
| [Seismology](/ai/seis.md) | When one earthquake arrives at two distant stations. | A station at 120° recording a crisp on-time P as sharp as the one at 95°, or the quiet band sitting at a fixed distance in kilometres rather than a fixed angle. | The shadow zone appearing at all, at the angle the globe predicts, from every earthquake regardless of where it starts. | Open archives and a clock; the arrival differences are minutes, not seconds. |
| [Atmosphere](/ai/atmo.md) | The pressure wave of one volcanic eruption, on ordinary barometers thousands of kilometres apart. | Each barometer recording the pulse only once, or t₁ + t₂ changing with the station's distance by more than a few percent, as an echo off an edge would make it, or the second pulse arriving later at the farther stations, as a bounce off a dome would. | A second pulse arriving from the other side, earlier the farther the station, with t₁ + t₂ the same everywhere to within a few percent. | A barometer logged once a minute (airport stations are open) and the eruption time; the pulse is about 0.7 hPa. |

| [Atmosphere](/ai/atmo.md) | The same kind of pressure wave in 1883, read by hand on the barographs of some fifty observatories. | A full lap (III − I, IV − II) that changes with the station's position, as echoes off an edge or a dome would make it, or no regular later passages at all. | The same lap of about 35½ hours at every station from Calcutta to Washington, seven passages at many of them, and the interval I → II falling in a straight line with the angle from the volcano. | The printed tables of the 1888 Royal Society report (public domain) and a subtraction; no position, no eruption time. |
| [Atmosphere](/ai/atmo.md) | Every lap of a pressure wave timed at one station, from Krakatoa (1883), the 1961 Novaya Zemlya explosion and Hunga Tonga (2022, seven days of barometers), pooled into one radius. | Laps that differ from one event, instrument or station to the next by more than the wind can explain, or returns after a lap that never cluster. | Laps of 35 to 36 hours whatever the year, the instrument and the place: 35.1 h in Japan in 1961, 36.1 h across the United States in 2022, about 35½ h on the barographs of 1883. | Times printed in 1888 and 1962, and seven days of public airport barometers picked without any Earth model; one fixed speed, 310 m/s. |
| [Magnetism](/ai/mag.md) | The angle a freely tilting compass needle takes. | Dips that miss tan I = 2 tan λ by more than the ~10° the field's non-dipole part allows, with a miss that grows steadily toward one pole instead of scattering from region to region; or a dip that does not change sign exactly once between the two magnetic poles. The law is the field's leading term, not an exact one: a few degrees of scatter refute nothing. | The dipole law holding at all across latitudes — this is the one test that constrains the shape without using a radius. | A dip needle to ±1°; the law predicts 63.4° at 45°, which is far outside that. |
| [Sun](/ai/sun.md) | Who is in daylight at one instant. | Polled answers that no great circle can separate — two places 180° apart in longitude both in daylight at the same second. | A day–night boundary that is a great circle, moving at 15°/h, with no place ever lit on both sides of the disc. | A handful of correspondents and a synchronised clock; no instrument at all. |
| [Twilight](/ai/twi.md) | How long the sky stays lit after sunset. | The Earth's shadow measured at or below the antisolar point, or climbing at a constant ratio instead of an accelerating one. | A dark shadow edge appearing opposite the Sun at all, with its elevation equal to the Sun's depression. | A phone camera and a timer; the boundary moves degrees per minute. |
| [Azimuth](/ai/azim.md) | The compass bearing of the Sun at a stated second. | A measured azimuth departing from the great-circle bearing to the published sub-solar point by more than your sighting error. | The bearing matching the great circle rather than the flat map, which points the other way round the horizon. | ±2° with a good compass, once magnetic declination is applied; the models differ by tens of degrees south of the tropics. |
| [Eclipses](/ai/ecl.md) | When totality begins and how long it lasts, at a named place, on 2 August 2027. | Tarifa not total from 08:45:05 UT ±15 s for 4 min 39 s ±10 s; Luxor total at any time but 10:02–10:08 UT; Marseille seeing totality at all. | Totality at Tarifa (the best-fitting flat shadow stays ~4,300 km away), or at Luxor near 10:05 UT rather than about 06:09 UT. | A clock set to the second (a phone synced to network time) and a filtered view of the Sun; the models differ by hours and thousands of kilometres. |
| [Theodolite](/ai/ct.md) | One star, one straight line of sight, its altitude read at both ends of that line. | The two ends returning the same altitude — difference zero within your error — repeatably, at 9 km and at 131 km alike. | That difference growing in proportion to s: the plane predicts exactly 0.000° with no free parameter, and the globe predicts γ = s/R, which is 27′ at 50 km. | A GPS-synchronised clock to ±1 s, which is 0.18′. The hard part is the refraction setting: it is worth 15′ and must be fixed before the comparison, not after. |
| [GPS](/ai/gps.md) | How long a satellite stays above your horizon. | One satellite tracked continuously above the horizon for more than 5 h 04 min, or a constellation that repeats on 24 h rather than 23 h 56 m. | Any satellite setting at all, or the sidereal repeat: fixed emitters over a plane never set and repeat on the solar day. | A phone GNSS status app and a clock; the 4-minute daily drift is unmistakable in a week. |
| [Aviation](/ai/avia.md) | How long airliners take on long routes, timed both ways, and which way a free gyro drifts. | Round-trip airborne times on the southern routes (Sydney–Santiago, Perth–Johannesburg) about twice what their great-circle distances need, or a free heading indicator drifting the same way in both hemispheres. | Round-trip times proportional to great-circle distances, with one speed near the filed cruise speeds; inertial units finding true north and their latitude from the Earth's rotation. | Public flight-tracking times over a couple of weeks, both directions averaged; a heading indicator, a clock and a compass. |
| [Rotation](/ai/rot.md) | The rotation that ring lasers and falling balls feel about the local vertical. | Two horizontal ring lasers at different latitudes reading the same rotation, or careful drops landing on the plumb point on average. | A beat ratio between Wettzell and Christchurch of sin 49.14° / sin 43.58° = 1.097, and balls landing east by ⅓ ω g t³ cos φ; a disc predicts 1 and no deflection, a plane at rest zero for both. | Published ring-laser frequencies and dimensions; for the drops, hundreds of falls of 20 m or more and a plumb line to 0.01 mm. |
| [Orbit](/ai/orb.md) | The yearly swing of starlight and of Doppler shifts, and the Sun's Doppler shift through the day. | Zenith stars that stay put through the year to better than 1″, or a solar Doppler curve through the day that a lamp a few thousand km up fits as well as the rotating observer does. | A common yearly swing of about ±20″ in every star, a Sun 3.4 % wider in January, and a daily solar Doppler curve that the best lamp misses by 27 m/s where the parameter-free globe leaves 1 m/s. | A zenith camera or published catalogue positions; public solar spectra (HARPS-N) or a home spectroscope at about 1 m/s for the daily curve. |
| [Satellites](/ai/sat.md) | One day of carrier-phase Doppler from 80 receivers on 79 navigation satellites, fitted with the orbits, the receivers, GM and Ω all free. | Receivers held on one plane fitting the Doppler as well as free ones, or satellites needing different GM for their periods. | Receivers settling on a ball around the centre the orbits go round, 6,357 to 6,381 km from it, from a start on a flat map; one GM for 79 satellites at three heights; the best plane missing by over a hundred m/s where the ball leaves millimetres. | Public RINEX files of the IGS and a least-squares fit of a few hundred unknowns. |
| [Moon](/ai/moon.md) | Laser times of flight to the Moon from one station through a night. | Ranges as smooth with the station at rest (R = 0) as with any other radius. | One radius, near 6,366 km for Grasse, that makes the Moon's distance from the centre smooth to a metre, where a station at rest leaves about 10 km. | Public normal points (EDC/DGFI) and a lunar theory good to about 10″. |

## What would not settle anything, and why

**A horizon that looks flat.** At two metres above the sea the horizon is 5 km away and drops 0.04° below eye level — forty times finer than the width of a pencil held at arm's length. Both models predict you see a straight line. A photograph of one is not evidence for either.

**An oval star trail.** As soon as the camera is not aimed at the celestial pole, the image of a circle in the sky is a conic, and a real lens adds its own distortion. Both models produce ovals. The star tab measures angles instead, for exactly this reason.

**A laser that crossed a lake.** Without a documented eye height, a measured distance, a stated time of day and a temperature profile, a laser shot over water is not a measurement of anything. Refraction over a cold surface on a warm afternoon routinely reaches several times the standard coefficient. This cuts both ways: it is also why laser shots are not counted here when they did show curvature.

**Anything an official body says.** Not one row of the table above needs you to trust an agency. Every threshold is reachable with a phone, a stopwatch, a protractor or a pendulum, and the two rows that use published data — earthquake arrival times and the star catalogue — name archives that are open, are maintained by rival institutions in different countries, and would have to be falsified in concert.

> **The one that keeps the page honest.** Any single test can be met with “your instrument was off”, and often fairly. That is why the page's real claim is not any one row: it is that one radius, R ≈ 6,371 km, satisfies every row at once. To refute that you do not need to beat one threshold — you need a flat arrangement that beats two of them with the same parameters. None has ever been shown, and the page would print it if one were.
